\>We welcome suggestions for additional practices, tasks, implementations, and references from within and beyond your sector. This profile prioritizes content and examples that generalize and offer broad, transferable value across all 16 critical infrastructure sectors, even if they may be focused on one sector or application. Highly specialized or unique content is still welcome and valuable for potential future sector-specific companion resources, developed by, or in partnership with, sector organizations.

\>This profile addresses SI risk from an operational and consequence-containment perspective, intentionally deconflicting with and referencing cybersecurity-focused control-level guidance. Security-adjacent content still appears where it best illustrates an SI-specific failure mode, or where a control area sits at the boundary between operational and cybersecurity risk. Our intent is to address the operational context specific to critical infrastructure and to point to cybersecurity-specific resources that will cover it in depth. We welcome suggestions on how to bridge this profile with such resources.

\> We welcome suggested additions to “Search Keywords” that would help readers scanning for concepts relevant to their sector or role find their way to the right Practice and Task.

\> References currently appear at all three levels: some at the Practice level, covering multiple Tasks and Implementations at once rather than repeating them; others at the Task and Implementation levels, specific to that item. Adding operational context to these references is ongoing work. We welcome thoughts on how to make these references and associated contextualizations more useful.

## How Far to Go: Measures as a Matter of Degree {#how-far-to-go:-measures-as-a-matter-of-degree}

Many of the measures in this profile are a matter of degree rather than something an organization either does or does not do: how independent a safeguard is, how finely access is divided, how much is logged, how often something is reviewed. The difficult decision is usually where to sit. Phrases such as “as independent as practical” or “shares as little as practical” refer to that decision.

* **Choosing where to sit:** How far to go is set by the consequence of a shared failure, weighed against the resources available, which are always finite. This is a design basis decision, as when infrastructure is designed for a flood of a chosen severity rather than for any flood. It should be made deliberately for the consequences involved, and what would happen beyond it should still be understood.
* **Recording what remains:** Any dependency or gap that remains is a decision, made within any regulatory or contractual obligations and accepted by someone with the authority to accept that level of risk ([Implementation 3.9.2: Define Decision Authority and Reassessment Triggers](#implementation-3.9.2:-define-decision-authority-and-reassessment-triggers)). It is recorded with its reason, so that it can be revisited when the system, its use, or the available resources change, and checked first when something goes wrong ([Implementation 3.9.6: Keep a Record of Design Decisions and Accepted Risks](#implementation-3.9.6:-keep-a-record-of-design-decisions-and-accepted-risks)).
* **Preparing alternatives:** Alternatives such as reverting, isolating, suspending, or switching to a backup are available only to the extent that the organization has prepared them, and each carries its own considerations, including the cost of keeping it ready.
* **Resources as a tension:** Because every measure draws on finite resources, this profile does not repeat that point in every item. It names “available resources” as one side of a tension only where a measure draws on a resource that other protections also depend on, such as operators’ attention or qualified reviewers’ time, and where the right choice changes with how much of that resource there is.
* **Side effects that cannot be resourced:** A side effect listed under Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider assumes that a measure addressing it elsewhere can be resourced. Where it cannot, the choice returns to the item that caused it, and becomes a tension to balance there.

\> TBD: whether efficiency and cost should also be treated as considerations in their own right, alongside the Trustworthiness Characteristics.

## Practice 1: Establish Requirements for Success {#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success}

*Define requirements and benchmarks for performance, safety, and security across the entire end-to-end system, including hardware, control logic, data sources, human operators, as well as automated, agentic, and SI components.*

Requirements set before a solution is chosen give the organization a baseline for judging existing and proposed systems. They help it check that those systems align with its mission and operational resilience goals while achieving the desired improvements. This helps ensure that where SI is adopted, it delivers measurable operational value. These requirements provide a verifiable framework for system acceptance and ongoing oversight, supporting clear accountability and audit-readiness throughout the asset lifecycle. Because these requirements are defined independently of any particular solution, a valid outcome of this Practice is the determination that SI is not the appropriate means of meeting them here, whether because a non-SI approach serves them better, or because a local constraint prevents an otherwise suitable SI system from meeting them in this specific deployment. This Practice is related to several others, for example [Practice 2: Define SI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service Expectations](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations), which helps ensure that any trade-offs still result in acceptable overall levels of robustness, resilience, and quality of service, and [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior), which sets the policies that bound SI behavior once the system is running.

**To the Reviewer:** > Specific, standardized risk management scoring metrics are considered too domain- and sector-specific for this document - instead, we encourage sector-specific organizations to develop such metrics. Having said that, what additional resources would you like to see, be it in this document or possible companion resources, that might facilitate organizations developing such metrics?

**Search Keywords:** operational baseline, success criteria, system acceptance, factory acceptance test (FAT), site acceptance test (SAT), operating envelope, TEVV scope, cyber-physical consequence tiering, performance benchmark, key performance indicator (KPI), legacy process baselining, edge-case stress testing, domain-specific terminology, business case for SI, non-SI alternative evaluation, audit-readiness, requirements matrix

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Valid:** Contributes the statement of what success means for this deployment, written before a solution is chosen, so that whether an SI system is the right means here is decided on evidence rather than assumed, and revisited when the operating context changes ([Implementation 1.1.3: Establish Triggers for Re-Validating Requirements on Change of Operating Context](#implementation-1.1.3:-establish-triggers-for-re-validating-requirements-on-change-of-operating-context)). This Practice does not cover the safeguards that maintain service and safety when performance departs from those requirements. For that, see [Practice 2: Define SI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service Expectations](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations).  
* **Accurate:** Contributes the reference that performance is judged against, set across the end-to-end system rather than the SI component alone, with minimum and preferred levels stated in advance. This Practice does not cover setting the consequence-based thresholds for how much of a given kind of error the organization is willing to carry, or the control responses when they are crossed. For that, see [Implementation 3.1.3: Define Acceptable Risk Thresholds and Associated Control Responses](#implementation-3.1.3:-define-acceptable-risk-thresholds-and-associated-control-responses).  
* **Accountable:** Contributes acceptance criteria fixed in advance, together with evidence that they were met, so that a decision to proceed rests on a documented bar and can be reviewed against it later. This Practice does not cover capturing what the system did once in service. For that, see [Practice 10: Implement Multi-Tiered SI System Logging and Audit Capabilities](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities).

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Secure:** Contributes security requirements set alongside performance and safety for the end-to-end system before a solution is chosen, including the adversities the system is expected to withstand, such as manipulated inputs, so that security is a condition a candidate SI system must meet rather than a property added afterward. This Practice does not cover mapping the ways an adversary could exploit the system once it is chosen. For that, see [Task 3.8: Scope and Map the Expanded SI Attack Surface and Risk Surface](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface).

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Valid versus Robust:** Where a deployment’s conditions are stable and well understood, drawing the requirements tightly makes both the bar and the evidence clear. Where conditions vary widely, a tightly drawn scope makes acceptance easier while leaving behavior outside that scope uncharacterized, and the organization carries whatever falls there. One way to balance this is to require behavior beyond the stated scope to be characterized separately before acceptance, for example through the edge-case testing in [Task 2.3: Establish Protocols for and Regularly Perform Systematic and Achievable Testing, Evaluation, Validation, and Verification (TEVV)](#task-2.3:-establish-protocols-for-and-regularly-perform-systematic-and-achievable-testing,-evaluation,-validation,-and-verification-\(tevv\)). Others include widening the scope and funding the evidence it then needs, or declining the deployment where neither is affordable.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MAP 1.4** (on defining SI business value): This Practice calls for SI adoption to be justified by measurable operational value rather than purely technological optimization, and that the value be stated in terms that the organization can check later; it does not cover determining whether the trade-offs made to obtain that value deviate from acceptable service levels. For that, see for example [Practice 2: Define SI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service Expectations](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations).  
* **GOVERN 1.2** (on defining trustworthy SI policies): This Practice turns the Trustworthiness Characteristics into benchmarks that a specific system can be accepted or rejected against; it does not cover setting the standing policies that bound SI behavior once the system is running. For those, see for example [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior).  
* **MEASURE 1.1** (on selecting and prioritizing measurements): This Practice covers performance, safety, and security benchmarks across the end-to-end system, and treats what cannot be measured directly as requiring additional verification rather than assumption; it does not cover enumerating the risks those measurements should be prioritized against. For that, see for example [Task 3.8: Scope and Map the Expanded SI Attack Surface and Risk Surface](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface).  
* **MANAGE 1.1** (on authorizing the system): This Practice covers the acceptance criteria and audit-ready evidence on which a proceed decision rests; it does not cover identifying who holds the authority to make that decision. For that, see for example [Implementation 3.9.1: Establish Accountable Ownership](#implementation-3.9.1:-establish-accountable-ownership).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Who owns the requirements for each SI deployment, and who decides whether the evidence meets them?  
* Where the requirements show that SI is not the appropriate means, who makes that call, and what is done instead?  
* What time and expertise are set aside for requirements work, baselining, and testing, including that of operators and subject matter experts, and where does it come from?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Section 2.1, “Consider the OT Business Case for AI Use,” is the closest external counterpart to this Practice: it treats whether to adopt SI as a question to be answered rather than assumed. Sections 4.1 and 4.2 cover monitoring and oversight mechanisms, and safety and failsafe mechanisms.  
* **Guidance** [Roles and Responsibilities Framework for Artificial Intelligence in Critical Infrastructure](https://www.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/2024-11/24_1114_dhs_ai-roles-and-responsibilities-framework-508.pdf), from the United States Department of Homeland Security. Part III, Critical Infrastructure Owners and Operators, sets out what that role is expected to carry, which is the perspective from which this Practice is written.  
* **Standard** [ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023, Systems and software engineering: system life cycle processes](https://www.iso.org/standard/81702.html), published jointly by ISO, IEC and IEEE. Clause 6.4.2, the stakeholder needs and requirements definition process, is the general systems-engineering form of what this Practice asks for, and is useful where an organization already runs a lifecycle process that SI requirements should join rather than sit beside.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-218A, Secure Software Development Practices for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models: An SSDF Community Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218A), July 2024, from NIST. Tasks PO.1.1 and PO.1.2, under practice PO.1, Define Security Requirements for Software Development, cover identifying and documenting security requirements for the infrastructure and processes used to develop SI models and for the software built with them, and PO.1.2 recommendation R1 notes that such requirements may come from laws, regulations, contracts and standards. This is the security portion of the requirements this Practice establishes, from the side of an organization that develops or fine-tunes models; NIST SP 800-218A places the deployment and operation of SI systems outside its scope.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v1r1, Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v1r1), from NIST. Appendix H.2, Stakeholder Needs and Requirements Definition, gives the security form of this Practice: its outcomes include characterizing the adversities presented by the environment, defining stakeholder protection needs, and transforming prioritized protection needs into stakeholder requirements, alongside security-oriented performance measures.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control SA-4, Acquisition Process, calls for security and privacy functional, strength of mechanism, and assurance requirements, together with acceptance criteria, to be included in the acquisition contract for a system, component, or service, which is where requirements set under this Practice reach a vendor.

### Task 1.1: Identify Current Requirements {#task-1.1:-identify-current-requirements}

Knowing what the current process actually has to achieve gives the organization the reference against which any SI system is judged. Catalog the functional, safety, and performance requirements for the operational processes the SI system is intended to support or augment. Include requirements that are met today only because a person is present to notice something, such as an implausible reading, or that rest on informal checks and unwritten limits. These are often absent from written procedures, and an SI system that takes over part of the task will not meet them unless they are stated. Distinguish requirements that apply regardless of who or what performs the task from those that assume a human performer, such as a licensed operator’s duties or a human-in-the-loop clause in a safety case. The latter can limit what an SI system may be permitted to do at all. Organizations with an established requirements capture process for new systems, or a management of change process, can build on that process here, with particular attention to what people currently do that is not written down. Organizations without one can start from the documentation review and walk-throughs in [Implementation 1.1.1: Operational Baseline Review](#implementation-1.1.1:-operational-baseline-review).

This Task helps ground SI-specific objectives in established mission-critical benchmarks, and contributes the reference for system acceptance and ongoing oversight. It also helps ensure that visibility is maintained into the expected benefits to be gained relative to the trade-offs elsewhere, and highlights when those benefits might no longer be present. Establishing operational success criteria also involves evaluating the initial Risk Surface under [Task 3.8: Scope and Map the Expanded SI Attack Surface and Risk Surface](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface), to help keep optimization gains from introducing unmitigated exposure elsewhere.

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Valid:** Contributes the specification of expected conditions and use: mission scope, operating envelopes, environmental parameters and functional dependencies across sensors, networks, control software, actuators and operators, recorded as a structured requirements matrix that remains auditable ([Implementation 1.1.2: Structured Requirements Mapping](#implementation-1.1.2:-structured-requirements-mapping)). This Task does not cover testing the delivered system against that specification. For that, see [Task 1.3: Implement Evaluation and Test Plans, Including TEVV, Across the SI Lifecycle](#task-1.3:-implement-evaluation-and-test-plans,-including-tevv,-across-the-si-lifecycle).  
* **Safe:** Contributes classification by consequence: requirements that reach physical machinery, environmental safety or human life are classified as such, which is what raises verification rigor and calls for deterministic boundary constraints ([Implementation 1.1.2: Structured Requirements Mapping](#implementation-1.1.2:-structured-requirements-mapping)). This Task does not cover defining those constraints or the states entered when one is exceeded. For those, see [Implementation 3.2.2](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints) and [Implementation 3.2.3](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior).

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Fair:** Requirements are elicited through internal functions such as engineering, operations, safety, compliance and legal ([Implementation 1.1.2: Structured Requirements Mapping](#implementation-1.1.2:-structured-requirements-mapping)), so obligations toward the people a service reaches enter through the roles that already hold them. Because this Task is the authoritative list that later testing works from, a service obligation absent here is absent from acceptance. [Task 1.4: Establish the SI System’s Domain Knowledge and Linguistic Alignment Requirements](#task-1.4:-establish-the-si-system’s-domain-knowledge-and-linguistic-alignment-requirements) carries part of this for systems that work in natural language, by making comprehension of community language variation a success criterion. \>TBD \- Whether evenness of service across the populations an operator serves belongs in the requirements matrix for SI systems that allocate, prioritize or triage rather than communicate. This entry is incomplete until that is settled. Suggestions welcome.  
* **Secure:** The requirements matrix records operating envelopes, the adverse and adversarial conditions the system is designed to withstand, and which requirements reach physical machinery, environmental safety, or human life ([Implementation 1.1.2: Structured Requirements Mapping](#implementation-1.1.2:-structured-requirements-mapping)). An attacker could use it to find the limits the system is built around, and the functions where a failure would do most harm. Protecting the matrix is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MAP 1.1** (on defining operating context): This Task documents the operational processes, deployment settings, operating envelopes and environmental conditions that the SI system will meet, drawn from safety manuals, SOPs and SLAs that already exist; it does not cover deriving the adverse and adversarial conditions that it catalogs. For those, see for example [Task 3.8: Scope and Map the Expanded SI Attack Surface and Risk Surface](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface).  
* **MAP 1.6** (on defining and communicating user requirements): This Task elicits requirements from engineering, operations, safety, compliance and legal subject matter experts and records them as a structured requirements matrix that remains auditable later; it does not cover testing the delivered system against them. For that, see for example [Task 1.3: Implement Evaluation and Test Plans, Including TEVV, Across the SI Lifecycle](#task-1.3:-implement-evaluation-and-test-plans,-including-tevv,-across-the-si-lifecycle).  
* **MAP 2.1** (on defining SI system task and methodology): This Task defines the operational tasks and mission scope that the SI system and the wider system are expected to perform, together with their dependencies on sensors, networks, control software, actuators and human operators; it does not cover selecting the model class or the method by which those tasks are implemented.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which expected benefits are recorded alongside the requirements, so that their loss can be noticed later?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 600-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1), July 2024, from NIST. Suggested actions MP-1.1-001 and MP-1.1-002, under MAP 1.1, cover identifying the intended purposes of a generative SI system, including whether it is fine-tuned or draws on retrieval-augmented data, and documenting its expected and acceptable context of use with domain experts: assumptions and limitations, direct value to the organization, and the intended operational environment. These are the generative-AI-specific counterparts of the operational requirements this Task catalogs.

#### Implementation 1.1.1: Operational Baseline Review {#implementation-1.1.1:-operational-baseline-review}

A baseline review shows the organization what the targeted process is required to achieve today, including what is done in practice but not written down. Perform a baseline review of existing operational documentation, such as safety manuals, standard operating procedures (SOPs), and service level agreements (SLAs), for the targeted process. Compare the written procedures with how the process is actually run, through walk-throughs, shift observation or interviews with operators, and record where the two differ, including workarounds. Recent incident and near-miss reports, permits and contracts can also hold requirements that the procedures do not state.

Distill these into a “Requirements Summary” that explicitly lists measurable success criteria (e.g., latency or throughput targets) along with minimum and ideal thresholds for performance. Where the SI system is later developed or supplied by one party and validated by another, both can agree on these thresholds before testing, so that the same thresholds serve validation, pre-deployment checks and monitoring. This implementation differs from [Task 1.2: Create Quantitative Baselines for Existing Systems in Both Normal and Challenging Conditions](#task-1.2:-create-quantitative-baselines-for-existing-systems-in-both-normal-and-challenging-conditions) by focusing on establishing a baseline from which improvements can be measured.

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by CISA. Section 2.1 closes with a fictional example assessment of SI for predictive maintenance on an industrial generator. It states requirements, corresponding safety and security requirements and success metrics as measurable targets, such as a 25% reduction in downtime, a 15% decrease in maintenance costs and a cap of 80% on network bandwidth for data aggregation. It is a worked example of the measurable success criteria and thresholds that a Requirements Summary lists.  
* **Commentary** [Artificial Intelligence Model Risk Management: Observations from a Thematic Review](https://www.mas.gov.sg/publications/monographs-or-information-paper/2024/artificial-intelligence-model-risk-management), Information Paper, December 2024, from the Monetary Authority of Singapore, drawn from a review of banks. Paragraph 6.3.8 reports that most banks set criteria or thresholds that define acceptable performance, and that these thresholds need to be clearly defined, documented and agreed by developers and validators. It adds that such thresholds were usually specific to the use case and could later support validation, pre-deployment checks, monitoring and change management. This is a financial-sector example of the agreed thresholds this Implementation asks for.

#### Implementation 1.1.2: Structured Requirements Mapping {#implementation-1.1.2:-structured-requirements-mapping}

A structured requirements matrix lets the organization see, for each requirement, where it came from, what will meet it once the SI system is in place, and how it will be verified. Conduct cross-functional requirements analysis with SMEs, including those from engineering, operations, safety, compliance, and legal departments, and front-line personnel who will supervise, rely on, or override the SI system, to translate high-level mission goals into a structured requirements matrix for the SI system, and the broader operational system within which it operates.

Requirements should explicitly define the operational task and mission scope, including the tasks that the system (AI and overall) is expected to perform, and its functional dependencies across sensors, network backbones, control software, physical actuators, and human operators in the oversight loop.

They should also define the conditions and constraints under which the system is expected to perform those tasks, including:

* Defined Operating Envelopes such as quantified input/output ranges (e.g., deterministic setpoint limits, clinical dosage thresholds, transaction execution ceilings), latency ceilings, and physical tolerance boundaries.  
* Environmental Operating Conditions, including physical, digital, and operational boundary parameters (e.g., sensor noise thresholds, data schema variations, network latency ranges, equipment wear tolerances).  
* Adverse and Adversarial Conditions, including enumerating expected environmental stresses (e.g., weather events, process upsets, sensor degradation) and attack surfaces as mapped in [Task 3.8: Scope and Map the Expanded SI Attack Surface and Risk Surface](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface) (e.g., prompt injection, data poisoning, compromised telemetry) and corresponding explicit behavioral requirements, such as those outlined in [Implementation 3.2.3: Specify Fail-Safe States and Fallback Behavior](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior).  
* Classification by physical consequence, such as explicit classification of requirements that directly impact physical machinery, environmental safety, or human life (see [Implementation 3.1.3: Define Acceptable Risk Thresholds and Associated Control Responses](#implementation-3.1.3:-define-acceptable-risk-thresholds-and-associated-control-responses)), triggering elevated verification rigor (see [Implementation 12.1.1: Artifact Risk Classification](#implementation-12.1.1:-artifact-risk-classification)) and deterministic boundary constraints (see [Implementation 3.2.2: Define and Independently Enforce Deterministic Operational Constraints](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints)).  
* Other non-functional requirements, such as specific auditability standards and data retention periods (see [Task 10.1: Define Decision-Level Logging and Metadata Retention Policies](#task-10.1:-define-decision-level-logging-and-metadata-retention-policies)).

For each requirement, record its source, how it is met today (by an engineered safeguard, a written procedure or operator judgment alone) and what will meet it once the SI system is in place, such as the SI system, a deterministic constraint, a human approval step or an existing safety function. Requirements met today by operator judgment alone, and that cannot be measured, warrant particular attention. An SI system can erode them without any indicator changing. Record how each requirement will be verified, and restate any that cannot be verified as written, such as “never unsafe under any input”, in a verifiable form, or allocate it to a layer where it can be verified.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which functions and front-line roles take part in requirements mapping for each SI system?

**References:**

* **Research** [Recent policy developments on AI in the labour market](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/recent-policy-developments-on-ai-in-the-labour-market_c0ffced7-en.html), OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 63, July 2026, from the OECD Directorate for Employment, Labour and Social Affairs. Section 7, Box 7 and Table 2, reports that the G7 countries, Costa Rica and Colombia all recommend involving workers in occupational safety and health matters, and many require it, because workers often know where risks arise. This is the reason for bringing front-line personnel into requirements analysis.  
* **Standard** [ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023, Systems and software engineering: system life cycle processes](https://www.iso.org/standard/81702.html), published jointly by ISO, IEC and IEEE. Clause 6.4.3, the system requirements definition process, asks that requirements be analyzed for characteristics including traceable and verifiable, with conflicts identified and resolved. It keeps bidirectional traceability to verification methods and to allocated requirements, and refers to ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 for detail on requirement characteristics. This bears on recording a verification method and an allocation for each row of the matrix.

#### Implementation 1.1.3: Establish Triggers for Re-Validating Requirements on Change of Operating Context {#implementation-1.1.3:-establish-triggers-for-re-validating-requirements-on-change-of-operating-context}

Re-validation triggers help an organization notice when the rules a system must meet have changed, even though the system itself has not. Define the events that invalidate the Requirements Summary produced in [Implementation 1.1.1: Operational Baseline Review](#implementation-1.1.1:-operational-baseline-review), and require re-validation when those events occur rather than only on a fixed review cycle.

For assets that relocate, that serve users or customers in more than one jurisdiction, or whose governing rule set is contract-dependent, the applicable standards, regulations, and customer-specific terms can change without any change to the SI system itself. Examples include:

* a mobile or relocatable asset entering a different regulatory jurisdiction, where a different set of national, sectoral, or customer-specific requirements becomes applicable,  
* an asset that stays where it is but begins to serve another jurisdiction, such as a system hosted in one country being opened to customers in another,  
* a change in contract status such as going off-contract or being stacked, and  
* the layering of customer-specific procedural requirements on top of a regional baseline.

For each trigger, record who is responsible for detecting it, who decides on the response, what depth of re-validation it calls for, from a desk review to a full re-evaluation under [Task 1.3: Implement Evaluation and Test Plans, Including TEVV, Across the SI Lifecycle](#task-1.3:-implement-evaluation-and-test-plans,-including-tevv,-across-the-si-lifecycle), and whether operation may continue in the meantime. Where the organization already runs a management of change process, these triggers can be added to it rather than kept separately.

Where the applicable rules are encoded in the SI system in its prompts, retrieval corpus or rule base, or in the guardrails and safety wrappers around it, treat the change as a required system update under [Task 7.5: Conduct Impact Assessments and Risk Management for SI System and Model Updates](#task-7.5:-conduct-impact-assessments-and-risk-management-for-si-system-and-model-updates). Where the rules are not encoded, but the SI system relies on standard operating procedures that reflect them, the trigger should raise an explicit action to review and, where necessary, rewrite those procedures before operation continues. Without such triggers, an SI system may continue to perform correctly against a rule set that no longer applies to the asset, producing outputs that are internally consistent and externally non-compliant. For SI systems built on pre-trained models, guidance, procedures, or regulations that changed after the model’s training cutoff are a further trigger. The model may continue to reproduce the superseded version unless current sources are supplied and take precedence. Where a trigger can be anticipated, such as a planned relocation, opening service to a new jurisdiction, or a change in contract status, re-validate before it takes effect, so that operation need not be suspended when it does.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which events trigger re-validation, who detects each, who decides the response, and what depth of re-validation does each call for?  
* Are the triggers added to an existing management of change process or kept separately?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-37r2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations: A System Life Cycle Approach for Security and Privacy](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-37r2), from NIST. Appendix F, Event-Driven Triggers and Significant Changes, lists changes to the environment of operation that may trigger an event-driven authorization action where they are likely to affect the security and privacy posture of the system. These include moving to a new facility, adding new core missions or business functions, and establishing new or modified laws, directives, policies or regulations. The first and last are changes in where a system operates or in the rules it must meet, rather than in the system itself, which is the category of trigger this Implementation defines. Its Type and Facility Authorizations subsection describes a single authorization for a common version of a system deployed to multiple locations, with the official responsible at each site accepting the risk of deploying it there. This separates acceptance of the system from acceptance of the setting it is placed in, the distinction this Implementation relies on when a relocatable asset enters a different setting.

### Task 1.2: Create Quantitative Baselines for Existing Systems in Both Normal and Challenging Conditions {#task-1.2:-create-quantitative-baselines-for-existing-systems-in-both-normal-and-challenging-conditions}

Measuring how the existing process performs, in hard conditions as well as normal ones, lets the organization tell whether an SI system is an improvement, and where it may be more brittle. Establish quantitative performance baselines for current legacy or manual processes to provide a comparative metric for evaluating SI system effectiveness. These baselines capture performance under both normal and stressed operating conditions, enabling technical managers to identify specific risks and measure improvements associated with the adoption of SI. This Task differs from [Implementation 1.1.1: Operational Baseline Review](#implementation-1.1.1:-operational-baseline-review) by focusing on minimum performance under challenging conditions to help ensure that performance gains do not result in increased brittleness.

Record the uncertainty of each baseline and the stressed conditions for which there is too little data to set one, along with any known gaps or reporting bias in the historical records it draws on. What can be claimed about the SI system’s relative performance under those conditions is limited in the same way. Where the measured baseline falls short of a requirement identified in [Task 1.1: Identify Current Requirements](#task-1.1:-identify-current-requirements), record the shortfall, so that a decision to require more of the SI system than the existing process achieves is made knowingly.

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Valid:** Contributes the measured “before” that a claimed improvement is checked against ([Implementation 1.2.1: Establish Manual or Legacy Process Performance and Safety Baselines](#implementation-1.2.1:-establish-manual-or-legacy-process-performance-and-safety-baselines)), which is what lets a conclusion that an SI system is not the right means here rest on evidence. This Task does not cover benefits for which the legacy process offers no counterpart, such as a capability that did not previously exist.  
* **Robust:** Contributes the comparison point beyond expected conditions: the manual or legacy process measured under stress and edge cases ([Implementation 1.2.2: Develop High-Fidelity Operational Baselines Including Edge-Case Performance Under Stress](#implementation-1.2.2:-develop-high-fidelity-operational-baselines-including-edge-case-performance-under-stress)), so brittleness introduced by an SI system appears as a like-for-like difference rather than as a surprise in service. This Task does not cover characterizing the SI system’s own behavior in those conditions. For that, see [Task 2.3: Establish Protocols for and Regularly Perform Systematic and Achievable Testing, Evaluation, Validation, and Verification (TEVV)](#task-2.3:-establish-protocols-for-and-regularly-perform-systematic-and-achievable-testing,-evaluation,-validation,-and-verification-\(tevv\)).

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Privacy-Enhanced:** Baselining a manual process measures the people who carry it out, and records kept at that level describe how individuals work. Aggregating the measures, and agreeing their use with the workforce, can limit this. Governing those records belongs with the organization’s existing workforce monitoring and privacy practice.  
* **Fair:** A baseline drawn from historical service records carries any unevenness in past service across locations or populations. An SI system that matches such a baseline can reproduce that unevenness while appearing to perform as well as the process it supports or replaces. Comparing performance for the groups served, as well as in aggregate, can show this.  
* **Secure:** A stressed-condition baseline records the conditions under which the existing process, and the people running it, perform worst, such as a plant upset or an alarm flood ([Implementation 1.2.2: Develop High-Fidelity Operational Baselines Including Edge-Case Performance Under Stress](#implementation-1.2.2:-develop-high-fidelity-operational-baselines-including-edge-case-performance-under-stress)). An attacker could use it to time an attack for when operators are least able to respond. Protecting the baseline records is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Accurate versus Robust:** Where only normal operation is baselined, a candidate that improves the average compares well. Where the stressed baseline is measured as well, a candidate that is sharper on average and weaker at the edges shows the trade, and the two comparisons can point to different decisions. One way to balance this is to set an acceptance bar on the stressed baseline as well as the normal one, so that an average gain does not by itself carry the decision. Others include accepting the trade with the brittleness recorded as a known limitation, or keeping the legacy path available for the conditions in which it performs better, with the resources for that allocated under [Task 11.1: Identify and Prioritize SI-Dependent Essential Functions](#task-11.1:-identify-and-prioritize-si-dependent-essential-functions).

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MAP 3.1** (on understanding benefits): This Task measures how the manual or legacy process actually performs before anything is deployed, so a claimed benefit can be checked against a documented “before” rather than an estimate; it does not cover examining benefits for which the legacy process offers no counterpart, such as a capability that did not previously exist.  
* **MAP 3.2** (on understanding costs): This Task baselines performance under stressed and edge-case conditions as well as normal ones, so that brittleness introduced by the SI system shows up as a like-for-like comparison rather than as a surprise in service; it does not cover relating the resulting costs to a level of risk the organization is willing to carry. For that, see for example [Implementation 3.1.3: Define Acceptable Risk Thresholds and Associated Control Responses](#implementation-3.1.3:-define-acceptable-risk-thresholds-and-associated-control-responses).  
* **MANAGE 2.1** (on allocating resources): This Task documents how the viable non-AI alternative performs, including under stress, so that keeping that alternative becomes a costed choice rather than an assumption; it does not cover allocating the resources needed to keep it available. For that, see for example [Task 11.1: Identify and Prioritize SI-Dependent Essential Functions](#task-11.1:-identify-and-prioritize-si-dependent-essential-functions).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Is acceptance judged on the normal baseline, the stressed baseline, or both? (see the Accurate versus Robust tension in [Task 1.2: Create Quantitative Baselines for Existing Systems in Both Normal and Challenging Conditions](#task-1.2:-create-quantitative-baselines-for-existing-systems-in-both-normal-and-challenging-conditions))  
* Where a candidate is weaker at the edges, is the brittleness accepted and recorded, or is the legacy path kept for those conditions?  
* Who collects the baseline measures, over what period, and whose time and budget does it draw on?

**References:**

#### Implementation 1.2.1: Establish Manual or Legacy Process Performance and Safety Baselines {#implementation-1.2.1:-establish-manual-or-legacy-process-performance-and-safety-baselines}

Before deploying an SI system, measure and document the current performance and safety metrics of the manual or legacy process it will support or replace, giving the organization a concrete “before” picture to compare against once the SI system is live. Sources can include historian data, work orders, logbooks, and incident and alarm records over a period long enough to cover seasonal and other expected variation. Record the spread and the worst cases as well as averages, together with any gaps in the data.

Use measures that can be taken again in the same way after deployment, so that the comparison is like-for-like. Where the AI system will perform the task differently from the people or process it supports, measure the outcomes that the process delivers rather than the steps it follows. Some of those steps may have no counterpart in the AI system. The same baseline can later serve as the reference from which deviation thresholds for post-deployment monitoring are set.

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-1), from NIST. Section 1.2.1, Risk Measurement, names the human baseline as a measurement challenge. AI systems intended to augment or replace human activity need some form of baseline metrics for comparison, and this is difficult to systematize because AI systems carry out different tasks, and perform tasks differently, than humans. This bears on choosing outcome measures for the “before” picture.  
* **Research** [NIST AI 800-4, Challenges to the Monitoring of Deployed AI Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.800-4), March 2026, from NIST. Section 3.2.1, Functionality, reports that practitioners found establishing performance baselines and thresholds difficult. Workshop attendees asked whether performance baselines had been established, and highlighted the need for deviation thresholds, set after the baseline, to trigger corrective actions or reviews. This bears on taking the “before” measure in a form that later monitoring can use.

#### Implementation 1.2.2: Develop High-Fidelity Operational Baselines Including Edge-Case Performance Under Stress {#implementation-1.2.2:-develop-high-fidelity-operational-baselines-including-edge-case-performance-under-stress}

Extend the baseline in [Implementation 1.2.1: Establish Manual or Legacy Process Performance and Safety Baselines](#implementation-1.2.1:-establish-manual-or-legacy-process-performance-and-safety-baselines) to include performance under stressed or edge-case conditions, not just normal operation, so that any brittleness introduced by the AI system can be identified by comparing like-for-like stress performance rather than only normal-condition performance.

For example, in process control, the number of alarms presented to operators can be counted during normal operation and during a plant upset, and the same counts repeated after a change to show whether performance has improved. Counts after an upset can be recorded for fixed periods, such as the first minute and the next ten minutes, together with the type of upset. Stressed conditions to baseline can be drawn from the adverse conditions enumerated in [Implementation 1.1.2: Structured Requirements Mapping](#implementation-1.1.2:-structured-requirements-mapping).

Where records of stressed conditions are few, operator training simulator sessions and exercises that introduce, for example, the loss of a sensor, a communications outage or an equipment trip can supply the stressed-condition baseline, measuring detection, response time, errors and recovery.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which stressed and edge-case conditions are baselined, and how is each reproduced?

**References:**

* **Guidance** Health and Safety Executive (2000), [Better alarm handling](https://www.hse.gov.uk/pubns/chis6.pdf), Chemicals Sheet No 6, from Great Britain’s workplace health and safety regulator. Step 1 asks how many alarms occur during normal operation and how many during a plant upset, and gives a separate rate target for each. Step 3 repeats the original measurements to measure progress. It is a worked example, from process plant, of a baseline taken under normal and stressed conditions and measured again after a change.  
* **Research** Bransby, M. L. and Jenkinson, J. (1998), [The management of alarm systems: a review of current practice in the procurement, design and management of alarm systems in the chemical and power industries](https://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/ukgwa/20230103120103/https://www.hse.gov.uk/research/crr_pdf/1998/crr98166.pdf), HSE Contract Research Report 166, research for Great Britain’s Health and Safety Executive drawing on visits to 15 chemical and power plants. Volume 1, Section 4.6, Number of alarms during a major plant upset, reports that operators find alarm systems significantly less helpful after an upset than in normal operation. It suggests recording counts for set periods after an upset, with the type of upset. This bears on measuring the stressed-condition baseline.

### Task 1.3: Implement Evaluation and Test Plans, Including TEVV, Across the SI Lifecycle {#task-1.3:-implement-evaluation-and-test-plans,-including-tevv,-across-the-si-lifecycle}

Testing repeated across the lifecycle helps an organization confirm whether an SI system still meets its requirements after acceptance, as the system’s behavior and the conditions of its use change. Develop and execute a systematic testing, evaluation, validation, and verification (TEVV) program that assesses AI performance against established requirements, as defined in [Task 1.1: Identify Current Requirements](#task-1.1:-identify-current-requirements) and, in particular, [Implementation 1.1.2: Structured Requirements Mapping](#implementation-1.1.2:-structured-requirements-mapping), at each stage of the asset lifecycle, and against previous baselines (if any). The system under test should be the AI system as deployed, including, where present, the model version, prompts and configuration, retrieval and data pipelines, tools, safety wrappers and interfaces, together with the operators who act on its outputs.

This Task serves as the anchor for TEVV considerations throughout this profile. It supports the generation of verifiable, audit-ready evidence, with re-evaluation as environments change handled under [Implementation 2.3.4: Recurrent Risk Evaluations](#implementation-2.3.4:-recurrent-risk-evaluations). Specialized applications of this framework appear throughout this profile. For example, [Task 2.3: Establish Protocols for and Regularly Perform Systematic and Achievable Testing, Evaluation, Validation, and Verification (TEVV)](#task-2.3:-establish-protocols-for-and-regularly-perform-systematic-and-achievable-testing,-evaluation,-validation,-and-verification-\(tevv\)) extends TEVV to anomaly and edge-case behavior. [Implementation 4.1.3: Regularly Practice and Evaluate Intervention Processes](#implementation-4.1.3:-regularly-practice-and-evaluate-intervention-processes) applies TEVV to override and intervention procedures. [Implementation 7.5.2: Perform Automated “Champion-Challenger” Assessment](#implementation-7.5.2:-perform-automated-“champion-challenger”-assessment) applies it to champion-challenger assessment, and [Task 11.4: Establish System Integrity Re-Validation and Re-Commissioning Protocols](#task-11.4:-establish-system-integrity-re-validation-and-re-commissioning-protocols) applies it to system re-commissioning.

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Valid:** Contributes the evidence that a delivered system meets the requirements and operating envelopes set in [Task 1.1: Identify Current Requirements](#task-1.1:-identify-current-requirements), with scope, environment and pass/fail criteria fixed per lifecycle stage before testing begins ([Implementation 1.3.1: Define TEVV Scope and Requirements per SI System](#implementation-1.3.1:-define-tevv-scope-and-requirements-per-si-system)), and with the conditions beyond which that evidence does not hold recorded alongside it. This Task does not cover detecting the loss of validity that appears only after the operating environment moves. For that, see [Implementation 2.3.4: Recurrent Risk Evaluations](#implementation-2.3.4:-recurrent-risk-evaluations) for scheduled re-evaluation, and [Task 3.4: Monitor for Anomalous SI Behavior](#task-3.4:-monitor-for-anomalous-si-behavior) for continuous runtime monitoring.  
* **Safe:** Contributes the verification that a system exceeding its defined boundaries derates or transitions predictably, and the rule that a system whose evidence does not support autonomy is held in a more restrictive oversight mode, with the oversight capacity that mode needs confirmed as available rather than assumed ([Implementation 1.3.1: Define TEVV Scope and Requirements per SI System](#implementation-1.3.1:-define-tevv-scope-and-requirements-per-si-system)). This Task does not specify the fallback states themselves. For those, see [Implementation 3.2.3: Specify Fail-Safe States and Fallback Behavior](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior).  
* **Transparent:** Contributes the acceptance record: test plans, dataset provenance documentation, model cards and empirical results held as one package for regulatory audit, lifecycle review and post-incident evaluation ([Implementation 1.3.4: Generate and Maintain Audit-Ready TEVV Evidence](#implementation-1.3.4:-generate-and-maintain-audit-ready-tevv-evidence)). This Task does not cover capturing what the system did in service. For that, see [Practice 10: Implement Multi-Tiered SI System Logging and Audit Capabilities](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities).

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Secure:** TEVV evidence records where the system was found weak, which conditions were not tested, and which assumptions the results depend on ([Implementation 1.3.1](#implementation-1.3.1:-define-tevv-scope-and-requirements-per-si-system) and [Implementation 1.3.4](#implementation-1.3.4:-generate-and-maintain-audit-ready-tevv-evidence)). An attacker could use it to aim manipulated inputs or faults at the conditions known to be untested or poorly handled. Protecting that evidence is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Valid versus Safe:** Where an application can sustain a planned outage, such as a report summarization tool or an off-peak batch process, testing during an authorized window yields evidence about the system that will actually run ([Implementation 1.3.2: Categorization of Testing Environments](#implementation-1.3.2:-categorization-of-testing-environments)). Where service delivery or a physical control loop cannot tolerate disruption, that evidence has to come instead from staging mirrors, hardware-in-the-loop rigs, simulators or digital twins, whose behavior may differ from the live system in ways the test will not show. One way to balance this is to record the difference between the test environment and the live system as a stated limit on the evidence, and to bound what is claimed from it. Others include raising fidelity for the specific behaviors that carry the most consequence, or confirming a narrow set of them live during scheduled downtime.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MAP 2.3** (on applying scientific methodologies): This Task fixes TEVV scope, test environment and pass/fail criteria per lifecycle stage before testing begins, and keeps destructive and adversarial testing off live production paths, except during scheduled downtime as discussed in [Implementation 1.3.1](#implementation-1.3.1:-define-tevv-scope-and-requirements-per-si-system) and [Implementation 1.3.2](#implementation-1.3.2:-categorization-of-testing-environments); it does not address the data availability, representativeness and suitability that MAP 2.3 also names. For those, see for example [Task 7.2: Validate, Select, and Prepare Data for SI Systems](#task-7.2:-validate,-select,-and-prepare-data-for-si-systems).  
* **MEASURE 1.3** (on involving independent assessors): This Task has the roles that design, execute, review and accept tests named, with their independence from the developer or supplier scaled to consequence ([Implementation 1.3.1: Define TEVV Scope and Requirements per SI System](#implementation-1.3.1:-define-tevv-scope-and-requirements-per-si-system)); it does not cover setting up the consultation with affected communities that MEASURE 1.3 also names.  
* **MEASURE 2.5** (on measuring validity and reliability): This Task demonstrates validity and reliability against the requirements and operating envelopes set in [Task 1.1: Identify Current Requirements](#task-1.1:-identify-current-requirements), and records the conditions beyond which that evidence does not hold; it does not cover detecting the loss of validity that appears only after the operating environment moves. For that, see for example [Implementation 2.3.4: Recurrent Risk Evaluations](#implementation-2.3.4:-recurrent-risk-evaluations).  
* **MEASURE 2.6** (on measuring safety): This Task verifies that a system exceeding its defined boundaries derates or transitions predictably, and constrains it to a more restrictive oversight mode where the evidence does not support autonomy; it does not specify what the fallback states themselves should be. For that, see for example [Implementation 3.2.3: Specify Fail-Safe States and Fallback Behavior](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Where live testing is not possible, how much difference between the test environment and the live system is accepted? (see the Valid versus Safe tension in [Task 1.3: Implement Evaluation and Test Plans, Including TEVV, Across the SI Lifecycle](#task-1.3:-implement-evaluation-and-test-plans,-including-tevv,-across-the-si-lifecycle))  
* Who staffs and funds TEVV across the lifecycle, including independent assessors and test environments, and what is done where that capacity is not available?

**References:**  
The following references illustrate how different critical infrastructure sectors have formalized TEVV-equivalent processes. Readers should look for analogous frameworks within their own sector’s regulatory or standards environment.

* **Regulation** [DoD Manual 5000.101, “Operational Test and Evaluation and Live Fire Test and Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence-Enabled and Autonomous Systems,” December 9, 2024](https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodm/5000101p.pdf), a policy issuance of the United States Department of Defense, binding on DoD components. Section 4 sets out the process for operational and live fire test and evaluation of SI-enabled and autonomous systems.  
* **Regulation** [DoD Directive 3000.09, “Autonomy in Weapon Systems,” January 25, 2023](https://www.esd.whs.mil/portals/54/documents/dd/issuances/dodd/300009p.pdf), from the same department. Section 3 covers verification and validation and testing and evaluation of autonomous and semi-autonomous systems.

#### Implementation 1.3.1: Define TEVV Scope and Requirements per SI System {#implementation-1.3.1:-define-tevv-scope-and-requirements-per-si-system}

For AI systems deployed in safety-critical operational roles in critical infrastructure, define TEVV scope requirements that map to the categories defined in [Implementation 1.1.2: Structured Requirements Mapping](#implementation-1.1.2:-structured-requirements-mapping) and are proportionate to consequence severity of errors identified during risk assessments within [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior) and explicitly account for failure modes specific to critical infrastructure, including model drift, adversarial manipulation, and degraded-mode operation.

Where the organization already grades consequence through hazard analysis methods, such as hazard and operability studies (HAZOP) or failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA), those results can be used to scale TEVV rigor rather than a separate scheme being devised.

Test suites should be proportionate to the severity of the system’s potential physical consequences and evaluate performance across:

* Nominal & Operating Envelope Testing: Validating system execution against the defined input/output ranges, setpoint limits, and latency ceilings established under [Implementation 1.1.2: Structured Requirements Mapping](#implementation-1.1.2:-structured-requirements-mapping).  
* Adverse & Adversarial Stress Testing: Assessing system stability and containment logic against the specific environmental stresses and attack vectors cataloged under [Task 3.8](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface) and [Implementation 1.1.2](#implementation-1.1.2:-structured-requirements-mapping).  
* Degraded-Mode & Fallback Verification: Verifying that when operating parameters exceed [Implementation 1.1.2: Structured Requirements Mapping](#implementation-1.1.2:-structured-requirements-mapping) boundaries, the system predictably initiates derated operations or transitions to an independent safe fallback state ([Implementation 3.2.3: Specify Fail-Safe States and Fallback Behavior](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior)).

Establish pass/fail criteria for each lifecycle stage including pre-deployment, post-incident, and periodic drift or degradation checks. Test and Evaluation (T\&E) planning documentation, of the kind already used for many traditional critical infrastructure systems to specify what will be tested, under what conditions, and against what success criteria before testing begins, provides a useful model for defining these requirements up front, rather than determining them ad hoc during testing.

Where an AI system’s outputs vary between runs on the same input, state how many repetitions each test needs and what proportion should pass. Demonstrating a low rate of rare, high-consequence failures by testing alone can need an impractically large number of trials, so record what mix of testing, analysis, simulation and architectural safeguards is relied on instead. Record what will not be tested and why, the assumptions on which the results depend, and the controls that compensate, so that these limits are visible to whoever decides whether to accept the risk. That person needs the information, time, and authority to make the decision, not only the role.

Define who designs, executes, reviews and accepts the tests, and how independent of the developer or supplier those roles are, with greater independence for higher-consequence systems. Independence can come from an internal function not involved in development or from a qualified external party. State which evidence supplied by a vendor is accepted as it stands and which is verified independently. Where few qualified people are available, for example in a small organization or a field office, one person may have to hold more than one of these roles. Where that happens, record it, and how the conflict is offset, such as by an external review of the test plan or of the results ([Implementation 3.9.6: Keep a Record of Design Decisions and Accepted Risks](#implementation-3.9.6:-keep-a-record-of-design-decisions-and-accepted-risks)).

Where an AI system cannot be shown to satisfy reliability requirements for autonomous operation, constrain it to a more restrictive oversight mode, appropriate to the consequence severity of the application, until TEVV evidence supports a less restrictive oversight mode (see [Task 4.5: Define Operational Regimes for Human-on-the-Loop and Human-Out-of-the-Loop Operation](#task-4.5:-define-operational-regimes-for-human-on-the-loop-and-human-out-of-the-loop-operation) for specification of modes).

Confirm that the oversight capacity required by that mode is actually available, rather than assuming it: high algorithmic error rates can quickly exceed operator triage capacity, and that capacity is shared with every other system the same operators watch. Where it is not available, limit use of the AI system to what the available oversight capacity can support, as discussed in [Task 4.4: Attention Governance and Alert/Alarm Flood Mitigation](#task-4.4:-attention-governance-and-alert/alarm-flood-mitigation). To reduce the risk of accidental operational outages caused by evaluation overhead, procurement and engineering policies should explicitly avoid high-load active adversarial testing, automated input fuzzing, or dense red-teaming (testing a system by deliberately seeking to compromise it as an attacker would) vectors on live, production model paths.

All destructive profiling or exploratory boundary testing should be restricted to isolated staging environments, offline hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) test rigs, high-fidelity digital twins (detailed virtual replicas of physical equipment or processes that are kept up to date with real data), or during scheduled downtime, with sufficient time and resources to recover if necessary.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* How is TEVV scope scaled to consequence severity, and who accepts what is left untested?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53Ar5, Assessing Security and Privacy Controls in Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53Ar5), from NIST. Section 2.4.2, Assessment Methods, defines depth (rigor and level of detail) and coverage (scope and breadth) attributes for examination, interview and testing, each with basic, focused and comprehensive values, and notes that as assurance requirements increase, the rigor and scope of assessment tend to increase as well, which is a model for making TEVV scope proportionate to consequence severity as this Implementation asks.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control enhancement CA-2(1), Independent Assessors, describes impartial assessors as free from conflicts of interest regarding the development, operation or management of the system. It notes that independent assessments can come from within the organization or be contracted outside it, and that the authorizing official sets the required level of independence by risk. This bears on scaling evaluator independence to consequence.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Appendix F.7.4, the OT discussion of CA-8, Penetration Testing, notes that OT systems are sensitive to timing and limited resources, gives a replicated, virtualized or simulated system as a compensating control, and schedules any offline testing during planned outages where possible. Appendix C.3.4 records outages caused by testing on live systems.  
* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by CISA. Section 1.2 covers the secure AI system development lifecycle and Section 3.3 covers AI testing and evaluation.  
* **Standard** ISA/IEC 62443-4-1, Security for industrial automation and control systems, Part 4-1: Secure product development lifecycle requirements, from the International Society of Automation and the International Electrotechnical Commission. Clause 9, Practice 5: Security Verification and Validation Testing, is the industrial control equivalent of the verification requirements set here.  
* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025), March 2025, from NIST. Sections 2.1 and 3.1 classify attacks on predictive and generative systems by learning stage, attacker goals and objectives, and attacker capabilities and knowledge, which can be used to structure the adversarial portion of lifecycle test coverage. Section 3.3.3, discussing evaluations of generative models against direct prompting attacks, notes that evaluations measure model vulnerabilities at a particular moment in time and that assessments may change as new attacks are developed, more data is collected after training, or capabilities improve. This supports setting pass/fail criteria for periodic and post-incident checks as well as for pre-deployment.  
* **Regulation** [DoD Manual 5000.101, Section 4.1](https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodm/5000101p.pdf), a policy issuance of the United States Department of Defense. Covers the process for planning operational test and evaluation of SI-enabled systems.

**\>To the Reviewer:** Implementation references are intended to help those implementing these tasks find further reading, be it to help them implement this task, or to better understand where this task fits in with other things that they may already be familiar with, including other policies and regulations. We would like to provide just enough context to help the reader determine what is useful (particularly if we’re referencing long documents) but we also need to keep this short as most of these implementations will have references. We are trying a few different ways of doing this and while we do this, the references will look different in different places in this document. Let us know what you think about this balance and which ones you prefer\!

#### Implementation 1.3.2: Categorization of Testing Environments {#implementation-1.3.2:-categorization-of-testing-environments}

Choosing a suitable test environment helps the organization gather evidence about the system while limiting the risk to live operations. TEVV activities across the system lifecycle should be conducted within a validated environment tailored to the operational nature of the underlying infrastructure. For critical applications where service delivery, safety constraints, or physical control loops cannot tolerate production path disruption or performance overhead, adhere to the production path testing exclusions defined in [Implementation 1.3.1: Define TEVV Scope and Requirements per SI System](#implementation-1.3.1:-define-tevv-scope-and-requirements-per-si-system).

Testing, including active verification, automated input fuzzing, and adversarial red-teaming should be restricted to non-production systems such as staging mirrors, hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) test rigs, simulators, or high-fidelity digital twins. For critical applications that possess regular, planned downtime or can sustain temporary outages without safety impacts (e.g., administrative or transactional batch processors, data summarization tools, or off-peak fraud queues), it may be safe to test directly on the active production system strictly during authorized maintenance or scheduled outage windows. Where feasible, this may be preferable to testing on simulators or staging systems, whose behavior may unintentionally differ from the live system. This does not preclude advancing an SI system through these environments in stages, with criteria to be met at each stage before testing moves closer to the live system.

A digital twin or simulator supports assurance only to the extent that it has itself been validated against the process it represents. A simulation that has not been checked against measurements from the real equipment can repeat its own errors at scale. Where no validated twin is available, other options include hardware-in-the-loop rigs, replay of recorded operational data, phased commissioning, and passive shadow mode. In passive shadow mode, sometimes called a silent trial, the AI system runs on live inputs in parallel with normal operation, and its outputs do not affect that operation. Passive shadow mode does not show how operators respond to the AI system’s outputs, or how the process behaves once the AI system’s own actions change it.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which SI systems can be tested in an authorized window on the live system, and which only in staging, simulation or hardware-in-the-loop environments?  
* What criteria must be met at each stage before testing moves closer to the live system?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control enhancement CM-3(2), Testing, Validation, and Documentation of Changes, tests and validates changes before they are finalized, and its discussion asks that testing not interfere with operations, that testers understand the health, safety and environmental risks of the facility or process, that operational systems may need to be replicated or taken offline, with tests scheduled during planned outages whenever possible, and that compensating controls be used where testing cannot be conducted on operational systems. That parallels the split this Implementation draws between non-production environments and testing in scheduled outage windows.  
* **Working Document** [Preliminary Report](https://www.scsp.ai/robotics-preliminary-report/), October 2026, from the National Security Commission on Robotics for Advanced Manufacturing. Under Finding 9, the discussion of robotics data notes that, for contact-rich industrial tasks, a simulation is only useful if it matches real equipment, materials and friction, and that the only way to check that match is against measurements from real machines. It adds that a simulation without real-world grounding repeats its own mistakes at scale. This bears on validating a digital twin before relying on its results.  
* **Research** [Tikhomirov, L. et al., “A scoping review of silent trials for medical artificial intelligence”, Nature Health 1, 532-554](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44360-025-00048-z), 2026\. The introduction defines a silent trial as prospective, noninterventional testing of AI models in the intended setting, with outputs produced in parallel to the standard of care and without affecting it. Its main use is to find out whether a model keeps its performance in a live context. The review of 75 studies also found that few verified outputs against an in situ ground truth. This healthcare example bears on passive shadow mode as a testing option.

#### Implementation 1.3.3: Evaluate SI System Behavior Against Requirements and Operational Baselines {#implementation-1.3.3:-evaluate-si-system-behavior-against-requirements-and-operational-baselines}

Evaluating an SI system against its requirements and against the baselines of the existing process shows the organization where the SI system improves on that process and where the SI system falls short. Assess AI system performance against TEVV requirements defined in [Implementation 1.3.1: Define TEVV Scope and Requirements per SI System](#implementation-1.3.1:-define-tevv-scope-and-requirements-per-si-system), and the operational baseline reviewed in [Implementation 1.1.1: Operational Baseline Review](#implementation-1.1.1:-operational-baseline-review), and the quantitative baselines measured under [Task 1.2: Create Quantitative Baselines for Existing Systems in Both Normal and Challenging Conditions](#task-1.2:-create-quantitative-baselines-for-existing-systems-in-both-normal-and-challenging-conditions). DoD 5000.101 Section 4.3 Test Execution provides examples of high level guidance to understand operational test and evaluation considerations. Record each violation of a constraint defined under [Implementation 3.2.2: Define and Independently Enforce Deterministic Operational Constraints](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints) during evaluation as a finding that needs a recorded disposition, even where aggregate measures pass. Where operators act on the AI system’s outputs, evaluate the operators and the AI system together, including how often operators catch incorrect outputs, how often they accept them, and how workload and response time compare with the baseline.

For AI agents and agentic AI systems, evaluate the sequence of actions as well as the end result, including the plan, which tools are called and in what order, and whether the AI system seeks human input where it should. An AI system can reach the required result through intermediate actions that would not be acceptable, such as attempting to bypass an access control or fabricating data to complete a task.

**References:**

* **Research** [Agentic AI in Organisations: Early Insights from Practitioner Interviews](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/agentic-ai-in-organisations_1257a26f-en.html), OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 65, 2026, from the OECD Directorate for Science, Technology and Innovation and the Tokyo Centre of the GPAI Expert Community, drawing on interviews with 25 organizations. Section 4.1 reports that assessing agentic behavior over extended sequences of actions, including planning quality, tool-call order and when to seek user input, remains an open challenge; Section 3.3 gives examples of agents reaching the desired result through undesirable intermediate behavior; and Section 4.2 lists agent-specific metrics some organizations use, such as intent resolution, tool-calling accuracy and task adherence.

#### Implementation 1.3.4: Generate and Maintain Audit-Ready TEVV Evidence {#implementation-1.3.4:-generate-and-maintain-audit-ready-tevv-evidence}

Keeping test evidence in a form others can check helps the organization show later, even without the original team, what was tested and what was found, for audits, lifecycle reviews, and incident investigations. TEVV activities should produce structured, verifiable evidence suitable for regulatory audit, lifecycle review, and post-incident evaluation.

Where evidence includes a verification result, state what the property was proven over: the AI system’s own internal model or records, or over the whole end-to-end system, including the physical process and its ground truth. A property proven over a model holds for the world only as far as the model is faithful to it.

Where the AI system’s behavior depends on its configuration, the evidence should also record the configuration tested, such as prompts, tool settings and the settings of any safety wrapper, and the test environment. Linking each result to the requirement it verifies in [Implementation 1.1.2: Structured Requirements Mapping](#implementation-1.1.2:-structured-requirements-mapping) can help show which requirements are supported by evidence.
