Recording who reviewed the results, who accepted them and the basis for that decision can help a later reviewer reconstruct the test without the original team.

To establish operational trust, evidence packages should pair governance evidence (test plans, dataset provenance documentation, model cards) with technical evidence (empirical evaluation results, simulation logs, boundary test receipts). Record with each result the version of the AI system, its data and its test datasets, and how each has changed since earlier testing, so that the evidence remains traceable to the system actually in service. Keeping evidence packages, configurations, and test datasets for each version has a storage and curation cost, which bears on how long they are kept. Records about a version can lose their meaning once that version is updated or retired, unless what they refer to is kept with them (see [Task 10.1](#task-10.1:-define-decision-level-logging-and-metadata-retention-policies) and [Practice 13](#practice-13:-establish-procedures-for-retiring-si-systems-and-withdrawing-their-authority)).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* How long is TEVV evidence kept, and which configuration details are recorded with it?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53Ar5, Assessing Security and Privacy Controls in Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53Ar5), from NIST. Section 2.3, Building an Effective Assurance Case, describes compiling evidence from development artifacts and assessments, and from operational records such as remediation actions, incident reports and continuous monitoring results, into a form decision makers can use, and defines an assurance case as a body of evidence organized into an argument that a claim about a system holds, needed for properties such as safety or reliability. That parallels this Implementation’s pairing of governance evidence with technical evaluation evidence.  
* **Research** [Mitchell, M. et al., “Model Cards for Model Reporting”, FAT\* ’19: Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency](https://doi.org/10.1145/3287560.3287596), January 2019\. The abstract proposes model cards: short documents that accompany trained machine learning models and give benchmarked evaluation across relevant conditions, the context in which the models are intended to be used, and details of the performance evaluation procedures. This is the source of the model cards that this Implementation lists among governance evidence.  
* **Regulation** [DoD Manual 5000.101, “Operational Test and Evaluation and Live Fire Test and Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence-Enabled and Autonomous Systems,” December 9, 2024](https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodm/5000101p.pdf), a policy issuance of the United States Department of Defense, binding on DoD components. Section 4.1.b, OT\&E and LFT\&E Plans, requires plans to identify how inputs or outputs to AI components have been modified over time through data and model versioning, and how changing aspects of system performance relate to prior testing. This Implementation suggests the same versioning record for evidence outside that setting.  
* **Guidance** [AI Shared Responsibility Framework, version 1.0](https://www.coalitionforsecureai.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/CoSAI-Shared-Responsibility-Framework.pdf), Workstream 2: Preparing Defenders for a Changing Cybersecurity Landscape, 26 May 2026, from the Coalition for Secure AI, an OASIS Open Project. Appendix A.7, Evidence Requirements, sorts evidence into governance, technical, operational, assessment and attestation categories. It lists by layer the artifacts each accountable party is expected to hold, such as model cards, training data documentation and red team reports from the AI model provider. This bears on what an operator assembling a TEVV evidence package can ask its suppliers for.

### Task 1.4: Establish the SI System’s Domain Knowledge and Linguistic Alignment Requirements {#task-1.4:-establish-the-si-system’s-domain-knowledge-and-linguistic-alignment-requirements}

For AI systems that interact in natural language (including chatbots, summarization tools, schematic/diagram parsers, and user interfaces that generate unique textual or graphical human output), identify and document domain-specific knowledge, industry terminology, operational ontologies, graphical conventions, and community context that the AI system needs to understand in order to perform its intended function accurately and safely.

Especially for multimodal and language models trained on large, general datasets, success criteria should include a verified understanding of sector-specific jargon, graphical symbols, units of measure and sign conventions, operational nuances, and community variations to language, particularly where colloquial variations exist or where domain-specific conventions can be expected to diverge from those of the broader community. For example, an open circuit breaker interrupts current, while an open valve permits flow.

Success criteria can also cover how the AI system behaves at the edge of its domain knowledge, such as whether it flags a term or question that it does not recognize rather than resolving it to a familiar meaning. Where outputs carry exact identifiers, such as equipment tags or procedure numbers, the criteria can require that they be reproduced exactly rather than paraphrased.

For high-consequence applications, including otherwise benign AI systems, such as chatbots, or parsers of scanned technical diagrams that provide outputs that are used for high-consequence decisions, verification of understanding should be commensurate with the consequence. This may exclude post-hoc statistical explanations that are not guaranteed to reflect the AI system’s understanding (see [Implementation 4.6.2](#implementation-4.6.2:-derive-confidence-and-rationale-for-learned-components-from-their-decision-processes) and [Implementation 8.1.2](#implementation-8.1.2:-identify-si-systems-that-may-not-satisfy-root-cause-analysis-requirements)) and/or necessitate additional verification of the AI system’s outputs. This helps ensure that the system’s outputs, whether in optimization, predictive maintenance, digital twins, report summarization, or AI-generated code, procedures, and configurations, are aligned with the precise technical, conceptual, safety, and execution logic requirements of the industry and the community it serves.

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Valid:** Contributes the sector knowledge requirement: the terminology, operational ontologies, graphical conventions and community context an AI system needs to hold for this industry, written as success criteria, verified in proportion to consequence, and with post-hoc statistical explanation ruled out as evidence of understanding. This Task does not cover testing a delivered system against those criteria. For that, see [Task 2.4: Perform Linguistic and Domain-Context Robustness Testing](#task-2.4:-perform-linguistic-and-domain-context-robustness-testing).  
* **Accurate:** Contributes contextual accuracy as a stated benchmark rather than general fluency: whether sector terms, symbols and priorities are read as the sector uses them, so that a plausible summary which misreads a critical alert fails a criterion ([Implementation 1.4.2: Administrative & Support](#implementation-1.4.2:-administrative-&-support)). This Task does not cover verifying the artifacts the system generates once they exist. For that, see [Practice 12: Independently Verify SI-Generated Operational Logic and Artifacts Across Their Lifecycle](#practice-12:-independently-verify-si-generated-operational-logic-and-artifacts-across-their-lifecycle).  
* **Fair:** Contributes comprehension across community and colloquial language variation as an explicit success criterion, so that uneven understanding across the populations an operator serves fails a stated requirement instead of passing unremarked. This Task does not cover evaluating unevenness in the decisions that follow or in the outcomes they produce.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Accurate versus Explainable & Interpretable:** Where a domain requirement can be written as a checkable distinction, such as separating a forced outage from planned maintenance ([Implementation 1.4.1: Maintenance & Operations](#implementation-1.4.1:-maintenance-&-operations)), demonstrated understanding and measured accuracy move together. Where the requirement is tacit institutional knowledge ([Implementation 1.4.4: Requirements for SI-Generated Code, Configurations, Procedures, and Other Logic](#implementation-1.4.4:-requirements-for-si-generated-code,-configurations,-procedures,-and-other-logic)), a system can score well on the part that was written down, while the evidence that it holds the rest is exactly what this Task declines to take from post-hoc statistical explanation. One way to balance this is to raise verification of the outputs themselves in proportion to consequence, which this Task provides for. Others include writing the tacit knowledge down before the requirement is set, or limiting the system’s role to the part of the domain that can be stated. For where a stated part could be implemented symbolically, see [Task 4.6: Ensure that Confidence and Rationale Shown to Personnel Reflect How the SI System Reached Its Output](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output).

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MAP 2.2** (on defining AI system utility and oversight needs): This Task documents the sector terminology, operational ontologies and graphical conventions that a system must hold, so that its knowledge limits can be stated for one industry rather than in general; it does not cover defining the oversight mode applied where those limits are reached. For that, see for example [Task 4.5: Define Operational Regimes for Human-on-the-Loop and Human-Out-of-the-Loop Operation](#task-4.5:-define-operational-regimes-for-human-on-the-loop-and-human-out-of-the-loop-operation).  
* **MEASURE 2.9** (on measuring interpretability and explainability): This Task requires understanding to be verified in proportion to consequence, and treats post-hoc statistical explanations as insufficient evidence that the system understood the domain; it does not cover whether the confidence and rationale shown to an operator at run time reflect how the output was produced. For that, see for example [Task 4.6: Ensure that Confidence and Rationale Shown to Personnel Reflect How the SI System Reached Its Output](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output).  
* **MEASURE 2.11** (on measuring fairness, accuracy, and bias): This Task makes comprehension of community and colloquial language variation an explicit success criterion, so that uneven understanding across communities fails a stated requirement instead of passing unremarked; it does not cover evaluating bias in the system’s decisions or in the outcomes they produce.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which domain distinctions are written as checkable requirements, and which tacit knowledge needs expert review instead? (see the Accurate versus Explainable & Interpretable tension in [Task 1.4: Establish the SI System’s Domain Knowledge and Linguistic Alignment Requirements](#task-1.4:-establish-the-si-system’s-domain-knowledge-and-linguistic-alignment-requirements))  
* Whose time is set aside for eliciting tacit knowledge and agreeing reference interpretations, and how is it balanced against their operational duties?

#### Implementation 1.4.1: Maintenance & Operations {#implementation-1.4.1:-maintenance-&-operations}

For a predictive maintenance or digital twin system, require the AI to demonstrate mastery of technical standards (e.g., distinguishing between “forced outage” and “planned maintenance”) to help ensure correct prioritization. Where the system learns from or retrieves maintenance work orders, the failure descriptions in them may have been recorded by technicians rather than maintenance experts, and their accuracy can be uncertain. Subject matter experts who understand the equipment, maintenance protocols and failure mechanisms can help set the reference interpretations against which this mastery is verified. Where a sector body publishes defined terms, those definitions can form part of that reference. For example, the electric sector’s glossary defines a forced outage as the condition in which equipment is unavailable due to unanticipated failure.

**References:**

* **Research** [Kang, J. et al., “A data quality management framework for equipment failure risk estimation: Application to the oil and gas industry”, Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence 136 (2024) 108834](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.engappai.2024.108834). Section 3.2.3, Data labeling, notes that maintenance technicians rather than maintenance experts often record the failure descriptions in maintenance work orders, so the accuracy of those reports and of the identified root cause can be uncertain. It adds that labeling such data requires an understanding of equipment operations, maintenance protocols and failure mechanisms held by subject matter experts. This bears on the reference interpretations that mastery of technical standards is verified against.  
* **Standard** [NERC Glossary of Terms](https://www.nerc.com/glossary-of-terms), from the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC), online glossary as saved on 16 October 2026\. The entry for Forced Outage defines it as the removal from service availability of a generating unit, transmission line or other facility for emergency reasons, and as the condition in which the equipment is unavailable due to unanticipated failure. This Implementation uses the definition only as an example of a published sector term against which an AI system’s interpretation can be checked.

#### Implementation 1.4.2: Administrative & Support {#implementation-1.4.2:-administrative-&-support}

For report summarization or customer service systems, establish “Contextual Accuracy” benchmarks to verify that LLM-based tools correctly interpret industry-specific jargon without introducing “hallucinations” or misprioritizing critical alerts. Such benchmarks can include explicit checks that a summary preserves the quantities, units, dates and obligations stated in its source. Scoring such benchmarks generally depends on reviewers with domain expertise. Where reviewers disagree on whether an output is in error, recording the disagreement, rather than only a consolidated rating, can help identify the items that are hardest to judge. For testing against these benchmarks, see [Implementation 2.4.3: Technical Accuracy and “Plausible Hallucination” Audits](#implementation-2.4.3:-technical-accuracy-and-“plausible-hallucination”-audits).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Who scores the contextual accuracy benchmarks, and with what domain expertise?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 600-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1), July 2024, from NIST. Section 2.2, Confabulation, describes confidently presented but erroneous or false content, colloquially called hallucinations. It notes that this is particularly relevant for open-ended prompts for long-form responses and in domains that require highly contextual or domain expertise, and it gives the example of a confabulated summary of patient information leading to an incorrect diagnosis. This bears on the summarization benchmarks in this Implementation.  
* **Research** [Schiller, C. A., “The Human Factor in Detecting Errors of Large Language Models: A Systematic Literature Review and Future Research Directions”](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.09743), preprint, March 2024\. Section 4, Human factors in LLM error detection, finds that the reviewed studies relied on a very small number of evaluators with domain expertise, typically two or three. Where evaluators disagreed, the studies consolidated their ratings into one rather than examining why they disagreed. This bears on how contextual accuracy benchmarks are scored.

#### Implementation 1.4.3: Infrastructure Optimization {#implementation-1.4.3:-infrastructure-optimization}

Define the specific operational states and physical constraints the system should “understand” (e.g., grid stability terminology in Energy) to help ensure optimization recommendations are technically valid. In the electric sector, for example, published definitions of System Operating Limits and Interconnection Reliability Operating Limits can supply part of this vocabulary. A system that performs well against one set of operating protocols may not carry over to another function in the same sector. The states and constraints defined should therefore be those of the functions that the system will actually support, and the scope of its testing should be taken as the range in which it is used.

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Real-Time System Operations](https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/our-work/white-papers/whitepaper-ai-and-ml-in-real-time-system-operations.pdf), White Paper Revision 1, November 2024, from the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC). Chapter 1, Key Terms, defines reliability, robustness and resilience for the bulk power system, with reliability measured against operational requirements such as those in NERC’s Reliability Terminology. In Chapter 3, Bias in Training Models notes that an LLM trained on one Reliability Coordinator’s operating protocols will likely not function effectively for generating regulatory reports, and that the scope of testing should be taken as the range of functions in which the tool is used.  
* **Standard** [NERC Glossary of Terms](https://www.nerc.com/glossary-of-terms), from the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC), online glossary as saved on 16 October 2026\. The entries for System Operating Limit and Interconnection Reliability Operating Limit define the facility ratings, voltage limits and stability limits used to assess operating states, and the subset of those limits whose violation could lead to instability, uncontrolled separation or cascading outages. They are examples of the operational states and physical constraints that this Implementation asks to be defined.

#### Implementation 1.4.4: Requirements for SI-Generated Code, Configurations, Procedures, and Other Logic {#implementation-1.4.4:-requirements-for-si-generated-code,-configurations,-procedures,-and-other-logic}

Success criteria that reflect what experienced staff know, as well as what is written down, help generated code, configurations, and procedures fit how the site actually works. For AI systems that generate artifacts that affect execution, including by other systems (e.g., code and configurations) and by people (e.g., procedures, summaries of manuals), set success criteria that capture both formal documented specifications and as much of the relevant tacit institutional knowledge as practical.

Tacit knowledge is often unwritten. Experienced staff may be unaware of all they know, but they can often explain why they acted as they did. Asking them to explain past decisions can help bring this knowledge into the success criteria. Converting it into written criteria generally takes repeated dialogue among the people who hold it. For generated code, formal criteria can include a check that each software package it references is a known, intended dependency. Code-generating AI systems can reference packages that do not exist, and a name that does resolve may not be the package intended: it may be an unrelated or unmaintained package with a similar name, or a malicious one that an attacker has published under that name. A check that the package merely exists is therefore not sufficient. For validation of the generated artifacts against these criteria, see [Implementation 12.2.3: Validation Against Tacit and Formal Requirements](#implementation-12.2.3:-validation-against-tacit-and-formal-requirements). For generated code and configurations, the formal specifications can include the target language or dialect, the platform and firmware version that it will run on, and site naming conventions.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which generated artifacts need validation before use, and how is the rigor of that validation set?

**References:**

* **Research** [Nonaka, I., “A Dynamic Theory of Organizational Knowledge Creation”, Organization Science 5(1), 14-37](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2635068), February 1994\. Section 2.2 draws on Polanyi to describe tacit knowledge as personal, rooted in action and context, and hard to formalize and communicate. Section 2.4 calls the conversion of tacit into explicit knowledge externalization, triggered by successive rounds of meaningful dialogue, and Section 3.2 describes it as a difficult process involving repeated, time-consuming dialogue. This bears on writing tacit knowledge into success criteria.  
* **Guidance** [NIST IR 8367, Psychological Foundations of Explainability and Interpretability in Artificial Intelligence](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.IR.8367), from NIST. Section 4.1.3 draws on engineering management literature on the tacit nature of expertise. It notes that human experts may not be consciously aware of how they obtained an outcome, yet are often able to describe why they did what they did, and that experts can be queried for their rationales. This bears on eliciting the tacit institutional knowledge that this Implementation asks success criteria to capture.  
* **Research** [Spracklen, J. et al., “We Have a Package for You\! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs”, 34th USENIX Security Symposium](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity25/presentation/spracklen), 2025\. Section 1, Introduction, describes package hallucination, in which generated code recommends or references a package that does not exist, and how an adversary can publish a malicious package under that name. The abstract reports average hallucinated-package rates of at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models. This bears on the formal criteria for generated code in this Implementation.

## Practice 2: Define SI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service Expectations {#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations}

*Establish expectations of, and safeguards to maintain, essential service delivery and functional safety when SI system performance deviates from expected levels, regardless of the cause.*

Because an SI system can depart from expected performance for reasons that are hard to foresee, a layered set of safeguards helps an organization keep essential functions running: some that act on the effect whatever its cause, and others that depend on recognizing a particular cause, each where it fits. Such safeguards should be considered at multiple points in the system to reduce the likelihood of cascading failures. These include usage thresholds and rate controls ([Task 2.1: Establish SI Usage Thresholds and Rate Control Mechanisms](#task-2.1:-establish-si-usage-thresholds-and-rate-control-mechanisms)), redundant paths, and watchdog controllers ([Task 2.2: Establish Requirements for Redundancy in SI-Driven Functions](#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions)).

Where an SI system is hosted by a third party or reached over external networks, its availability and latency also depend on networks and providers outside the organization’s control. The safeguards should then also cover a slowed or lost external service. Related Practices include [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior), which defines the deterministic boundaries and fail-safe states these safeguards fall back to, and [Practice 4: Define Procedures for Emergency Avoidance Override, Recovery, and Situational Awareness](#practice-4:-define-procedures-for-emergency-avoidance-override,-recovery,-and-situational-awareness), which covers operator intervention when operators are called on. [Practice 11: Maintain SI-Aware Mission Continuity and Disaster Recovery Planning](#practice-11:-maintain-si-aware-mission-continuity-and-disaster-recovery-planning) covers sustained operation when the SI system is unavailable for an extended period.

**Search Keywords:** graceful degradation, fail-operational, quality of service (QoS), rate limiting, dynamic throttling, process-informed guardrails, watchdog controller, enforcement application, heterogeneous redundancy, defense in depth, digital twin testing, hardware-in-the-loop (HIL), distribution drift, concept drift, time-to-divergence, parameter cycling, multi-vendor interoperability, inductive bias, shortcut learning

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Resilient:** Contributes the layered safeguards that keep essential service delivery and functional safety in place while SI performance is away from expected levels, through fallback to reduced capability or to a known-safe mode of operation. This Practice does not cover sustained operation during, or recovery from, a prolonged SI system outage, which [Practice 11: Maintain SI-Aware Mission Continuity and Disaster Recovery Planning](#practice-11:-maintain-si-aware-mission-continuity-and-disaster-recovery-planning) covers.  
* **Robust:** Contributes the expectation itself: the range of conditions and uses across which SI performance should hold, and the testing that shows where it stops holding. This Practice does not cover establishing the level of performance required in the first place, which [Practice 1: Establish Requirements for Success](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success) covers.  
* **Reliable:** Contributes expectations for repeated re-checking against a maintained reference ([Implementation 2.3.1: Baseline SI System Performance](#implementation-2.3.1:-baseline-si-system-performance)), so that gradual departure from expected performance is found on a schedule, before it becomes deficient. This Practice does not cover the moment-to-moment detection of sudden departures, which [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior) covers.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Secure and Safe:** Redundant paths, independent monitors, and fallback routes each add a further way for an instruction to reach the process, whether that instruction is malicious or simply wrong. Examples include a switchover forced by a faulty sensor or a fallback that has fallen out of step with the system it backs up. [Task 3.8: Scope and Map the Expanded SI Attack Surface and Risk Surface](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface) covers the scoping of the attack and risk surface that grows as they are added.  
* **Fair:** Rate limits, throttling and fallback to reduced capability decide which requests are served when capacity is short, and those served by lower-priority functions bear the delay. Where such priorities are set, they should be explicit and consistent with the organization’s service obligations.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Robust versus Resilient:** Where the SI system meets a departure it was designed to absorb, holding performance and degrading gracefully point the same way. Where safeguards are set to keep the SI-enabled function performing across a wider range of conditions, the boundary at which the fallback should engage becomes harder to observe, and the fallback, when it does engage, starts from further outside familiar territory and potentially with less available time, power, control overhead, or other resources to degrade gracefully. One way to balance this is to fix the point at which the fallback engages from the consequence of being wrong rather than from how far the SI system can be pushed. Others include treating the wider range as a documented allowance that prompts review rather than as normal operation.  
* **Accurate versus Robust:** Where operation stays close to the conditions the SI system was tested in, closer agreement with the reference and steadiness across conditions move together. Where the expectation is set to hold across a wide range of conditions, an SI system tuned for its best average agreement may become more fragile where conditions differ significantly from the average. One way to balance this is to state the required performance separately for normal and for stressed conditions, so that the two are procured, tested and accepted as distinct expectations, with [Task 1.2](#task-1.2:-create-quantitative-baselines-for-existing-systems-in-both-normal-and-challenging-conditions)’s normal and stressed baselines for the existing process as a point of comparison. Others include accepting a narrower range of conditions of use and carrying the remainder on the fallback.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MEASURE 2.6** (on measuring safety): This Practice covers the fail-safe behavior, derated modes and boundary testing that a demonstration of failing safely rests on; it does not cover setting the residual risk tolerance against which acceptable safety is judged. For that, see for example [Implementation 3.1.3: Define Acceptable Risk Thresholds and Associated Control Responses](#implementation-3.1.3:-define-acceptable-risk-thresholds-and-associated-control-responses).  
* **MEASURE 2.7** (on measuring security and resiliency): This Practice covers the resilience half of that evaluation, in redundancy, graceful degradation, and layered safeguards that sustain service delivery when SI performance deviates; it does not cover cataloging the adversarial exposure that MEASURE 2.7 pairs resilience with. For that, see for example [Task 3.8: Scope and Map the Expanded SI Attack Surface and Risk Surface](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface).  
* **MANAGE 2.4** (on decommissioning or superseding SI systems): This Practice covers the automatic mechanisms, from rate limits through redundant paths to watchdog controllers, that disengage an SI system whose behavior is inconsistent with intended use; it does not cover the operator-initiated intervention that follows. For that, see for example [Practice 4: Define Procedures for Emergency Avoidance Override, Recovery, and Situational Awareness](#practice-4:-define-procedures-for-emergency-avoidance-override,-recovery,-and-situational-awareness).  
* **MANAGE 2.2** (on ensuring sustained value): This Practice covers the quality-of-service floor that a deployed SI system continues to deliver while it degrades; it does not cover defining the value that the system was adopted to deliver. For that, see for example [Practice 1: Establish Requirements for Success](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* What minimum level of service is kept for each essential function while the SI system is degraded, within any regulatory or contractual obligations?  
* When SI performance departs from expected levels, who decides whether to keep operating, throttle the system, or move to the fallback, and do they have the information and authority to act in time?  
* Where an SI system depends on a service or network outside the organization’s control, what happens to service delivery when that external service is slow or unavailable?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Section 4.1.1, Framing OT Risk, notes that OT may have strict availability or recovery requirements and that failures in one system or process can easily cascade to others. Its Table 3 gives example impact definitions, from outages across sites to public confidence, people and the environment.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v1r1, Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v1r1), from NIST. Its Appendix E states the design principles for trustworthy secure design. Protective Failure (E.23) holds that the failure of one system element should be contained, so that it does not cause unacceptable loss or trigger a further loss scenario, which is the cascading failure this Practice asks a layered approach to reduce; Loss Margins (E.18), Defense in Depth (E.9) and Protective Recovery (E.24) carry the rest of the layering. Section 3.5 reasons in terms of loss, and its Table 2 names limited capacity, being diminished delivery of function, service or capability, as one of the dimensions along which loss can be limited.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v2r1, Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v2r1), from NIST. Table 3 defines the Continue objective as maximizing the duration and viability of essential mission or business functions during adversity, and Table D-1 breaks it into minimizing degradation of service delivery, minimizing interruptions in service delivery and ensuring that ongoing functioning is correct, which corresponds to the service delivery floor this Practice sets. The discussion of the goals in Table 2 counts structural failures and unexpectedly high performance loads as adversity alongside attacks, so the objective is not limited to adversary action. In Table D-4, the Consistency Analysis approach to Coordinated Protection is defined as determining whether and how protections can be applied in a coordinated, consistent way that minimizes interference, potential cascading failures or coverage gaps, which bears on this Practice’s call for safeguards at multiple points that reduce the likelihood of cascading failures.  
* **Standard** ANSI/ISA-62443-3-3-2013, Security for industrial automation and control systems, Part 3-3: System security requirements and security levels, from the International Society of Automation, a technical society that develops automation standards, approved as an American National Standard. Clause 11, Resource Availability, is the industrial control counterpart of the service delivery floor this Practice sets.  
* **Guidance** [Adapting Zero Trust Principles to Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/adapting-zero-trust-principles-operational-technology), published 29 April 2026 by the Zero Trust Operational Technologies Security Working Group, a joint initiative of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the Department of War and the Department of Energy, with the Department of State, the Federal Bureau of Investigation and NIST contributing. Pages 12 and 13, on network and microsegmentation, hold that isolation prevents cascading failures across interconnected systems and that segmentation limits the blast radius of a cyber or operational incident, so the reasoning reaches a malfunctioning SI path and not only a compromised one. The guide’s Table 1 states what OT segmentation is for in contrast to IT segmentation: system availability and system safety rather than data confidentiality, with an extremely low tolerance for downtime because disruptions can have physical consequences.  
* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Section 2.3 notes that some OT devices come with built-in SI that may require internet connectivity to function, and suggests asking vendors whether they can operate on premises or without continuous access to the internet or vendor cloud. Section 2.4 adds that cloud integration may cause data transmission latency. This bears on quality-of-service expectations for externally hosted SI.

### Task 2.1: Establish SI Usage Thresholds and Rate Control Mechanisms {#task-2.1:-establish-si-usage-thresholds-and-rate-control-mechanisms}

Limits on how much and how fast an SI system can act help keep unexpected behavior from overwhelming the equipment, systems, and people around it. Define and implement technical constraints on the volume, frequency, and scope of SI-driven actions, communications, and resource usage, particularly where there are physical and safety limitations or constrained resources.

This Task reduces the potential for rapid, automated system instability and resource bottlenecks by helping ensure that SI interactions remain within predefined operational tolerances and do not overwhelm upstream or downstream legacy systems. Record the operational basis for each threshold, such as the equipment rating or process constraint it reflects, so that it can be reviewed when the process, the equipment or the SI system changes. Rate limiting and throttling are established practice for networks, application interfaces, and alarm systems, and this Task applies them to what an SI system can do.

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Resilient:** Contributes a ceiling on how fast a departure can propagate, so that an SI system behaving unexpectedly consumes a bounded amount of resource, control authority and operator attention before the wider system falls back to its fail-safe state or other fallback behavior ([Implementation 2.1.1: Implement Baseline Rate Limiting](#implementation-2.1.1:-implement-baseline-rate-limiting)). This Task does not cover the independent mechanism that acts once that ceiling is reached. For that, see [Task 2.2: Establish Requirements for Redundancy in SI-Driven Functions](#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions), and for the fail-safe state or other fallback behavior the wider system falls back to, [Implementation 3.2.3: Specify Fail-Safe States and Fallback Behavior](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior).  
* **Safe:** Contributes limits placed where SI activity meets physical and resource constraints, holding the volume, frequency and scope of automated action within what the surrounding equipment and legacy systems were built to absorb. This Task does not cover defining the operating boundary that an individual command should respect, which [Implementation 3.2.2: Define and Independently Enforce Deterministic Operational Constraints](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints) covers.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Transparent:** An SI system held at a limit continues to operate while its activity is being constrained, so the constraint is a fact about the deployment that should be recorded and notified rather than inferred. [Implementation 2.1.1: Implement Baseline Rate Limiting](#implementation-2.1.1:-implement-baseline-rate-limiting) directs notification of limit events, and [Practice 10: Implement Multi-Tiered SI System Logging and Audit Capabilities](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities) covers retention of the record.  
* **Secure:** The recorded thresholds and their basis show how much activity the SI system may carry out before it is limited, and what happens when a limit is reached. An attacker could use them to keep malicious activity just under a limit, or to trip a limit on purpose and force the fallback. Protecting the threshold records is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Safe versus Safe:** Where the SI system’s demand is steady, a fixed ceiling holds automated activity inside what the surrounding equipment can absorb. Where a fast-moving abnormal condition calls for a higher volume of valid commands, such as a rapid pressure excursion or a cascading equipment fault, the same ceiling can suppress correct action at the moment it matters most. Options include [Implementation 2.1.2: Develop Process-Informed Guardrails](#implementation-2.1.2:-develop-process-informed-guardrails), which sets the permitted rate from the state of the process rather than as a single fixed value across all operating conditions. Where prepared in advance, other options include raising the ceiling for a declared abnormal condition, or treating a limit reached during an excursion as a trigger for the fallback in [Task 2.2: Establish Requirements for Redundancy in SI-Driven Functions](#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions) rather than as a cap held in place. Each carries its own considerations, such as who may declare the abnormal condition and whether the fallback is ready to take over.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MAP 4.2** (on establishing risk controls for SI system components): This Task covers rate limits, process-informed guardrails and throttles as the internal controls placed around the SI component itself; it does not cover the independent mechanism that acts once those controls are exceeded. For that, see for example [Task 2.2: Establish Requirements for Redundancy in SI-Driven Functions](#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions).  
* **MEASURE 2.4** (on monitoring deployed SI systems): This Task covers the automatic response to production monitoring, throttling the SI system when its behavior departs from expected patterns; it does not cover defining the detection regime that recognizes the departure. For that, see for example [Task 3.4: Monitor for Anomalous SI Behavior](#task-3.4:-monitor-for-anomalous-si-behavior).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* How is each rate ceiling set, and what headroom is kept for abnormal conditions that call for a higher volume of valid commands? (see the Safe versus Safe tension in [Task 2.1: Establish SI Usage Thresholds and Rate Control Mechanisms](#task-2.1:-establish-si-usage-thresholds-and-rate-control-mechanisms))  
* Who may change a rate limit, including during an abnormal condition, and how is the change recorded?

#### Implementation 2.1.1: Implement Baseline Rate Limiting {#implementation-2.1.1:-implement-baseline-rate-limiting}

Rate limit the various resources and actions that an AI system can take, including consuming AI generation resources (often measured in tokens), making configuration change requests, taking control actions, and requesting attention from humans and other systems. This reduces the likelihood that automated activity will saturate critical networks or cause instability in other systems, particularly legacy systems that may not be designed for the rapid changes in resource usage or control that can result from some AI systems. It may also highlight signs of malfunction, such as a runaway loop or an SI system whose behavior has drifted, as well as adversarial action or interference.

Limits on AI generation resources also bound cost, since a runaway agent loop or retry storm can exhaust a usage budget while it loads other systems, and a budget exhausted part-way through operation can itself withdraw a capability that operations rely on. For agentic systems, such limits can include step, recursion-depth, time and per-run cost ceilings on each execution. A limit that halts use when it is exceeded can be more dependable than an alerting threshold, since a fast-accumulating workload can outpace an alert. Where several AI workloads compete for the same constrained resource, which of them yield when the resource is short is for the organization to decide in advance, within any regulatory or contractual obligations. Giving priority to workloads that support the essential mission protects core service delivery, and the workloads that yield bear the delay, which may fall on obligations of their own. Record the priority and the reason for it. Allocating the resource by priority rather than only by quota is one way to enforce the priority. Retries can multiply load as well. Where several layers of a system each retry a failed request, one action can become many attempts on the system underneath. A retry budget that fails requests once it is used up can help contain this.

Enforce rate limits at a point outside the AI system that it cannot reconfigure, such as a gateway, a broker or the receiving system, and avoid giving the AI system credentials that would let it reach the resource without passing that point. Limits can apply to each AI agent identity as well as in aggregate, so that several agents together stay within what a downstream system tolerates and a limit event can be attributed to the agent that caused it (see [Implementation 5.1.2: Establish Unique Identities for SI Service Accounts and Agents](#implementation-5.1.2:-establish-unique-identities-for-si-service-accounts-and-agents)).

Ensure that when rate limits are hit, the system’s overall behavior falls back to its fail-safe state and that operators are notified via non-disruptive alerts where appropriate ([Implementation 3.2.3](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior) and [Task 4.4](#task-4.4:-attention-governance-and-alert/alarm-flood-mitigation)). For requests that do not act on the physical process, such as generation or configuration change requests, rejecting the request with a clear error, queuing it or degrading the service can be the fallback behavior instead, as with the retry budget above. This may be particularly important where AI is used to improve efficiency in normal times, resulting in either more systems utilizing the same allocated resources or the same systems being allocated fewer resources. Such rate limits act as a first line of defense against overload, particularly in unusual or unforeseen situations where the efficiency gains may not hold.

To safeguard operator cognitive capacity and minimize alert fatigue, notification delivery metrics should follow exception batching, aggregation, and soft-throttling strategies, some of which are discussed in [Task 4.4: Attention Governance and Alert/Alarm Flood Mitigation](#task-4.4:-attention-governance-and-alert/alarm-flood-mitigation). Rate limits should account for legitimate increases in command frequency during upset or abnormal operating conditions. An AI system responding correctly to a fast-moving abnormal condition, such as a rapid pressure excursion or a cascading equipment fault, may need to issue a higher volume of valid commands than during steady-state operation, and a rate limit tuned only to normal conditions could suppress legitimate corrective actions at the moment they matter most. Rate limit thresholds should therefore be informed by [Implementation 2.1.2: Develop Process-Informed Guardrails](#implementation-2.1.2:-develop-process-informed-guardrails), rather than applied as a single fixed ceiling across all operating conditions.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which workloads yield when a shared resource is short, and why? Where is that priority recorded?  
* What retry budget applies at each layer?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-genai-llm-top-10-2026/), Version 2026, from the OWASP GenAI Security Project, a volunteer community project of the Open Worldwide Application Security Project. LLM06:2026, Unbounded Consumption, names denial of wallet and recursive agent tool-calling loops among its examples. Its mitigations include limits on tokens and estimated cost rather than on requests alone, hard spending caps that halt inference rather than alert, and step, recursion-depth, time and per-run cost limits on agent executions, which bear on the cost and agentic limits in this Implementation.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control SC-6, Resource Availability, allocates defined resources by priority or quota. Its discussion describes priority protection as keeping lower-priority processes from delaying or interfering with higher-priority ones, which bears on deciding which AI workloads yield a shared resource to those that support the essential mission.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Section 2.4, Comparing OT and IT System Security, notes that OT and their real-time operating systems are often resource-constrained, that legacy systems often lack resources common on modern IT systems, and that indiscriminate use of IT practices in OT may cause availability and timing disruptions, which bears on this Implementation’s concern for legacy systems not designed for rapid changes in load.  
* **Commentary** [“Addressing Cascading Failures,” Chapter 22 of *Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems*](https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/), written by M. Ulrich, from Google, published by O’Reilly Media. Its section on retries shows how retries issued at several layers multiply the attempts that reach the lowest layer. It suggests limiting retries per request and setting a server-wide retry budget beyond which requests fail rather than retry. This bears on the retry storms that this Implementation’s limits bound.

#### Implementation 2.1.2: Develop Process-Informed Guardrails {#implementation-2.1.2:-develop-process-informed-guardrails}

Process-informed guardrails let an SI system use more resources or act more freely when the process can absorb it, and hold it tighter when it cannot. They dynamically determine the appropriate rate at which AI systems should be utilizing resources or taking actions. For example:

* An AI-based optimization system may use more tokens during quiet periods.  
* Rapid changes to power grid load distribution should be avoided when the grid is running close to capacity.  
* The number of units or feeders that an AI system may adjust at once, and the minimum interval between adjustments to the same control loop, may be set tighter during startup and shutdown than in steady operation.

These guardrails should be deterministic and based on the application’s needs. Such guardrails give the AI system flexibility to use additional resources or take additional actions when the application requires it, such as during quieter periods, while maintaining tight control during rapid change or heightened activity. Complex guardrails can cause problems of their own, such as tripping into a restrictive mode when it is not wanted or entering feedback cycles. Keeping the rules simple, with a way to quickly disable or retune them, can help. Disabling or retuning a guardrail removes or weakens a protection, so who may do it, and under what conditions, is for the organization to decide in advance. The tighter limits apply only in uncommon conditions and so are seldom exercised, and a path that is rarely used may not work when it is needed. Exercising it regularly can help.

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Section 4.1 cautions that with active AI systems directly influencing control, problems can escalate before operators become aware of them. Where AI is actively updating control logic, it asks for safety thresholds, alternative sensor output, or state changes that add human-in-the-loop intervention points, which bears on tightening control of AI action as process conditions change.  
* **Commentary** [“Addressing Cascading Failures,” Chapter 22 of *Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems*](https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/), written by M. Ulrich, from Google, published by O’Reilly Media. Its section on load shedding and graceful degradation notes that a degraded mode is seldom exercised in steady-state operation, and that the code path never used often does not work. It adds that complex degradation logic can trip when not desired or enter feedback cycles, and suggests a way to quickly turn such logic off or retune it. This bears on keeping process-informed guardrails simple and exercised.

#### Implementation 2.1.3: Implement Anomaly-Driven Detection and Throttling {#implementation-2.1.3:-implement-anomaly-driven-detection-and-throttling}

This should be based on patterns of expected behavior of the AI system, particularly in situations where tight guardrails may be difficult to develop. For example, statistical process control can flag outliers in the values an AI system produces, and a session whose tool calls or token use depart from their established baseline can be throttled or paused. A Shewhart control chart can reveal a sudden shift while CUSUM and EWMA charts accumulate small deviations over time and can reveal a slow drift (see Dolin 2026). The baselines and deviation ranges come from [Implementation 3.4.2: Establish Operational Baselines and Deviation Thresholds](#implementation-3.4.2:-establish-operational-baselines-and-deviation-thresholds); this Implementation supplies the automatic throttling response.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which deviations from expected behavior trigger throttling, and which only raise an alert?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Section 4.1 asks operators to implement anomaly detection and behavioral analytics, and notes that as processes mature, software safety thresholds can shift from setpoints to anomaly detection of increasingly sophisticated faults. Its worked example monitors a predictive maintenance system with statistical process control that detects outliers in predicted downtime values, which bears on detection where fixed guardrails are hard to define.  
* **Guidance** [OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/), Version 2026, December 2025, from the Agentic Security Initiative of the OWASP Gen AI Security Project, a volunteer community project of the Open Worldwide Application Security Project. ASI08, Cascading Failures, lists rate limiting and monitoring among its mitigations, to detect fast-spreading commands and throttle or pause on anomalies, with quotas, progress caps and circuit breakers as blast-radius guardrails. This is the throttling response that this Implementation pairs with detection.  
* **Research** [Statistically Valid Post-Deployment Monitoring Should Be Standard for AI-Based Digital Health](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2506.05701), by P. Dolin, W. Li, G. Dasarathy and V. Berisha, Arizona State University, arXiv preprint version 3, February 2026\. A position paper on clinical AI. Appendix D, on choosing a statistical test, describes Shewhart control charts for detecting sudden shifts, and CUSUM and EWMA charts for persistent small changes and gradual drift in monitored features. This bears on matching the detector to the kind of departure being throttled.

### Task 2.2: Establish Requirements for Redundancy in SI-Driven Functions {#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions}

Establish a risk-proportionate redundancy strategy to maintain continuous operations during AI degradation, distribution drift, or system failure. Redundancy requirements should be commensurate with consequence severity. This may range from heterogeneous AI model and infrastructure redundancy (for complex digital workflows where non-AI fallbacks are technically infeasible) up to deterministic, rule-based software algorithms or out-of-band independent deterministic physical interlocks (for high-consequence cyber-physical systems). This Task supports the system’s resilience through graceful degradation (operating in reduced capability or derated modes) or transition to a known fail-safe state, including handover to legacy/manual control, which reduces the impact of a total loss of service due to AI component failure. This Task complements [Task 3.4: Monitor for Anomalous SI Behavior](#task-3.4:-monitor-for-anomalous-si-behavior). Redundancy and fallback are familiar from safety and continuity engineering. What SI changes is that redundant models built on similar data, or hosted by the same provider, can fail together. Where a sector’s safety practice credits independent protection layers, such as a safety instrumented system designed to IEC 61511, neither the AI system nor a monitor of it should be credited as such a layer unless it meets that practice’s requirements for independence and integrity.

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Resilient:** Contributes the graded fallback that keeps a function available while the AI system is not: secondary models on distinct architectures, training distributions and hosting where a non-AI path is infeasible, rising to deterministic algorithms or physical interlocks where consequence is high ([Implementation 2.2.1: Maintain Backup Systems Proportionate to Consequence](#implementation-2.2.1:-maintain-backup-systems-proportionate-to-consequence)). This Task does not cover defining the state that the control system enters once the AI system is disengaged, which [Implementation 3.2.3: Specify Fail-Safe States and Fallback Behavior](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior) covers.  
* **Reliable:** Contributes an independent, non-AI check on whether the AI system is still performing as required, in continuous monitoring of output integrity, execution latency and setpoint stability ([Implementation 2.2.2: Deploy “Watchdog” Controllers](#implementation-2.2.2:-deploy-“watchdog”-controllers)). This Task does not cover producing the evidence that the fallback operates as intended when called on. For that, see [Task 2.3: Establish Protocols for and Regularly Perform Systematic and Achievable Testing, Evaluation, Validation, and Verification (TEVV)](#task-2.3:-establish-protocols-for-and-regularly-perform-systematic-and-achievable-testing,-evaluation,-validation,-and-verification-\(tevv\)), and, for periodic confirmation that standby infrastructure still functions, [Implementation 11.3.2: Maintain Isolated Standby Infrastructure and Allocated Reserves](#implementation-11.3.2:-maintain-isolated-standby-infrastructure-and-allocated-reserves).

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Secure and Safe:** Each redundant path, and each monitor able to force a transition, is a further route by which the process can be commanded or stopped, whether by a deliberate actor or by a fault, such as a stale reading or a mis-set threshold that trips the fallback when nothing is wrong. [Implementation 2.2.2: Deploy “Watchdog” Controllers](#implementation-2.2.2:-deploy-“watchdog”-controllers) hardens the watchdog itself through read-only telemetry access and isolation from the AI application stack, which also keeps a malfunctioning SI system from disabling its own monitor, and tunes trip thresholds against false trips. [Task 3.8: Scope and Map the Expanded SI Attack Surface and Risk Surface](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface) covers scoping the exposure that the wider redundancy strategy adds. Records of watchdog trip thresholds, and of how each watchdog responds to loss of contact, show an attacker how to force a fallback at a moment of their choosing. Protecting them is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice, as for other safety system settings.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Safe versus Resilient:** Where the process can absorb a transition at any point, tripping to the fallback on a watchdog signal serves continuity and safety together. Where the trip would land during an active process transition or a critical control maneuver, the transition is itself the hazard, and a corrupted input or a deliberate actor can force it. One way to balance this is the state-aware interlocks and rate-of-change validation on the trigger in [Implementation 2.2.2: Deploy “Watchdog” Controllers](#implementation-2.2.2:-deploy-“watchdog”-controllers), so that the trip is qualified by what the process is doing. Others include sequencing the fallback so that it reaches a deterministic state in steps rather than at once.  
* **Resilient versus Resilient:** Where a non-AI path is infeasible, secondary models on distinct architectures, training distributions and hosting remove the single point of failure in the implementation. Where the shared exposure is to the operating environment instead, such as distribution drift that reaches every model built on similar data, that heterogeneity does less, while a deterministic algorithm or a physical interlock holds under the same drift and carries less of the function. One way to balance this is the redundancy gradient in [Implementation 2.2.1: Maintain Backup Systems Proportionate to Consequence](#implementation-2.2.1:-maintain-backup-systems-proportionate-to-consequence), which sets the degree of independence by the severity of consequences rather than from what is convenient to build. Others include pairing the two, with the deterministic path bounding the heterogeneous one.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MANAGE 2.4** (on decommissioning or superseding AI systems): This Task covers the independent, non-AI watchdog that disengages or supersedes an AI system whose output, latency or setpoint stability falls outside intended use; it does not cover defining the state that the control system enters once the AI system is disengaged. For that, see for example [Implementation 3.2.3: Specify Fail-Safe States and Fallback Behavior](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior).  
* **MEASURE 2.6** (on measuring safety): This Task covers the redundancy gradient and watchdog controllers that make failing safely an implemented property rather than an assumed one; it does not cover producing the evidence that those mechanisms work. For that, see for example [Task 2.3: Establish Protocols for and Regularly Perform Systematic and Achievable Testing, Evaluation, Validation, and Verification (TEVV)](#task-2.3:-establish-protocols-for-and-regularly-perform-systematic-and-achievable-testing,-evaluation,-validation,-and-verification-\(tevv\)).  
* **GOVERN 6.2** (on establishing contingency plans for critical third parties): This Task covers the runtime contingency for a failing third-party model, in secondary models built on distinct architectures, training distributions and hosting infrastructure; it does not cover the pre-acquisition visibility that identifies which third-party dependencies are high-risk. For that, see for example [Practice 6: Integrate Visibility of the External Supply Chain of SI into Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* How is the level of redundancy for each SI-driven function matched to consequence severity?  
* Where the trip could land during an active process transition, how is the watchdog’s response timed or interlocked? (see the Safe versus Resilient tension in [Task 2.2: Establish Requirements for Redundancy in SI-Driven Functions](#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions))  
* Who funds and maintains each backup path, including keeping it current with the primary and exercising it?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v2r1, Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v2r1), from NIST. Section D.5.2.6, Maintain Redundancy, states that because malware can propagate across homogeneous resources, redundancy should be applied together with diversity and considered at multiple layers, and that the extent of redundancy is set by analysis of single points of failure and shared resources. The same reasoning applies to a failure mode shared by similar AI models, and it supports the heterogeneous and layered redundancy this Task asks for. Table D-2 introduces the use of heterogeneity to minimize common mode failures, with the purpose of limiting the loss of critical functions due to the failure of replicated common critical components.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Section 2.3.7, Safety Systems, describes the safety instrumented system as specifically designed in accordance with IEC 61511, and as often independent from all other control systems, so that a failure of the basic process control system will not impact its functionality. This bears on whether an AI system or its watchdog can be credited as an independent protection layer.

#### Implementation 2.2.1: Maintain Backup Systems Proportionate to Consequence {#implementation-2.2.1:-maintain-backup-systems-proportionate-to-consequence}

A backup that is current and ready lets an essential function continue when the SI system cannot be relied on. Establish a risk-proportionate redundancy gradient for AI-driven functions, matching the level of architectural isolation to the severity of consequences of failure, as assessed against the thresholds in [Implementation 3.1.3: Define Acceptable Risk Thresholds and Associated Control Responses](#implementation-3.1.3:-define-acceptable-risk-thresholds-and-associated-control-responses). For lower and moderate-consequence applications where non-AI fallbacks are technically infeasible, organizations should deploy heterogeneous AI redundancy, utilizing secondary models built on distinct architectures, training distributions, and hosting infrastructure to mitigate single-points-of-failure and shared model drift. Where a non-AI fallback, such as a documented manual procedure, is feasible, it remains an option at any consequence level. For high-consequence or cyber-physical functions, redundancy should escalate to include independent, deterministic algorithmic fallbacks or out-of-band non-AI physical safety interlocks ([Implementation 3.2.2: Define and Independently Enforce Deterministic Operational Constraints](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints)). Develop and communicate expected guarantees of performance during fail-over procedures so that downstream entities can prepare for potential impacts. Keep the backup current with the primary. Configuration changes, such as new equipment, revised limits or renamed tags, should be carried into the backup through the same change process. Keeping a backup current takes ongoing effort, and resourcing it is part of the redundancy decision (see [Task 11.3: Pre-Allocate Operational Resources for Alternative Service Delivery](#task-11.3:-pre-allocate-operational-resources-for-alternative-service-delivery)). Where an existing conventional control scheme is retained as the backup, it should keep its tuning, alarms and interlocks once the AI system is introduced. For periodic confirmation that backup infrastructure still functions, see [Implementation 11.3.2: Maintain Isolated Standby Infrastructure and Allocated Reserves](#implementation-11.3.2:-maintain-isolated-standby-infrastructure-and-allocated-reserves).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* For which functions is a fallback independent of the SI system infeasible, and is heterogeneous redundancy accepted there? (see the Resilient versus Resilient tension in [Task 2.2: Establish Requirements for Redundancy in SI-Driven Functions](#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions))

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v2r1, Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v2r1), from NIST. Section D.5.2.5, Plan and Manage Diversity, warns that diversity can be more apparent than real, as when alternative implementations run on the same underlying operating system or reuse software components, and calls for analysis of the architectural approach to diversity. This applies to secondary models that share a foundation model, training data or hosting provider. Table D-4 makes the same point for the Diversity technique, noting that reliance on common libraries and infrastructures means analysis is needed to verify the extent of diversity. Its Design Diversity approach (for example, N-version programming and mixed hardware and software implementations) and Supply Chain Diversity approach (using multiple independent supply chains for critical components, with the example of analyzing components from different suppliers for common elements) correspond to the levels of independence in this redundancy gradient.

#### Implementation 2.2.2: Deploy “Watchdog” Controllers {#implementation-2.2.2:-deploy-“watchdog”-controllers}

An independent watchdog helps an organization detect, at machine speed, that an SI system has stopped performing as required, and fail over without waiting for a person to notice. Watchdog controllers, also referred to as “enforcement applications,” are based on independent, deterministic architectures that monitor AI output and automatically perform fail-over, consistent with [Implementation 3.2.3: Specify Fail-Safe States and Fallback Behavior](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior). Deploy independent watchdog controllers to continuously monitor AI system health, execution latency, setpoint stability, and output integrity. Output integrity checks can include plausibility against the state and capacity of the physical process, for example flagging a recommended flow above what the installed pumps can deliver. They can also include agreement with an independent estimate, such as a simple physical model or a conventional controller running in parallel, with sustained divergence between the two flagged. Checks on the inputs that the AI system relies on, for freshness, range and expected source, can help catch a fault before it reaches the output.

To help keep watchdog mechanisms from introducing unmanaged complexity, secondary attack surfaces, or weaponized failover vectors, organizations should enforce:

* Determinism (Non-AI Assurance): Watchdog logic should be strictly non-AI, lightweight, and deterministic. Example implementations may include dedicated hardware timers, separate Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) or microcontrollers, with minimal, formally verified software logic that shares as little as practical with the primary AI application stack, and where anything is shared, records what it is (see *How Far to Go*). Note that a notionally deterministic system can still exhibit non-deterministic behavior due to input/sensor noise, errors, wear, etc.  
* Independence and Tamper Resistance: Watchdog controllers should operate out-of-band on hardened, privileged infrastructure with read-only telemetry access, helping ensure that an upstream malfunction or mistaken change, as well as an upstream compromise (of the AI system or otherwise), prompt injection, or network intrusion, cannot modify watchdog setpoints, disable execution checks, or corrupt trip logic. Note that the watchdog itself may be part of the attack surface as discussed in [Task 3.8: Scope and Map the Expanded SI Attack Surface and Risk Surface](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface).  
* Mitigation of Destructive/Forced Failover: Watchdog trigger thresholds should still incorporate state-aware interlocks and rate-of-change validation to help prevent corrupted inputs or malicious actors from forcing an unintended failover during sensitive operational windows (e.g., during active process transitions or critical control maneuvers). Thresholds can be tuned by running the watchdog in a monitoring-only mode alongside the AI system before it is given authority to trigger fail-over, with its false and missed trips reviewed periodically after that. A watchdog that trips too readily is at risk of being disabled or bypassed, as alarms that cause nuisance have been in process plants.

How the watchdog responds when it loses contact with the AI system, such as a missed heartbeat or stale telemetry, is a choice to make deliberately for each system and to record with its reason. Failing toward the fail-safe state is the usual default, but where an abrupt move to it during an active process transition is itself the hazard, loss of contact can instead pass through the same state-aware interlocks, which may delay reaching the fallback. The record of tradeoffs described in [Task 3.1: Identify Risk Trade-offs](#task-3.1:-identify-risk-trade-offs) is one place to keep that choice.

Triggers should initiate safe, deterministic fallback sequences ([Implementation 3.2.3: Specify Fail-Safe States and Fallback Behavior](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior)) rather than uncoordinated abrupt shutdowns. Ensure the watchdog itself is included within [Implementation 3.4.3: Monitor Validation Control Integrity](#implementation-3.4.3:-monitor-validation-control-integrity). Notify operators of any watchdog-triggered fail-over per [Task 4.2: Ensure that Personnel Are Able to Gain and Maintain Situational Awareness](#task-4.2:-ensure-that-personnel-are-able-to-gain-and-maintain-situational-awareness), so that a failure the watchdog catches does not go unnoticed by operators.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* How does each watchdog respond when it loses contact with the SI system, and where is that choice recorded?  
* How are trip thresholds tuned between missed trips and false trips?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Section 2.3.7, Safety Systems, describes a safety instrumented system as often independent from all other control systems, so that a failure of the basic process control system will not impact its functionality, and historically as physically and logically separated from the rest of the control system. That is the independence this Implementation asks of a watchdog relative to the AI application stack.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control AC-25, Reference Monitor, is written for access control enforcement, but it specifies a mechanism that is tamperproof, always invoked, and small enough to be subject to analysis and testing, which are the properties this Implementation asks of watchdog logic. Control enhancement SI-13(5), Failover Capability, provides real-time or near real-time automatic switchover to an alternate system upon failure of the primary system.  
* **Research** Bransby, M. L., and Jenkinson, J., [The management of alarm systems](https://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/ukgwa/20230103120103/https://www.hse.gov.uk/research/crr_pdf/1998/crr98166.pdf), Contract Research Report 166/1998, funded by the Health and Safety Executive, Great Britain’s workplace health and safety regulator. Volume 1, Section 2.2, Incidents reported, describes a refinery near miss in which operators were overwhelmed by alarms and the alarm hooter had been disconnected because of the nuisance it caused. This bears on tuning watchdog trip thresholds so that the watchdog is not bypassed.

**\> To the Reviewer:** \> We understand that terms like “watchdog” controllers can vary from industry to industry. We’d love further suggestions as to other terms that might be used for such concepts, both here and in other places in this document, to make sure that we’re all on compatible pages even if we all use different terminology.

### Task 2.3: Establish Protocols for and Regularly Perform Systematic and Achievable Testing, Evaluation, Validation, and Verification (TEVV) {#task-2.3:-establish-protocols-for-and-regularly-perform-systematic-and-achievable-testing,-evaluation,-validation,-and-verification-\(tevv\)}

Perform rigorous testing and analysis specifically focused on the AI system’s behavior in anomalous or edge-case conditions and environments, extending the TEVV protocols established in [Task 1.3: Implement Evaluation and Test Plans, Including TEVV, Across the SI Lifecycle](#task-1.3:-implement-evaluation-and-test-plans,-including-tevv,-across-the-si-lifecycle) to govern specialized boundary and stress conditions. This Task contributes verifiable evidence that fail-safe mechanisms and manual overrides operate as intended, supporting long-term reliability. It also supports rigorously identifying the attack and risk surface as discussed in [Task 3.8: Scope and Map the Expanded SI Attack Surface and Risk Surface](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface) and supports the evaluation of downstream risk as discussed in [Task 3.5: Define and Control Risks to Adjacent and Related Systems](#task-3.5:-define-and-control-risks-to-adjacent-and-related-systems).

Where an AI system can produce different outputs from the same input, as many generative AI systems and some planners that use randomized search can, a single test run may not represent its behavior. Running each test case repeatedly and reporting the spread of results, as well as the typical result, can help show how often a failure occurs. Boundary and stress tests should exercise the AI function as it is integrated with the systems around it, including the control system, the operator interface and the fallback path, as well as the AI component on its own. Incidents, near-misses reported under [Task 8.6: Establish Non-Punitive Reporting for SI-Related Near-Misses](#task-8.6:-establish-non-punitive-reporting-for-si-related-near-misses) and interventions by the watchdog controllers of [Implementation 2.2.2: Deploy “Watchdog” Controllers](#implementation-2.2.2:-deploy-“watchdog”-controllers) can each add a case to the edge-case test set, so that later testing covers conditions the AI system has already met in service.

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**
