For that, see for example [Task 4.4: Attention Governance and Alert/Alarm Flood Mitigation](#task-4.4:-attention-governance-and-alert/alarm-flood-mitigation).  
* **MEASURE 2.5** (on measuring validity and reliability): This Task converts the documented limits of a model’s generalizability into quantitative drift thresholds, each with a defined response when the operating environment moves beyond it; it does not cover establishing those limits. For the testing that establishes them, see [Task 2.3: Establish Protocols for and Regularly Perform Systematic and Achievable Testing, Evaluation, Validation, and Verification (TEVV)](#task-2.3:-establish-protocols-for-and-regularly-perform-systematic-and-achievable-testing,-evaluation,-validation,-and-verification-\(tevv\)).  
* **GOVERN 4.3** (on establishing AI incident response and information-sharing processes): This Task makes an AI failure identifiable at the moment it occurs, by treating silent recovery as a choice to be justified for each application rather than as the default; it does not cover the analysis that follows once a failure has been identified. For that, see for example [Practice 8: Incorporate SI-Aware Incident Analysis and Response Procedures](#practice-8:-incorporate-si-aware-incident-analysis-and-response-procedures).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Who tracks how notifications perform once in service, and who decides when one is redesigned or removed?  
* Who periodically tests the notification paths, and how often?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Section 6.3.1, Anomalies and Events, recommends basing OT alerting thresholds on baselines of normal behavior and setting them with the expected response time in mind. In Appendix F.7.18, the OT discussion of SI-6 notes that shutting down and restarting OT may not always be feasible when an anomaly is identified.  
* **Standard** ANSI/ISA-62443-3-3, from the American National Standards Institute and the International Society of Automation. Sets system-level security requirements and security levels for industrial automation and control systems.  
* **Standard** ISA-18.2, Management of Alarm Systems for the Process Industries, from the International Society of Automation. Covers alarm prioritization and what makes an alarm actionable, which is the established practice a requirement to fail loudly has to sit inside if the resulting alarms are to stay actionable.  
* **Standard** [IEC 60601-1-8:2006, Medical electrical equipment, Part 1-8: General requirements for basic safety and essential performance, Collateral Standard: General requirements, tests and guidance for alarm systems in medical electrical equipment and medical electrical systems](https://www.iso.org/standard/41986.html), 2006, from the International Electrotechnical Commission. As its title states, it sets general requirements, tests and guidance for alarm systems in medical electrical equipment and systems. It is a healthcare counterpart to ISA-18.2 for making a failure known in a form that stays actionable.  
* **Research** Bransby, M. L., and Jenkinson, J., [The management of alarm systems](https://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/ukgwa/20230103120103/https://www.hse.gov.uk/research/crr_pdf/1998/crr98166.pdf), Contract Research Report 166/1998, funded by the Health and Safety Executive, Great Britain’s workplace health and safety regulator. Section 2.3 notes that where automatic protection guards against hazards to people or the environment, pre-alarms are almost always installed as well, giving the operator a chance to intervene before the protection operates. This is a process-industry precedent for failing loudly as a step separate from the fail-safe action.  
* **Guidance** Health and Safety Executive (2000) [Better alarm handling](https://www.hse.gov.uk/pubns/chis6.pdf), Chemicals Sheet No 6, from Great Britain’s workplace health and safety regulator. Step 1 asks whether alarms are necessary and require operator action, and whether large numbers of alarms are acknowledged in quick succession. Step 3 repeats those measurements to see whether alarm performance is now reasonable. These bear on tracking notification performance and on notifications acknowledged without action.

**\>To the Reviewer:** \>This concept is one that is familiar to the OT community and, for that matter, the electronic and mechanical engineering disciplines. For example, in many cases the purpose of an electrical or mechanical fuse is to cause a piece of equipment to “fail loudly” even if it could have kept going for a little bit longer (but then may have caused more damage when it finally failed). A fuse also stops the equipment; in this profile, failing loudly refers only to making the failure known, and stopping is the separate choice of a fail-safe state.  
\>What would be examples of sector-specific guidance/regulations relating to the concept of “failing loudly” that would be applicable to AI (both within OT/ICS and otherwise)?

#### Implementation 3.3.1: Context-Specific Failure Modes {#implementation-3.3.1:-context-specific-failure-modes}

Matching each application’s failure notification to its consequences helps operators notice the failures that matter without being flooded by those that do not. Conduct an engineering assessment for each application to determine its failure notification requirements. For example, silent resilience (e.g., automated retries or soft failovers) may be appropriate for non-critical administrative tasks where internal algorithmic recovery does not alter physical processes or mask safety margins. Conversely, for safety-critical IT/OT/ICS applications, a ‘fail loudly’ protocol should be enforced with explicit human notifications, even if the system continues to operate, perhaps in a degraded capacity. Set the priority of each such notification from the consequence if the operator does not respond. When setting the point at which it is raised, allow for the time that response takes. The assessment should include failures that do not announce themselves, for example an SI system producing confident output on inputs outside the conditions it was validated for, a display that continues to show the last output after the SI system has stopped updating it, or a change in behavior after a vendor update to an acquired SI system. For each, record how the failure would be detected and how long detection would take. Where the organization already performs a process hazard analysis (PHA) or failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA), this assessment can extend that analysis with SI-specific failure scenarios rather than starting a separate one.

These notification states should be programmatically linked to the independent safety wrappers in [Task 3.2: Implement Independent Guardrails for SI Outputs](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs) so that an unacknowledged ‘loud’ failure automatically forces a transition to a deterministic fallback state (per [Implementation 3.2.3: Specify Fail-Safe States and Fallback Behavior](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior)). To limit alarm floods and alert fatigue, utilize containment techniques such as time-delay hysteresis, dynamic deadbands (control and sensor ranges where minor fluctuations are ignored and assumed to be noise), and state-based alarm aggregation to compress rapid automated iterations into a single operational event change. See [Task 4.4: Attention Governance and Alert/Alarm Flood Mitigation](#task-4.4:-attention-governance-and-alert/alarm-flood-mitigation) for further details.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* For each application, is silent recovery acceptable, or should it fail loudly? (see the Resilient versus Transparent tension in [Task 3.3: Establish Failure Notification Requirements](#task-3.3:-establish-failure-notification-requirements))  
* What priority does each notification carry?

**References:**

* **Guidance** Health and Safety Executive (2000) [Better alarm handling](https://www.hse.gov.uk/pubns/chis6.pdf), Chemicals Sheet No 6, from Great Britain’s workplace health and safety regulator. For effective alarm prioritization, it advises using about three priorities and basing them on the potential consequences if the operator fails to respond. This is the basis for the priority of a loud failure set here.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Section 6.3.1, Anomalies and Events, notes that OT components are often remote and not continually staffed, so a threshold may need to be set to alert earlier to allow for the expected response time. This bears on the point at which a loud failure is raised. Section 4.1.1, Framing OT Risk, suggests that organizations may consider incorporating cyber attack and IT failure scenarios into their process hazard analysis (PHA) or failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) processes. This is the precedent for extending an existing hazard analysis with SI-specific failure scenarios here.  
* **Research** Bransby, M. L., and Jenkinson, J., [The management of alarm systems](https://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/ukgwa/20230103120103/https://www.hse.gov.uk/research/crr_pdf/1998/crr98166.pdf), Contract Research Report 166/1998, funded by the Health and Safety Executive, Great Britain’s workplace health and safety regulator. Appendix 12 reports that no site visited used more than three normally displayed priorities, and that an approach-to-trip alarm may outrank the trip itself if the operator can still act. Section 5.3.2 and Appendix 10 describe deadband, de-bounce timers, shelving and single line annunciation for repeating alarms. These bear on the priorities and containment techniques set here.

#### Implementation 3.3.2: Establish Maximum Drift Thresholds {#implementation-3.3.2:-establish-maximum-drift-thresholds}

Drift thresholds help an organization act before shifts in operating conditions, data, or task take an SI system outside what it was trained and tested for. Establish quantitative monitoring and thresholds against which the AI system is continuously or periodically evaluated for how far the real-world operating environment, data inputs, task, and system context can shift from the historic conditions on which the system was trained before mitigations are put in place, defining the specific thresholds that determine when the periodic evaluations in [Implementation 2.3.4: Recurrent Risk Evaluations](#implementation-2.3.4:-recurrent-risk-evaluations) or the continuous monitoring in [Task 3.4: Monitor for Anomalous SI Behavior](#task-3.4:-monitor-for-anomalous-si-behavior) should trigger a fail-safe response. Where ground-truth outcomes are delayed or never observed at runtime, as is common in predictive maintenance, alarm prioritization and fraud triage, define these thresholds on observable proxies that do not depend on labels, such as shifts in the distribution of inputs, shifts in the distribution of predictions or scores, operator override rates and guardrail interception rates, and apply label-dependent measures in the evaluations under [Implementation 2.3.4: Recurrent Risk Evaluations](#implementation-2.3.4:-recurrent-risk-evaluations) as outcomes become available.

Determine if exceeding a maximum drift threshold should result in notifications, forced fail-over, or other restrictions on the operation of the system. Minimum responses should include operator notification. For safety-critical applications, responses should include automatic restriction of AI authority or, where a deterministic backup system has been prepared, forced failover to it. A forced failover is itself a transition with its own hazards, such as a step change at handover, which [Implementation 3.2.3: Specify Fail-Safe States and Fallback Behavior](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior) addresses. Drift thresholds should account for seasonal, operational, and environmental variation relevant to the critical infrastructure sector, in addition to the physical degradation and changes over time of underlying OT hardware. Set each threshold from the tighter of the range over which validation demonstrated acceptable performance and the error that the process can tolerate. Apparent good performance beyond the validated range should not by itself widen a threshold. Compare current behavior with the original baseline as well as with recent operation, so that slow drift that never crosses a short-window threshold can still be detected. Cumulative methods, such as CUSUM or EWMA control charts, can help detect small, persistent shifts. Averages across operating regimes, such as seasonal or load conditions, can mask a decline in one regime, and breaking measures down by regime can help reveal it. Drift can also arrive through the supply chain with no change in the process, for example a vendor update to a hosted model, a changed retrieval source, or a replaced sensor. [Task 6.2: Align SI and Existing CI Asset Lifecycle Management](#task-6.2:-align-si-and-existing-ci-asset-lifecycle-management) covers detecting unannounced changes of this kind.

For example, an AI model trained on summer demand patterns in a water distribution system should have explicit thresholds that detect and flag degraded performance during winter conditions before that degradation can cause operators to miss a safety-relevant alert. Similarly, a healthcare diagnostic AI should flag drift in clinical parameters when shifted between different patient demographics, and a financial liquidity model should trigger boundaries during sudden, non-historical macroeconomic shocks. Where output quality can degrade before any shift is detectable in input statistics, as with SI systems making investment recommendations or credit decisions, thresholds can also be set on performance against a human-reviewed benchmark sample on a defined cadence, such as the validated standard dataset in [Implementation 2.3.1: Baseline SI System Performance](#implementation-2.3.1:-baseline-si-system-performance). For SI systems that answer from what they learned in training, facts that changed after training, such as revised procedures, setpoints, or regulations, are a form of drift that input statistics will not show. Drift thresholds should be reviewed and recalibrated at a defined interval or whenever a significant change in the operational environment occurs. This implementation mitigates hazard risk associated with silent AI performance degradation. An AI model trained on historical operational data can progressively lose accuracy as the operational environment shifts, without generating any visible failure or alert. Operators could continue to rely on the AI’s outputs without realizing its reliability has degraded below acceptable thresholds.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* What response, beyond operator notification, does exceeding each drift threshold trigger?  
* At what interval are the thresholds reviewed?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Principle 4, Embed Oversight and Failsafe Practices Into AI and SI-enabled OT Systems, pages 18 to 20\. Section 4.1 directs establishing safe operating bounds for OT devices that detect AI drift and model changes affecting safety and performance, and maintaining a known good state or thresholds for safe behavior. Section 4.2 covers the failsafe mechanisms a breached threshold can hand control to.  
* **Research** [NIST AI 800-4, Challenges to the Monitoring of Deployed AI Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.800-4), March 2026, from NIST. Section 3.2.1, Functionality, reports practitioners’ difficulty in establishing performance baselines and the deviation thresholds that trigger corrective action or review. It names missing ground-truth datasets as a barrier, quoting Dolin et al. that post-deployment labels are often delayed, costly or entirely unavailable. This bears on the label-free proxies in this Implementation.  
* **Guidance** [SR 11-7 Attachment, Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management](https://www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/srletters/2011/sr1107a1.pdf), April 2011, from the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. Written for banks, its Section V treats a high override rate found in ongoing monitoring as a sign that the model may need revision. It also describes benchmarking against alternative data or models, and cautions against false comfort from a close match. These bear on the override-rate proxy and the benchmark-based thresholds here.  
* **Research** Dolin, P., Li, W., Dasarathy, G., and Berisha, V., [Statistically Valid Post-Deployment Monitoring Should Be Standard for AI-Based Digital Health](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2506.05701), arXiv:2506.05701v3, February 2026, from Arizona State University. Written for clinical AI, its Introduction notes that average performance metrics can mask degradation in specific patient subgroups. Section 5.1 tests performance against the pre-deployment baseline, and Appendix D describes CUSUM charts for persistent small changes and EWMA charts for gradual drift. These bear on the baseline comparison, control charts and regime breakdown here.

#### Implementation 3.3.3: Actionable Operator Decision & Escalation Pathways {#implementation-3.3.3:-actionable-operator-decision-&-escalation-pathways}

Agreeing in advance how far to rely on SI output in each operating condition helps personnel respond consistently, rather than judging trust under pressure. Establish clear, pre-authorized decision pathways that dictate how personnel respond to AI outputs across normal, degraded, and emergency operating conditions. Organizations should operationalize these pathways into simplified quick-reference guides, HSI prompts, and standard operating procedures. Examples to consider include:

* **Trust & Execute:** Routine, high-confidence recommendations within validated baseline operating envelopes (as specified in [Implementation 1.1.2: Structured Requirements Mapping](#implementation-1.1.2:-structured-requirements-mapping) and validated under [Implementation 1.3.1: Define TEVV Scope and Requirements per SI System](#implementation-1.3.1:-define-tevv-scope-and-requirements-per-si-system)) and within the consequence thresholds set under [Implementation 3.1.3: Define Acceptable Risk Thresholds and Associated Control Responses](#implementation-3.1.3:-define-acceptable-risk-thresholds-and-associated-control-responses), executed without further review where organizational policy permits, and notified for visibility.  
* **Spot-Check & Investigate:** Recommendations with moderate confidence, derived as in [Implementation 4.6.2: Derive Confidence and Rationale for Learned Components from Their Decision Processes](#implementation-4.6.2:-derive-confidence-and-rationale-for-learned-components-from-their-decision-processes), or novel input parameters (e.g., an unusual maintenance condition, borderline prior-authorization claim, or atypical network routing request), requiring a brief manual plausibility check before execution.  
* **Escalate to Oversight:** Persistent, non-critical model anomalies or recurring “soft” failures that do not threaten immediate safety or service continuity but indicate algorithmic drift or data schema shifts (as discussed in [Implementation 3.3.2: Establish Maximum Drift Thresholds](#implementation-3.3.2:-establish-maximum-drift-thresholds)), routed to the role holding decision authority for the capability along the escalation paths defined in [Implementation 3.9.3: Establish Escalation to Empowered Authority](#implementation-3.9.3:-establish-escalation-to-empowered-authority).  
* **Immediate Emergency Override:** Any AI output that intersects with deterministic safety/policy wrappers (as discussed in [Task 3.2: Implement Independent Guardrails for SI Outputs](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs)), violates hard physical or financial limits, or occurs during an unannounced multi-system outage. For this pathway, define in advance which roles may move the SI-enabled function to its fallback without seeking further authorization, consistent with the tiers in [Implementation 4.1.2: Establish Tiered Intervention Procedures, Training, and Authorization](#implementation-4.1.2:-establish-tiered-intervention-procedures,-training,-and-authorization). How the organization treats a good-faith decision to move to the fallback, where the SI output later proves to have been correct, is for it to decide, within any regulatory or contractual obligations. Protecting such decisions removes a reason to hesitate when the pathway calls for action, and it also weakens the check against moves made without adequate grounds. Record the position taken and make it known to the roles concerned.

Defining these pathways does not by itself establish that personnel apply them as intended. Periodically assess whether personnel assign outputs to the correct pathway under realistic workload and time pressure, particularly at the boundary between Trust & Execute and Spot-Check & Investigate, where repeated correct outputs can condition personnel to treat later recommendations as routine (see [Implementation 9.2.1](#implementation-9.2.1:-include-role-specific-training-on-si-failure-modes) and [Implementation 9.2.2](#implementation-9.2.2:-implement-realistic-incident-simulation-training)).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which pathways are used, and where is the boundary between Trust & Execute and Spot-Check & Investigate?  
* Does organizational policy permit Trust & Execute at all?  
* Which roles may move the SI-enabled function to its fallback without further authorization?  
* How is a good-faith move to the fallback treated when the SI output later proves correct?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Section 4.1, under human-in-the-loop decision-making, advises bringing the recommendations of more passive AI systems into an existing change management process. Where AI is actively updating control logic, it advises safety thresholds, alternative sensor output or state changes that add human intervention points, since problems can escalate before operators become aware of them. These correspond to the pathways this Implementation distinguishes by how directly an output acts.  
* **Research** [Endsley, M. R., and Kiris, E. O., The Out-of-the-Loop Performance Problem and Level of Control in Automation](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1518/001872095779064555), *Human Factors* 37(2), pages 381 to 394, 1995, from the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society. In an experiment with an expert system, operators were slower to perform a navigation task manually after the automation failed than those who had performed it manually throughout. Situation awareness was lowest under full automation and intermediate at intermediate levels. This bears on the Trust & Execute pathway and on the periodic assessment asked for here.

### Task 3.4: Monitor for Anomalous SI Behavior {#task-3.4:-monitor-for-anomalous-si-behavior}

Define policies and procedures for detecting acute, undesired, unexpected, and unusual AI system behavior, as continuous, real-time monitoring that complements the scheduled batch evaluations in [Implementation 2.3.4: Recurrent Risk Evaluations](#implementation-2.3.4:-recurrent-risk-evaluations) and operates against the thresholds defined in [Implementation 3.3.2: Establish Maximum Drift Thresholds](#implementation-3.3.2:-establish-maximum-drift-thresholds). This includes violations and near violations of constraints defined in [Implementation 3.2.2: Define and Independently Enforce Deterministic Operational Constraints](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints) as well as other metrics such as unusual changes in performance or output, even if they remain within safe constraints. The SI system being monitored should not be able to modify or suppress the monitoring, telemetry or alerts that concern its own behavior.

Detection of regular anomalous behavior should also feed into the estimation of drift velocity in [Implementation 2.3.4: Recurrent Risk Evaluations](#implementation-2.3.4:-recurrent-risk-evaluations). This includes distinguishing, where feasible, between anomalies likely caused by incidental drift or error and those consistent with deliberate interference. The pattern of change can be one indicator. Slow, gradual change in performance is more often consistent with drift, while abrupt change in one or more dimensions is more often consistent with an attempt at compromise. Neither pattern settles the question on its own.

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Reliable:** Contributes the continuous check that the AI system still performs as it did when it was accepted, covering near-violations and changes in output that stay inside the safe constraints, together with confirmation that the safety wrapper is still functioning, whether it has stopped through fault, misconfiguration or tampering, so degradation arising between scheduled evaluations is caught. This Task does not cover setting the limits those observations are judged against, which [Implementation 3.3.2: Establish Maximum Drift Thresholds](#implementation-3.3.2:-establish-maximum-drift-thresholds) covers.  
* **Secure:** Contributes the runtime separation of an anomaly consistent with drift or error from one consistent with deliberate interference. This Task does not cover monitoring access boundaries or privilege escalation by AI entities, which [Task 5.4: Implement Continuous Monitoring of SI Entities Against Access and Action Boundaries and Expectations](#task-5.4:-implement-continuous-monitoring-of-si-entities-against-access-and-action-boundaries-and-expectations) covers.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Privacy-Enhanced:** Observing output patterns means retaining outputs, and for an AI system working on records or documents those outputs carry whatever the source carried. [Implementation 10.1.3: Forensic Integrity and Privacy-Preserving Log Partitioning](#implementation-10.1.3:-forensic-integrity-and-privacy-preserving-log-partitioning) sets the masking and partitioning arrangements for telemetry that holds sensitive material.
* **Secure:** The observability requirements, baselines, and deviation ranges set here describe what is watched and what counts as normal. An attacker who knows them could keep activity inside the normal range, or act through something that is not observed. Protecting them is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice. The telemetry itself is protected under [Practice 10: Implement Multi-Tiered SI System Logging and Audit Capabilities](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities).

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Secure versus Reliable:** Where the cause of an anomaly is clear, the response follows from it. Where one observation could be drift or could be interference, the reliability response of recalibrating or widening the baseline and the security response of preserving state and investigating point in opposite directions, and handling manipulation as drift adapts the AI system toward the manipulated distribution. One way to balance this is to hold the baseline and escalate under [Implementation 3.4.4: Define Runtime Anomaly Escalation Procedures](#implementation-3.4.4:-define-runtime-anomaly-escalation-procedures) until the cause is established; others include preserving the evidence while continuing to operate under tightened constraints.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MEASURE 2.4** (on monitoring deployed AI systems): This Task defines the observable behaviors, operational baselines and deviation ranges by which a deployed AI system is watched continuously, including whether its validation controls are still functioning; it does not cover the scheduled evaluation that runs alongside that monitoring. For that, see for example [Implementation 2.3.4: Recurrent Risk Evaluations](#implementation-2.3.4:-recurrent-risk-evaluations).  
* **MEASURE 3.1** (on tracking known and emerging risks): This Task tracks emergent behavior against an operational baseline, and distinguishes, where feasible, anomalies caused by drift or error from those consistent with deliberate interference; it does not cover tracking risks that leave no observable trace in the system’s own behavior.  
* **MANAGE 2.3** (on responding to emerging risks): This Task defines the escalation procedure that a sustained or recurring anomaly should trigger where it matches no previously characterized failure mode; it does not cover the intervention and recovery that follow. For those, see for example [Practice 4: Define Procedures for Emergency Avoidance Override, Recovery, and Situational Awareness](#practice-4:-define-procedures-for-emergency-avoidance-override,-recovery,-and-situational-awareness).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Who watches the monitoring, at what hours, and what happens to an alert raised when no one with authority to act is available?  
* Where continuous monitoring is not affordable for a system, what monitoring interval is accepted, and what risk remains between checks?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v2r1, Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v2r1), from NIST. Table D-2 defines the Analytic Monitoring technique as monitoring and analyzing a wide range of properties and behaviors on an ongoing basis and in a coordinated way, with the purpose of detecting potential adverse conditions and revealing their extent, which corresponds to the continuous monitoring this Task establishes. Section C.2 notes that an advanced persistent threat can take advantage of, or make its behavior appear to result from, human error, structural failure or natural disaster. That supports this Task’s request that anomalies consistent with drift be distinguished, where feasible, from those consistent with deliberate interference.  
* **Guidance** [AI Data Security: Best Practices for Securing Data Used to Train & Operate AI Systems](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/ai-data-security-best-practices-securing-data-used-train-operate-ai-systems), version 1.0, May 2025, joint Cybersecurity Information Sheet from the National Security Agency’s Artificial Intelligence Security Center, CISA, the FBI and partner agencies in Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom. Its section on data drift notes that slow, gradual changes in performance more likely indicate drift, and abrupt, dramatic changes more likely indicate an attempt to compromise the model. This is one heuristic for the distinction this Task asks for.

#### Implementation 3.4.1: Define Observability Requirements {#implementation-3.4.1:-define-observability-requirements}

Observation in operation helps an organization see what an SI system actually does, especially where the system’s behavior is learned rather than specified. Identify observable AI system behaviors and metrics, including output patterns, decision frequencies, and validation control states, and, where the SI system depends on recurring data feeds or transformation pipelines, indicators of upstream data health, such as missing or late feeds, unexpected changes in record counts, schema or unit changes, or mapping failures. Include the inputs the SI system receives as well as its outputs, intermediate states and errors, the model and configuration versions in effect, and its use of resources and data. The frequency and repetition of inputs can also be worth observing, since high-frequency or repetitive inputs can be signs of automated attempts at compromise.

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Section 4.1 asks owners and operators to take inventory of AI components and of the components that rely on them, and to log and monitor the inputs and outputs of these components.  
* **Guidance** [AI Incident Response Framework, Workstream 2: Preparing Defenders for a Changing Cybersecurity Landscape](https://www.coalitionforsecureai.org/defending-ai-systems-a-new-framework-for-incident-response-in-the-age-of-intelligent-technology/), version 1.0, 27 October 2025, from the Coalition for Secure AI, an OASIS Open Project. Section 3.3.1, Preparation Phase, lists the monitoring infrastructure for AI systems, including input and output logging, system prompt versioning, configuration management, API usage analysis, resource utilization and data access patterns, and recommends establishing API usage baselines. A fuller list of the observables this Implementation identifies.  
* **Guidance** [Deploying AI Systems Securely: Best Practices for Deploying Secure and Resilient AI Systems](https://media.defense.gov/2024/Apr/15/2003439257/-1/-1/0/CSI-DEPLOYING-AI-SYSTEMS-SECURELY.PDF), version 1.0, April 2024, joint Cybersecurity Information Sheet from the National Security Agency’s Artificial Intelligence Security Center, CISA, the FBI and partner agencies in Australia, Canada, New Zealand and the United Kingdom. Under actively monitoring model behavior, it asks for logs covering inputs, outputs, intermediate states and errors, and for monitoring of configuration settings for unauthorized changes. Under robust logging and monitoring, it advises watching for high-frequency or repetitive inputs as possible signs of compromise attempts.  
* **Guidance** [AI Data Security: Best Practices for Securing Data Used to Train & Operate AI Systems](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/ai-data-security-best-practices-securing-data-used-train-operate-ai-systems), version 1.0, May 2025, joint Cybersecurity Information Sheet from the National Security Agency’s Artificial Intelligence Security Center, CISA, the FBI and partner agencies in Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom. Among the causes of data drift, it lists a change in the upstream data pipeline that the training data does not represent, such as units changing from miles to kilometers. The data-health indicators here are meant to catch this kind of change.

#### Implementation 3.4.2: Establish Operational Baselines and Deviation Thresholds {#implementation-3.4.2:-establish-operational-baselines-and-deviation-thresholds}

Define what normal AI system behavior looks like under authorized operating conditions, and establish the deviation ranges to determine abnormal behavior. Draw these baselines from the normal behavior of the process and of the people working with the SI system, as well as from the SI system’s own outputs. This can help reduce nuisance alerts. Organizations that already baseline network traffic and process behavior for OT anomaly detection can extend that practice to the SI system. Those that do not can start with the process variables that the SI system reads or influences. Where a baseline is updated automatically, as some behavioral anomaly detection tools do, review each update before it takes effect, so that a gradual shift does not become the new normal without a decision to accept it. Where updates come too often to review one by one, a fallback is to limit how far each update can move the baseline and to review the accumulated change at intervals. A slow shift that stays within those limits can still become the new normal between reviews. Record the assumptions and operating conditions under which each baseline was established, and the corrective action or review that each deviation threshold triggers. Where the SI system works across distinct operating modes, for example startup, steady operation, peak demand or a maintenance outage, establish the baseline and deviation ranges for each mode, from a period that covers it. A single baseline across modes can raise anomaly alerts at mode transitions and during upsets, when operators are busiest.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Are automatic baseline updates allowed, and how is each one reviewed?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v2r1, Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v2r1), from NIST. Table D-4 lists Behavior Validation as an approach to the Substantiated Integrity technique: validating the behavior of a system, service or device against defined or emergent criteria such as requirements or patterns of prior usage, and learning which behaviors are normal and which are suspicious, which is the baseline and deviation range this Implementation defines.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Section 6.3.1, Anomalies and Events, asks that OT alerting thresholds be based on baselines of normal network traffic and data flows and of normal human and OT process behavior, to reduce false positive and nuisance alarms. Appendix E.2.5, Behavioral Anomaly Detection, notes that some such tools use AI and ML algorithms to update the baseline automatically as the environment evolves.  
* **Research** [NIST AI 800-4, Challenges to the Monitoring of Deployed AI Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.800-4), March 2026, from NIST. Section 3.2.1, Functionality, records workshop attendees asking what assumptions monitoring starts from and whether performance baselines were established. Attendees then highlighted the need for deviation thresholds, set after the baselines, that trigger corrective actions or reviews. This bears on the baselines and deviation ranges defined here.  
* **Research** Bransby, M. L., and Jenkinson, J., [The management of alarm systems](https://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/ukgwa/20230103120103/https://www.hse.gov.uk/research/crr_pdf/1998/crr98166.pdf), Contract Research Report 166/1998, funded by the Health and Safety Executive, Great Britain’s workplace health and safety regulator. Section 5.3.6.5 notes that certain alarms are only relevant in particular plant operating modes, such as shut down, starting-up and steady operation, and that alarm limits may be changed according to mode. Section 5.3.6.6 reports that alarm systems imposed the biggest load on operators in the period after a major plant upset. These bear on the per-mode baselines here.

#### Implementation 3.4.3: Monitor Validation Control Integrity {#implementation-3.4.3:-monitor-validation-control-integrity}

Checking that guardrails and watchdogs are still enforcing lets an organization rely on what they do, not only on their presence in a record. Establish continuous monitoring of the states of the validation controls (the safety wrappers of [Task 3.2: Implement Independent Guardrails for SI Outputs](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs) and the watchdogs of [Implementation 2.2.2: Deploy “Watchdog” Controllers](#implementation-2.2.2:-deploy-“watchdog”-controllers)) to validate that mechanisms are actively and correctly functioning. This includes confirming that each control is operating in its intended enforcement state, blocking or otherwise acting on a violation rather than only detecting or alerting on it, since a control left in a detect-only or alert-only mode can appear in inventories and assurance records as implemented while stopping nothing. Confirm this state in the production configuration at commissioning and after changes made under [Task 7.3: Manage Version Control and Logging for Internal SI Safety Mechanisms](#task-7.3:-manage-version-control-and-logging-for-internal-si-safety-mechanisms). Where practical, confirm it by exercising the control, for example by presenting a known out-of-bounds test command in a test or maintenance mode and confirming, from records independent of the control, that it was refused, rather than relying on the control’s own report of its state. Confirm that each control remains in the path it was placed in, for example by reconciling the number of SI outputs produced with the number the control evaluated, and by checking for output paths that do not pass through the intercept points identified in [Implementation 3.2.1: Identify SI Output Intercept Points](#implementation-3.2.1:-identify-si-output-intercept-points). Check the code, rule sets and configuration of each control against the approved versions held under [Task 7.3: Manage Version Control and Logging for Internal SI Safety Mechanisms](#task-7.3:-manage-version-control-and-logging-for-internal-si-safety-mechanisms), at startup and at a defined frequency. Where a control is bypassed or overridden, record who authorized it, when it began and when it is due to end, and raise a notification if it remains in place past that time. Run this monitoring separately from the controls it checks, with its own credentials and hosting where practical. Define in advance whether the SI-enabled function continues, is restricted, or moves to the fallback in [Implementation 3.2.3: Specify Fail-Safe States and Fallback Behavior](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior) when a control is found not to be functioning.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* What happens to the SI-enabled function when a validation control is found not to be functioning?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-137, Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) for Federal Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-137), from NIST. Section 3.2.1, Determine Metrics, states that metrics are fundamentally flawed without assurance that all security controls are implemented correctly, that collecting metrics from security controls that have not been assessed is like using a broken or uncalibrated scale, and that without assurance of the correct implementation and continued effectiveness of controls not associated with a metric, root-cause analysis may be narrowed to a predetermined list and overlook the true problem. This supports monitoring the state of the validation controls themselves rather than only what they report.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v2r1, Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v2r1), from NIST. Section D.5.2.1, Limit the Need for Trust, states that where a system element is required to have a given level of trustworthiness, some attestation mechanism is needed to verify that it has and continues to retain it, which applies to the validation controls in Task 3.2 that the rest of the system relies on. Section D.5.2.8, Leverage Health and Status Data, cautions that components can report health and status data erroneously or maliciously, so a control reporting itself as active is not by itself evidence that it is enforcing.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control SI-7, Software, Firmware, and Information Integrity, employs integrity verification tools to detect unauthorized changes to defined software, firmware and information, and enhancement SI-7(1) performs those integrity checks at startup, at defined transitional states or events, or at a defined frequency. These bear on checking each control against its approved version.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Their Executive Summary says that the keys of OT assets such as programmable logic controllers and safety systems should be in the “Run” position at all times unless they are being actively programmed. This is the OT counterpart of confirming that a validation control is in its intended enforcement state, not only that it is present.

#### Implementation 3.4.4: Define Runtime Anomaly Escalation Procedures {#implementation-3.4.4:-define-runtime-anomaly-escalation-procedures}

Escalation criteria help a sustained or recurring anomaly reach people who can investigate and respond, while the evidence is still intact. Extend communications actions defined under [Implementation 3.2.4: Define Further Logging and Communication Actions](#implementation-3.2.4:-define-further-logging-and-communication-actions) to cover sustained or recurring behavioral anomalies of AI systems. Define the criteria at which a sustained or recurring anomaly is escalated for investigation as a possible incident, and at that point hand it to the procedures in [Practice 8: Incorporate SI-Aware Incident Analysis and Response Procedures](#practice-8:-incorporate-si-aware-incident-analysis-and-response-procedures). Where an anomaly could reflect either drift or deliberate interference, preserve the relevant records and system state before recalibrating or retraining the model, so that the cause can still be investigated. Preserving state has a storage and handling cost. How long it is kept can follow the retention decided under [Task 10.1: Define Decision-Level Logging and Metadata Retention Policies](#task-10.1:-define-decision-level-logging-and-metadata-retention-policies), and the preserved records should identify the model version, prompts, configuration, and other state and information that influenced the output ([Implementation 10.1.5: Define What Each Operational Record Is For](#implementation-10.1.5:-define-what-each-operational-record-is-for)).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* At what point is a sustained or recurring anomaly escalated as a possible incident?  
* While the cause is unclear, is the baseline held and the anomaly escalated, or does operation continue under tightened constraints? (see the Secure versus Reliable tension in [Task 3.4: Monitor for Anomalous SI Behavior](#task-3.4:-monitor-for-anomalous-si-behavior))

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-61r3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-61r3), April 2025, from NIST. In Table 3, subcategory DE.AE-08 has incidents declared when adverse events meet defined incident criteria, and the notes to RS.MA ask that triage, prioritization, escalation and elevation be based on a set of risk evaluation factors. These are the criteria this Implementation asks to be defined for SI anomalies. Subcategory RS.AN-07 asks that incident data and metadata be collected with their integrity and provenance preserved, which bears on preserving records and state before recalibration.  
* **Guidance** [AI Incident Response Framework, Workstream 2: Preparing Defenders for a Changing Cybersecurity Landscape](https://www.coalitionforsecureai.org/defending-ai-systems-a-new-framework-for-incident-response-in-the-age-of-intelligent-technology/), version 1.0, 27 October 2025, from the Coalition for Secure AI, an OASIS Open Project. Section 3.3.2, Detection and Analysis Phase, lists escalation triggers among the manual review elements, and asks responders to validate whether anomalous behavior constitutes a security incident and to make escalation procedures match incident severity.

### Task 3.5: Define and Control Risks to Adjacent and Related Systems {#task-3.5:-define-and-control-risks-to-adjacent-and-related-systems}

Because a failure in an SI system can affect other systems through its outputs, its access, and the infrastructure and resources it shares, sometimes faster than people can intervene, planning for those effects helps an organization limit how far a failure spreads. Define and control risks to other systems that may be affected by a failure in this system, including:

* Systems that are intentionally interdependent with this system, where errors travel along functional, data, or operational dependencies (“cascading failures”).  
* Systems that may be unrelated except for shared adjacency in a physical, logical, network, resource, supply chain, or other sense (“splash damage” or “blast radius”).  
* Systems and parties outside the organization that are affected through shared capacity, such as demand on grid or water capacity, or through disruption to neighboring communities, where the effect can return to the organization as direct risk or as indirect risk, such as regulatory or community opposition.

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Safe:** Contributes containment of consequence beyond the AI system’s own function: execution confined to isolated segments, and limits on shared resources such as compute, bandwidth, power and exclusive sensor access, so a failure reaches a bounded set of assets. This Task does not cover bounding what the AI system is permitted to reach in the first place, which [Task 5.3: Implement Principles of Least Agency and Least Privilege for SI Entities](#task-5.3:-implement-principles-of-least-agency-and-least-privilege-for-si-entities) covers.  
* **Resilient:** Contributes the common-cause analysis that redundancy rests on: whether systems and safeguards that are functionally independent share a facility, a power or cooling supply, a network path, a hypervisor or a municipal substrate. This Task does not cover establishing the redundancy itself, which [Task 2.2: Establish Requirements for Redundancy in SI-Driven Functions](#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions) covers.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Secure:** The dependency and shared-infrastructure maps built under this Task show which systems a failure would reach, and which safeguards share a facility, power supply, network path, or service. An attacker could use them to choose a single point whose failure disables several systems or safeguards at once. Protecting them is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Safe versus Reliable:** Where an AI system’s demand for a shared resource is steady, a hard limit protects the systems alongside it while the SI-enabled function continues to perform as required. Where demand rises during the same upset that raises demand elsewhere, the limit removes capacity from the function at the point it is most needed. One way to balance this is the graded arrangement in [Implementation 3.5.4: Define and Implement Resource Limiting](#implementation-3.5.4:-define-and-implement-resource-limiting), where a soft limit and a notification precede the hard limit; others include reserving capacity for the highest-consequence function, or defining the state the function enters when it is throttled.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MAP 5.1** (on identifying risk likelihood and impacts): This Task identifies impacts on systems that share physical space, network paths, logical substrates or scarce resources with the AI system, and on systems downstream of it; it does not cover impacts at the AI system’s own decision points. For those, see for example [Task 3.1: Identify Risk Trade-offs](#task-3.1:-identify-risk-trade-offs).  
* **MAP 3.3** (on documenting application scope of the AI system): This Task bounds the scope an AI system can reach, by confining its execution to isolated segments and capping the shared resources it may consume; it does not cover defining the intended scope from which those bounds should be derived. For that, see for example [Practice 1: Establish Requirements for Success](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success).  
* **GOVERN 4.2** (on documenting impact): This Task requires that impacts estimated beyond the facility perimeter be recorded as bounded engineering assumptions where telemetry is unavailable, so that the limits of the assessment stay visible to a later reader; it does not cover communicating those impacts to the operators of the affected systems.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which external parties, such as utilities or neighboring operators, are told about dependencies or exposure the analysis finds, and by whom?  
* Who resources analysis of shared infrastructure that the organization does not own or see into?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v2r1, Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v2r1), from NIST. Table D-2 gives the Segmentation technique the purpose of containing adversary activities and non-adversarial stresses, such as fires and floods, to the enclave, segment or facility in which they arise. It gives the Realignment technique the purpose of minimizing connections between mission-critical and non-critical services, so that a failure of non-critical services is less likely to affect mission-critical ones. These are the containment aims this Task applies to the failure of an AI system. Section C.3 counts alterations in behavior that affect external systems, which can cascade beyond the system of interest, among the effects cyber resiliency engineering considers.  
* **Incident Report** [Incident Review: Considering Simultaneous Voltage-Sensitive Load Reductions](https://www.nerc.com/pa/rrm/ea/Documents/Incident_Review_Large_Load_Loss.pdf), January 2025, from the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC). On July 10, 2024, a transmission line fault led to the customer-initiated, simultaneous loss of about 1,500 MW of voltage-sensitive load, mostly data centers transferring to backup power. Much of it came from a protection scheme that counts voltage disturbances and moves the facility off the grid until it is manually reconnected. NERC notes that grid planning has historically considered large generation losses rather than load losses of this size. This bears on the third category above: the combined response of many facilities reaching the regional grid that they and others depend on.

#### Implementation 3.5.1: Map Direct Functional and Algorithmic Dependencies {#implementation-3.5.1:-map-direct-functional-and-algorithmic-dependencies}

A map of where SI outputs go helps an organization plan monitoring, containment, and recovery before an error spreads. Trace and document downstream logical, algorithmic, and operational paths of AI outputs to identify how errors, whether in control outputs, direct executable code, or human-mediated summaries, could trigger a chain reaction through connected assets. These dependencies often extend beyond traditional IT/OT/ICS boundaries; for example, an AI agent defending an IT network might erroneously disable authentication traffic, physically locking personnel out of a facility. To capture these risks more fully, organizations should conduct a high-value asset (HVA) assessment that extends outward to map functional dependencies on upstream suppliers and downstream customers. This can help limit how far automated errors propagate along the extended supply chain. Include undeclared consumers, such as systems or spreadsheets that read the SI system’s outputs without its owner’s knowledge, and algorithmic couplings, where two automated systems, possibly operated by different organizations, react to each other’s outputs and form a feedback loop that neither owner sees. For each dependency, record what the downstream system does if the SI output it receives is wrong, late or missing, and whether a person reviews that output before it takes effect. Treat a dependency found in testing or operation that is not on the map as a finding, and update the map when the SI system or a connected system changes.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* How far upstream and downstream, including outside the organization, does the dependency map reach?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v2r1, Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v2r1), from NIST. Section 3.2.3.1, Identify Critical Resources, Sources of Fragility, and Attack Surfaces, identifies critical resources from functional flows and mission threads, noting that a resource can be critical at one point in a flow and not at another, and notes that network or graph analysis can show how tightly elements are connected and that graphical analysis of the distribution of component types can help determine how easily a given stress could propagate, an approach this Implementation adapts to errors in AI outputs.

#### Implementation 3.5.2: Identify Indirect Shared Infrastructure and Collateral Damage Exposure {#implementation-3.5.2:-identify-indirect-shared-infrastructure-and-collateral-damage-exposure}

Finding what an SI system shares with otherwise unrelated systems helps an organization reduce the chance that a single failure disables several of them at once, including safeguards assumed to be redundant. Audit the operational environment to identify functionally independent systems that are vulnerable to collateral damage from an AI failure. Evaluation criteria should include cross-cutting environmental and infrastructure commonalities, such as:

* Physical Proximity: Independent physical assets co-located in the same facility or enclosure, or that share the same power, cooling, or other physical resources.  
* Network Topography: Systems sharing the same network switches, backbones, or uplink paths.  
* Logical Substrates: Unrelated applications sharing the same hypervisor, underlying cloud tenant, base operating system image, or database instance.  
* Shared Services: Systems relying on the same identity provider, time source, remote access gateway, vendor update channel, model provider, inference endpoint or retrieval store.

This mapping should also consider whether a single event or action could affect multiple identified safeguards at once, rather than assuming redundant controls fail independently. Common-cause analysis is established practice in safety and reliability engineering. Organizations that use it can build on it here, applying it to the SI system and the services it relies on. This includes the case where the same model, vendor product or update channel is deployed across many sites or organizations, so that one defect, update or manipulation can affect them at once and remove a fallback that several of them share. Diversity in fallback arrangements can help limit this exposure; see [Task 2.2: Establish Requirements for Redundancy in SI-Driven Functions](#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions). This asset assessment should, where possible, reach outward past the facility’s immediate perimeter to evaluate shared municipal substrates, such as the regional electrical grid, water networks, or telecommunication backbones, where a localized AI failure or resource-saturation event could cause regional collateral damage.

Where direct technical visibility or telemetry past the facility’s perimeter is unavailable, organizations should utilize qualified engineering approximations and best-available sector intelligence to estimate these external impacts. These estimations should be explicitly documented as bounded technical assumptions, so that the limits of the data stay visible and the assessment can proceed without complete external information. The task of mapping internal dependencies is common to [Implementation 7.6.1: Internal Dependency Mapping (Orphan System Prevention)](#implementation-7.6.1:-internal-dependency-mapping-\(orphan-system-prevention\)). Maintaining this map can reduce the effort needed when this system is later decommissioned. This mapping is also the basis for identifying what depends on an AI system at retirement, under [Implementation 13.3.3: Determine and Record What Happens to Everything that Depended on the System](#implementation-13.3.3:-determine-and-record-what-happens-to-everything-that-depended-on-the-system).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* How far past the facility perimeter does the assessment reach, and which external impacts are recorded as bounded assumptions?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v2r1, Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v2r1), from NIST. Section D.5.2.6, Maintain Redundancy, states that the extent of redundancy is established through analysis of single points of failure and shared resources, and that trends to convergence undermine it. Its example is an organization using Voice over Internet Protocol, which cannot claim alternate paths for phone, email and instant messaging. Section D.5.1.1, Focus on Common Critical Assets, makes common infrastructures, shared services and shared data repositories high priorities for the application of cyber resiliency techniques because they are common to multiple missions. This supports the common-cause view this Implementation takes of functionally independent systems.  
* **Guidance** [NIST AI 600-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1), July 2024, from NIST. Section 2 names algorithmic monocultures as an ecosystem-level risk, and its footnote describes how repeated use of the same model or algorithm can increase susceptibility to correlated failures, such as unexpected shocks, because multiple actors rely on the same algorithm. This bears on the same model deployed across many sites or organizations.  
* **Research** [2025 Long-Term Reliability Assessment](https://www.nerc.com/our-work/assessments/long-term-reliability-assessments), January 2026, from the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC). Recommendation 2 notes that inverter-based resources respond to disturbances based on programmed logic and inverter controls, and that their tripping during grid faults has caused sudden loss of generation, over wide areas in some cases. The common thread NERC identifies is a shared lack of ride-through capability that lets a minor disturbance become a major one. Under Data Centers and Large Commercial and Industrial Loads, it also reports an event in which data centers and other power electronic loads transferred load to backup generation at the same time, a reduction of about 1,500 MW that caused frequency overshoot and high voltages on the grid. Written about the grid rather than AI systems, these are sector examples of many independent assets failing together because they share the same control behavior, and of a facility’s collective response reaching the regional grid.  
* **Incident Report** [Incident Review: Considering Simultaneous Voltage-Sensitive Load Reductions](https://www.nerc.com/pa/rrm/ea/Documents/Incident_Review_Large_Load_Loss.pdf), January 2025, from the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC). On July 10, 2024, a transmission line fault led to the customer-initiated, simultaneous loss of about 1,500 MW of voltage-sensitive load, mostly data centers transferring to backup power. Much of it came from a protection scheme that counts voltage disturbances and moves the facility off the grid until it is manually reconnected. NERC notes that grid planning has historically considered large generation losses rather than load losses of this size. This is the primary account of the large-load event that the 2025 assessment summarizes, and it bears on the shared municipal substrates this Implementation asks to be evaluated.

#### Implementation 3.5.3: Impact Compartmentalization (Sandboxing) {#implementation-3.5.3:-impact-compartmentalization-\(sandboxing\)}

Compartmentalization limits how far a misbehaving or compromised SI system can reach, especially toward safety functions. Restrict AI agent execution to isolated micro-segments of the network or other infrastructure. For example, an AI optimizing valve pressure should not be able to affect core safety instrumented systems (SIS). Apply the same separation to the paths used to administer and update the SI system: a segment that contains safety functions should not be administered from a less critical environment. Organizations that already zone their OT networks, for example under the ISA/IEC 62443 series, can treat the SI system and its management paths as further assets to place in those zones. For robots and other physical SI systems, the paths to compartmentalize can include wireless connectivity, cloud services and remote maintenance as well as the plant network. Where legacy network architecture makes micro-segmentation infeasible, a minimal implementation is read-only integration: the SI system receives process data, for example from a replicated historian or through a one-way gateway, and has no network path by which to write to the process, so any recommendation it makes is entered by a person or by a separately controlled system. Scale the strength of isolation to the consequence of failure, for example from process or container isolation for low-consequence tasks to a separate host or network zone for SI systems near operational technology. Where practical, make compartments non-persistent, so that an agent’s execution environment is discarded and recreated, rather than cleaned, after a session that misbehaved or may have been compromised.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* How strong is the isolation for each SI system, given the consequence of its failure?  
* Where micro-segmentation is infeasible, is read-only integration used instead?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control enhancement SC-7(21), Isolation of System Components, uses boundary protection mechanisms to isolate components that support different missions or business functions, and its discussion notes that such isolation limits the potential harm from both hostile cyber-attacks and errors, which supports confining an AI agent so that it cannot reach a safety instrumented system.  
* **Guidance** [Principles of operational technology cyber security](https://www.cyber.gov.au/publication/principles-of-operational-technology-cyber-security), 2024, from the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre, co-sealed by CISA, NSA, the FBI and cybersecurity agencies of several other countries. Principle 4, Segment and segregate OT from all other networks, notes the long-recognized need to separate more critical OT networks, such as those essential to safety, from less critical ones. It adds that a more critical environment should never be administered from a less critical environment. These bear on the SIS example and on the administration paths in this Implementation.  
* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by CISA. Section 4.1 asks operators to prefer push-based or brokered architectures that move required features or summaries out of OT without granting persistent inbound access, and to use one-way transfer patterns and audited staging buffers where data must reach business networks. This bears on the read-only integration this Implementation names for legacy networks.  
* **Working Document** [Preliminary Report](https://www.scsp.ai/robotics-preliminary-report/), October 2026, from the National Security Commission on Robotics for Advanced Manufacturing, an initiative of the Special Competitive Studies Project. Under National Framework, it notes that a modern robot often combines sensors, wireless connectivity, proprietary software, cloud services, remote maintenance and the ability to act physically inside a facility. It adds that a network-isolated packaging cell does not have the same risk profile as a connected mobile robot. This bears on the paths this Implementation compartmentalizes for physical SI systems.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v2r1, Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v2r1), from NIST. Table D-4 lists Non-Persistent Services as an approach to the Non-Persistence technique: refreshing services periodically, or generating them on demand and terminating them when no longer needed, with the informal description that a service should not run indefinitely because it may have been compromised while executing. This bears on non-persistent compartments here.

#### Implementation 3.5.4: Define and Implement Resource Limiting {#implementation-3.5.4:-define-and-implement-resource-limiting}

Limits on an SI system’s use of shared resources help keep other systems, including safeguards, supplied when an agentic system consumes resources quickly. Limits set too tightly can starve the SI system itself, so they are a balance against what its task needs. Identify limited resources that the AI agent or system shares with other systems (AI or otherwise), such as compute, tokens, exclusive hardware/sensor access, power, network bandwidth, and cooling. Define and implement appropriate soft and hard limits on the AI system’s use of these resources, along with appropriate notifications for when these limits are approached or exceeded. Where consumption accumulates quickly, it can outpace a notification, so a hard limit should stop the consumption rather than only report it. Include the resources that monitoring, logging and enforcement controls themselves depend on. Where these share a host with the SI system, a runaway agentic loop can exhaust that host before those controls act, so place them on separate resources or reserve capacity for them. Spare capacity that depends on other workloads staying idle is not a reserve. Where the SI system competes for the same power, compute, cooling or bandwidth as the physical or public service it supports, establish in advance which SI workloads yield, and in what order, so that the SI system does not take resources that the mission itself needs. Enforce these limits outside the SI system, for example at a gateway, in the operating system, in the orchestration layer or at the controller, so that the SI system cannot raise them.

For agentic and multi-agent systems, these limits can include per-agent budgets for tokens, time and tool calls that fail closed when exceeded. They can also include a circuit breaker that halts an agent after a defined number of consecutive failed or anomalous actions. Bound retries with randomized backoff and a retry budget, so that one agent caught in a retry loop cannot saturate a dependency it shares with others. Retrying at several layers at once multiplies the attempts that reach that dependency. Idempotency keys on state-changing actions can mean that a retried action is not carried out twice.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Where are the soft and hard limits set for each shared resource?  
* Which SI workloads yield first, and in what order, when a shared resource runs short? (see the Safe versus Reliable tension in [Task 3.5: Define and Control Risks to Adjacent and Related Systems](#task-3.5:-define-and-control-risks-to-adjacent-and-related-systems))

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control SC-6, Resource Availability, protects the availability of defined resources by allocating them by priority or quota, so that lower-priority processes cannot delay higher-priority ones and no process obtains more than a predetermined amount, which is the control form of the limits this Implementation places on an AI system’s share of compute, bandwidth and other shared resources.  
* **Guidance** [OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-genai-llm-top-10-2026/), Version 2026, from the OWASP GenAI Security Project, a volunteer community project of the Open Worldwide Application Security Project. LLM06:2026, Unbounded Consumption, notes that agentic architectures and tool-use protocols can amplify a single request into cascading downstream operations. Its mitigations include hard spending caps that halt inference when exceeded, rather than alerting thresholds that fast-accumulating workloads can outpace, and agentic circuit breakers with step, recursion-depth, time and per-run cost limits. These bear on the hard limits and agent budgets in this Implementation.  
* **Commentary** [Ulrich, M., *Addressing Cascading Failures*](https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/), Chapter 22 of *Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems*, 2017, from Google, published by O’Reilly Media. Under Retries, it shows how naive retries can keep an overloaded backend from recovering. It recommends randomized exponential backoff, a limit on retries per request, and a server-wide retry budget beyond which requests fail rather than retry. It shows how retrying at several layers multiplies attempts. Under Resource limits, it cautions against relying on slack capacity whose availability depends on other jobs. These bear on bounded retries and on reserved capacity in this Implementation.

### Task 3.6: Mitigate Automation Complacency and Skills Degradation {#task-3.6:-mitigate-automation-complacency-and-skills-degradation}

To sustain safe operation when an SI system is unavailable or wrong, establish continuous readiness and training protocols that keep critical human capabilities exercised. Reliance on an SI system is often the intended result of adopting one, be it to make new aspects of the task possible or perform existing tasks with more efficiency. Where it takes over work people did before, it reduces the occasions on which those capabilities are used (see Bainbridge 1983). That the reliance is intended does not make this erosion less of a hazard. It makes it an expected consequence that this Task plans for.

Practice to sustain these capabilities has to be arranged rather than left to routine operation. This Task requires organizations to identify critical human capabilities that should be preserved, helping operators retain the technical expertise, cognitive situational awareness, and manual or legacy override proficiency necessary to manage operations during prolonged AI outages or catastrophic failures. Note that this includes full manual overrides (where system velocity makes this possible, see [Task 4.5: Define Operational Regimes for Human-on-the-Loop and Human-Out-of-the-Loop Operation](#task-4.5:-define-operational-regimes-for-human-on-the-loop-and-human-out-of-the-loop-operation)), the ability to monitor and operate deterministic fallback or legacy systems ([Task 3.2: Implement Independent Guardrails for SI Outputs](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs)), and decision-making processes necessary to perform appropriately risk-managed unplanned shutdowns ([Practice 11: Maintain SI-Aware Mission Continuity and Disaster Recovery Planning](#practice-11:-maintain-si-aware-mission-continuity-and-disaster-recovery-planning)). Organizations with established operator qualification and emergency drill programs can extend them to the skills an SI system takes over. Those without such programs can start from the manual procedures in [Task 11.2: Define Manual and Alternative Operating Procedures for Long-Term Mission Continuity](#task-11.2:-define-manual-and-alternative-operating-procedures-for-long-term-mission-continuity).

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Resilient:** Contributes periodic exercise of the fallback path under real load: drills in which deterministic controllers and analog backups take over the operation while independent safety protections, such as trips and limits, stay active, which is what separates a documented fallback from a demonstrated one. This Task does not cover sustained operation once the fallback is carrying the process, which [Task 11.2: Define Manual and Alternative Operating Procedures for Long-Term Mission Continuity](#task-11.2:-define-manual-and-alternative-operating-procedures-for-long-term-mission-continuity) covers.  
* **Bias Managed:** Contributes a bound on one human-cognitive error source, automation bias, by placing active verification at high-consequence boundary thresholds so that agreement with an AI output is an act rather than a default. This Task does not address the notification rate that produces desensitization, which [Task 4.4: Attention Governance and Alert/Alarm Flood Mitigation](#task-4.4:-attention-governance-and-alert/alarm-flood-mitigation) covers.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Reliable:** Simulating a failure of the AI system is itself an operational action, and a drill placed in a window judged low-risk can still meet a real disturbance. [Implementation 3.6.2: Scheduled “Manual Control” Drills](#implementation-3.6.2:-scheduled-“manual-control”-drills) directs drills that cannot be run safely on the live system to non-production environments, which [Implementation 1.3.2: Categorization of Testing Environments](#implementation-1.3.2:-categorization-of-testing-environments) categorizes.  
* **Privacy-Enhanced:** The engagement indicators in [Implementation 3.6.4: Monitor Aggregate Engagement Indicators](#implementation-3.6.4:-monitor-aggregate-engagement-indicators) are drawn from how individual operators work, so they also produce a record about individuals. How that record is governed, and by which function, is for the organization to decide, within any regulatory or contractual obligations. Existing workforce monitoring and privacy practice already handles comparable records, while indicators drawn from how individual operators work may also bear on labor arrangements that practice does not cover. Record where governance of that record sits.
* **Secure:** Drill schedules and after action reports show when an operation will run without its SI system, and where the fallback or the operators fell short.
