An attacker could use them to time an attack for a drill window or to target a known weakness in the fallback. Protecting them is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Safe versus Safe:** Where verification steps are reserved for high-consequence boundary thresholds, operator engagement is spent where the consequence is greatest. Where they are applied widely, the same steps become routine, and a check performed routinely returns agreement without examination while still consuming capacity needed elsewhere. One way to balance this is the restriction to high-consequence thresholds in [Implementation 3.6.3: Cognitive Engagement by Design](#implementation-3.6.3:-cognitive-engagement-by-design), deployed with the calm technology and mixed-initiative choices in [Implementation 4.4.4: Applying Consolidation and Low-Cognitive-Load Design Techniques](#implementation-4.4.4:-applying-consolidation-and-low-cognitive-load-design-techniques); others include varying when the check falls so that it is not anticipated, having the operator record an assessment before the SI recommendation is shown, or moving the exercise into scheduled drills.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MAP 3.4** (on defining operator proficiency): This Task identifies the manual and interpretive skills that day-to-day AI reliance erodes, and requires periodic audited verification that operators can still run the infrastructure without AI assistance; it does not cover delivering the instruction that builds those skills. For that, see for example [Task 9.2: Deliver Specialized Training on Human-SI Interaction and Automation Bias](#task-9.2:-deliver-specialized-training-on-human-si-interaction-and-automation-bias).  
* **GOVERN 4.1** (on establishing a risk-aware culture): This Task designs the operator interface against passive monitoring, placing active verification steps at high-consequence boundaries so that trust in an AI output stays deliberate; it does not address the alert fatigue that too many such checkpoints would cause. For that, see for example [Task 4.4: Attention Governance and Alert/Alarm Flood Mitigation](#task-4.4:-attention-governance-and-alert/alarm-flood-mitigation).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Who provides the time away from operating duties, the trainers, and any simulator that this Task calls for?  
* Where that resourcing is not available, how much reliance on the SI system is accepted, and what risk remains?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Real-Time System Operations](https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/our-work/white-papers/whitepaper-ai-and-ml-in-real-time-system-operations.pdf), White Paper Revision 1, November 2024, from the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC). In Chapter 3, Out of the Loop Syndrome extends the existing practice of maintaining reliability through a tool failure to AI systems, asking whether, if the tool failed spontaneously, operators understand the state of the system well enough to keep it operating reliably for a period of time. Automaticity describes how operators who verify a tool’s recommendations at first can, over time, shift to accepting them by habit, and cautions that remedies which force extreme attention onto operators tend to backfire.  
* **Research** [Bainbridge, L., *Ironies of Automation*, *Automatica* volume 19 number 6, 1983, pages 775 to 779](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0005109883900468). *Automatica* is the journal of the International Federation of Automatic Control, an international body whose members are national control engineering organizations. A seminal paper on the human factors of automated process control. Its subject is the process-control computers of 1983, and the mechanisms it identifies are relevant to AI systems. Section 1.1.1 sets out why manual skills decay when unused, so that “a formerly experienced operator who has been monitoring an automated process may now be an inexperienced one”, and section 2.3 discusses what maintaining them requires, including hands-on control periods and simulator practice.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 1270, Towards a Standard for Identifying and Managing Bias in Artificial Intelligence](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.1270), March 2022, from NIST. The Glossary defines automation complacency as humans over-relying on automated systems or having their skills attenuated by that over-reliance, and Fig. 2 lists it among individual human biases. Section 3.3.1 describes how experts may lean on the presumed objectivity of automation. The definition covers both halves of this Task: the complacency and the skills degradation.  
* **Guidance** [FAA AC 120-71B, *Standard Operating Procedures and Pilot Monitoring Duties for Flight Deck Crewmembers*](https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/advisory_circulars/index.cfm/go/document.information/documentID/1030486), 10 January 2017, from the United States Federal Aviation Administration. Paragraph 6.7, item 9, asks that pilots be trained to transition seamlessly between levels of flight guidance and flight control automation, including manual flight. Paragraph 6.9.2.2 suggests staying in the loop by mentally flying the aircraft while the autopilot flies it. Appendix A lists SAFO 13002, Manual Flight Operations, among related guidance. These are an aviation counterpart to keeping manual capability exercised under automation.

#### Implementation 3.6.1: Baseline Human Competency Retention {#implementation-3.6.1:-baseline-human-competency-retention}

Knowing which skills an SI system puts at risk, and checking those skills, gives an organization evidence, rather than an assumption, of whether manual operation remains possible. Identify and document the core operational skills (e.g., manual loop tuning, raw data interpretation, manual dispatch) that risk being eroded by day-to-day AI reliance. Incorporate periodic, audited training or, commensurate with available operational resources, simulator-based testing to verify that human operators can safely run the infrastructure without AI assistance. Existing job task analyses and operator qualification programs can supply the starting list of skills. Where possible, record operators’ proficiency in these skills before the SI system takes over the work, and set for each skill the level that the manual procedures in [Task 11.2: Define Manual and Alternative Operating Procedures for Long-Term Mission Continuity](#task-11.2:-define-manual-and-alternative-operating-procedures-for-long-term-mission-continuity) assume. Treat a fall below that level as a finding that calls for a response, such as retraining, more frequent drills or narrower reliance on the SI system.

Include personnel who joined after the AI system was adopted and may never have performed these tasks without it. For them the question is whether the skill was acquired, not whether it was retained. Confidence built while working with AI assistance is not evidence of acquisition, so verify it with the same audited training or simulator-based testing before relying on these personnel for manual operation.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which skills are preserved, and what proficiency level do the manual procedures assume for each?

**References:**

* **Research** [AI adoption in the education system: International insights and policy considerations for Italy](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/ai-adoption-in-the-education-system_69bd0a4a-en.html), OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 52, December 2025, from the OECD Centre for Skills with Fondazione Agnelli. Section 6, under Educators’ supervision, describes learners who outsource effort to AI tutors and develop a false sense of mastery that shows only outside the tool’s parameters. The evidence is from generative AI in schools, offered for the mechanism this Implementation guards against in new personnel.

#### Implementation 3.6.2: Scheduled “Manual Control” Drills {#implementation-3.6.2:-scheduled-“manual-control”-drills}

Regular drills show whether people and fallback systems can actually carry the operation without the SI system, and keep the skills to do so fresh. Where appropriate, establish a routine cadence of scheduled operational drills analogous to facility “live-load generator exercising” or “blackout drills” in OT, paper-based charting and manual triage cycles in healthcare, or offline transaction reconciliation procedures in finance. During designated low-risk or off-peak windows, simulate a failure of the AI system. The failure could include a loss of availability or a combination of other failures as identified in [Task 3.1: Identify Risk Trade-offs](#task-3.1:-identify-risk-trade-offs). Include failures that are harder to recognize than a loss of availability, such as an SI system that stops updating without raising an alarm or that gives confident but incorrect advice. Include a loss of the SI system during an event that is already abnormal. Exercise the return from manual operation to SI-supported operation as well. These drills should be designed to achieve two primary outcomes:

* Technical Validation: Verify that fallback deterministic control systems and analog backups successfully assume the operational load, and that independent safety protections act as designed, without data loss or safety breaches.  
* Human Readiness: Force human operators to actively manage operations via legacy or manual methods, preserving the critical muscle memory, tactical domain skills, and situational awareness required to safely navigate a real-world, unannounced AI outage.

For applications where this is not possible within safety or regulatory constraints, they should be performed within non-production systems, see [Implementation 1.3.2: Categorization of Testing Environments](#implementation-1.3.2:-categorization-of-testing-environments) for further details.

Evaluate each drill against criteria set in advance, such as time to recognize the failure, time to reach stable manual control and errors made, and compare the results with the levels set under [Implementation 3.6.1: Baseline Human Competency Retention](#implementation-3.6.1:-baseline-human-competency-retention). Record findings and follow-up actions in an after action report. Treat a sustained decline, or a fallback that cannot carry the load, as a finding to act on, for example by narrowing reliance on the SI system or recording the residual risk. Where safety allows, some drills can be unannounced to the operators taking part, with a controller able to restore the SI system at once. Spread participation across shifts and crews, so that readiness is not demonstrated by the same few people.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* How often are drills run, on the live system or in a non-production environment?  
* Are any drills unannounced, and with what safeguards?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v2r1, Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v2r1), from NIST. Table D-4 describes the Self-Challenge approach to Coordinated Protection as affecting mission or business processes or system elements adversely in a controlled manner to validate the effectiveness of protections, with examples including role-based training exercises, fault injection, testing automated incident response and tabletop exercises, which is what a scheduled drill that takes the AI system away during a low-risk window does. Its discussion calls for such exercises throughout the system life cycle and with different scopes.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-84, *Guide to Test, Training, and Exercise Programs for IT Plans and Capabilities*](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-84), September 2006, from NIST. Section 2 describes functional exercises, which allow personnel to validate their operational readiness in a simulated operational environment. Section 5.5 describes the after action report that documents findings and recommendations from a functional exercise, and the action items assigned from it. This bears on evaluating each drill and following up on what it finds.

#### Implementation 3.6.3: Cognitive Engagement by Design {#implementation-3.6.3:-cognitive-engagement-by-design}

Interface design that asks for active judgment at the right moments helps operators keep thinking for themselves rather than approving SI output by habit. Design the human-system or human-machine interface (HSI or HMI), and any other point at which a person reviews or approves SI output, including human-in-the-loop approval steps in agentic workflows that have no dedicated HMI, to discourage passive monitoring. Consider active human verification step-throughs or plausibility checks for truly high-consequence AI recommendations to counter the psychological tendency of operators to automatically trust machine outputs (automation bias). To balance active human validation against cognitive exhaustion, these checkpoints can be reserved for high-consequence operational boundary thresholds. They should be deployed flexibly, utilizing the mixed-initiative and calm technology design choices referenced in [Implementation 4.4.4: Applying Consolidation and Low-Cognitive-Load Design Techniques](#implementation-4.4.4:-applying-consolidation-and-low-cognitive-load-design-techniques) to limit how far alert fatigue drives superficial operator compliance. [Implementation 3.6.4: Monitor Aggregate Engagement Indicators](#implementation-3.6.4:-monitor-aggregate-engagement-indicators) covers measuring whether these design choices keep personnel engaged.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which review and approval points get active verification steps? (see the Safe versus Safe tension in [Task 3.6: Mitigate Automation Complacency and Skills Degradation](#task-3.6:-mitigate-automation-complacency-and-skills-degradation))

**References:**

* **Research** [Endsley, M. R. and Kiris, E. O., *The Out-of-the-Loop Performance Problem and Level of Control in Automation*, *Human Factors* volume 37 number 2, 1995, pages 381 to 394](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1518/001872095779064555), from the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society. In an experiment, people who had worked with an automated decision aid were slower to decide after it failed. The authors attribute the loss of situation awareness mainly to a shift from active to passive processing of information. They report that the level of operator control is a major factor in moderating that loss. This bears on designing the interface against passive monitoring.  
* **Guidance** [OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/), Version 2026, December 2025, from the Agentic Security Initiative of the OWASP Gen AI Security Project, a volunteer community project of the Open Worldwide Application Security Project. ASI09, Human-Agent Trust Exploitation, describes people approving agent actions without independent validation, with automation bias making abuse look legitimate. Its Adaptive Trust Calibration mitigation adjusts the required human oversight to contextual risk and uses confidence-weighted cues that prompt users to question high-impact actions. This bears on extending this Implementation to approval steps in agentic workflows.

#### Implementation 3.6.4: Monitor Aggregate Engagement Indicators {#implementation-3.6.4:-monitor-aggregate-engagement-indicators}

Aggregate engagement indicators can show an organization where its interface and workload are wearing down operators’ attention, before a drill or an incident does. Consider tracking aggregate indicators of engagement at the review and approval points designed under [Implementation 3.6.3: Cognitive Engagement by Design](#implementation-3.6.3:-cognitive-engagement-by-design), such as the share of recommendations accepted without modification and the time spent reviewing before approval. Many of these can be drawn from the decision-level records kept under [Practice 10: Implement Multi-Tiered SI System Logging and Audit Capabilities](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities). Use them to adjust the interface and workload, rather than to assess individual operators, and agree their scope with the personnel concerned. A sustained shift, such as acceptance rising toward every recommendation or review times falling, can also prompt an earlier drill under [Implementation 3.6.2: Scheduled “Manual Control” Drills](#implementation-3.6.2:-scheduled-“manual-control”-drills) or a check of the skills identified under [Implementation 3.6.1: Baseline Human Competency Retention](#implementation-3.6.1:-baseline-human-competency-retention).

Whether such indicators are collected, who may see them and how the resulting record is governed is for the organization to decide, within any regulatory or contractual obligations, such as privacy law and labor agreements. Aggregate indicators can show where the design is not keeping people engaged. They also produce a record drawn from how individuals work, which can discourage candid use if its scope is not bounded. Record the scope agreed and who may see the indicators.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Are aggregate engagement indicators collected, who may see them, and how is the record governed?

### Task 3.7: Govern and Mitigate Risks from Unauthorized, Transient, and “Shadow SI” Systems {#task-3.7:-govern-and-mitigate-risks-from-unauthorized,-transient,-and-“shadow-si”-systems}

Bringing unrecorded SI tools under review helps an organization account for SI capabilities that could otherwise act on its systems and data without appearing in any risk assessment. Establish organizational policies, procurement gates, and contractor onboarding workflows to detect, restrict, and manage risks associated with unvetted or unauthorized SI systems, locally run models obtained outside procurement, including freely available open-source models, and agentic tools brought into the operational environment by internal personnel or third-party contractors. In combination with [Practice 7: Manage Internal SI Supply Chain and Data Provenance](#practice-7:-manage-internal-si-supply-chain-and-data-provenance), this Task helps bring any AI capability utilized within the facility’s physical or logical boundary into the organization’s risk profile and configuration management baselines.

Transient SI systems, such as short-lived agents, pilots and experiments, are within scope while they run. Record them when they start and set an end date. When they end, withdraw the authority they held, as in [Task 13.2: Withdraw All Authority and Confirm the Result](#task-13.2:-withdraw-all-authority-and-confirm-the-result). Unvetted SI tools on hosts that can reach control systems, such as engineering workstations, maintenance laptops and remote access hosts, warrant particular attention. In the electric sector, for example, sharing operational reports with an external generative AI service raises concern about disclosure of Critical Energy Infrastructure Information (CEII). Control logic or configurations generated by such tools have not been through the verification in [Practice 12: Independently Verify SI-Generated Operational Logic and Artifacts Across Their Lifecycle](#practice-12:-independently-verify-si-generated-operational-logic-and-artifacts-across-their-lifecycle). Organizations with established arrangements for shadow IT and unapproved software can extend those arrangements to SI tools.

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Secure:** Contributes visibility of AI capability that entered the environment outside procurement: contractor attestation, detection of traffic to public AI endpoints, and scanning for unapproved applications and local models, so an AI system operating outside the credential directory becomes known. This Task does not cover denying those entities access, which [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools) covers.  
* **Privacy-Enhanced:** Contributes the point at which an undeclared external AI service becomes visible, where condition reports, operational records or facility information may otherwise leave through an endpoint nobody cataloged. This Task does not cover governing the dataflows of services the organization has authorized, which [Task 6.3: Identify and Control Dataflows Across the SI Supply Chain](#task-6.3:-identify-and-control-dataflows-across-the-si-supply-chain) covers.  
* **Valid:** Contributes the precondition for evaluating an SI tool at all. A tool brought in without a formal evaluation process has not been tested for this use. Even if it is never connected to anything, an engineer or operator may act on what it tells them, or copy its output into a configuration or a decision. This Task does not cover performing that evaluation, which [Task 1.3: Implement Evaluation and Test Plans, Including TEVV, Across the SI Lifecycle](#task-1.3:-implement-evaluation-and-test-plans,-including-tevv,-across-the-si-lifecycle) covers.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Privacy-Enhanced:** Detection works by observing the traffic and endpoints that personnel and contractors use, so it also produces a record of how individuals work. How that record is governed, and by which function, is for the organization to decide, within any regulatory or contractual obligations. Existing workforce monitoring and privacy practice already handles comparable records, while a record of how individuals use SI tools may raise questions that practice was not written for. Record where governance of that record sits.
* **Secure:** The attestations and detection results gathered here describe which SI tools are in use, and which endpoints and hosts are watched. Someone wishing to use an unvetted tool unseen, or an attacker looking for an unmonitored route out, could use them to avoid detection. Protecting them is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Secure, Valid and Privacy-Enhanced versus themselves:** Where sanctioned tooling covers the work people need to do, restricting unvetted SI tools removes exposure, whether to attack, to untested output or to records leaving through an uncataloged service, at a modest cost. Where it leaves the need unmet, the same restriction moves the use to personal devices and accounts, which detection, logging and evaluation reach less well than the corporate network did. One way to balance this is to pair each restriction with a sanctioned route that meets the underlying need; others include a time-bounded permit for a declared tool under the attestation in [Implementation 3.7.1: SI Attestation](#implementation-3.7.1:-si-attestation), or accepting the restriction and resourcing the gap it leaves.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **GOVERN 1.6** (on building the AI inventory): This Task brings AI that entered the environment without procurement, including contractor tooling and locally run models obtained outside procurement, into the same inventory as sanctioned systems; it does not cover registration of components the organization has deliberately acquired. For those, see for example [Task 6.2: Align SI and Existing CI Asset Lifecycle Management](#task-6.2:-align-si-and-existing-ci-asset-lifecycle-management).  
* **GOVERN 6.1** (on establishing third-party risk management processes): This Task treats contractor attestation and onboarding as the point at which third-party AI use becomes declarable at all; it does not cover setting the trustworthiness and visibility requirements that a vetted vendor should meet. For those, see for example [Task 6.1: Develop Policies for SI Supply Chain Requirements](#task-6.1:-develop-policies-for-si-supply-chain-requirements).  
* **MANAGE 3.1** (on monitoring and responding to third-party risks): This Task detects use of external commercial AI services by logging traffic to known API endpoints and scanning for unapproved models and containers; it does not cover monitoring the actions of AI entities that hold authorized credentials. For those, see for example [Task 5.4: Implement Continuous Monitoring of SI Entities Against Access and Action Boundaries and Expectations](#task-5.4:-implement-continuous-monitoring-of-si-entities-against-access-and-action-boundaries-and-expectations).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which restrictions on unvetted SI tools apply, and what sanctioned route meets the need each one leaves? (see the Secure, Valid and Privacy-Enhanced versus themselves tension)  
* Who owns detection of unvetted SI use and follow-up of what is found, given that it falls between IT security, business units, and contractors?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Section 6.3.1, Anomalies and Events, lists “Unauthorized devices connecting to the network” and “Unauthorized communication to external IPs” among events OT detection should recognize. The OT discussion of CM-7(5) in Appendix F.7.5 notes that the set of applications that run in OT is relatively static, making allowlisting practical.  
* **Guidance** [AI Shared Responsibility Framework, version 1.0](https://www.coalitionforsecureai.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/CoSAI-Shared-Responsibility-Framework.pdf), Workstream 2: Preparing Defenders for a Changing Cybersecurity Landscape, from the Coalition for Secure AI, an OASIS Open Project. Page 4 names the condition this Task exists for: unsanctioned AI usage thriving in the gray areas between IT security, business units and external vendors, where, left unassigned, no single group monitors for rogue usage or owns the risk of sensitive data exposure. Page 15 gives a detection list covering discovery of ungoverned AI tool usage, network monitoring for AI service API calls and web usage, departmental AI spending and subscription tracking, and risk assessment of what is found, alongside criteria for when tool usage should escalate into a governed enterprise system. Its responsibility matrix places accountability for shadow AI detection on the operating organization rather than on any provider.  
* **Guidance** [Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Real-Time System Operations](https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/our-work/white-papers/whitepaper-ai-and-ml-in-real-time-system-operations.pdf), White Paper Revision 1, November 2024, from the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC). In Chapter 3, under Informational Leakage, it reports concerns raised in interviews and surveys about Critical Energy Infrastructure Information (CEII) being sent to or returned by generative AI systems. It notes that a generative tool may include information in a report that an operator would not have wanted there. This bears on the CEII example in this Task.

#### Implementation 3.7.1: SI Attestation {#implementation-3.7.1:-si-attestation}

Consider requiring third-party contractors and integrators to sign a formal attestation declaring any AI-backed analytical tools, Large Language Models (LLMs), or automated code/configuration generation software utilized during their contract period. These should be cataloged in the organization’s AI system inventory and subject to appropriate risk management controls as described in [Implementation 7.1.1: Create and Maintain a Master SI Asset List](#implementation-7.1.1:-create-and-maintain-a-master-si-asset-list) (regarding inventory) and [Task 1.3](#task-1.3:-implement-evaluation-and-test-plans,-including-tevv,-across-the-si-lifecycle) and [Practice 5](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools) and [Practice 7](#practice-7:-manage-internal-si-supply-chain-and-data-provenance) (regarding controls). The attestation contributes visibility, so that the organization can determine whether and how the SI use could affect operations ([Implementation 3.1.1: Identify SI System Decision Points and Potential Outcomes of SI System Errors](#implementation-3.1.1:-identify-si-system-decision-points-and-potential-outcomes-of-si-system-errors)) and route it to controls proportionate to its consequences ([Implementation 3.1.3: Define Acceptable Risk Thresholds and Associated Control Responses](#implementation-3.1.3:-define-acceptable-risk-thresholds-and-associated-control-responses)). The attestation does not by itself authorize the use. Contractors and integrators can be asked to sign it because it can be made a term of their contract. Staff can instead make a periodic declaration under the organization’s acceptable-use policy. Vendors are covered by the disclosure obligations in [Implementation 6.1.1: Add SI Disclosure to Existing Procurement Policies](#implementation-6.1.1:-add-si-disclosure-to-existing-procurement-policies) rather than by a separate attestation. How the first round of attestation treats existing undeclared use, and how later discrepancies are followed up, is for the organization to decide, within any regulatory or contractual obligations. A period in which existing use can be declared without penalty, and follow-up that does not penalize honest disclosure, encourage the declarations the attestation depends on. Sanctions for undeclared use deter it, but they can also discourage disclosure. Record the approach and the reason for it. Early in such a program, a rise in declared or detected use can indicate improving visibility rather than growing risk. Compare attestations with the results of [Implementation 3.7.2: SI Use Detection](#implementation-3.7.2:-si-use-detection), and follow up on differences in either direction.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Who signs an attestation, and who makes a periodic declaration instead?  
* How is existing undeclared use treated in the first round, and how are later discrepancies followed up?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-161 Revision 1, Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management Practices for Systems and Organizations](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/161/r1/upd1/final), from NIST. Section 3.1.2, The Role of C-SCRM in the Acquisition Process, lists self-attestation among acceptable methods for validating supplier adherence, alongside certifications, site visits and third-party assessments. It asks that the type and rigor of the method be commensurate with the criticality of what is acquired. This bears on using the attestation to route an SI use to proportionate controls.  
* **Commentary** [Artificial Intelligence Model Risk Management: Observations from a Thematic Review](https://www.mas.gov.sg/publications/monographs-or-information-paper/2024/artificial-intelligence-model-risk-management), Information Paper, December 2024, from the Monetary Authority of Singapore, drawn from a review of banks. Paragraph 5.1.2 reports that control functions often lead the identification of AI, for example by setting up attestation processes or acting as the final arbiter of whether AI is being used. Section 5 also describes processes to keep AI inventories complete, capturing the approved scope of use. These bear on feeding attestations into the SI system inventory.

#### Implementation 3.7.2: SI Use Detection {#implementation-3.7.2:-si-use-detection}

Detection can find SI use that declarations miss, whether brought in by people or embedded in equipment. Incorporate the detection and logging of traffic to known public commercial AI API endpoints. Include scanning for unapproved AI applications, including containerized applications and software models. Monitor for unusual high-volume traffic that may indicate an unauthorized AI system ingesting data. Reviews of cloud accounts, SI service subscriptions and spending, and issued API keys can reveal SI services that traffic monitoring misses. In OT zones that are not expected to make outbound connections, consider alerting on any connection to an SI service endpoint rather than only logging it. Not all unvetted SI is brought in by people: smart sensors, vision systems and industrial gateways can carry embedded inference engines that arrive through ordinary procurement, do not appear in IT asset inventories and make no calls to external SI endpoints, so identifying them may require device-level inventory and the vendor disclosures in [Implementation 6.1.1: Add SI Disclosure to Existing Procurement Policies](#implementation-6.1.1:-add-si-disclosure-to-existing-procurement-policies) rather than inference from network traffic.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* In which OT zones does any connection to an SI service endpoint raise an alert?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control enhancement CM-8(3), Automated Unauthorized Component Detection, detects unauthorized hardware, software and firmware components and sets actions such as isolating them. Its discussion cautions that some types of components, such as IoT devices and sensors, cannot host the software agents that detection mechanisms may depend on. This bears on scanning for unapproved SI applications and on device-level visibility of embedded inference engines.  
* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by CISA. Section 3.2 asks operators to collect flow logs and access logs for AI endpoints and to track data egress by asset and identity. Section 2.3 notes that some OT devices now come with built-in AI technology, and asks operators to require vendors to explain how AI is embedded in their products. These bear on the traffic-based and the device-level detection in this Implementation.

### Task 3.8: Scope and Map the Expanded SI Attack Surface and Risk Surface {#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface}

To show what exposure an SI deployment adds and where controls are needed, catalog the AI Risk Surface introduced by AI deployment across all lifecycle stages. It includes both the adversarial exploitation vectors (the AI Attack Surface) and the non-adversarial, systemic vulnerability vectors. Evaluate how SI systems, whose outputs can vary or fail in ways that are hard to predict, expand operational risk beyond traditional cybersecurity boundaries to encompass all SICI Trustworthiness Characteristics described in the Trustworthiness Characteristics table\. Who carries out this evaluation is for the organization to decide. It calls for technical knowledge of the SI system, and also for a view across the Trustworthiness Characteristics, which can be wider than any one technical function covers. Record who performed it. For example, an agent that reads incoming vendor email and can raise work orders can be steered by instructions placed in that email, a path that perimeter defenses see only as ordinary email.

To enable the evaluation of the reachable risk surface of third-party AI components, vendors should provide the disclosures, described in [Implementation 6.1.5: Operational SI Hazard Reachability Disclosures](#implementation-6.1.5:-operational-si-hazard-reachability-disclosures), to formally declare which upstream model limitations are operationally contained before deployment.

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Secure:** Contributes the catalog of AI-specific adversarial exposure: the interfaces at which a crafted input can reach inference, from direct and indirect prompt injection to training data poisoning, model extraction and tool invocation. This Task does not cover placing controls at the interfaces it finds. For those, see [Task 3.2](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs) and [Practice 5](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools).  
* **Safe:** Contributes the half of the picture where harm arises with no attacker present: feedback loops or distribution shifts driving controllers out of limits, plausible hallucinations in generated logic, and opaque pathways that slow a response. This Task does not cover weighing the consequence of each exposure, which [Task 3.1: Identify Risk Trade-offs](#task-3.1:-identify-risk-trade-offs) covers.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Secure:** The catalog states where an AI system can be reached and which hazards a deployment has left reachable, which an adversary who obtains it could use to choose where to attack. How the catalog is classified and handled is for the organization to decide, within any regulatory or contractual obligations, under its existing information classification and handling practice. Wide access helps those who have to act on it, and every additional reader is another route by which it can reach an adversary. Record the handling decided on.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Safe versus Safe:** Where a hazard has been shown unreachable in this deployment and the control that makes it so is stable, treating it as contained lets attention go to the deviations that can occur. Where autonomy is widened, one agent is chained to another, or the operating environment moves, the same hazard can become reachable while the record still shows it contained. One way to balance this is the periodic coupling analysis in [Implementation 3.8.3: Dynamic Risk Surface Coupling Analysis](#implementation-3.8.3:-dynamic-risk-surface-coupling-analysis), which treats a widened risk surface as a trigger to re-evaluate the guardrails a containment claim rested on; others include time-bounding a containment claim, or re-confirming it whenever guardrail scope changes.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MAP 4.1** (on understanding AI component-level risks): This Task catalogs the adversarial vectors that can reach AI inference logic, including direct and indirect prompt injection, data poisoning, model extraction and malicious tool invocation; it does not cover obtaining the vendor statements that show which upstream model limitations remain reachable in deployment. For those, see for example [Implementation 6.1.5: Operational SI Hazard Reachability Disclosures](#implementation-6.1.5:-operational-si-hazard-reachability-disclosures).  
* **MEASURE 2.7** (on measuring security and resiliency): This Task covers the attack and risk surface that a security and resilience evaluation is scoped against, which is the identification MEASURE 2.7 refers back to the MAP function for; it does not cover carrying out that evaluation. For that, see for example [Task 2.3: Establish Protocols for and Regularly Perform Systematic and Achievable Testing, Evaluation, Validation, and Verification (TEVV)](#task-2.3:-establish-protocols-for-and-regularly-perform-systematic-and-achievable-testing,-evaluation,-validation,-and-verification-\(tevv\)).  
* **GOVERN 1.2** (on defining trustworthy AI policies): This Task turns each Trustworthiness Characteristic into a category of operational exposure to be mapped, so that safety, explainability, privacy, fairness and accuracy are examined as vulnerability surfaces rather than as aspirations; it does not cover defining the characteristic set or the terms used for it.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Who carries out the risk-surface evaluation?  
* How is the catalog classified and handled?  
* Where the evaluation needs expertise the organization does not hold, where does it come from, and which characteristics are covered less thoroughly as a result?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Mitigating Artificial Intelligence (AI) Risk: Safety and Security Guidelines for Critical Infrastructure Owners and Operators](https://www.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/2024-04/24_0426_dhs_ai-ci-safety-security-guidelines-508c.pdf), April 2024, from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. Its cross-sector analysis sets out three categories of system-level AI risk: attacks using AI, attacks targeting AI systems, and failures in AI design and implementation. Appendix A lists subcategories of each, including brittleness, inscrutability, overreliance by human operators and statistical bias among design and implementation failures. The second and third categories correspond to the attack surface and the non-adversarial risk surface this Task catalogs.

#### Implementation 3.8.1: SI Attack Surface Mapping (Adversarial Exposure) {#implementation-3.8.1:-si-attack-surface-mapping-\(adversarial-exposure\)}

A catalog of the ways an adversary can reach an SI system supports decisions about which interfaces to remove and where to defend the rest. Identify and catalog technical AI-specific attack vectors, such as direct and indirect prompt injection, training data poisoning, evasion, including physically realizable attacks on what a camera or sensor observes, model extraction, context window manipulation, and malicious tool/API invocation. Document all interfaces where adversarial inputs can reach AI inference logic, including tool outputs, the tool and agent descriptions advertised by connected servers, and content from nominally trusted sources such as documentation and instruction files that organizations publish for agents to read, and consider whether each is needed ([Implementation 7.2.4: Select and Prepare the Inputs Each SI System Receives](#implementation-7.2.4:-select-and-prepare-the-inputs-each-si-system-receives)). A connected server can change a tool’s description or behavior after it has been reviewed. Consider pinning reviewed tool definitions, for example by content hash, and treating a change as a new interface to assess. Organizations with established attack surface analysis and threat modeling can build on it here, extending it to interfaces specific to SI systems, such as prompts, retrieved content, and tool descriptions.

For each interface, record who can write to it, which trust boundary it crosses and what the SI system can do with what arrives there. Include the channels through which model weights and updates arrive, and the system prompts and guardrail configurations held under [Task 7.3: Manage Version Control and Logging for Internal SI Safety Mechanisms](#task-7.3:-manage-version-control-and-logging-for-internal-si-safety-mechanisms). Trace each viable path to its worst plausible consequence. For example, an injection that can only alter a summary read by an engineer differs from one that can lead to a setpoint change. Where a path continues past the SI system into OT, the adversary behaviors cataloged in MITRE ATT\&CK for ICS can help describe its later steps.

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025), March 2025, from NIST. Section 2.2 covers evasion attacks, and section 2.2.1 describes physically realizable ones, such as stickers applied to road signs to evade a sign classifier. Section 2.3 covers poisoning attacks on predictive systems and section 2.4.4 model extraction. Section 3.2 covers data and model poisoning in the generative AI supply chain, and sections 3.3 and 3.4 cover direct prompting attacks and indirect prompt injection. Section 3.5 covers agents that select and call tools, where a prompt injection can become an action taken in the environment, and notes that security research on agents is still at an early stage. Published counterparts for most of the vectors this Implementation asks to be cataloged, with the mitigations reported for each where the taxonomy has them.  
* **Guidance** [MITRE ATLAS, maintained by MITRE, a not-for-profit organization in the United States that operates federally funded research and development centers](https://atlas.mitre.org/). A matrix of tactics and techniques observed in attacks on SI-enabled systems, structured after the same organization’s ATT\&CK matrix for enterprise systems. Organized by the stage of an attack rather than by the kind of attack, which is the axis that matches documenting the interfaces at which an adversarial input reaches inference.  
* **Guidance** [OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/), Version 2026, December 2025, from the Agentic Security Initiative of the OWASP Gen AI Security Project, a volunteer community project of the Open Worldwide Application Security Project. ASI04, Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities, notes that agentic systems often load tools and agent personas at runtime, creating a live supply chain. Its examples include tool-descriptor injection: instructions hidden in a tool’s metadata that the host agent takes as trusted guidance. Its mitigations include pinning tools and configurations by content hash, with rollback on drift. These bear on tool descriptions as input paths and on pinning reviewed definitions.  
* **Guidance** [Model Context Protocol Specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/), revision 2026-07-28, from the Model Context Protocol project. Under Security and Trust & Safety, Tool Safety states that tools represent arbitrary code execution. It adds that descriptions of tool behavior, such as annotations, should be considered untrusted unless obtained from a trusted server. This bears on treating the tool descriptions advertised by connected servers as an input path.

#### Implementation 3.8.2: System-Wide Risk Surface Mapping (Non-Adversarial Trustworthiness Exposure) {#implementation-3.8.2:-system-wide-risk-surface-mapping-\(non-adversarial-trustworthiness-exposure\)}

Map system vulnerabilities across all SICI Trustworthiness Characteristics where non-deterministic AI behavior can cause physical, operational, or administrative harm without an active attacker. For example:

* Safety & Resilience: Unintended feedback loops or distribution shifts driving physical controllers out of safe limits.  
* Explainability & Forensic Auditability: Opaque decision pathways that impede real-time operator situational awareness or post-event root-cause analysis.  
* Privacy & Data Protection: Systemic ingestion or leakage of sensitive telemetry, facility blueprints, or personally identifiable information (PII) into retrieval repositories or prompts.  
* Fairness & Bias: Algorithmic distortion causing unequal resource dispatch, asymmetric hazard detection across different equipment ages/vendors, or biased administrative reviews.  
* Accuracy & Reliability: Plausible hallucinations in report summaries, diagnostic feeds, or AI-generated execution logic.  
* Resilience & Concentration: Many organizations relying on the same model, vendor, or hosted service, so that a single silent update or failure produces a correlated, sector-wide event that no single organization’s risk assessment can see. Shared reliance can also lower the quality of decisions in normal operation, without any single triggering event, and the effect can be hard to notice while it occurs (see Kleinberg and Raghavan 2021). Findings of this kind can be shared through [Implementation 8.6.4: Share De-Identified Incident Records for Collective Learning](#implementation-8.6.4:-share-de-identified-incident-records-for-collective-learning).

Where the sector already uses a structured hazard analysis method, such as a hazard and operability study (HAZOP), failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA) or system-theoretic process analysis (STPA), consider extending it to include the SI system as a component whose outputs can be wrong, late, missing, overconfident or outside their intended scope. Link each hazard found to the safeguards that address it, and record where there is none.

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 600-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1), July 2024, from NIST. Section 2 counts ecosystem-level risk among the scopes at which risk can arise, with algorithmic monocultures as its example. Its footnote describes these as repeated use of the same model or algorithm leading to correlated failures because multiple actors rely on it. Suggested action GV-1.3-005 names algorithmic monoculture among risks to track. This bears on the concentration example in this Implementation.  
* **Research** [Kleinberg, J. and Raghavan, M., *Algorithmic monoculture and social welfare*, *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences* volume 118 number 22, 2021](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2018340118). It models many decision-makers relying on the same algorithm, with examples from employment and lending. Beyond the familiar risk of correlated failures in adverse conditions, it shows that shared reliance can lower the overall quality of decisions in normal operation, even when the shared algorithm is more accurate for each user alone. The Conclusion adds that such effects might be difficult to notice while they occur. This bears on the concentration example in this Implementation.  
* **Commentary** [Artificial Intelligence Model Risk Management: Observations from a Thematic Review](https://www.mas.gov.sg/publications/monographs-or-information-paper/2024/artificial-intelligence-model-risk-management), Information Paper, December 2024, from the Monetary Authority of Singapore, drawn from a review of banks. Paragraph 7.2.1 counts among the added risks of third-party and generative AI the concentration risks that arise when multiple financial institutions, or even third-party providers, rely on common underlying generative AI models. This bears on the concentration example, as observed in one sector.

#### Implementation 3.8.3: Dynamic Risk Surface Coupling Analysis {#implementation-3.8.3:-dynamic-risk-surface-coupling-analysis}

Because an SI system, its uses, and its operating environment can change after deployment, regular review helps an organization notice when the system’s risk surface has grown or shrunk. Conduct periodic evaluations of how changes in the operating environment, data distribution drift, increased agentic autonomy, or multi-agent chaining expand or contract the system’s risk surface over time. Include interactions between the attack surface and the non-adversarial risk surface. An adversary can steer inputs toward conditions in which the SI system is known to perform poorly. A non-adversarial change, such as a new operating mode, a replaced sensor or an updated model, can open or widen an attack path. Adding a tool, a permission or a data source to an agent can enlarge both surfaces at once. Have risk surface expansion trigger re-evaluation of independent guardrails, automatically where practical and otherwise through the reassessment triggers in [Implementation 3.9.2: Define Decision Authority and Reassessment Triggers](#implementation-3.9.2:-define-decision-authority-and-reassessment-triggers), ([Task 3.2: Implement Independent Guardrails for SI Outputs](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs)) and of the oversight thresholds established under [Implementation 4.5.1: Define Engineering Time-Constant Thresholds](#implementation-4.5.1:-define-engineering-time-constant-thresholds), since a widened risk surface can move a path across a threshold that was previously satisfied. Autonomy can also widen without a deliberate decision. For example, oversight can relax gradually after a run of successes, through bulk approvals or relaxed policies, so include changes in how oversight is exercised in practice among the changes evaluated.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* How often is the coupling analysis repeated, and how long does a containment claim stand without re-confirmation? (see the Safe versus Safe tension in [Task 3.8: Scope and Map the Expanded SI Attack Surface and Risk Surface](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface))

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v2r1, Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v2r1), from NIST. Table 2 discusses, under the Adapt goal, changes in the technical environment, naming artificial intelligence among them, and in the operational environment, and states that analyses of such changes and of interactions between them can reveal how they modify the attack surface or introduce fragility, which is the coupling analysis this Implementation performs as the AI system’s environment and autonomy change.  
* **Guidance** [OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/), Version 2026, December 2025, from the Agentic Security Initiative of the OWASP Gen AI Security Project, a volunteer community project of the Open Worldwide Application Security Project. ASI08, Cascading Failures, describes a single fault propagating across agents, tools and workflows. Its observable symptoms include rapid fan-out and feedback loops between agents. Among its examples is a governance drift cascade, in which human oversight weakens after repeated success and bulk approvals or policy relaxations propagate configuration drift across agents. These bear on multi-agent chaining and on the gradual widening of autonomy this Implementation evaluates.

### Task 3.9: Assess and Document Organizational Readiness for Each SI-Enabled Capability {#task-3.9:-assess-and-document-organizational-readiness-for-each-si-enabled-capability}

Determine whether the governance and oversight mechanisms applicable to an SI-enabled capability are executable for the specific capability and operating context. Make this determination before deployment, and again whenever a material change occurs. For the conditions that trigger reassessment, see [Implementation 3.9.2: Define Decision Authority and Reassessment Triggers](#implementation-3.9.2:-define-decision-authority-and-reassessment-triggers). This assessment is capability- and context-specific rather than a general organizational maturity assessment. This does not preclude also reviewing broader readiness for the same capability, such as training, procedures, safeguards and logging. This Task adds the question of whether its governance can be carried out. An organization may have established AI policies and governance structures while still lacking the accountability, authority, escalation paths, operational capability, or enforceability necessary to govern a particular SI-enabled capability. This is distinct from [Task 4.5: Define Operational Regimes for Human-on-the-Loop and Human-Out-of-the-Loop Operation](#task-4.5:-define-operational-regimes-for-human-on-the-loop-and-human-out-of-the-loop-operation), which concerns whether a person can intervene in a single machine-speed action as it happens. This Task concerns whether a governance decision, once made, can be enforced at all, be it before deployment, throughout operation, or after material change. The conditions under which a capability is retired, and the authority to decide, are identified under [Implementation 13.1.1: Identify Retirement Triggers, Including Those Outside the Organization’s Control](#implementation-13.1.1:-identify-retirement-triggers,-including-those-outside-the-organization’s-control) and recorded, with the deciding authority, under [Implementation 3.9.2: Define Decision Authority and Reassessment Triggers](#implementation-3.9.2:-define-decision-authority-and-reassessment-triggers). Record the determination, including what was assessed, the gaps that remain, and any conditions placed on operation, such as advisory use only or a limited scope. Where a gap remains, the capability may proceed only under a recorded decision by the role that holds authority to accept that risk under the same Implementation. That decision can rest on a compensating measure, or on reducing the capability’s scope or delegated authority to what can be governed.

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Accountable:** Contributes the demonstration that a governance decision reaches the system’s operating state: that restriction, suspension, rollback or reduction of delegated authority takes effect, within a window set against consequence, confirmable without relying on the capability’s own report, and holding until an authorized decision changes it. This Task does not cover intervention in a single machine-speed action as it happens. [Task 4.1: Establish “Break-Glass” Intervention Procedures](#task-4.1:-establish-“break-glass”-intervention-procedures) covers procedures while [Task 4.5: Define Operational Regimes for Human-on-the-Loop and Human-Out-of-the-Loop Operation](#task-4.5:-define-operational-regimes-for-human-on-the-loop-and-human-out-of-the-loop-operation) covers the feasibility of intervention.  
* **Valid:** Contributes a readiness determination made for this capability in this operating context, re-opened when the capability, use case, delegated authority or environment materially changes, so the determination does not outlive the conditions it was made under. This Task does not cover determining whether the AI system suits the deployment, which [Task 1.3: Implement Evaluation and Test Plans, Including TEVV, Across the SI Lifecycle](#task-1.3:-implement-evaluation-and-test-plans,-including-tevv,-across-the-si-lifecycle) covers.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Reliable:** Demonstrating that a suspension or a rollback takes effect means exercising it, and exercising it on a live deployment interrupts the function it governs. [Implementation 1.3.2: Categorization of Testing Environments](#implementation-1.3.2:-categorization-of-testing-environments) categorizes the environments in which such exercises belong, and names the applications for which an authorized outage window is the safer place.  
* **Secure:** A readiness determination that is slow or demanding for low-consequence capabilities can delay their approved use and lead personnel to adopt SI tools outside it, which [Task 3.7: Govern and Mitigate Risks from Unauthorized, Transient, and “Shadow SI” Systems](#task-3.7:-govern-and-mitigate-risks-from-unauthorized,-transient,-and-“shadow-si”-systems) addresses. Scaling the depth of the determination to the delegated authority and the consequence, as [Implementation 3.9.2: Define Decision Authority and Reassessment Triggers](#implementation-3.9.2:-define-decision-authority-and-reassessment-triggers) asks, can limit this. The readiness record itself lists the gaps that remain and the conditions placed on operation. An attacker could use it to find a capability whose restriction or suspension cannot yet be enforced. Protecting it is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Accountable versus Resilient:** Where the restricted capability is not the one keeping a service running, authority that holds until an authorized decision reverses it is the protection intended. Where it is, a restriction that cannot be lifted quickly extends the loss of that service. One way to balance this is to settle the restoration decision and its authority at the same time as the restriction, so reversal is an authorized path rather than an exception; others include scoping the restriction to the function at issue rather than the whole capability, which the range of decisions in [Implementation 3.9.5: Demonstrate Operational Enforceability](#implementation-3.9.5:-demonstrate-operational-enforceability) anticipates, or carrying the service on the continuity arrangements in [Practice 11: Maintain SI-Aware Mission Continuity and Disaster Recovery Planning](#practice-11:-maintain-si-aware-mission-continuity-and-disaster-recovery-planning) while the restriction holds.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **GOVERN 2.1** (on establishing roles and responsibilities): This Task identifies an accountable owner for the SI-enabled capability, and tests that escalation paths terminate with a role empowered to act rather than only to receive or record; it does not cover the operator-level pathways for responding to individual AI outputs. For those, see for example [Implementation 3.3.3: Actionable Operator Decision & Escalation Pathways](#implementation-3.3.3:-actionable-operator-decision-&-escalation-pathways).  
* **GOVERN 1.3** (on establishing risk management processes): This Task scales the depth of governance to the authority delegated to a capability and to the consequence of its actions, and re-opens the readiness determination on material change; it does not cover setting the thresholds that place a capability in a consequence class. For those, see for example [Implementation 3.1.3: Define Acceptable Risk Thresholds and Associated Control Responses](#implementation-3.1.3:-define-acceptable-risk-thresholds-and-associated-control-responses).  
* **MANAGE 2.4** (on decommissioning or superseding AI systems): This Task requires evidence, before deployment, that a decision to restrict, suspend, revert or reduce a capability’s delegated authority can be made effective, verifiable and durable in the running system; it does not cover the orderly removal of an AI component at end of life. For that, see for example [Task 13.2: Withdraw All Authority and Confirm the Result](#task-13.2:-withdraw-all-authority-and-confirm-the-result).  
* **GOVERN 1.5** (on establishing monitoring and review processes): This Task defines the material changes that should re-open a readiness determination, which gives the review an event trigger rather than only a calendar; it does not cover setting a frequency for periodic review.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Where a gap remains, does the capability proceed, and under what conditions? (see the Accountable versus Resilient tension)  
* Who performs the readiness assessment, and how independent is that person or team from those who want to deploy the capability?

#### Implementation 3.9.1: Establish Accountable Ownership {#implementation-3.9.1:-establish-accountable-ownership}

A named owner and deputy help make sure that someone can decide about an SI-enabled capability when a decision is needed. Identify an accountable owner for the SI-enabled capability and for the governance decisions about it. Document who is responsible for these decisions across the SI lifecycle. This includes deciding whether the capability may be deployed, may continue operating, or may operate under modified conditions. Transfer ownership explicitly when the owner changes role, or when the capability passes from a project team to operations. The owner needs the visibility, time, resources, access, support, and authority to make these decisions, not only the title. [Implementation 3.9.3](#implementation-3.9.3:-establish-escalation-to-empowered-authority) and [Implementation 3.9.4](#implementation-3.9.4:-assess-operational-capability) test whether these are in place.

Name a deputy who can act for the owner when the owner is unavailable. Some frameworks and obligations, such as SP 800-37, limit which actions can be delegated. Decide in advance which actions the deputy may take. Review this when the system’s environment or tasks change, especially before a period of higher risk. Stopping or restricting the capability may reduce some risks while raising others (see [Practice 4: Define Procedures for Emergency Avoidance Override, Recovery, and Situational Awareness](#practice-4:-define-procedures-for-emergency-avoidance-override,-recovery,-and-situational-awareness)). Record the actions that are delegated, in which circumstances, and why.

A capability might lose its owner, for example when the owner leaves and no successor has been named. The organization decides whether the capability may keep operating during such a gap, and under what interim arrangement, within any regulatory or contractual obligations. Continued operation avoids disrupting the function the capability supports. Operation without an owner leaves no one to make the decisions this Implementation assigns. Record the interim arrangement and how long it may last.

Where responsibilities span several organizational functions, identify the role accountable for resolving conflicting recommendations or decisions. Where one person holds several roles, check that this creates no conflict of interest. Some frameworks and obligations, such as SP 800-37, limit which roles one person may hold. One example is whether the person who approves continued operation of the capability may also own the system. Where few qualified people are available, for example in a small organization, a field office, or a niche application, one person may be the only one able to hold both roles. In that case, record this and how the conflict is offset, such as by an independent review ([Implementation 3.9.6: Keep a Record of Design Decisions and Accepted Risks](#implementation-3.9.6:-keep-a-record-of-design-decisions-and-accepted-risks)).

Where a vendor supplies the capability, the accountable owner is still within the organization. The organization decides where the leader of the operational function that the capability serves sits in this structure, within any regulatory or contractual obligations. That leader bears the operational consequences and often knows the process best. That leader also feels the production pressure to keep the capability running. Record where the leader sits and why.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Who is the accountable owner, and who is the deputy?  
* Which actions may the deputy take, and in which circumstances?  
* Where does the leader of the operational function the capability serves sit in this structure?  
* Where one person holds roles that conflict, how is the conflict offset?  
* Can the capability keep operating during a gap in ownership, and for how long?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-37r2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations: A System Life Cycle Approach for Security and Privacy](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-37r2), from NIST. Appendix D, Roles and Responsibilities, describes the authorizing official as a senior official with the authority to formally assume responsibility and accountability for operating a system, and as the only official who can accept the associated security and privacy risk. The authorizing official is the closest RMF counterpart to the accountable owner in this Implementation; the RMF system owner is a different role. Appendix D also limits what the authorizing official may delegate to a designated representative. Task P-1, Risk Management Roles, addresses conflicts of interest when one individual holds several roles, including whether an authorizing official may also own the system being authorized.  
* **Guidance** [Model risk management principles for banks, Supervisory Statement SS1/23](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/prudential-regulation/publication/2023/may/model-risk-management-principles-for-banks-ss), updated 16 April 2026, from the Prudential Regulation Authority of the Bank of England. It is written for UK banks that use internal models for regulatory capital. Principle 2.4, Roles and responsibilities, asks firms to document roles for each stage of the model lifecycle, with the organizational independence and seniority each requires, and to document model owners for all models. Principle 2.6 keeps senior management responsible for model risk when a model comes from a third party. These bear on documenting ownership across the lifecycle, including for supplied capabilities.

#### Implementation 3.9.2: Define Decision Authority and Reassessment Triggers {#implementation-3.9.2:-define-decision-authority-and-reassessment-triggers}

Settling decision authority in advance helps a change to an SI-enabled capability, or to its context, reach someone with the authority to act. Document who has authority to accept risk, restrict deployment or operation, suspend use, require remediation, roll back the capability, or reduce its delegated authority. Define the scope and limits of that authority in relation to the potential consequences associated with the capability and its operating context. The depth of governance should scale with both the authority granted to the SI-enabled capability and the potential consequence of its actions.

Establish conditions that trigger reassessment of organizational readiness following material changes to the SI-enabled capability, use case, delegated authority, operating environment, dependencies, or potential consequences. For each trigger, identify who monitors for it, who is notified when it activates, and whether the capability continues, is restricted or is suspended while the reassessment is under way. Where the organization operates a management-of-change process, such as those common in process safety and operational technology, routing these triggers through it can help keep a change to an SI-enabled capability from taking a separate, less rigorous path. Where a material change means the organization can no longer confirm that previously established governance or enforcement paths remain effective, re-open the readiness determination rather than assuming that the prior determination remains valid. Material risk acceptances should also carry a review date or a review frequency proportionate to their consequence, since the conditions an acceptance rests on, such as the threat, regulatory or dependency environment, can change gradually without activating any single defined trigger.

Two other parts of the profile define re-evaluation triggers: [Implementation 2.3.4](#implementation-2.3.4:-recurrent-risk-evaluations), and [Implementation 3.8.3](#implementation-3.8.3:-dynamic-risk-surface-coupling-analysis). Where either trigger activates for a capability whose governance rests on a prior readiness determination, treat it as a material change for the purposes of this Implementation. The authority tiers referred to here should be consistent with those established in [Implementation 4.1.2: Establish Tiered Intervention Procedures, Training, and Authorization](#implementation-4.1.2:-establish-tiered-intervention-procedures,-training,-and-authorization).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which reassessment triggers apply, who watches each, and what happens to the capability meanwhile?  
* What review date or frequency applies to each material risk acceptance?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-37r2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations: A System Life Cycle Approach for Security and Privacy](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-37r2), from NIST. Task R-4, Authorization Decision, places explicit acceptance of risk with the authorizing official and states that it cannot be delegated, and has the decision convey terms and conditions for operation and an authorization termination date or review frequency. Task M-6, Ongoing Authorization, has the same official determine on an ongoing basis whether risk remains acceptable and, if not, possibly issue a denial of authorization. Together they are an established model for documenting who holds authority to accept risk and to restrict or stop operation, as this Implementation asks; the reassessment triggers correspond to the event-driven triggers in Appendix F.  
* **Guidance** [Adapting Zero Trust Principles to Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/adapting-zero-trust-principles-operational-technology), 29 April 2026, from CISA, the Department of War and the Department of Energy with partners. The Configuration and Change Management section, on page 10, asks that all changes follow a formalized Management of Change (MOC) process, so that they are reviewed and approved before implementation, typically by a multi-disciplinary board covering engineering, safety and operational review. This bears on routing reassessment triggers through an existing management-of-change process.

#### Implementation 3.9.3: Establish Escalation to Empowered Authority {#implementation-3.9.3:-establish-escalation-to-empowered-authority}

Escalation that ends with someone empowered to act lets a risk beyond one person’s authority be decided, not only recorded. Define escalation paths that move AI risk information to a role with sufficient authority to make the required governance decision. Identify escalation points for circumstances in which the risk, consequence, scope, or required response exceeds the decision authority of the person or function initially receiving or identifying the issue. Identify an alternate for each role at which an escalation path terminates, so that the path does not end with a person who is unavailable. Test or otherwise validate that escalation paths terminate with a role empowered to act rather than solely with a role responsible for receiving or documenting the issue. Evidence that a role is empowered can include past instances in which an escalation to it led to the capability, or its use, being changed. Where the escalation concerns an in-progress operational anomaly rather than a governance decision, [Implementation 4.1.2: Establish Tiered Intervention Procedures, Training, and Authorization](#implementation-4.1.2:-establish-tiered-intervention-procedures,-training,-and-authorization) applies. This Implementation covers escalation of the governance decision itself.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Where does each escalation path terminate, and who is the alternate?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-39, Managing Information Security Risk: Organization, Mission, and Information System View](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-39), from NIST. Section 2.3.1, Governance, has senior leaders determine which risk management decisions are reserved for specific senior roles and which can be delegated, and states that clear assignment and accountability for accepting risk is essential. Section 2.3.2, Risk Executive (Function), includes elevating risk from shared responsibility with external providers to appropriate decision-making authorities. These bear on identifying where each escalation path should terminate.  
* **Guidance** [SR Letter 11-7 Attachment, Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management](https://www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/srletters/2011/sr1107a1.pdf), April 2011, from the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, for U.S. banks. Section III states that challenge may fail to be effective without the influence to have model issues addressed, and that this influence comes from explicit authority, stature and support from higher management. Section V adds that influence may be shown by instances in which models or their use were changed as a result of validation. These bear on validating that a role is empowered to act.

#### Implementation 3.9.4: Assess Operational Capability {#implementation-3.9.4:-assess-operational-capability}

Assess whether existing organizational functions collectively provide sufficient capability to execute the governance requirements applicable to the SI-enabled capability. Consider whether accountability, decision authority, escalation, lifecycle responsibilities, monitoring, and control execution operate together sufficiently for the intended use and operating context. Where these conditions are met, existing governance structures may be extended to cover the SI-enabled capability. Where authority, accountability, lifecycle coverage, or operational capability is fragmented or absent, establish additional governance mechanisms as necessary. Where the assessment turns on whether a governance decision could actually be carried out, use the five properties in [Implementation 3.9.5: Demonstrate Operational Enforceability](#implementation-3.9.5:-demonstrate-operational-enforceability) as the test, rather than a general judgment of sufficiency. Where the assessment turns on whether personnel can actually perform the roles assigned to them, apply the role-specific training and competency requirements in [Implementation 9.2.1: Include Role-Specific Training on SI Failure Modes](#implementation-9.2.1:-include-role-specific-training-on-si-failure-modes) and the simulation training in [Implementation 9.2.2: Implement Realistic Incident Simulation Training](#implementation-9.2.2:-implement-realistic-incident-simulation-training). Organizational capability includes the people who exercise it. Repeat the assessment whenever a reassessment trigger in [Implementation 3.9.2: Define Decision Authority and Reassessment Triggers](#implementation-3.9.2:-define-decision-authority-and-reassessment-triggers) activates, including any increase in the authority delegated to the capability. Include in the assessment whether the organization can sustain the affected functions if the capability is lost, drawing on the procedures in [Task 11.2: Define Manual and Alternative Operating Procedures for Long-Term Mission Continuity](#task-11.2:-define-manual-and-alternative-operating-procedures-for-long-term-mission-continuity) and the drills in [Implementation 11.5.2: Execute High-Fidelity Simulation Drills Involving Total SI Infrastructure Loss and Recovery](#implementation-11.5.2:-execute-high-fidelity-simulation-drills-involving-total-si-infrastructure-loss-and-recovery).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Where the assessment finds a function fragmented or absent, who provides the people, time, and budget to close the gap, and does the capability wait until it is closed?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by CISA. Section 3.2, Integrating AI Into Existing Security and Cybersecurity Frameworks, asks operators to embed AI system assessments within existing risk evaluation, mitigation and monitoring processes. Section 3.1 lists the stakeholders an AI governance structure should include, among them leadership, OT and IT subject matter experts and cybersecurity teams, and asks for clear roles and responsibilities. These bear on deciding whether existing functions can be extended to cover the capability.  
* **Guidance** [Deploying AI Systems Securely: Best Practices for Deploying Secure and Resilient AI Systems](https://media.defense.gov/2024/Apr/15/2003439257/-1/-1/0/CSI-DEPLOYING-AI-SYSTEMS-SECURELY.PDF), Joint Cybersecurity Information, version 1.0, April 2024, from the National Security Agency’s Artificial Intelligence Security Center with CISA, the FBI and four other national cybersecurity agencies. Under Secure the deployment environment, it suggests that the person accountable for AI system cybersecurity be the same person accountable for the organization’s cybersecurity in general.
