* **MANAGE 2.1** (on allocating resources): This Task treats operator attention as a resource that has to be sized for correlated surges up to the organization’s design basis across every system drawing on the same oversight pool, rather than for average per-system load; it does not cover considering the viable non-AI alternative systems that MANAGE 2.1 also names.  
* **MEASURE 1.2** (on continuously improving measurement): This Task reassesses whether an established alarm-management practice remains effective once AI introduces non-deterministic failure modes; it does not cover evaluating whether a given display is understood by the audience that reads it. For that, see for example [Task 4.2: Ensure that Personnel Are Able to Gain and Maintain Situational Awareness](#task-4.2:-ensure-that-personnel-are-able-to-gain-and-maintain-situational-awareness).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which alarms and notifications are kept outside the reach of SI-driven suppression?  
* Where an SI system suppresses, groups, or re-prioritizes notifications, who owns those rules: the owner of the alarm system, the owner of the SI system, or both together?

**References:**

* **Guidance** Health and Safety Executive (2000) [Better alarm handling](https://www.hse.gov.uk/pubns/chis6.pdf), Chemicals Sheet No 6, from Great Britain’s workplace health and safety regulator. States target alarm rates for process plant: no more than one every ten minutes in normal operation, and no more than ten in the first ten minutes after a major upset.  
* **Guidance** [EEMUA Publication 191, “Alarm Systems: A Guide to Design, Management and Procurement”](https://www.eemua.org/products/publications/print/eemua-publication-191), from the Engineering Equipment and Materials Users’ Association, a UK association of industrial plant owner-operators. The underlying baseline for alarm metrics in process industries, and the source of the targets above.  
* **Incident Report** [Health and Safety Executive (1997) The Explosion and Fires at the Texaco Refinery, Milford Haven, 24 July 1994](https://www.jesip.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Texaco-Refinery-Explosion.pdf). In the final 10.7 minutes two operators had to recognize, acknowledge and act on at least 275 alarms, arriving at one every two to three seconds, and the report records operators cancelling alarms for their nuisance value without recognizing what they meant.  
* **Guidance** [The Joint Commission (2013) Sentinel Event Alert 50: Medical device alarm safety in hospitals](https://www.jointcommission.org/en-us/knowledge-library/newsletters/sentinel-event-alert/issue-50), from the US non-profit that accredits healthcare organizations, issued on the basis of aggregated reported events. Documents the same failure in a sector with entirely different equipment.  
* **Research** [McFarlane, D.C. (1999), “Coordinating the Interruption of People in Human-Computer Interaction”, INTERACT’99, pages 295 to 303](https://www.interruptions.net/literature/McFarlane-Interact99-Coordinating.pdf). The first empirical comparison of the four ways a system can time an interruption, immediate, negotiated, mediated and scheduled, which is the evidence behind Implementation 4.4.4: *Applying Consolidation and Low-Cognitive-Load Design Techniques*‘s discussion of when to interrupt. No method was best on every measure: interrupting immediately got interruptions handled promptly at the cost of more errors, and scheduling them minimized task switching at a heavy cost to other performance, which is why timing is a design choice to make for each kind of alert rather than a default.  
* **Research** [Simon, H. (1971), “Designing Organizations for an Information-Rich World”](https://gwern.net/doc/design/1971-simon.pdf). The origin of the framing this Task opens with, that a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention.  
* **Research** Bransby, M.L. and Jenkinson, J., [The management of alarm systems](https://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/ukgwa/20230103120103/https://www.hse.gov.uk/research/crr_pdf/1998/crr98166.pdf), HSE Contract Research Report 166/1998, funded by Great Britain’s Health and Safety Executive. Section 5.2.4 treats alarm systems as part of the plant’s defense against hazard, so that changes to them need control, with closer review for alarms claimed in the hazard analysis. Section 5.3.6.7 notes open questions about whether AI and expert-system alarm processing developed on a limited range of transients will be effective in unexpected situations. Both bear on SI-driven suppression in this Task.

**\>To the Reviewer:** \>This is still rather a nascent field and, while there are academic publications specific to the topic of AI-induced cognitive overload and similar issues, we’re having some trouble finding good references that would speak to an end-user audience. Would pointing to more academic references where there is a lack of industry publications be useful here or would it be more likely to cause confusion?

#### Implementation 4.4.1: Recognizing Novel SI-Driven Alert Floods in Unfamiliar Domains {#implementation-4.4.1:-recognizing-novel-si-driven-alert-floods-in-unfamiliar-domains}

Recognizing an alert flood early lets an organization apply mitigation techniques that other sectors have already developed. Domains with no prior experience managing alarm floods may not recognize the pattern when AI introduces it, or know that established mitigation techniques exist. For example, a fraud-detection system entering a confused state can flood a review queue with false positives; a summarization tool can generate excessive content when it should stay silent; a hospital’s AI-assisted clinical decision support can generate alert volumes comparable to those long documented in traditional medical device alarm fatigue, but without the institutional awareness built up around that older problem. Simple measurements can help recognize the pattern early, such as the average notification rate over a week of normal operation, the few sources that produce most notifications, the number in set periods after an upset, and how useful personnel find the notifications. Measures to reduce this risk range from training personnel to recognize alert-flood patterns as they emerge in the tool they’re using and developing procedures for manual prioritization, to automated triage and consolidation of output (e.g., rate-limiting generated content, grouping duplicate flags). Other signs that notifications exceed what personnel can handle include notifications acknowledged with no resulting action, a growing backlog of items awaiting review, notifications that stand unresolved for long periods, and approval requests from SI systems being approved in batches. Counting notifications per person across all the SI systems that person attends to, rather than per system, can show a flood that no single system’s count reveals. A rate agreed in advance as a flood, with a defined response such as partial suspension of a non-essential SI system under [Implementation 4.1.2: Establish Tiered Intervention Procedures, Training, and Authorization](#implementation-4.1.2:-establish-tiered-intervention-procedures,-training,-and-authorization), can help personnel act on it.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* What notification rate per person counts as a flood, and what response does it trigger?

**References:**

* **Research** [Bransby, M.L. and Jenkinson, J., The management of alarm systems](https://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/ukgwa/20230103120103/https://www.hse.gov.uk/research/crr_pdf/1998/crr98166.pdf), HSE Contract Research Report 166, 1998, funded by Great Britain’s Health and Safety Executive. Section 4 gives simple measures of alarm system performance: the average rate over a week (4.4), the ten most frequent alarms (4.5), the number in set periods after a major upset (4.6), and how useful operators find the alarms (4.8). A domain new to the problem can apply them to SI-generated notifications.  
* **Guidance** [The Joint Commission (2013) Sentinel Event Alert 50: Medical device alarm safety in hospitals](https://www.jointcommission.org/en-us/knowledge-library/newsletters/sentinel-event-alert/issue-50), 8 April 2013, from the US non-profit that accredits healthcare organizations. Estimates that between 85 and 99 percent of alarm signals do not require clinical intervention. It recommends inventorying alarm-equipped devices and setting guidelines for alarm settings that identify when alarm signals are not clinically necessary. This is the institutional awareness that this Implementation’s hospital example refers to.

#### Implementation 4.4.2: Adapting Existing Alarm Management for Complex, Adaptive or Otherwise Unpredictable Systems {#implementation-4.4.2:-adapting-existing-alarm-management-for-complex,-adaptive-or-otherwise-unpredictable-systems}

Organizations with mature, trusted alarm-management practices can build on them for AI-generated notifications, but may find that those practices don’t transfer cleanly to some AI systems. Traditional mitigations often assume alarms correspond to discrete, mechanical fault states (e.g., a stuck valve or tripped breaker).

Established practice treats an alarm as an indication that requires a response from personnel. An SI-generated notification that cannot be given a defined response can be logged or shown as status rather than presented as an alarm. An SI system’s notification behavior can change after an update, retraining, a change to its system prompts or prompt templates, configuration or input data, or a change in a model or service it obtains from a supplier, with no change to the process it monitors, so such changes can be treated as triggers to review its notifications against the alarm system’s criteria and rates.

Examples of ways in which AI-generated alarms can differ from those in more traditional systems include:

* An AI system may report the same underlying error in slightly different ways.  
* Adaptive AI systems may respond inconsistently to an underlying error, resulting in hidden or inconsistent alarms.  
* Inconsistent AI alerts may result in only downstream systems alerting while the system that is the root cause stays silent.  
* Agentic systems can build dependencies dynamically and in ways that may not be documented, so a failure may cause unexpected and seemingly unrelated systems to send notifications of failure.  
* Machine learned detection algorithms and thresholds may be undocumented and applied inconsistently, making it difficult to determine what any given alert means.

These differences arise from complexity, adaptation and randomness, whether in the inputs (such as sensor noise) or in how the SI system produces its outputs, rather than from SI as such. Some existing automation, including systems that already use SI techniques, shows them too; SI tends to make them more common and more pronounced.

The dependency mapping in [Implementation 3.5.1](#implementation-3.5.1:-map-direct-functional-and-algorithmic-dependencies) and [Implementation 3.5.2](#implementation-3.5.2:-identify-indirect-shared-infrastructure-and-collateral-damage-exposure) can help make the dependency chains described above more visible in advance, even though it does not resolve the underlying detection problem. Some partial approaches, not specific to critical infrastructure or to AI, exist in the broader IT/software observability field, such as similarity-based alert clustering and distributed tracing, but these generally assume mature instrumentation that many current AI deployments, and especially OT environments, may not yet have in place. Adapting existing alarm rationalization, for example by rationalizing SI alerts by category rather than individually, may also serve as a partial approach where those categories are stable enough to document. This is particularly challenging in agentic systems, which can make dependency decisions dynamically and without documenting them. For multi-agent systems, observable symptoms of a fault spreading between agents can be monitored as alarm conditions in their own right, such as rapid fan-out from a single decision, oscillating retries or feedback loops between agents, and repeated identical requests. Rate limits and circuit breakers that throttle or pause propagation when such a symptom appears can help contain a feedback loop while personnel diagnose its cause. Limiting retries for each request and across a whole service, and avoiding retries at several layers at once, can also help, because attempts issued at each layer multiply.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which SI-generated notifications are presented as alarms, and which are logged or shown as status?

**References:**

* **Commentary** [Understanding and Applying the ANSI/ISA 18.2 Alarm Management Standard](https://www.isa.org/getmedia/55b4210e-6cb2-4de4-89f8-2b5b6b46d954/PAS-Understanding-ISA-18-2.pdf), 2010, from PAS, a commercial supplier of alarm management software and services. Section 11 summarizes the rationalization activities of ANSI/ISA-18.2-2009, including justifying the need for each alarm, determining its setpoint or logical condition and priority, and documenting the operator action and consequences. That per-alarm basis is the legacy practice whose assumptions this Implementation’s examples show SI-generated alarms may not meet.  
* **Guidance** [OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/), Version 2026, December 2025, from the Agentic Security Initiative of the OWASP Gen AI Security Project, a volunteer community project of the Open Worldwide Application Security Project. ASI08, Cascading Failures, lists observable symptoms of a fault propagating across agents as detection hooks, including rapid fan-out, oscillating retries or feedback loops between agents, and downstream queue storms or repeated identical intents. Its mitigations include rate limiting that throttles or pauses on anomalies, and circuit breakers between planner and executor. These bear on the multi-agent feedback-loop case in this Implementation.  
* **Commentary** [Ulrich, M., “Addressing Cascading Failures”](https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/), Chapter 22 of the Google SRE book, 2017, from Google, published by O’Reilly Media. Defines a cascading failure as one that grows through positive feedback. The Retries section advises limiting retries per request, a server-wide retry budget, and avoiding retries at several layers, since attempts multiply. It notes that overload produces secondary symptoms that can look like the root cause. These bear on the multi-agent feedback-loop case and on alerts that point away from the root cause.

**\>To the Reviewer:** \>Mitigating this is still an open research topic, particularly in agentic systems. Are there other partial mitigations, especially for the multi-agent feedback-loop case, that we’re missing?

#### Implementation 4.4.3: Managing Correlated Multi-System Attention Surges {#implementation-4.4.3:-managing-correlated-multi-system-attention-surges}

Planning for correlated surges helps an organization keep oversight workable when many SI systems need attention at once, whether by adding capacity or by reducing and prioritizing the requests. A single external event can trigger a simultaneous surge of attention requests across many AI-controlled systems at once, overwhelming a limited pool of human operators even if each individual system’s alert volume is otherwise manageable. The common cause need not be external: SI systems that share an underlying model or training data can fail together, so that a single fault produces a correlated surge. Reduced staffing is frequently among the expected benefits of adopting an AI system. Where it is, the oversight capacity the AI system depends on is drawn from the same pool that the expected benefit reduces, and sizing the two separately can produce a shortfall that neither decision would have chosen. For example, a widespread power failure or loss of traffic signals can cause an entire autonomous vehicle fleet to simultaneously request remote operator attention, exceeding the capacity of the remote operations center. Measures to address this risk include: Identifying which AI-driven systems draw on the same oversight capacity, and estimating what external events could cause them to request attention simultaneously.

Designing and resourcing oversight capacity and escalation procedures explicitly for correlated surges, not just average or independent per-system load. How large a surge to design for is a design basis decision, made for the consequences involved. What would happen in a larger surge should still be understood, and planned for where feasible, for example by reducing what the systems ask of operators or the autonomy they are given. One way to make this testable is to compare the attention requests expected in such a surge with the oversight capacity available to answer them, and to treat a shortfall as a limit on the autonomy that can be authorized ([Implementation 3.9.2: Define Decision Authority and Reassessment Triggers](#implementation-3.9.2:-define-decision-authority-and-reassessment-triggers)). Accounting for oversight capacity as a cost of the AI system rather than as a resource already available, so that it enters the tradespace of benefits and control costs that [Practice 1](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success), [Practice 2](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations), and [Practice 3](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior) define. Developing automated alert triaging mechanisms so that limited operator attention is not spent sorting through large quantities of alerts or addressing low priority issues. Re-checking oversight capacity when staffing levels, shift patterns, training, or authorizations change, rather than only when the AI systems drawing on it change. A pre-defined surge mode can defer non-essential notifications and approval requests while safety-critical alarms continue unchanged. Where agents wait on human approval, deciding in advance what each does when approval does not arrive in time, such as holding in its fail-safe state under [Implementation 3.2.3: Specify Fail-Safe States and Fallback Behavior](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior), can keep a surge from producing either a queue of unattended requests or actions taken without approval.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* What does each agent do when a human approval does not arrive in time?  
* How is oversight capacity sized against surge demand?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 600-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1), July 2024, from NIST. Section 2 names algorithmic monocultures resulting from repeated use of the same model as an ecosystem-level risk. Its footnote 3 defines these as increased susceptibility to correlated failures when multiple actors rely on the same algorithm, with employment and lending as examples. This bears on SI systems that share an underlying model and so can request attention together.  
* **Guidance** [Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Real-Time System Operations](https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/our-work/white-papers/whitepaper-ai-and-ml-in-real-time-system-operations.pdf), White Paper Revision 1, November 2024, from the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC). In Chapter 3, Implications to Workforces notes that if SI tools increase operator productivity, resulting management decisions may add responsibilities or tasks to the system operator. That would increase cognitive load and decrease the time available to review and interact with SI results and recommendations. This bears on sizing oversight capacity together with the staffing benefit expected from the SI system.

#### Implementation 4.4.4: Applying Consolidation and Low-Cognitive-Load Design Techniques {#implementation-4.4.4:-applying-consolidation-and-low-cognitive-load-design-techniques}

Once alarm flood risks are identified, apply techniques that reduce the rate and cognitive cost of notifications without hiding genuinely urgent, isolated signals. Examples of measures to consider include:

* Implementing basic consolidation, such as grouping repeated identical alerts into a single notification.  
* Prioritizing notifications by the potential consequences if personnel fail to respond, using a small number of priority levels.  
* Suppressing notifications that follow predictably from a known root cause, or from a deliberate change of operating state such as a unit that personnel have shut down, while keeping the root-cause notification.  
* Applying user-interface design choices that reduce distraction (often referred to as calm technology or mixed-initiative interfaces) such as:  
  * exception batching,  
  * trend dashboards,  
  * dynamic deadbands, or  
  * time-delay hysteresis.


  These should be matched to the specific application, oversight mode, and the range of personnel familiarity likely to encounter these notifications, from regular operators to occasional external responders. Testing consolidation logic with personnel against realistic scenarios, including one in which an isolated urgent signal arrives during a flood, can show whether it reduces load without hiding a distinct problem.

Note that there is a trade-off between many of these measures. For example, aggressive batching reduces fatigue but risks delaying a genuinely urgent, isolated signal. Where a notification is suppressed or shelved, keeping a list of shelved notifications that personnel can readily see, making it easy to restore one, and reviewing the list at shift handover can help keep a temporary measure from hiding the notification indefinitely.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which notifications are consolidated or suppressed, and how is the consolidation logic tested with personnel? (see the Safe versus Reliable tension in [Task 4.4: Attention Governance and Alert/Alarm Flood Mitigation](#task-4.4:-attention-governance-and-alert/alarm-flood-mitigation))

**References:**

* **Guidance** Health and Safety Executive (2000) [Better alarm handling](https://www.hse.gov.uk/pubns/chis6.pdf), Chemicals Sheet No 6, from Great Britain’s workplace health and safety regulator. For effective alarm prioritization, it suggests using about three priorities based on the potential consequences if the operator fails to respond. Step 2 gives quick technical measures from the EEMUA guide, including tuning nuisance alarm settings, adjusting deadbands on repeating alarms and suppressing alarms from out-of-service plant. These are process-industry counterparts to the measures in this Implementation.  
* **Research** [Bransby, M.L. and Jenkinson, J., The management of alarm systems](https://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/ukgwa/20230103120103/https://www.hse.gov.uk/research/crr_pdf/1998/crr98166.pdf), HSE Contract Research Report 166, 1998, funded by Great Britain’s Health and Safety Executive. Section 5.3.2 rates deadband and shelving as excellent techniques for repeating alarms. Appendix 10 names three features of the shelving systems seen: quick access to the list of shelved alarms, easy unshelving, and a check of that list at shift changeover. These bear on the hysteresis and suppression measures here.

### Task 4.5: Define Operational Regimes for Human-on-the-Loop and Human-Out-of-the-Loop Operation {#task-4.5:-define-operational-regimes-for-human-on-the-loop-and-human-out-of-the-loop-operation}

Knowing where a person can intervene in time, and where they cannot, helps an organization rely on human oversight where it works and on automated protections elsewhere. Identify operational contexts where real-time, manual human-in-the-loop (HITL) oversight is physically or technically infeasible due to tight system time constants (such as stability anomalies operating in milliseconds, real-time industrial control loops, or machine-speed cyber defense events). Oversight of any mode degrades into a purely nominal or superficial check where the unfolding event outruns what the operator can be relied upon to do about it, particularly in situations where fatigue or stress are factors; the oversight thresholds established under [Implementation 4.5.1: Define Engineering Time-Constant Thresholds](#implementation-4.5.1:-define-engineering-time-constant-thresholds) are what make this testable rather than assumed.

For these regimes, formally define the boundaries where the human-on-the-loop oversight mode (action proceeds, with intervention capability retained) or the human-out-of-the-loop oversight mode (autonomous execution with retrospective post-hoc review) should substitute for the human-in-the-loop mode, and specify the deterministic automated protections required to support them. A named oversight mode, or a level on an autonomy scale, carries little meaning unless it is stated together with the operating envelope, the task, the supervision arrangement and the fallback assumptions it was defined for. The oversight mode in force should also be evident to the personnel involved, together with what the SI system may currently do without them and what it will do next if no one intervenes. Aviation treats confusion about the active autoflight mode as a recognized vulnerability, and asks that crews be able to identify the current mode and anticipate the next (see FAA AC 120-71B).

Operating in a less direct oversight mode does not remove human decision-making; it moves it earlier and later. Even where real-time intervention is infeasible, a specific role holds the oversight authority to decide whether the system may operate in that mode, on what conditions, and when to suspend or roll it back ([Implementation 3.9.2: Define Decision Authority and Reassessment Triggers](#implementation-3.9.2:-define-decision-authority-and-reassessment-triggers)). That role needs the visibility, time, resources, access, and support to exercise the authority. Entering a less direct oversight mode should be a deliberate and recorded act by that role, not something the SI system does on its own. Leaving it when its conditions no longer hold, for example for a fallback state under [Implementation 3.2.3: Specify Fail-Safe States and Fallback Behavior](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior), need not wait for a person. This Task separates the paths where human intervention can be relied upon from those where it cannot, so that automated boundaries carry the role where a person cannot.

**Search Keywords:** human-on-the-loop, human-out-of-the-loop, human-in-the-loop, supervisory control, closed-loop control, system time constant, control loop rate, human reaction time, operator response time, response time budget, automated fail-safe, infeasible oversight, autonomy regime

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Safe:** Contributes the test that decides whether human intervention counts as a safety control: whether what the operator would have to do is something a person can be relied upon to do in the time available, and documenting the paths where it cannot. This Task does not cover the replacement protection, which [Task 3.2: Implement Independent Guardrails for SI Outputs](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs) covers.  
* **Accountable:** Contributes the human decision that remains when real-time intervention is infeasible: a named role decides whether a regime may be entered, on what conditions, and when to suspend it. This Task does not cover defining that authority, which [Implementation 3.9.2: Define Decision Authority and Reassessment Triggers](#implementation-3.9.2:-define-decision-authority-and-reassessment-triggers) does.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Transparent:** Out-of-the-loop operation moves the whole review to afterward. [Implementation 4.5.2: Establish Deterministic Boundary Constraints for Automated Regimes](#implementation-4.5.2:-establish-deterministic-boundary-constraints-for-automated-regimes) requires a log when a deterministic boundary blocks a command, but autonomous actions that stay within bounds depend on telemetry captured under [Practice 10: Implement Multi-Tiered SI System Logging and Audit Capabilities](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities).  
* **Secure:** Where entry to or exit from an oversight mode depends on sensor, communications or system health signals, a manipulated signal can push the system into a less direct mode, or force repeated reversions. Making entry a deliberate act limits the first; the state-aware interlocks and rate-of-change validation in [Implementation 2.2.2: Deploy “Watchdog” Controllers](#implementation-2.2.2:-deploy-“watchdog”-controllers) limit the second. The time-constant analysis in [Implementation 4.5.1: Define Engineering Time-Constant Thresholds](#implementation-4.5.1:-define-engineering-time-constant-thresholds) also shows which paths outrun human intervention and rely on automated boundaries alone. An attacker could use it to aim at those paths. Protecting it is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Accountable versus Safe:** Where the operator can be relied upon to act, keeping a person in the loop contributes both accountability and safety. Where they cannot, the two separate; human oversight may identify a responsible party while making the system less safe, because a person who cannot act in time can delay or interrupt the process at a point where the delay is itself hazardous. One way to balance this is to move the human decision to a point where there is sufficient time and information to make it well, such as deciding in advance whether the system may run in this mode and on what conditions. Others include changing the process so that intervention becomes feasible, or not operating in that mode.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **GOVERN 3.2** (on defining human-AI configuration): This Task differentiates the human-in-the-loop, human-on-the-loop and human-out-of-the-loop oversight modes and fixes the boundaries between them; it does not cover defining the intervention procedure that applies once a person is in the loop. For that, see for example [Task 4.1: Establish “Break-Glass” Intervention Procedures](#task-4.1:-establish-“break-glass”-intervention-procedures).  
* **MAP 1.1** (on defining operating context): This Task adds the process time constants to the documented operating context, so that the feasibility of real-time human oversight is established rather than assumed; it does not cover the intended purposes and user expectations that MAP 1.1 also names.  
* **MEASURE 2.6** (on measuring safety): This Task covers the human reaction and execution times that a response-time safety metric has to be set against, and requires deterministic boundaries able to execute a fallback state with no human present; it does not cover producing evidence that those boundaries hold. For that, see for example [Task 2.3: Establish Protocols for and Regularly Perform Systematic and Achievable Testing, Evaluation, Validation, and Verification (TEVV)](#task-2.3:-establish-protocols-for-and-regularly-perform-systematic-and-achievable-testing,-evaluation,-validation,-and-verification-\(tevv\)).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which operating contexts run human-on-the-loop or human-out-of-the-loop, and which role holds the authority to approve them? (see the Accountable versus Safe tension)  
* Where neither a person nor an automated boundary can act in time on a path, does the organization change the process, add a protection, or not operate in that mode?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Section 4.2, Embed Safety and Failsafe Mechanisms, asks that AI systems be able to fail gracefully without disrupting critical operations, and that the new failure states an AI system introduces, including how to bypass or replace it, be written into existing functional safety and incident response procedures. Those are the deterministic protections this Task calls for where real-time human intervention is infeasible.  
* **Standard** ISA-84 / IEC 61511, Functional Safety: Safety Instrumented Systems for the Process Industry Sector (defining automated protective layers independent of human operator loops).  
* **Guidance** [FAA AC 120-71B, *Standard Operating Procedures and Pilot Monitoring Duties for Flight Deck Crewmembers*](https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/advisory_circulars/index.cfm/go/document.information/documentID/1030486), 10 January 2017, from the United States Federal Aviation Administration. Paragraph 6.9.1 records that safety data have shown autoflight mode confusion to be a potential vulnerability, and asks that pilots be able to identify, interpret and anticipate autoflight modes. Paragraph 6.9.2 describes the flight mode annunciators as the source for depicting “who is doing what.” This bears on making the oversight mode in force evident to personnel.

#### Implementation 4.5.1: Define Engineering Time-Constant Thresholds {#implementation-4.5.1:-define-engineering-time-constant-thresholds}

Audit automated processes to identify paths where the window between an AI anomaly and an irreversible consequence is shorter than what human intervention can be relied upon to achieve. For these paths, document that real-time human intervention is not a primary risk mitigation control. Where the process already has a hazard analysis, this window corresponds to what process safety practice calls the process safety time, with the SI anomaly as the initiating failure, and the existing analysis may provide a starting figure. An SI system can also shorten the window, for example by acting faster than the process normally changes, or by issuing the same action to many assets at once, so that the consequence arrives at all of them before an operator has dealt with the first. What can be relied upon depends on the time available and on what the operator has to do with it. The time an operator needs should be established for the specific role, interface and staffing level, for example through the exercises in [Implementation 4.1.3: Regularly Practice and Evaluate Intervention Processes](#implementation-4.1.3:-regularly-practice-and-evaluate-intervention-processes), and should include the time to gain situational awareness of the system’s state ([Task 4.2: Ensure that Personnel Are Able to Gain and Maintain Situational Awareness](#task-4.2:-ensure-that-personnel-are-able-to-gain-and-maintain-situational-awareness)), not only the time to act. Where the time is measured in minutes, an operator may be able to detect, diagnose, and act. Where it is measured in seconds, a memorized response to an unambiguous trigger is the most dependable option. For example, FAA guidance on standard operating procedures (see FAA AC 120-71B) advises avoiding such responses wherever possible and limiting unavoidable ones to fewer than three items containing no conditional decision steps. Judging whether an AI-selected action is appropriate is likely to be a conditional decision that does not meet that bound. Time is not the only limit. An operator can rarely be expected to verify in real time that a complex AI system is following its rules, and can judge only whether its actions, perhaps with an accompanying explanation, appear acceptable (see Bainbridge 1983). Where the system was adopted because it handles cases human judgment handles poorly, that judgment is what the oversight arrangement relies on. This even applies to an attentive operator, and is compounded where automatic control masks a developing problem by compensating for it up until the point where human intervention becomes necessary. See [Task 3.2: Implement Independent Guardrails for SI Outputs](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs) for automated controls, as well as [Implementation 4.2.3](#implementation-4.2.3:-human-centered-interfaces-for-si-uncertainty-and-actionable-triggers), [Task 4.6](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output), [Task 4.4](#task-4.4:-attention-governance-and-alert/alarm-flood-mitigation), and [Implementation 11.2.3](#implementation-11.2.3:-human-factors-and-cognitive-transition-protocols-for-control-handoffs) for further details.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* What operator response time is assumed for each role, and from what evidence?

**References:**

* **Research** [Lisanne Bainbridge, “Ironies of Automation”, Automatica volume 19 number 6, 1983, pages 775 to 779](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0005109883900468). Automatica is the journal of the International Federation of Automatic Control, an international body whose members are national control engineering organizations. A seminal paper on the human factors of automated process control. Its subject is the process-control computers of 1983, and the mechanisms it identifies are relevant to AI systems. Section 1.1.3 sets out why an operator cannot verify in real time that an automated system is following its rules.  
* **Guidance** [FAA AC 120-71B, *Standard Operating Procedures and Pilot Monitoring Duties for Flight Deck Crewmembers*](https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/advisory_circulars/index.cfm/go/document.information/documentID/1030486), 10 January 2017, from the United States Federal Aviation Administration, the civil aviation authority of the United States. The AC states that it is not mandatory and does not constitute a regulation. Paragraph 4.2.5 gives the conditions under which a response may be relied on from memory: avoided wherever possible, clearly identified, emphasized in training, fewer than three items, and containing no conditional decision steps.  
* **Research** [Endsley, M.R. and Kiris, E.O., “The Out-of-the-Loop Performance Problem and Level of Control in Automation”, Human Factors 37(2), 1995](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1518/001872095779064555), from the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society. In its experiment, decisions after an expert system broke down took longer for participants who had worked under higher levels of automation, and they were less aware of what had been happening. This bears on counting the time to regain situational awareness, not only the time to act, in operator response time.

#### Implementation 4.5.2: Establish Deterministic Boundary Constraints for Automated Regimes {#implementation-4.5.2:-establish-deterministic-boundary-constraints-for-automated-regimes}

Identified human-out-of-the-loop operational regimes should include independent, non-AI deterministic safety wrappers detailed in [Task 3.2: Implement Independent Guardrails for SI Outputs](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs). Make these wrappers as independent of the SI system as practical. Where they share sensors, power, or networks with it, record which. Ensure that these physical process boundaries have total authority to block unsafe autonomous commands, execute fallback states per [Implementation 3.2.3: Specify Fail-Safe States and Fallback Behavior](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior), and log the event prior to subsequent human administrative review. Where practical, and in proportion to the consequences, keep this boundary logic small enough to be analyzed and tested independently of the SI system it constrains and, where the severity of consequences warrants, formally verified, as for the watchdog logic in [Implementation 2.2.2: Deploy “Watchdog” Controllers](#implementation-2.2.2:-deploy-“watchdog”-controllers).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* At what severity of consequence is the boundary logic formally verified, and who has the expertise to do it?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Section 2.3.7, Safety Systems, describes a safety instrumented function as sensors, logic solvers and final control elements that bring a system to a safe state when predetermined thresholds are violated. It notes that a safety instrumented system is often independent of the basic process control system, so that a failure of the latter does not impair it. That is the established process-industry form of the independent boundary this Implementation asks for.

### Task 4.6: Ensure that Confidence and Rationale Shown to Personnel Reflect How the SI System Reached Its Output {#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output}

Establish requirements that any confidence indication or rationale shown to personnel is derived from the process by which the AI system produced its output, and that rationale displays are designed and tested for whether they help personnel decide. This applies to routine decision support as well as to intervention. A rationale can be persuasive without being accurate as an explanation: an explanation constructed after the fact can look reasonable without corresponding to how the output was produced. For this reason, post-hoc attribution tools such as SHAP or LIME are not the primary source of the rationale shown to personnel; where their output is shown, it is treated as presentation rather than as an account of how the output was produced. Rationale displays have also been found to increase acceptance of incorrect recommendations as well as correct ones ([Implementation 4.6.1: Design Rationale Displays that Give Personnel Something to Check](#implementation-4.6.1:-design-rationale-displays-that-give-personnel-something-to-check)).

How accurately a rationale can reflect the AI system’s process depends on how the AI system reasons. For learned components, confidence and rationale can be derived from calibrated probabilities and decision-level telemetry ([Implementation 4.6.2: Derive Confidence and Rationale for Learned Components from Their Decision Processes](#implementation-4.6.2:-derive-confidence-and-rationale-for-learned-components-from-their-decision-processes)). Where the AI system, or part of it, reasons symbolically or is a self-interpretable model, the rationale can be a trace of the steps it actually applied ([Implementation 4.6.3: Display Execution Traces from Symbolic, Hybrid, and Self-Interpretable Components](#implementation-4.6.3:-display-execution-traces-from-symbolic,-hybrid,-and-self-interpretable-components)). Where a learned model performs well but cannot be inspected, an interpretable model distilled from it can sometimes be deployed in its place, so that the rationale is again such a trace ([Implementation 4.6.4: Distill Learned Models into Interpretable Models that Can Be Verified](#implementation-4.6.4:-distill-learned-models-into-interpretable-models-that-can-be-verified)).

In either case, a rationale shows at most how the AI system reached its output, not that the output is correct. This Task complements [Task 4.2](#task-4.2:-ensure-that-personnel-are-able-to-gain-and-maintain-situational-awareness) and [Task 4.4](#task-4.4:-attention-governance-and-alert/alarm-flood-mitigation), which address what information reaches personnel and in what volume, by addressing whether the confidence and rationale in that information reflect how the output was produced. Recording the confidence and rationale that were displayed, alongside the output, under [Task 10.1: Define Decision-Level Logging and Metadata Retention Policies](#task-10.1:-define-decision-level-logging-and-metadata-retention-policies) lets a later review establish what personnel were shown when they decided. Those records stay meaningful only if the model version, prompts, configuration, and other state and information that influenced the output at the time are also kept, which adds storage and management overhead ([Implementation 10.1.5: Define What Each Operational Record Is For](#implementation-10.1.5:-define-what-each-operational-record-is-for); see also [Practice 13: Establish Procedures for Retiring SI Systems and Withdrawing Their Authority](#practice-13:-establish-procedures-for-retiring-si-systems-and-withdrawing-their-authority)).

**Search Keywords:** explanation fidelity, faithful explanation, explanation accuracy, introspective explanation, post-hoc explanation, SHAP, LIME, rationale display, decision support, confidence calibration, reasoning trace, rule trace, interpretable model, self-interpretable model, decision tree, hybrid AI, neuro-symbolic AI, over-reliance, automation bias, distillation, model distillation, surrogate model, behavioral cloning, learning from demonstration

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Explainable & Interpretable:** Contributes explanation accuracy (see NIST IR 8312): the confidence and rationale that personnel see are derived from the process that produced the output, or are treated as presentation where they are not. This Task does not cover deciding how that information is laid out or when it reaches personnel. For that, see [Task 4.2: Ensure that Personnel Are Able to Gain and Maintain Situational Awareness](#task-4.2:-ensure-that-personnel-are-able-to-gain-and-maintain-situational-awareness).  
* **Safe:** Contributes a check against rationale displays that make incorrect recommendations more convincing: rationale is designed to be checked, and can be tested for whether personnel still reject incorrect recommendations. This Task does not cover the means of intervening. For that, see [Task 4.1: Establish “Break-Glass” Intervention Procedures](#task-4.1:-establish-“break-glass”-intervention-procedures).

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Secure:** Detailed confidence values and rationale can tell an adversary how the SI system responds to its inputs. Where an adversary can query a learned component and see its confidence scores, those scores can be used to craft inputs that it misclassifies (see NIST AI 100-2e2025). Limiting who can see the more detailed views, under [Task 5.2: Determine and Implement Specific Access Requirements](#task-5.2:-determine-and-implement-specific-access-requirements), can reduce this without withholding what personnel need to decide.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Accurate versus Explainable & Interpretable:** Where the knowledge a decision depends on can be stated as rules, constraints, or a self-interpretable model, the two need not separate: a symbolic or hybrid design can make the rationale an operator sees the reasoning the AI system actually used ([Implementation 4.6.3: Display Execution Traces from Symbolic, Hybrid, and Self-Interpretable Components](#implementation-4.6.3:-display-execution-traces-from-symbolic,-hybrid,-and-self-interpretable-components)). Where that knowledge cannot readily be stated, a learned model may perform better, and its rationale can be checked only indirectly ([Implementation 4.6.2: Derive Confidence and Rationale for Learned Components from Their Decision Processes](#implementation-4.6.2:-derive-confidence-and-rationale-for-learned-components-from-their-decision-processes)). Whether interpretable models must in general give up accuracy is disputed (see NIST IR 8312), and the answer depends on how much of the domain can be stated, the same condition behind the tension in [Task 1.4: Establish the SI System’s Domain Knowledge and Linguistic Alignment Requirements](#task-1.4:-establish-the-si-system’s-domain-knowledge-and-linguistic-alignment-requirements). One way to balance this, where the choice of approach is still open and operators must be able to check the reasoning at the moment of decision, is to weigh a symbolic or hybrid design for the part of the decision that can be stated. Others include distilling an interpretable model from a learned one and deploying it where it performs well enough for the application ([Implementation 4.6.4: Distill Learned Models into Interpretable Models that Can Be Verified](#implementation-4.6.4:-distill-learned-models-into-interpretable-models-that-can-be-verified)), relying more heavily on verifying the outputs of a learned model, or limiting its role to recommendations that personnel can check against independent evidence.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MEASURE 2.9** (on measuring interpretability and explainability): This Task requires that confidence and rationale shown to personnel derive from the process that produced the output, and rules out post-hoc attribution tools as the primary source; it does not cover capturing the decision-level telemetry that such a display depends on. For that, see for example [Implementation 10.1.2: Runtime Telemetry and Artifact Tracking](#implementation-10.1.2:-runtime-telemetry-and-artifact-tracking).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which personnel see detailed confidence values and rationale, and which see only a summary? (see the Secure effect)  
* Where a learned model’s rationale can be checked only indirectly, which decisions is it limited to?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 600-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1), July 2024, from NIST. Section 2.2, Confabulation, notes that generative AI outputs may include confabulated logic or citations that purport to justify or explain an answer, for example logical steps presented for an answer that is itself incorrect, and that this may mislead people into inappropriately trusting the output. This is the case this Task addresses when it asks that rationale shown to personnel derive from how the output was produced.  
* **Guidance** [NIST IR 8312, Four Principles of Explainable Artificial Intelligence](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.IR.8312). Section 2.3 distinguishes explanation accuracy (whether an explanation reflects how the system reached its output) from decision accuracy, and Section 2.4 describes knowledge limits (a system identifying cases it was not designed for or cannot answer reliably). Section 6.1 describes self-interpretable models, which are themselves the explanation, and records that whether they trade accuracy for interpretability is disputed. It covers models such as decision trees, decision lists, and regression, not knowledge-based or hybrid systems.  
* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025), March 2025, from NIST. Section 2.2.2, Black-Box Evasion Attacks, describes score-based attacks, in which an attacker who can query a model and obtain its confidence scores uses them to craft adversarial examples. This bears on the Secure effect of showing detailed confidence values to personnel.

#### Implementation 4.6.1: Design Rationale Displays that Give Personnel Something to Check {#implementation-4.6.1:-design-rationale-displays-that-give-personnel-something-to-check}

Where rationale is displayed, offer concise, “one-click” or hoverable rationale summaries highlighting the primary inputs, telemetry feeds, patient factors, transaction parameters, or business rules that drove the AI recommendation. Where a summary points to evidence that personnel can check for themselves, such as a sensor reading they can confirm against a second instrument, a transaction detail they can look up, or a rule they can compare with the governing procedure, it can help them judge a recommendation under time pressure without parsing raw logs. For example, where a language model summarizes a procedure or work order, citing the document, its revision and the passage relied on lets the reader confirm that the summary says what the source says. It can also reveal a summary that reflects an earlier revision the model saw in training rather than the current one. Rationale displays can help or hinder decisions, depending on the situation. A rationale can make a recommendation more convincing without making it easier to tell when it is wrong, and rationale displays have been found to increase acceptance of incorrect recommendations as well as correct ones (see Bansal 2021). Interface designers should therefore aim for rationale that gives personnel something to check rather than something to believe. They should also consider the time available to act: for responders who need only enough information to choose an emergency mode, see [Implementation 4.2.1: Develop Situational Awareness Processes and Procedures for Personnel Who May Need to Intervene in the SI System’s Operation](#implementation-4.2.1:-develop-situational-awareness-processes-and-procedures-for-personnel-who-may-need-to-intervene-in-the-si-system’s-operation). Where rationale is displayed to support decisions in the moment, consider testing under [Task 1.3: Implement Evaluation and Test Plans, Including TEVV, Across the SI Lifecycle](#task-1.3:-implement-evaluation-and-test-plans,-including-tevv,-across-the-si-lifecycle) whether it improves decisions for the personnel who will use it, including whether they still reject incorrect recommendations. For training personnel on the effect of rationale on reliance, see [Task 9.2: Deliver Specialized Training on Human-SI Interaction and Automation Bias](#task-9.2:-deliver-specialized-training-on-human-si-interaction-and-automation-bias).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Is displayed rationale tested under [Task 1.3: Implement Evaluation and Test Plans, Including TEVV, Across the SI Lifecycle](#task-1.3:-implement-evaluation-and-test-plans,-including-tevv,-across-the-si-lifecycle) to show whether it improves decisions for the personnel who use it?

**References:**

* **Research** [Bansal, G. et al., “Does the Whole Exceed its Parts? The Effect of AI Explanations on Complementary Team Performance”, Proceedings of the 2021 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems](https://doi.org/10.1145/3411764.3445717). A study of crowdworkers deciding with the help of AI recommendations on text classification and reasoning tasks. Explanations were either generated post-hoc (using LIME) or written by an expert, and neither reflected the model’s actual reasoning. They tended to raise accuracy when the AI was correct and lower it when it was wrong, with no net gain over showing a calibrated confidence score. The authors note the results may not generalize to expert users in high-stakes domains.

#### Implementation 4.6.2: Derive Confidence and Rationale for Learned Components from Their Decision Processes {#implementation-4.6.2:-derive-confidence-and-rationale-for-learned-components-from-their-decision-processes}

Confidence and rationale displays help personnel judge how far to rely on an SI output, when the displays reflect how that output was actually reached. To avoid misinforming personnel with uncalibrated confidence scores or plausible-sounding explanations that do not reflect reality, displayed confidence metrics, data freshness warnings, and rationale summaries should be derived from the underlying AI system’s decision making processes. For learned components, examples include calibrated model probabilities and tamper-evident, decision-level runtime telemetry captured at inference time. Calibration should be established on data representative of the deployment, such as the specific plant and its instruments, and rechecked when the model is retrained or when sensors or the process change ([Implementation 7.5.1](#implementation-7.5.1:-perform-pre-update-validation-and-re-calibration); [Implementation 2.3.4](#implementation-2.3.4:-recurrent-risk-evaluations)). Natural-language summaries generated by a language model should be treated as user-facing presentation layers rather than as evidence of model decision logic. Interface designers and system leads should not rely on post-hoc, perturbation-based explanation tools (such as SHAP or LIME) as primary sources for rationale displays, as these generate post-hoc hypotheses that need not correspond to the AI system’s actual decision logic or internal state. Such tools, with sanity checks, may still serve as secondary aids alongside rationale derived from decision-level telemetry.

For further discussion on capturing decision-level telemetry, see:

* [Implementation 8.1.2: Identify SI Systems that May Not Satisfy Root Cause Analysis Requirements](#implementation-8.1.2:-identify-si-systems-that-may-not-satisfy-root-cause-analysis-requirements) (Forensic interpretability gaps and limitations of post-hoc attributions).  
* [Implementation 10.1.2: Runtime Telemetry and Artifact Tracking](#implementation-10.1.2:-runtime-telemetry-and-artifact-tracking) (Capturing decision-level runtime telemetry rather than relying on post-hoc explanations).  
* [Implementation 12.1.2: Provenance and Traceability](#implementation-12.1.2:-provenance-and-traceability) (Linking generated logic strictly to hard inference-context metadata for audit paths).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Are post-hoc attribution tools used as secondary aids, and if so, with which sanity checks?

**References:**

#### Implementation 4.6.3: Display Execution Traces from Symbolic, Hybrid, and Self-Interpretable Components {#implementation-4.6.3:-display-execution-traces-from-symbolic,-hybrid,-and-self-interpretable-components}

Where the AI system, or part of it, reasons symbolically, for example by applying encoded rules, constraints, or a knowledge base, or is a self-interpretable model such as a decision tree, the displayed rationale can be a trace of the steps it actually applied rather than a hypothesis constructed after the fact (see Sheh 2021). For a planner or optimizer, such as a tool that proposes a switching sequence or a generation schedule, the trace can include the constraints that bound the solution and the alternatives it rejected. In a hybrid system, such a trace is an accurate explanation only of the symbolic part: facts supplied by learned components, such as a classification of a vibration signature as a bearing fault, enter the trace as premises and should be displayed with their own uncertainty ([Implementation 4.6.2: Derive Confidence and Rationale for Learned Components from Their Decision Processes](#implementation-4.6.2:-derive-confidence-and-rationale-for-learned-components-from-their-decision-processes)). For an agent that orchestrates tools, the recorded sequence of tool calls, their arguments and their returns is a trace of what it did, though not of why; the narrative it gives alongside is a presentation layer, as in [Implementation 4.6.2: Derive Confidence and Rationale for Learned Components from Their Decision Processes](#implementation-4.6.2:-derive-confidence-and-rationale-for-learned-components-from-their-decision-processes). Such a trace shows how the AI system reached its output, not that its rules are correct. The trace should be produced by the same execution that produced the output, rather than reconstructed afterward, and recorded with it ([Implementation 10.1.2: Runtime Telemetry and Artifact Tracking](#implementation-10.1.2:-runtime-telemetry-and-artifact-tracking)). Whether the displayed trace matches the logic actually executed can be checked in acceptance testing and again after changes to the rule base or software. Where a trace is too long to use under time pressure, it can be condensed by a deterministic approximation with known error, and the display should indicate that it has been condensed. For when such a design might be weighed against a learned model, see [Task 4.6: Ensure that Confidence and Rationale Shown to Personnel Reflect How the SI System Reached Its Output](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output).

**References:**

* **Research** [Sheh, R., “Explainable Artificial Intelligence Requirements for Safe, Intelligent Robots”, Proceedings of the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Intelligence and Safety for Robotics (ISR), pages 382 to 387](https://doi.org/10.1109/ISR50024.2021.9419498). A position paper on specifying explainability requirements for safety-critical robots. It distinguishes introspective explanations, drawn from the process that made the decision, from post-hoc explanations, and argues that local post-hoc methods such as LIME and SHAP hold only near the case being explained, within bounds that are hard to determine. It identifies decision trees, inductive logic programming, and models built on domain knowledge as able to give introspective explanations, argues that the trade-off against accuracy should be made deliberately, and notes that each stage of a system, from sensing to decision making, can have different explainability requirements. The paper does not address how explanations should be presented to operators.

#### Implementation 4.6.4: Distill Learned Models into Interpretable Models that Can Be Verified {#implementation-4.6.4:-distill-learned-models-into-interpretable-models-that-can-be-verified}

Distilling a learned model into one that people can read can give an organization a model whose own reasoning it can check, and sometimes verify, though it reproduces the original’s decisions only approximately. The best-performing machine learning technique for an application is often not interpretable at the level of abstraction people need. Where a trained opaque model performs well but its reasoning cannot be usefully inspected, consider using it as a demonstrator to train a self-interpretable model, such as a decision tree or rule set, that reproduces its decisions over the conditions the deployment will meet. This is behavioral cloning, first used to learn control rules from the logged actions of human operators (see Sammut 1992), with a trained model, planner, search over a simulation or digital twin, or other demonstrator in place of the human expert (see Sheh 2017; Bastani 2018).

The self-interpretable model may perform better trained this way than on the original data. The opaque model may build on a foundation model, be fine-tuned, or be trained at a scale the self-interpretable model’s algorithm cannot match, and it can supply what the original data cannot: synthetic examples to fill gaps, labels for the conditions the self-interpretable model actually meets during training, estimates of how much worse each alternative would be, and, in simulation, rare or hazardous conditions, including information that will not be available at deployment (see Sheh 2017; Bastani 2018).

If the self-interpretable model is the one deployed, its trace accurately explains what the AI system did ([Implementation 4.6.3: Display Execution Traces from Symbolic, Hybrid, and Self-Interpretable Components](#implementation-4.6.3:-display-execution-traces-from-symbolic,-hybrid,-and-self-interpretable-components)), and its rules can be reviewed by domain experts and checked against constraints such as those in [Implementation 3.2.2: Define and Independently Enforce Deterministic Operational Constraints](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints), in some cases formally (see Bastani 2018). It explains itself, not the opaque model: matching the opaque model’s outputs does not explain how the opaque model reached them (see NIST IR 8312). Where the opaque model remains the one deployed, the self-interpretable model can still be shown alongside it, with its measured agreement. This shows that a decision could have been reached by a line of reasoning a person can review, not that the opaque model reached it that way, so it should not be presented as an account of how the opaque model reached its outputs. Where the two disagree on a decision, no such line of reasoning should be shown for it, since the one on offer leads elsewhere. How much disagreement can be tolerated before the comparison stops being useful depends on the application and on the consequence of the decisions involved. Such distilled models can be more computationally efficient, allowing them to run offline on limited hardware.

The self-interpretable model need not copy its demonstrator. Its learning algorithm has its own inductive bias, a preference among hypotheses that fit the data equally well, such as for simpler rules. This can help: in early behavioral cloning of human aircraft pilots, the induced rules left out many of the pilots’ spurious actions, and the authors observed that the autopilot based on the self-interpretable model flew more smoothly than the pilots it learned from, while also providing insight into the decision-making process (see Sammut 1992). Some techniques for training self-interpretable models can also make use of background knowledge that the trained opaque model demonstrator lacks, such as engineering units, equations that model the system, quantities operators already use, or known constraints, so that their rules are stated in terms domain experts recognize and stay consistent with that knowledge (see Sammut 1992; Sheh 2021).

Measure and record how the self-interpretable model performs against ground truth, and under which conditions, and treat other conditions as untested under [Task 1.3: Implement Evaluation and Test Plans, Including TEVV, Across the SI Lifecycle](#task-1.3:-implement-evaluation-and-test-plans,-including-tevv,-across-the-si-lifecycle). Where the two models disagree, investigate rather than assume either is right: the self-interpretable model may have filtered out an error, or lost something the opaque model had right. The opaque model can be kept offline to flag disagreements and generate further training cases. The rules of the self-interpretable model can also be read for what they rely on. A rule keyed to something with no causal bearing on the decision, such as an instrument identifier or a timestamp artifact, can be a sign that the opaque model has learned a shortcut, and is worth investigating in the opaque model as well as in the explanation (see Geirhos 2020). Where the self-interpretable model fails verification, the failure may lie in the opaque model it was distilled from rather than in the distillation; in one simulated control task, neither the opaque controller nor the tree distilled from it was stable (see Bastani 2018). Repeat the distillation and its verification when the opaque model is retrained or the process or its instrumentation changes, treating the change as an update under [Task 7.5: Conduct Impact Assessments and Risk Management for SI System and Model Updates](#task-7.5:-conduct-impact-assessments-and-risk-management-for-si-system-and-model-updates).

Where the self-interpretable model cannot perform well enough, the decision may depend on more than can be stated in an interpretable form, which is itself evidence for the choice described in [Task 4.6: Ensure that Confidence and Rationale Shown to Personnel Reflect How the SI System Reached Its Output](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output). Where the opaque model works on high-dimensional raw inputs such as images, waveforms or text, distilling only the decision stage that acts on its perception outputs may be practical, with those outputs entering the self-interpretable model as premises with their own uncertainty, as in [Implementation 4.6.3: Display Execution Traces from Symbolic, Hybrid, and Self-Interpretable Components](#implementation-4.6.3:-display-execution-traces-from-symbolic,-hybrid,-and-self-interpretable-components). Conversely, one that performs well may still be too complex to use under time pressure. Its size can be limited during training, trading some performance for an explanation people can follow (see Sammut 1992), and the rationale shown can be condensed as in [Implementation 4.6.3: Display Execution Traces from Symbolic, Hybrid, and Self-Interpretable Components](#implementation-4.6.3:-display-execution-traces-from-symbolic,-hybrid,-and-self-interpretable-components) or reduced to what a responder needs as in [Implementation 4.2.1: Develop Situational Awareness Processes and Procedures for Personnel Who May Need to Intervene in the SI System’s Operation](#implementation-4.2.1:-develop-situational-awareness-processes-and-procedures-for-personnel-who-may-need-to-intervene-in-the-si-system’s-operation).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Is a distilled model deployed in place of the opaque model, or shown alongside it with its measured agreement? (see the Accurate versus Explainable & Interpretable tension in [Task 4.6: Ensure that Confidence and Rationale Shown to Personnel Reflect How the SI System Reached Its Output](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output))  
* How much disagreement between the two is tolerated before the comparison stops being shown?  
* Who has the expertise and time to distill and verify the interpretable model, including after each retraining?

**References:**

* **Research** [Sammut, C., Hurst, S., Kedzier, D. and Michie, D., “Learning to Fly”, Machine Learning: Proceedings of the Ninth International Workshop (ML92), Morgan Kaufmann, 1992, pages 385 to 393](https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-1-55860-247-2.50055-3). An early demonstration of behavioral cloning. The actions of human pilots in a flight simulator were logged and used to induce decision trees (with C4.5), which were converted into code and flown as an autopilot through take-off, climb, turn and landing. One autopilot was built per pilot, because different pilots flew the same plan in different ways. The authors report that the induced rules pruned away many of the pilots’ spurious actions, so the autopilot flew more smoothly than the person it learned from, which they note as of particular interest for safety-critical tasks. They also note that the rules are purely reactive, with no model of the domain’s causality, that rules built only from the primitive attributes logged by the simulator could not be understood by a human expert, and that higher-level attributes, supplied by the expert or constructed automatically, may be needed to simplify them.  
* **Research** [Sheh, R., “‘Why Did You Do That?’ Explainable Intelligent Robots”, The Workshops of the Thirty-First AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-17), Human-Aware Artificial Intelligence, WS-17-10](https://aaai.org/ocs/index.php/WS/AAAIW17/paper/view/15162). Describes behavioral cloning with decision trees, in which state-action pairs logged from a demonstrator train a model whose goal is to explain some aspect of the decision-making process, with the ability to replace the demonstrator a byproduct. Its section on cloning a non-causal agent uses as demonstrator a search with perfect information in a simulator, which could not itself be deployed, and treats the cloned tree as approximating that demonstrator’s policy from the noisy information the deployed agent actually has, while noting the gap between the two.  
* **Research** [Sheh, R., “Explainable Artificial Intelligence Requirements for Safe, Intelligent Robots”, Proceedings of the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Intelligence and Safety for Robotics (ISR), pages 382 to 387](https://doi.org/10.1109/ISR50024.2021.9419498). Identifies decision trees and inductive logic programming, which represent their decisions as IF-THEN-ELSE rules and first-order logic respectively, and application-specific models that include background knowledge of the application, such as equations of motion, with learned parameters that have a physical interpretation, as representations that directly support introspective explanations.  
* **Research** [Bastani, O., Pu, Y. and Solar-Lezama, A., “Verifiable Reinforcement Learning via Policy Extraction”, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 31 (NeurIPS 2018\)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/3327144.3327175). Describes VIPER, which uses a trained deep neural network policy as the demonstrator (the “oracle”) to train a decision tree policy by imitation learning, drawing on model compression and distillation, so that properties of the tree can be verified efficiently where verifying the network is typically very inefficient if not infeasible. In three simulated control tasks (a symbolic version of Atari Pong, a toy Pong game and cart-pole), extracted trees were verified for robustness, correctness and stability respectively. For cart-pole, neither the network nor the tree extracted from it was stable, and the stable tree was extracted from a different, model-based controller. Verification of the toy Pong tree found a case in which it could miss the ball; after a fix it was proved never to lose. Verifying correctness and stability relies on a model of the system dynamics (for cart-pole, an approximation to it), though robustness can be checked without one, and the guarantees apply to the tree rather than to the network it was extracted from.  
* **Guidance** [NIST AI 600-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1), July 2024, from NIST. Suggested actions MS-2.9-001 and MG-3.2-001 list model compression and surrogate models, and model compression and distillation, among the explanation techniques to apply and document for generative AI systems.  
* **Guidance** [NIST IR 8312, Four Principles of Explainable Artificial Intelligence](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.IR.8312). Section 6.3 notes that an explanation that can mimic a closed-box model’s predictions is not thereby accurate as an explanation of it, and describes models built to match the original on real input data but to answer differently on the perturbed inputs that perturbation-based explainers generate, so that the explanation describes behavior the model does not show in use. This is why performance in this Implementation is measured and recorded over stated conditions, and why the distilled model is treated as explaining itself.  
* **Research** [Geirhos, R. et al., “Shortcut Learning in Deep Neural Networks”, Nature Machine Intelligence, 2020](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-020-00257-z). Describes shortcuts as decision rules that perform well on standard benchmarks but fail to transfer to more challenging conditions. Its examples include a pneumonia classifier that had learned to identify which hospital a scan came from, for example from a hospital-specific metal token on the scan. This bears on reading a distilled model’s rules for signs that the opaque model learned a shortcut.

## Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools {#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools}

*Establish IdAM controls for SI agents and tools appropriate to their roles, auditability, risk, and oversight, throughout the SI system lifecycle.*

This Practice extends identity and access management for people and systems to SI agents and tools, so that each one is identified, limited to what its role needs, and traceable. Establishing these boundaries reduces the risk of malicious or unauthorized actions reaching risk-sensitive processes, and limits their impacts across the operational environment. Two kinds of boundary are involved. Access boundaries limit what an SI agent or tool can reach (least privilege). Action boundaries limit what it may do or set in motion with that access, at the point it acts (least agency) ([Task 5.3: Implement Principles of Least Agency and Least Privilege for SI Entities](#task-5.3:-implement-principles-of-least-agency-and-least-privilege-for-si-entities)).

Together they reduce both the attack surface, by limiting unauthorized access points and lateral pathways, and the overall risk surface, by bounding an agent’s autonomous authority, operational scope, and “blast radius,” whether the risk results from adversarial action or another source of error ([Task 3.5: Define and Control Risks to Adjacent and Related Systems](#task-3.5:-define-and-control-risks-to-adjacent-and-related-systems)). Both surfaces are defined in [Task 3.8: Scope and Map the Expanded SI Attack Surface and Risk Surface](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface). This applies zero trust principles to SI entities: an authenticated SI agent is not trusted with every action it can request, because an agent can act outside its intended scope without being compromised, so each consequential action is checked when it is taken, not only the access granted beforehand ([Implementation 5.2.2: Action-Level, Context-Aware Authorization Policies](#implementation-5.2.2:-action-level,-context-aware-authorization-policies)). Controls modeled after human user permissions are a starting point, but access and authority to act should be further restricted based on the actual need of individual SI agents and tools.

In general, authority that downstream agents or tools exercise at the request of a person or other agent should not exceed what the requester holds ([Implementation 5.3.2: Task-Bounded and Revocable Agent Authority](#implementation-5.3.2:-task-bounded-and-revocable-agent-authority)), so that the downstream agents or tools cannot be used to do what the requester could not. A different arrangement is sometimes deliberate: a downstream agent or tool may hold permissions the requester lacks, such as write access to a specialized device that may be hazardous if not used properly. While requesting people or agents may have permission to achieve an outcome with the device, such as causing it to enter a different operating mode, only the downstream agent or tool is trusted to do so properly, and in accordance with relevant risk management controls such as logging, rate limits, or oversight ([Implementation 5.3.3: Separate Privilege via Encapsulated Downstream Agents and Tools](#implementation-5.3.3:-separate-privilege-via-encapsulated-downstream-agents-and-tools)). The first limits what can be passed on, while the second places access with the agent or tool that is trusted, and controlled, to exercise it.

Access controls rely on effective asset visibility. SI systems that are deployed without authorization, such as personal LLM-based assistants or models downloaded and run locally without approval, may bypass identity and other risk management controls. Keeping such systems out is covered by [Task 3.7: Govern and Mitigate Risks from Unauthorized, Transient, and “Shadow SI” Systems](#task-3.7:-govern-and-mitigate-risks-from-unauthorized,-transient,-and-“shadow-si”-systems).
