Where it carries a fix, such as to safety, security, accuracy or reliability, holding it defers that benefit, so [Implementation 6.2.2: Track Vendor Updates and Third-Party Entity Changes Through Change Management Process](#implementation-6.2.2:-track-vendor-updates-and-third-party-entity-changes-through-change-management-process) describes an emergency path, where the organization has established one, with the update reviewed and recorded through the normal process as soon as practical afterward.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **GOVERN 1.6** (on building the AI inventory): This Task registers externally sourced models, tools and services in the existing asset management system at acquisition; inventory alone does not detect change, so this Task pairs registration with change control and telemetry.  
* **MANAGE 3.2** (on monitoring pre-trained model risks): This Task routes vendor model updates through change control and watches for unannounced version shifts; it does not cover behavioral drift within an unchanged model. For that, see for example [Task 3.4: Monitor for Anomalous SI Behavior](#task-3.4:-monitor-for-anomalous-si-behavior).  
* **MAP 4.2** (on establishing risk controls for AI system components): This Task treats change management and runtime telemetry as the internal controls applied to third-party components; it does not cover controls at the physical process boundary. For those, see for example [Task 3.2: Implement Independent Guardrails for SI Outputs](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Is an emergency path established for vendor releases that cannot wait, and which releases qualify because delay is judged an unreasonable risk? (see the Any characteristic a release could degrade versus any characteristic it would fix tension)

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Foundations for OT Cybersecurity: Asset Inventory Guidance for Owners and Operators](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-08/joint-guide-foundations-for-OT-cybersecurity-asset-inventory-guidance_508c.pdf), 13 August 2025, from CISA, EPA, NSA and FBI with the cybersecurity agencies of Australia, Canada, Germany, the Netherlands and New Zealand. Step 5, Implement Life Cycle Management, asks organizations to define the life cycle stages of each asset, from acquisition through decommissioning. It also asks for policies that follow the organization’s change management process and require inventory updates whenever devices are introduced or removed, even under emergency change authority. This bears on bringing externally sourced SI components into the same lifecycle and change control.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. The section Comparing OT and IT System Security notes that IT components typically have a lifetime on the order of three to five years, while deployed OT technology often lasts on the order of 10 to 15 years and sometimes longer. The discussion of OT cybersecurity program content adds that an OT system’s lifespan can exceed 20 years, so legacy systems may contain hardware and software that vendors no longer support. This bears on the mismatch this Task manages.

#### Implementation 6.2.1: Register Externally Sourced SI Components in Asset Management Systems {#implementation-6.2.1:-register-externally-sourced-si-components-in-asset-management-systems}

A register of externally sourced SI, including SI embedded in other products, helps an organization know what SI it depends on and where. Add every externally sourced AI model, tool, or service to the organization’s existing asset management system at the point of acquisition, capturing vendor, version, and purpose so it is visible alongside traditional IT and OT assets rather than tracked separately or not at all. Record SI functions that are present in an acquired product but disabled, since a license change or vendor update can enable them without a procurement event. The record can also identify the asset or process each component serves, its owner, its announced end of support, and its AIBOM and hazard reachability disclosure under [Implementation 6.1.2](#implementation-6.1.2:-require-sibom-for-mission-critical-applications) and [Implementation 6.1.5](#implementation-6.1.5:-operational-si-hazard-reachability-disclosures). Where the organization also keeps the list described in [Implementation 7.1.1: Create and Maintain a Master SI Asset List](#implementation-7.1.1:-create-and-maintain-a-master-si-asset-list), externally sourced components can be recorded in both, or the two reconciled, so that the organization does not hold two diverging accounts of its SI systems. Periodic reconciliation of the register against observed network traffic and supplier disclosures can reveal components that were never registered. Include SI capabilities embedded in OT devices and other products, as well as standalone SI models, tools and services. Record where each model is hosted and whether it needs connectivity to the vendor to function. For SI capabilities in OT, the high-priority fields already recommended for OT assets, such as asset criticality, manufacturer, model and the user accounts expected to access the asset, can be recorded for the SI component as well.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Are externally sourced components recorded in the asset management system, in the list under [Implementation 7.1.1: Create and Maintain a Master SI Asset List](#implementation-7.1.1:-create-and-maintain-a-master-si-asset-list), or in both with reconciliation?  
* How often is the register reconciled against observed network traffic and supplier disclosures?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control CM-8, System Component Inventory, maintains an inventory of system components at the granularity needed for tracking, including software version numbers and supplier information, and enhancement CM-8(1) updates it as part of component installations, removals and system updates, which is the existing control into which externally sourced AI models, tools and services are registered at the point of acquisition.  
* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by CISA. Section 2.3, Understanding the Role of OT Vendors in AI Integration, notes that some OT devices now come with built-in AI technology that may require internet connectivity to function. It asks operators to require vendors to clarify the supply chain of AI models in their products, such as where the models are hosted. This bears on what the asset record holds for embedded SI capabilities.  
* **Guidance** [Foundations for OT Cybersecurity: Asset Inventory Guidance for Owners and Operators](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-08/joint-guide-foundations-for-OT-cybersecurity-asset-inventory-guidance_508c.pdf), 13 August 2025, from CISA, EPA, NSA and FBI with the cybersecurity agencies of Australia, Canada, Germany, the Netherlands and New Zealand. Step 2 lists the high-priority attributes to collect, among them asset criticality, manufacturer, model, communication protocols and user accounts. Appendix A, Table 1, gives the benefit of each, for example that asset criticality lets assets be managed by operational role, safety impact and exposure to risk. This bears on the fields recorded for an SI component in an OT asset inventory.

#### Implementation 6.2.2: Track Vendor Updates and Third-Party Entity Changes Through Change Management Process {#implementation-6.2.2:-track-vendor-updates-and-third-party-entity-changes-through-change-management-process}

Where possible, route vendor-issued updates and third-party configuration changes through the organization’s standard change management process, helping ensure updates are reviewed and approved before deployment rather than applied silently. Where the deployment model does not allow an update to be gated, such as for cloud-hosted and vendor-managed models, document that as a known limitation and monitor the provider on an ongoing basis. Where earlier versions are not kept available, records of decisions made before the change may become hard to interpret (see [Task 10.1: Define Decision-Level Logging and Metadata Retention Policies](#task-10.1:-define-decision-level-logging-and-metadata-retention-policies)). Sometimes an update cannot wait for the full review, because the delay would itself create an unreasonable risk. Where the organization has established an emergency path like the one in [Implementation 7.4.1: Define and Implement Requirements for Approvals and Logging of Updates and Changes to SI Systems](#implementation-7.4.1:-define-and-implement-requirements-for-approvals-and-logging-of-updates-and-changes-to-si-systems), route such an update through it, so that the update is reviewed and recorded through the normal process as soon as practical afterward. Where no such path exists, options include deferring the update, landing it under containment as in [Implementation 6.1.1: Add SI Disclosure to Existing Procurement Policies](#implementation-6.1.1:-add-si-disclosure-to-existing-procurement-policies) where staging and tightened safety wrappers have been prepared, or suspending the SI system, each with its own considerations, such as continued exposure to the fault the update fixes. Some frameworks, such as SP 800-53’s CM-3, keep urgent changes within change control. 

Combine required disclosures, as discussed in [Implementation 6.1.1: Add SI Disclosure to Existing Procurement Policies](#implementation-6.1.1:-add-si-disclosure-to-existing-procurement-policies), with runtime monitoring and telemetry, as discussed in [Task 3.4: Monitor for Anomalous SI Behavior](#task-3.4:-monitor-for-anomalous-si-behavior), to detect unannounced behavioral shifts after the fact, rather than treating the component as static. Asking at procurement whether the vendor allows a model version to be pinned, so that updates are adopted deliberately rather than pushed, can show in advance whether such gating will be possible. Comparing each new AIBOM received under [Implementation 6.1.2: Require SIBOM for Mission-Critical Applications](#implementation-6.1.2:-require-sibom-for-mission-critical-applications) with the one recorded for the version in service can also reveal changes in base model, training data or external services that the vendor did not announce.

Changes to track include model version, training data provenance, inference endpoint, vendor-controlled configuration such as system prompts and guardrail or threshold settings, a change of the foundation model provider behind the same product, and change to the third-party entity itself, such as acquisition, sub-processor change, or end of support. Changes should trigger re-evaluation under [Implementation 2.3.4: Recurrent Risk Evaluations](#implementation-2.3.4:-recurrent-risk-evaluations). 

The depth of that re-evaluation can scale with consequence. For example, a library fix with no change in behavior may follow a standard path, while a new model version in a function that can affect setpoints or alarms can be tested against the same representative operating scenarios as its predecessor, including upset conditions, compared with it, and reviewed by whichever role the organization assigns to approve changes to that function. The process or safety owner knows the consequences of the function best, and also carries pressure to keep it in service. Record who reviews and why. Where one person has to both own the function and approve its changes, for example in a small organization or a specialized function with few qualified reviewers, record that and how the conflict is offset, such as by a second reviewer for safety-affecting changes ([Implementation 3.9.6: Keep a Record of Design Decisions and Accepted Risks](#implementation-3.9.6:-keep-a-record-of-design-decisions-and-accepted-risks)). In particular, newly released or substantially revised models and other system components, AI or otherwise, warrant elevated monitoring and testing for a defined period after adoption. Treat these as a distinct category with a documented exit criterion for returning them to routine monitoring. This includes tools, libraries and other dependencies that an agent invokes: an automatic version update to a tool can change what the agent produces while the agent stays entirely within its authorized scope, so access monitoring alone will not reveal it. 

Where the organization hosts the component, keeping the previous release available, with its hash recorded in a protected location, supports reverting to the last known good state if an update introduces problems. Reverting carries its own considerations, such as reintroducing faults the update fixed or losing compatibility with components that have since changed. [Implementation 7.4.1: Define and Implement Requirements for Approvals and Logging of Updates and Changes to SI Systems](#implementation-7.4.1:-define-and-implement-requirements-for-approvals-and-logging-of-updates-and-changes-to-si-systems) sets the equivalent requirement for changes to internally sourced components.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which role approves changes to each safety-affecting function, and how deep is the re-evaluation for each kind of change?  
* How long does elevated monitoring of a newly adopted component last, and what is its exit criterion?  
* How long are earlier vendor releases and their SIBOMs kept, so that past decisions stay interpretable and reverting stays possible?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control CM-3, Configuration Change Control, reviews and approves or disapproves configuration-controlled changes with explicit consideration of impact analyses, including unscheduled or unauthorized changes. Control SA-9, External System Services, applies where the organization has no direct control over a provider’s implementation of the required controls and calls for processes to monitor the provider’s compliance on an ongoing basis, which is the situation of a cloud-hosted model whose updates cannot be gated.  
* **Guidance** [Deploying AI Systems Securely: Best Practices for Deploying Secure and Resilient AI Systems](https://media.defense.gov/2024/Apr/15/2003439257/-1/-1/0/CSI-DEPLOYING-AI-SYSTEMS-SECURELY.PDF), Cybersecurity Information Sheet, version 1.0, April 2024, from the NSA Artificial Intelligence Security Center with CISA, the FBI and the national cybersecurity centers of Australia, Canada, New Zealand and the United Kingdom. Under Validate the AI system before and during use, it asks for hashes of each release of the AI model to be archived in a tamper-proof location, and for automated rollbacks so that the organization can revert to the last known good state. Under Update and patch regularly, it asks for a full evaluation before a new model version is redeployed. This bears on re-evaluating and reverting vendor updates.  
* **Guidance** [OpenSSF Model Signing (OMS) Specification, Version 1.0](https://github.com/ossf/model-signing-spec), from the AI/ML Working Group of the Open Source Security Foundation, a cross-industry body hosted by the Linux Foundation; checked against commit 91bf841, October 2026\. It defines a detached signature over every file in a model directory, made with a bare key, a certificate chain or Sigstore keyless signing (Section 4.1), so that the organization can confirm that an update came from the vendor and was not altered on the way. This bears on checking vendor-issued model updates before they enter change management.

#### Implementation 6.2.3: Manage End-of-Life Transitions for Externally Sourced SI Components {#implementation-6.2.3:-manage-end-of-life-transitions-for-externally-sourced-si-components}

Planning for a vendor component’s end of life helps an organization replace the component in time, since models and hosted services can be withdrawn on much shorter cycles than the equipment that depends on them. Organizations with established obsolescence management for equipment can build on it. Define a formal offboarding process for externally sourced AI components reaching end-of-life or vendor discontinuation, including secure decommissioning and confirmation that no dependent systems are left relying on an unsupported component. Procurement terms can ask the supplier to state how long it will provide security fixes for the component’s models, runtimes and libraries, matched where feasible to the expected service life of the equipment that depends on it. They can also ask for a minimum notice period before a model or hosted service is withdrawn, long enough for the sector’s replacement lead times. Recording each announced end-of-support date in the asset record under [Implementation 6.2.1: Register Externally Sourced SI Components in Asset Management Systems](#implementation-6.2.1:-register-externally-sourced-si-components-in-asset-management-systems), and reviewing approaching dates on a set cycle, can help the organization act on that notice in time. A successor model offered by the vendor should be treated as a new component under [Implementation 6.2.2: Track Vendor Updates and Third-Party Entity Changes Through Change Management Process](#implementation-6.2.2:-track-vendor-updates-and-third-party-entity-changes-through-change-management-process), even where it carries the same product name or the vendor states that it is equivalent. Vendor discontinuation is one of the external triggers for retirement recorded under [Implementation 13.1.1: Identify Retirement Triggers, Including Those Outside the Organization’s Control](#implementation-13.1.1:-identify-retirement-triggers,-including-those-outside-the-organization’s-control), and the withdrawal of the component’s authority follows [Task 13.2: Withdraw All Authority and Confirm the Result](#task-13.2:-withdraw-all-authority-and-confirm-the-result). Preparation can begin before any discontinuation is announced. Retaining enough knowledge of the component in-house, and a contingency plan for the case where the vendor’s model is no longer available or supported, can shorten the transition if the vendor ends the contract or leaves the market. Once the vendor’s model is gone, records of decisions it made may become hard to interpret, so deciding beforehand what to keep alongside them, such as the model version, prompts, configuration, and other state and information that influenced the output, can keep them usable ([Implementation 10.1.5: Define What Each Operational Record Is For](#implementation-10.1.5:-define-what-each-operational-record-is-for); see also [Practice 13: Establish Procedures for Retiring SI Systems and Withdrawing Their Authority](#practice-13:-establish-procedures-for-retiring-si-systems-and-withdrawing-their-authority)).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* What support period and withdrawal notice are asked of each supplier, and how much knowledge of each component is retained in-house?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-47 Revision 1, Managing the Security of Information Exchanges](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-47r1), from NIST. Section 3.4.1, Planned Discontinuance, sets out the steps for ending an exchange with an external party: written notification with reasons, timeline and responsible staff; scheduling that leaves time to notify affected users and identify alternative resources for continuing operations; agreement on the disposition of shared data, including purging moderate- or high-impact data; and updating security plans afterward. For an AI service, the shared data includes what the provider holds from inference requests and fine-tuning.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control SA-22, Unsupported System Components, replaces components when support is no longer available from the developer, vendor or manufacturer, or provides alternative sources of continued support, and its discussion covers components that remain essential to the mission after support ends, which is the situation this Implementation’s offboarding process addresses for discontinued AI models and services.  
* **Working Document** [NIST SP 800-218r1 ipd, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.2: Recommendations for Mitigating the Risk of Software Vulnerabilities](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218r1.ipd), initial public draft, as of December 2025, from NIST. Task PW.4.4, on verifying that acquired third-party software components comply with the organization’s requirements throughout their life cycles, gives as Example 4 checking that each component is still actively maintained and has not reached end of life, extending to components acquired through a merger or acquisition, and as Example 5 a plan of action for each component that is no longer maintained or will soon be unavailable. This Implementation applies the same discipline to externally sourced AI components.  
* **Guidance** [Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management, SR Letter 11-7 Attachment](https://www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/srletters/2011/sr1107a1.pdf), 4 April 2011, from the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, written for the banking organizations they supervise. Section V, under Validation of Vendor and Other Third-Party Products, stresses keeping as much knowledge in-house as possible in case the vendor or the bank ends the contract or the vendor is no longer in business. It asks banks to have contingency plans for when a vendor model is no longer available or cannot be supported by the vendor. This bears on preparing for offboarding before it is triggered.

### Task 6.3: Identify and Control Dataflows Across the SI Supply Chain {#task-6.3:-identify-and-control-dataflows-across-the-si-supply-chain}

Knowing and controlling the data that flows between SI systems and external services helps an organization keep sensitive and operational information within agreed handling terms, and notice flows it did not expect. Define and maintain visibility over the dataflows between AI systems and external vendors, platforms, and services they connect to. Ensure that data exchanged with these external dependencies, including telemetry, inference requests (a trained AI model producing an output for a given input), model updates, and any operational or sensitive information transmitted outside the organization is authorized, monitored, and bound by data handling policies. These dependencies include the foundation model providers and subprocessors behind the immediate supplier, with which the organization may have no contract. For each flow, consider whether it is needed and whether the data can be minimized, aggregated, anonymized or delayed, and whether the vendor may use the organization’s data to train models offered to other customers. Some information already carries handling obligations, for example Critical Energy Infrastructure Information in the electric sector, and these should be checked before a flow is permitted. Integrating an SI system should not open paths between operational networks and external services that existing segmentation deliberately closed: flows can instead pass through the existing demilitarized zone, or through push-based or brokered arrangements that do not grant persistent inbound access.

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Privacy-Enhanced:** Contributes containment of what leaves continuously rather than as a one-off transfer: inference requests and operational telemetry, cataloged in [Implementation 6.3.1: Catalog Data Egress Points and Third-Party Processing Destinations](#implementation-6.3.1:-catalog-data-egress-points-and-third-party-processing-destinations) and routed through restricted enclaves in [Implementation 6.3.2: Implement Egress Monitoring and Isolated, Access-Restricted Enclaves for SI Training and Telemetry](#implementation-6.3.2:-implement-egress-monitoring-and-isolated,-access-restricted-enclaves-for-si-training-and-telemetry). This Task does not address privacy risk arising from the AI system’s own outputs, which [Implementation 7.5.3: Integrate Privacy Impact Assessments (PIA) into Update Cycles](#implementation-7.5.3:-integrate-privacy-impact-assessments-\(pia\)-into-update-cycles) addresses in part, through privacy impact assessment at each significant update.  
* **Secure:** Contributes exfiltration detection at the AI egress path, watching cataloged destinations for unexpected volume or destination change ([Implementation 6.3.2: Implement Egress Monitoring and Isolated, Access-Restricted Enclaves for SI Training and Telemetry](#implementation-6.3.2:-implement-egress-monitoring-and-isolated,-access-restricted-enclaves-for-si-training-and-telemetry)), which is how loss of a model, training data or telemetry through a vendor endpoint becomes visible, whether through attack or misconfiguration. A destination change can also reveal a vendor endpoint or sub-processor change that was not announced, which [Task 6.2: Align SI and Existing CI Asset Lifecycle Management](#task-6.2:-align-si-and-existing-ci-asset-lifecycle-management) tracks. This Task does not cover authenticating the requesting AI entities, which [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools) does.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Secure:** The egress catalog in [Implementation 6.3.1: Catalog Data Egress Points and Third-Party Processing Destinations](#implementation-6.3.1:-catalog-data-egress-points-and-third-party-processing-destinations) and the per-tool-call records in [Implementation 6.3.2: Implement Egress Monitoring and Isolated, Access-Restricted Enclaves for SI Training and Telemetry](#implementation-6.3.2:-implement-egress-monitoring-and-isolated,-access-restricted-enclaves-for-si-training-and-telemetry) show what sensitive data leaves, by which paths, and which third parties hold it. An attacker could use them to pick the vendor or destination where the organization’s most sensitive data accumulates, or a path that monitoring does not cover. Protecting these records is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Privacy-Enhanced and Secure versus Reliable:** Reliability may depend on third party remote monitoring, such as by a vendor with specialized knowledge. Restricting or inspecting what leaves for third parties may impair system reliability as the vendor may be unable to respond to degradation appropriately, and may limit the vendor services and updates the SI system can draw on. One way to balance this is to agree with the vendor on a reviewed, minimized extract that supports its monitoring, as in [Implementation 6.3.2: Implement Egress Monitoring and Isolated, Access-Restricted Enclaves for SI Training and Telemetry](#implementation-6.3.2:-implement-egress-monitoring-and-isolated,-access-restricted-enclaves-for-si-training-and-telemetry). Others include vendor monitoring on premises under the organization’s access controls, or accepting less vendor support for less critical functions.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MANAGE 3.1** (on monitoring and responding to third-party risks): This Task monitors what leaves the organization to reach third-party AI services and applies egress controls; it does not cover monitoring the third party’s own behavior or performance. For that, see for example [Task 6.2: Align SI and Existing CI Asset Lifecycle Management](#task-6.2:-align-si-and-existing-ci-asset-lifecycle-management).  
* **MEASURE 2.10** (on measuring privacy): This Task covers the data-exposure inventory that a privacy-risk examination depends on; it does not cover performing that examination or assess privacy risk arising from the system’s own outputs.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which dataflows to third parties are permitted, and may a vendor use the organization’s data to train models offered to others?  
* How much telemetry is shared with vendors for remote monitoring? (see the Privacy-Enhanced and Secure versus Reliable tension)

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-47 Revision 1, Managing the Security of Information Exchanges](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-47r1), from NIST. Section 3.1.5, Step 5: Document Appropriate Agreements, with Table 1, Potential Agreements Matrix, maps the method of exchange and the impact level of the information to the agreements that may be needed, from an entry in a tracking system for low-impact exchanges to information exchange agreements, memoranda of understanding, non-disclosure and service-level agreements for higher-impact exchanges via database- or web-based services. Sending inference requests or telemetry to an external AI service is an exchange via a web-based service, and the matrix gives a starting point for the handling terms this Task asks to be in place.  
* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by CISA. Section 2.2 suggests not sharing sensitive data with AI models hosted in environments controlled by external parties, and Section 2.3 notes that operators may not want vendors to train AI on operational data. Section 2.4 asks that new connection paths work through the existing demilitarized zone or jump host infrastructure, and Section 4.1 prefers push-based or brokered architectures that do not grant persistent inbound access. This bears on the dataflow controls this Task asks for.  
* **Guidance** [Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Real-Time System Operations](https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/our-work/white-papers/whitepaper-ai-and-ml-in-real-time-system-operations.pdf), White Paper Revision 1, November 2024, from the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC). In Chapter 3, under Informational Leakage, it reports significant concern about the security of Critical Energy Infrastructure Information sent to or returned by generative AI systems. Energy sector only. This bears on checking the handling obligations that already attach to information before it flows to an SI vendor.

#### Implementation 6.3.1: Catalog Data Egress Points and Third-Party Processing Destinations {#implementation-6.3.1:-catalog-data-egress-points-and-third-party-processing-destinations}

A catalog of egress points helps an organization decide what data may leave, and notice when data goes somewhere unexpected. Identify every point where organizational data leaves the environment to reach a third-party AI vendor or service, and document what data is sent, why, and where it is processed, so the organization has as complete a picture of its external data exposure as practical. Include data that vendors reach through remote, cloud or offshore access, not only data that the organization sends. For each destination, record where the data resides and whether the vendor may use it to train or improve its SI systems. Connected equipment with embedded SI capabilities, such as robots that rely on cloud services and remote maintenance, can send operational data to the vendor in normal operation. Include such equipment, not only the SI services the organization calls directly. Also record how long each destination retains the data and any further parties, such as sub-processors or model providers, to which it passes the data. An SI product can contact destinations that its documentation does not list, such as for telemetry, update checks or remote support. Comparing supplier disclosures and AI bills of materials with observed network traffic can help find them.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Who maintains the catalog, and how often is it compared with observed network traffic?  
* How long may each destination keep the organization’s data, and to which further parties may it pass the data?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-47 Revision 1, Managing the Security of Information Exchanges](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-47r1), from NIST. Section 3.1.5.8, Logged in Tracking System, describes a log of information exchanges leaving the authorization boundary, kept in a spreadsheet, database, GRC tool or the system security plan. Section 3.1.4, Step 4: Identify Specific Protection Requirements, asks the parties to settle whether ownership transfers, how exchanged information is stored, whether it may be passed on to a third organization or system, and how it is destroyed, and to minimize the data exchanged. Those are the questions to answer for each external AI processing destination this Implementation catalogs.  
* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by CISA. Section 2.2, Manage OT Data Security Risks for AI Systems, asks operators to understand how AI vendors access and use their OT data, especially through remote, cloud or offshore access. Section 2.3 suggests a data usage policy that refers to data residency, communications paths, encryption and storage, noting that operators may not want vendors to train AI on operational data. Both bear on the fields this Implementation asks the catalog to record.  
* **Working Document** [National Security Commission on Robotics for Advanced Manufacturing, Preliminary Report](https://www.scsp.ai/robotics-preliminary-report/), October 2026\. Under Finding 3, the section on foreign component and software dependencies notes that a modern robot often combines sensors, wireless connectivity, proprietary software, cloud services and remote maintenance. It reports a 2026 case in which data from consumer robot vacuums was sent to cloud servers abroad as part of standard operation. Under Finding 9 it notes that factories and other robot users worry about giving their supplier a view into how they operate. This bears on cataloging what connected equipment sends to its vendor in normal operation.

#### Implementation 6.3.2: Implement Egress Monitoring and Isolated, Access-Restricted Enclaves for SI Training and Telemetry {#implementation-6.3.2:-implement-egress-monitoring-and-isolated,-access-restricted-enclaves-for-si-training-and-telemetry}

Egress monitoring and restricted paths help an organization detect unauthorized data transfers and limit what can leave if an SI system or vendor connection is compromised. Monitor the egress points cataloged in [Implementation 6.3.1: Catalog Data Egress Points and Third-Party Processing Destinations](#implementation-6.3.1:-catalog-data-egress-points-and-third-party-processing-destinations) for unexpected volume or destination changes, and route sensitive data used for AI training or telemetry through isolated, access-restricted environments rather than general-purpose network paths. Flows to a destination that is not in the catalog warrant attention, as well as changes at cataloged points. For data leaving OT networks, push-based or brokered transfer, using a unidirectional gateway where feasible, can help keep the enclave from becoming a persistent inbound path into control systems. Suppliers then receive a reviewed extract rather than live access to operational systems. Flow logs and access logs for SI endpoints that attribute egress to an asset and identity, together with data loss prevention inspection of prompts and outputs, can support this monitoring. Where agents choose at runtime which tools and external services to call, a catalog prepared in advance cannot list every destination; record at each tool call the classification of the data passed, its destination, and a hash of the payload, so that the path the data took can be reconstructed ([Implementation 8.1.5: Multi-Agent Cascade Reconstruction Capabilities](#implementation-8.1.5:-multi-agent-cascade-reconstruction-capabilities)).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Where is one-way or brokered transfer used for data leaving OT networks?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control enhancement SC-7(10), Prevent Exfiltration, addresses both intentional and unintentional exfiltration, and its techniques include traffic profile analysis to detect deviations from the expected volume and types of traffic, which is the monitoring of AI data egress points for unexpected volume or destination changes asked for here.  
* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by CISA. Section 3.2, Integrating AI Into Existing Security and Cybersecurity Frameworks, lists under robust security controls collecting flow logs and access logs for AI endpoints, tracking data egress by asset and identity, and integrating with data loss prevention for prompt and output inspection. This bears on how the egress monitoring in this Implementation can be instrumented.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Section 5.2.3.1, Network Architecture, describes a unidirectional gateway or data diode as an alternative to firewalls that permits authorized communication in only one direction. Appendix E.1.2 gives its common use at the boundary between operational and enterprise networks, letting traffic leave the operational network but not enter. This bears on how data reaches the enclave this Implementation describes from OT networks.

## Practice 7: Manage Internal SI Supply Chain and Data Provenance {#practice-7:-manage-internal-si-supply-chain-and-data-provenance}

*Establish operational oversight for SI assets that are under direct organizational control, including data and inference capabilities, once they have been acquired or developed.*

Keeping track of the SI systems an organization controls directly, the data that shapes their learned behavior, and the changes made to them helps the organization oversee, update, and retire each system deliberately. This Practice focuses on the mechanics of deployed systems internal to the organization, including:

* local training, transfer learning, and fine-tuning,   
* retrieval-augmented data repositories,   
* version control for safety wrappers,   
* local data provenance and flow,   
* localized SI model and system configurations, and   
* locally hosted inference. 

Keeping earlier versions of models, prompts, and retrieval sources after a change can also keep past decisions interpretable (see [Practice 10: Implement Multi-Tiered SI System Logging and Audit Capabilities](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities)) although this may carry substantial overhead for systems that update their behavior on a regular basis. In operational settings, these changes can go through the organization’s existing change management process, such as for process safety, or through a separate process for SI. An existing process brings established safety review and familiarity to operations staff, but may lack reviewers able to judge changes to models, data or prompts.

This Practice also describes the visibility needed to mitigate “Shadow SI” risks and helps keep internal modifications to automated logic traceable and mission-aligned. In addition, it includes measures that support [Task 3.7: Govern and Mitigate Risks from Unauthorized, Transient, and “Shadow SI” Systems](#task-3.7:-govern-and-mitigate-risks-from-unauthorized,-transient,-and-“shadow-si”-systems), and informs the need to update the SI attack and risk surface as discussed in [Task 3.8: Scope and Map the Expanded SI Attack Surface and Risk Surface](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface). 

[Practice 6](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management) and [Practice 7](#practice-7:-manage-internal-si-supply-chain-and-data-provenance) are two sides of the same SI supply chain. This Practice covers what the organization manages directly once a component is in its hands, whether acquired or developed. [Practice 6: Integrate Visibility of the External Supply Chain of SI into Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management) covers what can only be obtained from vendors and third parties, from before acquisition through the life of the contract. Where an internal SI system calls an external service, both apply: [Practice 6: Integrate Visibility of the External Supply Chain of SI into Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management) for what the vendor discloses and commits to, and [Implementation 7.4.2: Implement Regular Integrity Checks for Systems that Interface with External SI Services](#implementation-7.4.2:-implement-regular-integrity-checks-for-systems-that-interface-with-external-si-services) for what the organization checks for itself.

*Note on terminology:* In [Practices 6](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management) and 7, “SI supply chain” means the supply chain of the SI system itself: its models, data, software and services. SI systems used to manage an organization’s physical supply chain, such as logistics, routing or procurement optimization, are within scope as SI systems and are covered by the Practices that apply to any SI system, rather than by [Practices 6](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management) and 7.

**Search Keywords:** data provenance, data lineage, master AI asset list, AI asset inventory, model registry, fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), vector store, prompt versioning, configuration management, policy-as-code, policy lock, online learning governance, champion-challenger testing, catastrophic forgetting, privacy impact assessment (PIA), substrate substitution, model archiving, data poisoning prevention, feature selection, feature engineering, data preparation, input validation, input minimization

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Transparent:** Contributes a single internal account of what SI is running, at which version, built from which models, drawing on which data, and where that data came from, so that oversight rests on a maintained inventory rather than on what departments happen to report. This Practice does not cover components obtained from vendors before acquisition, which [Practice 6: Integrate Visibility of the External Supply Chain of SI into Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management) covers.  
* **Accountable:** Contributes a record, for each change to a model, its data, or the safety mechanisms around it, of who authorized the change and on what evidence, so that internal modifications to automated logic stay traceable. This Practice does not cover capturing what the SI system did in operation, which [Practice 10: Implement Multi-Tiered SI System Logging and Audit Capabilities](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities) covers.  
* **Secure:** Contributes protection against unauthorized change to what shapes SI behavior from the inside: the data it learns from or retrieves, its system prompts and safety filters, and the parameters of systems that adapt while running. This Practice does not cover deciding whether a specific action is permitted at the moment it is carried out, which [Practice 3](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior) and [Practice 5](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools) address.  
* **Any characteristic a change could degrade:** Contributes review of authorized changes to the same data, prompts, safety filters and adaptive parameters before they take effect ([Task 7.5: Conduct Impact Assessments and Risk Management for SI System and Model Updates](#task-7.5:-conduct-impact-assessments-and-risk-management-for-si-system-and-model-updates)), so that a well-intended change does not quietly lose behavior that was already correct, loosen a safety boundary, or otherwise degrade another characteristic by an unacceptable amount. This Practice does not cover setting the standard a change is judged against, which [Practice 1](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success) and [Practice 2](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations) cover.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Secure:** The asset list, data inventory, and SI bills of materials this Practice builds together describe what SI is running, where, on what data, and behind which controls. Together this information could help an attacker choose and plan an attack. [Task 7.3: Manage Version Control and Logging for Internal SI Safety Mechanisms](#task-7.3:-manage-version-control-and-logging-for-internal-si-safety-mechanisms) already treats sensitive system prompts as sensitive information; how the inventory itself is classified and handled is for the organization to decide, within any regulatory or contractual obligations, as with other descriptions of where its systems are exposed.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Any characteristic a change could degrade versus any characteristic it would fix:** Where a change to a model, its data, its prompts or its safety mechanisms can wait, full change control costs little and guards against a change that quietly degrades safety, security, reliability or another characteristic. Where the change is itself an urgent fix, the same review leaves the fault in place while it runs. If the normal review cannot wait, options include suspending the SI system under [Practice 4: Define Procedures for Emergency Avoidance Override, Recovery, and Situational Awareness](#practice-4:-define-procedures-for-emergency-avoidance-override,-recovery,-and-situational-awareness) until the reviewed change is ready, where the organization has prepared a way to carry on the function without it, or using an emergency change path, if the organization has chosen to establish one ([Implementation 7.4.1: Define and Implement Requirements for Approvals and Logging of Updates and Changes to SI Systems](#implementation-7.4.1:-define-and-implement-requirements-for-approvals-and-logging-of-updates-and-changes-to-si-systems)). Suspension carries its own considerations, such as the loss of the function and the extra load on personnel who take it over (see [Practice 11: Maintain SI-Aware Mission Continuity and Disaster Recovery Planning](#practice-11:-maintain-si-aware-mission-continuity-and-disaster-recovery-planning)). Changes made through an emergency path are reviewed and recorded through the normal process as soon as practical afterward. Until then, temporary measures such as closer monitoring or tighter guardrails can limit the risk of a change that has not yet been reviewed.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **GOVERN 1.6** (on building the SI inventory): This Practice covers the inventory of SI systems, models and data under direct organizational control, including legacy systems and those found by network scanning; it does not cover setting the resourcing of that inventory that GOVERN 1.6 also calls for.  
* **MAP 4.2** (on establishing risk controls for SI system components): This Practice covers internal controls for the components it governs: data provenance, version control for safety mechanisms, authorization of changes, and assessment of updates; it does not cover controls on third-party technologies before acquisition. For those, see for example [Practice 6: Integrate Visibility of the External Supply Chain of SI into Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management).  
* **GOVERN 1.7** (on establishing decommissioning processes): This Practice covers visibility that enables the retirement of internally developed models, datasets, and pipelines without breaking what depends on them or leaving unmonitored attack surfaces; it does not cover withdrawing the authority of an SI system that is still operating or ensuring that critical capability and information is preserved. For that, see for example [Practice 13: Establish Procedures for Retiring SI Systems and Withdrawing Their Authority](#practice-13:-establish-procedures-for-retiring-si-systems-and-withdrawing-their-authority).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Do changes to SI systems go through the existing management of change process, a separate process, or both, and who reviews changes to models, data or prompts?
* Who resources the inventory, data certification, and change review this Practice calls for, and what is deferred, with what remaining risk, when resources fall short?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-128, Guide for Security-Focused Configuration Management of Information Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-128), August 2011, with updates as of October 2019, from NIST. Section 2.2 organizes configuration management into planning, identifying and implementing configurations, controlling configuration changes and monitoring, and notes that monitoring identifies undiscovered or undocumented components and unauthorized changes. Section 2.3.4 treats a consolidated component inventory as the basis for visibility and control, and Section 2.3.7 keeps older approved baselines available for review or rollback. Section 3.3.2 asks that unscheduled changes, made when time does not allow the established process, still be managed and be reviewed as soon as practical afterward. Written for information systems, it is the established discipline this Practice extends to models, data, prompts and safety wrappers.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-218A, Secure Software Development Practices for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models: An SSDF Community Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218A), July 2024, from NIST. Section 2 notes that model source code is amenable to practices for versioning, lineage and reproducibility, but final weights are defined only after training and fine-tuning, where tracking collection, processing and training becomes limited, and asks organizations to document the parts those practices do not cover. Task PS.3.2 recommendation R1 asks that the provenance of a model and its components and derivatives be tracked. Both bear on this Practice’s lineage from base model to locally fine-tuned adapter.  
* **Guidance** [Establish Risks and Controls for the AI Supply Chain, version 1.0](https://www.coalitionforsecureai.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/risks-and-controls-for-the-ai-supply-chain-v1.pdf), 12 June 2025, from Workstream 1, Software Supply Chain Security for AI Systems, of the Coalition for Secure AI, an OASIS Open Project. Section 3.2.2, under Internal Model Security Considerations, calls the assumption that internally developed and stored models are inherently secure a common misconception: they remain open to data poisoning, and privileged insiders could modify them leaving few forensic traces. Section 4.1 asks executives to implement discovery processes identifying SI use within internal systems. Both bear on this Practice’s internal scope and its visibility of Shadow SI.

### Task 7.1: Maintain an Internal Registry of SI Deployments {#task-7.1:-maintain-an-internal-registry-of-si-deployments}

Catalog internal instances, versions, and specific use-cases of SI systems deployed across different departments, and the authorization associated with each (including legacy SI systems that predate formal authorization). This Task helps ensure that internal stakeholders have a clear inventory of “where” AI is operating within the organization, enabling consistent oversight and maintenance even when models are embedded in departmental workflows. Include SI systems embedded in vendor products and devices, such as analytics added to a data historian or inference on an edge device. Such systems can arrive through a routine update without any procurement decision; [Implementation 6.1.1: Add SI Disclosure to Existing Procurement Policies](#implementation-6.1.1:-add-si-disclosure-to-existing-procurement-policies) covers what vendors are asked to disclose. The registry can sit within the organization’s existing IT and OT asset inventory rather than in a separate list, as externally sourced components do under [Implementation 6.2.1: Register Externally Sourced SI Components in Asset Management Systems](#implementation-6.2.1:-register-externally-sourced-si-components-in-asset-management-systems). Whether registration is a condition of approval to connect an SI system to operational networks or data is for the organization to decide, within any regulatory or contractual obligations. Making it one helps keep the registry complete, at the cost of a step that can slow urgent connections. Linked to the data inventory and to AI bills of materials, the registry can also help locate the deployments affected when a vulnerability, a vendor model change or a data quality problem comes to light.

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Transparent:** Contributes a catalog of where AI is operating, at which version, for what purpose and under what authorization, including administrative tools and legacy systems that predate formal authorization, with lineage from base model to fine-tuned adapter and the data sources each draws on. This Task does not cover restricting or removing the unauthorized AI that scanning under [Implementation 7.1.3: Integrate Automated Internal Software and SI Bill of Material Management](#implementation-7.1.3:-integrate-automated-internal-software-and-si-bill-of-material-management) may find, which [Task 3.7: Govern and Mitigate Risks from Unauthorized, Transient, and “Shadow SI” Systems](#task-3.7:-govern-and-mitigate-risks-from-unauthorized,-transient,-and-“shadow-si”-systems) addresses.  
* **Accountable:** Contributes a named responsible contact for each AI system and an owner for each data source, including contacts for incident response. This Task does not cover establishing the team that acts when an incident occurs, which [Task 8.3: Designate Roles for SI Incident Governance](#task-8.3:-designate-roles-for-si-incident-governance) covers.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Secure:** The registry records where each SI system runs, what it can reach, who is responsible for it, and which controls surround it. An attacker could use it to pick the system with the most reach and the least protection, or to learn whose account or identity to target. Protecting the registry is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice, as with its other asset inventories.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **GOVERN 1.6** (on building the AI inventory): This Task covers the content of the inventory: names, versions, hosts, owners, dependencies, purpose, controls and model lineage for each internal AI system, with a companion data inventory; it does not cover disclosures obtained from vendors. For those, see for example [Practice 6: Integrate Visibility of the External Supply Chain of SI into Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management).  
* **MAP 4.1** (on understanding AI component-level risks): This Task covers the component record, including licensing, terms and usage restrictions for each data source, from which component-level and legal risks can be mapped; it does not cover assessing those risks.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Is the registry kept within the existing IT and OT asset inventory or as a separate list?  
* Is registration a condition of approval to connect an SI system to operational networks or data?
* Do the named contacts and data owners have the visibility, time, access, and authority to act on what the registry shows about their systems?

**References:**

* **Commentary** [Artificial Intelligence Model Risk Management: Observations from a Thematic Review](https://www.mas.gov.sg/publications/monographs-or-information-paper/2024/artificial-intelligence-model-risk-management), Information Paper, December 2024, from the Monetary Authority of Singapore, written for banks. Section 5.2, Inventory, reports that banks mostly keep a formal AI inventory. The inventory supports using AI only within the scope for which it was approved, and generally records purpose, scope of use, upstream and downstream dependencies, model status, approvals and responsible personnel. One bank aggregated its AI use case inventory with inventories of data, technology and controls. These observations bear on the authorization and the departmental use cases this Task asks the registry to record.  
* **Guidance** [Supervisory Statement SS1/23, Model risk management principles for banks](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/prudential-regulation/publication/2023/may/model-risk-management-principles-for-banks-ss), May 2023, updated 16 April 2026, from the Prudential Regulation Authority of the Bank of England, which sets its expectations for UK banks with internal model approval. Principle 1.2, Model inventory, expects a firm-wide inventory, alongside any kept by individual lines of business, covering models in use, under development or decommissioned, so that direct and indirect inter-dependencies between models can be identified. This bears on this Task’s catalog of SI systems deployed across different departments.

#### Implementation 7.1.1: Create and Maintain a Master SI Asset List {#implementation-7.1.1:-create-and-maintain-a-master-si-asset-list}

A master asset list helps the organization see in one place what SI systems it runs, what each one can affect, and what each one depends on. Document the names, versions, vendors, hosts (cloud vs on-premises), responsible contacts, dependencies (such as required authorizations, data, compute, and other resources), operational purpose, and risk management controls for all SI systems and models. Record also the processes or physical assets each SI system can affect, the network zone it sits in and what it can reach, whether it only advises or can act on the process, its oversight mode (human-in-the-loop, human-on-the-loop or human-out-of-the-loop, as [Task 4.5: Define Operational Regimes for Human-on-the-Loop and Human-Out-of-the-Loop Operation](#task-4.5:-define-operational-regimes-for-human-on-the-loop-and-human-out-of-the-loop-operation) defines them), the date of its last validation, and its status, such as pilot, production, suspended or retired. Keep entries for retired SI systems rather than deleting them, so that what was running at a given date can later be established. This includes AI systems used for logistical or administrative purposes, such as chatbots, meeting transcribers, and document summarization tools. Document model lineage and component hierarchy, tracking parent-child relationships between base foundation models, fine-tuned adapters (e.g., LoRAs), vector index embeddings, and quantized runtime distributions. Record each derivation, such as fine-tuning, quantization, format conversion, pruning or the addition of adapters, as a link in this lineage. Where known, record the training data cutoff of each model, so that a reviewer can tell what an output may have drawn from training rather than from current sources, such as a procedure revised or equipment replaced since. For SI systems that support essential functions, also record how long the mission is expected to depend on the system, alongside the periods covered by vendor support, contract, license and data rights, revalidation, and committed resources, and the earliest date at which any of these ends before that dependence does, with an accountable owner. Where a period is unknown or uncommitted, record it as an unresolved gap rather than as an absence of risk. Because the list records network zones, reach, oversight modes, and unresolved gaps, it shows an attacker which SI systems can act on a process and where coverage is weakest. Protecting it is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice (see also the Secure entry under [Task 7.1: Maintain an Internal Registry of SI Deployments](#task-7.1:-maintain-an-internal-registry-of-si-deployments)). Retirement triggers that follow from these dates are identified under [Implementation 13.1.1: Identify Retirement Triggers, Including Those Outside the Organization’s Control](#implementation-13.1.1:-identify-retirement-triggers,-including-those-outside-the-organization’s-control).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* For which SI systems are the dependence horizon and coverage periods recorded, and who owns each gap?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 600-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1), July 2024, from NIST. Suggested actions under GOVERN 1.6 ask that generative AI systems be enumerated into the AI system inventory (GV-1.6-001) and list items to consider in each entry (GV-1.6-003): data provenance information, known issues from bug tracking or incident databases, human oversight roles, special rights and sensitive data considerations, and the underlying foundation models, their versions and access modes. These correspond to several of the fields this Implementation asks the list to hold; the underlying foundation model and version are the first link of the model lineage it also asks for.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-218A, Secure Software Development Practices for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models: An SSDF Community Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218A), July 2024, from NIST. Task PS.3.1 note N1 states that AI models and their components may need to be added to an organization’s asset inventories at release, and task PS.3.2 recommendation R1 asks for the provenance of an AI model and its components and derivatives to be tracked, including the libraries, frameworks and pipelines used to build it. Section 2 notes that generative and dual-use foundation models present additional challenges in tracking versioning and lineage, which bears on the parent-child lineage this Implementation asks the list to record.  
* **Guidance** [Authoritative Guide to AI/ML-BOM: Drive Transparency, Compliance, and Security Across the AI Supply Chain](https://cyclonedx.org/capabilities/mlbom/), First Edition (Revision 1), 10 June 2026, from the CycloneDX AI/ML Working Group of the OWASP Foundation. The section Declaring a model’s pedigree lists fine-tuning, quantization, format conversion, pruning and adapters as ways models are derived from pre-trained models, and asks that these transformations be captured in the model’s lineage as a hierarchical graph of its ancestors. This is a machine-readable form for the parent-child lineage this Implementation asks the list to record.  
* **Guidance** [Implementing AI Bill of Materials (AI BOM) with SPDX 3.0: A Comprehensive Guide to Creating AI and Dataset Bill of Materials](https://spdx.dev/implementing-an-ai-bom/), October 2024, by K. Bennet, G. K. Rajbahadur, A. Suriyawongkul and K. Stewart, from Linux Foundation Research. The guide explains that SPDX 3.0 separates its AI and Dataset Profiles to clarify the provenance and training methods used in creating an ML model, and its comparison with IBM FactSheets (Table 3\) maps lineage questions, such as how the models were trained and which datasets they were trained on, to the informationAboutTraining field and trainedOn relationships. This is the SPDX counterpart of the CycloneDX lineage approach above.  
* **Guidance** [SR 11-7, Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management](https://www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/srletters/2011/sr1107a1.pdf), April 2011, from the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, written for banks. The Model Inventory section asks for information on models in use, under development or recently retired, with any variation that warrants separate validation entered as a separate model and cross-referenced. It also lists the time frame during which each model is expected to remain valid. This bears on the lineage entries and on the dependence and revalidation periods this Implementation asks the list to hold.

#### Implementation 7.1.2: Maintain a Data Inventory {#implementation-7.1.2:-maintain-a-data-inventory}

A data inventory helps the organization trace a problem with a data source to every SI system that depends on it, and use each source only as its terms allow. Document organizational data sources that are, or may be, used in AI systems. Use may include training, fine-tuning (further training an existing AI model on an organization’s own data to adapt it), retrieval augmentation, or agentic use. Data sources may be static knowledge bases, historic, and/or real-time feeds, or memory and context stores that are shared across SI systems or models and updated as they run. The inventory should identify the data’s:

* Source and provenance, including its origin and chain of custody. See [Task 7.2: Validate, Select, and Prepare Data for SI Systems](#task-7.2:-validate,-select,-and-prepare-data-for-si-systems).  
* Role within the AI system, such as for training or retrieval augmentation, and the SI systems listed under [Implementation 7.1.1: Create and Maintain a Master SI Asset List](#implementation-7.1.1:-create-and-maintain-a-master-si-asset-list) that use it, so that a problem with the data can be traced to each SI system that depends on it.  
* Data type and classification, including format and sensitivity level.  
* Metadata and versioning, including verification of integrity such as hashes, and, for documents such as operating procedures and equipment manuals used for retrieval, their revision status, so that superseded versions can be withdrawn from the index while a record is kept of which version was indexed when. That record keeps past outputs interpretable after the corpus changes (see [Task 10.1](#task-10.1:-define-decision-level-logging-and-metadata-retention-policies) and [Practice 13](#practice-13:-establish-procedures-for-retiring-si-systems-and-withdrawing-their-authority)).  
* Licensing, terms, and other restrictions on usage, including the uses in SI systems that the data is authorized for, restrictions on secondary use, and the approval needed before a new or materially expanded use.  
* Lineage and transformations performed, including cleaning, masking, gap-filling or estimation, and synthetic data generation, and whether each value is measured, modeled or imputed, so that estimated values are not later used or trained on as if they were measured.  
* For labeled data, the labeling method and who assigned the labels, such as domain experts, other personnel or an automated tool.  
* Quality and integrity metrics and checks performed.  
* Ownership and accountability, including contacts for incident response.  
* Security and access controls, including identity and access management, logging, and encryption requirements.  
* Hosting and storage location, including redundancy and backups.

The inventory records where data is stored and backed up, how it is protected, and which SI systems depend on it. An attacker could use it to choose the data source whose alteration would reach the most consequential SI systems. Protecting the inventory is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* What approval does a new or materially expanded use of a data source need?

**References:**

* **Research** [Artificial intelligence and open finance: Synergies, trade-offs and policy implications](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/artificial-intelligence-and-open-finance_eb511c3c-en.html), OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 61, 2026, from the OECD Directorate for Financial and Enterprise Affairs. Box 2 and Table 1 describe the Bank of Korea’s move to “AI-ready” data governance, which adds provenance and versioning to lineage to support reproducibility and auditability, and extends controls and accountability to derived artifacts such as embeddings, logs and features. This bears on this Implementation’s lineage, versioning and access-control fields, which can apply to data derived from a source as well as to the source.  
* **Working Document** [Preliminary Report](https://www.scsp.ai/robotics-preliminary-report/), October 2026, from the National Security Commission on Robotics for Advanced Manufacturing. Under Finding 9, the discussion of robotics data notes that a simulation is useful only if it matches real equipment, materials and friction, that the only way to check this is against measurements from real machines, and that simulated data therefore extends real data rather than replacing it. This bears on the inventory’s record of synthetic data and of whether each value is measured or generated, for SI systems in robotics and manufacturing.  
* **Standard** [ISO/IEC 12792:2025, Information technology: Artificial intelligence: Transparency taxonomy of AI systems](https://www.iso.org/standard/84111.html), first edition, November 2025, from ISO and IEC. Clause 10, Dataset-level taxonomy, sets out information items for documenting a dataset. Clause 10.3, Data provenance, asks whether data is real (measured, recorded) or generated, and Clause 10.8, Data preparation performed, asks who labeled the dataset and whether the labelers were domain experts. Annex A lists Datasheets for Datasets among data transparency templates. These offer a common structure for this inventory’s entries.

#### Implementation 7.1.3: Integrate Automated Internal Software and SI Bill of Material Management {#implementation-7.1.3:-integrate-automated-internal-software-and-si-bill-of-material-management}

Scanning and machine-readable bills of materials help the organization keep its inventory matched to what is actually running, and find SI that was never registered. Develop policies for regular scanning of internal networks for AI systems and behavior, and maintain AIBOMs for internally developed or modified AI systems in the same form as those requested of vendors under [Implementation 6.1.2: Require SIBOM for Mission-Critical Applications](#implementation-6.1.2:-require-sibom-for-mission-critical-applications). This integrates with information obtained in [Practice 6: Integrate Visibility of the External Supply Chain of SI into Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management). Some components, such as sensors and other IoT devices, cannot support a software agent, so scanning that depends on agents can miss them. In OT environments, a logical survey can be combined with physical inspection and with what documentation records. Periodically compare what scanning and detection find with the entries under [Implementation 7.1.1](#implementation-7.1.1:-create-and-maintain-a-master-si-asset-list): an observed SI system with no entry, such as a model downloaded and run without going through procurement, is a candidate for [Task 3.7: Govern and Mitigate Risks from Unauthorized, Transient, and “Shadow SI” Systems](#task-3.7:-govern-and-mitigate-risks-from-unauthorized,-transient,-and-“shadow-si”-systems), and an entry with no corresponding observation may indicate a retirement that was not recorded or a gap in scanning coverage. Track both kinds of discrepancy to closure. Generating AIBOMs in the build and deployment pipeline, rather than by hand, can help keep them current with each change to model weights, adapters, datasets, libraries, prompts and guardrails. Each AIBOM can be linked to the corresponding entry in the Master AI Asset List. AIBOMs and scanning results list components and their versions. An attacker could match these against known vulnerabilities to choose a way in. Protecting them is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice, as with software bills of materials.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* How often are scanning results reconciled with the asset list, and how is physical inspection combined with scanning in OT?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control enhancement CM-8(3), Automated Unauthorized Component Detection, detects unauthorized hardware, software and firmware components using automated mechanisms at a defined frequency. Its discussion notes that monitoring may be ongoing or by periodic scanning, and that some components, such as IoT devices and sensors, cannot support the agents that some detection mechanisms depend on. This is the established control form of the scanning this Implementation asks for.  
* **Guidance** [Foundations for OT Cybersecurity: Asset Inventory Guidance for Owners and Operators](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-08/joint-guide-foundations-for-OT-cybersecurity-asset-inventory-guidance_508c.pdf), 13 August 2025, from CISA with the EPA, NSA, FBI and partner agencies in Australia, Canada, Germany, the Netherlands and New Zealand. The section Steps to Develop an OT Asset Inventory and Taxonomy asks that assets be identified through physical inspection and a logical survey, and that the inventory’s scope consider assets identified in documentation and physical inspection. This bears on scanning for SI components embedded in OT, where network discovery alone can miss assets.  
* **Guidance** [OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-genai-llm-top-10-2026/), Version 2026, from the OWASP GenAI Security Project, a volunteer community project of the Open Worldwide Application Security Project. LLM04:2026, Supply Chain, mitigation 4 asks for an up-to-date, signed inventory of components using an SBOM extended to models, adapters and datasets with AIBOMs and ML SBOMs, with licenses tracked in the same inventory and audited regularly. This bears on the AIBOMs this Implementation asks to be maintained for internally developed or modified SI systems.

### Task 7.2: Validate, Select, and Prepare Data for SI Systems {#task-7.2:-validate,-select,-and-prepare-data-for-si-systems}

Knowing where data came from, and choosing what each SI system receives, helps the organization judge whether an SI system’s inputs are fit for its task. Document the source, cleaning process, permitted use policies, and authorization of internal datasets (e.g., maintenance logs, sensor telemetry) used to train, fine-tune or prompt AI models, and decide which of the available data each AI system should receive, and in what form. This includes operational data supplied by customers, partners or connected systems and processed by the SI system at runtime, together with the extraction, mapping and transformation steps applied to it before it reaches the SI system. This Task improves visibility into the risk of internal “data silos” that introduce biased or unvetted information into AI systems, whether for training or in retrieval-augmented or agentic systems. This visibility can also highlight opportunities to leverage data across departments while maintaining appropriate protections for that data. The outputs of this task should be documented as set out in [Implementation 7.1.2: Maintain a Data Inventory](#implementation-7.1.2:-maintain-a-data-inventory). Selecting and preparing what an AI system receives, at training and at runtime, also limits what it can learn from, be influenced by, or expose ([Implementation 7.2.4: Select and Prepare the Inputs Each SI System Receives](#implementation-7.2.4:-select-and-prepare-the-inputs-each-si-system-receives)).

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Bias Managed:** Contributes visibility into internal data silos that introduce biased or unvetted information, extended by [Implementation 7.2.3: Assess the Conditions Under Which Source Data Is Created](#implementation-7.2.3:-assess-the-conditions-under-which-source-data-is-created) to capture conditions that systematically drop or distort records before the data ever arrives, where certification of what did arrive cannot see the loss. This Task does not cover evaluating bias in the AI system’s outputs, which [Task 10.3: Implement Systematic Audit Review and Performance Trend Analysis](#task-10.3:-implement-systematic-audit-review-and-performance-trend-analysis) addresses.  
* **Secure:** Contributes a tamper-evident trail from source to AI system output for critical data, using cryptographic hashing and lineage tools, so that deliberate insertion or alteration of training or retrieval data can be traced. This Task does not cover restricting who may modify the data, which [Task 7.4: Define Authorization and Access Controls for SI Modifications](#task-7.4:-define-authorization-and-access-controls-for-si-modifications) covers.  
* **Valid:** Contributes inputs chosen and represented for the AI system’s task, and checked at runtime against the conditions under which it was tested, so that it is not relied on for data it was never validated with. The same hashes and lineage show where data reaching the SI system differs from what was certified, whether through corruption in transfer, overwriting or a wrong version, so that it is not trained on, or relying on, data that no one has checked.
