This Task does not cover setting the thresholds at which a shift from those conditions calls for action, which [Implementation 3.3.2: Establish Maximum Drift Thresholds](#implementation-3.3.2:-establish-maximum-drift-thresholds) covers.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Privacy-Enhanced:** Where critical data includes personal information, a source-to-output trail protected from alteration keeps a record that retention limits or deletion obligations may later require to be removed. [Implementation 10.2.2: Protect Logs from Alteration Where They Serve as Evidence](#implementation-10.2.2:-protect-logs-from-alteration-where-they-serve-as-evidence) gives ways to reconcile the two.
* **Secure:** Documentation of data sources, their preparation, and the SI systems they feed shows where inserted or altered data would have the most effect. An attacker could use it to aim poisoning at a weakly protected source that reaches a consequential SI system. Protecting this documentation is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Valid versus Robust:** Where anomalous records are sensor faults or entry errors, filtering them out improves the data an SI system learns from. Where they record genuine abnormal conditions, such as trips, startups, equipment failures or storms, the same filtering can remove the conditions the SI system most needs to recognize. Options include deciding with operations staff whether each class of outlier is a fault or a genuine condition. Where outliers are removed, the resulting gaps in coverage can be recorded in the data inventory under [Implementation 7.1.2: Maintain a Data Inventory](#implementation-7.1.2:-maintain-a-data-inventory).

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MAP 2.3** (on applying scientific methodologies): This Task covers documentation and certification of the suitability of internal data for an AI system, extended upstream to the field conditions in which records are created or lost, and the selection and preparation of the inputs the system receives; it does not cover experimental design or construct validation.  
* **MEASURE 2.11** (on measuring fairness, accuracy, and bias): This Task identifies where internal data sources and capture conditions introduce biased or systematically incomplete data before it reaches an AI system; it does not cover evaluating the bias in that system’s outputs. For that, see for example [Task 10.3: Implement Systematic Audit Review and Performance Trend Analysis](#task-10.3:-implement-systematic-audit-review-and-performance-trend-analysis).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Who decides whether each class of outlier is a fault or a genuine condition? (see the Valid versus Robust tension in [Task 7.2: Validate, Select, and Prepare Data for SI Systems](#task-7.2:-validate,-select,-and-prepare-data-for-si-systems))
* Who provides the expertise and time to document and certify data sources, and what happens to data that cannot be certified in time?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025), March 2025, from NIST. Section 2.3, Poisoning Attacks and Mitigations, covers adversarial manipulation of training data, and the mitigations in section 2.3.2 include protecting training data with access controls, data sanitization and validation, and mechanisms for dataset provenance and integrity attestation. Section 3.4.2 adds knowledge base poisoning, where a document inserted into a retrieval-augmented system’s knowledge base steers its output, which is the retrieval case this Task also covers.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-218A, Secure Software Development Practices for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models: An SSDF Community Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218A), July 2024, from NIST. Task PW.3.2, under practice PW.3, Confirm the Integrity of Training, Testing, Fine-Tuning, and Aligning Data Before Use, asks that the provenance of all such data be tracked when known and that data without known provenance be documented, and its note N1 records that provenance cannot always be verified but is still worth tracking. This is the development-side form of the documentation this Task asks for when an organization fine-tunes a model on its own data.

#### Implementation 7.2.1: Implement Data Quality Monitoring {#implementation-7.2.1:-implement-data-quality-monitoring}

Checking data before an SI system uses it helps the organization catch errors and gaps that the system would otherwise learn or repeat. Appropriately knowledgeable and resourced personnel should certify that organizational data to be used in an AI system, such as to train a model or to enable retrieval-augmented or database functionality, is appropriate for the task. Certification can include checking that the data is as expected and free of obvious errors, such as missing fields, duplicates, or uneven coverage of the conditions the SI system will meet. In operational settings, safety-related edge cases can be hard to capture in data, and operator expertise can help identify where they are missing. Data from external sources can be quarantined and tested on isolated systems before it enters internal repositories. Where data continues to arrive after it is certified, the runtime input checks in [Implementation 7.2.4: Select and Prepare the Inputs Each SI System Receives](#implementation-7.2.4:-select-and-prepare-the-inputs-each-si-system-receives) carry the monitoring forward, and the certification should be repeated when the source or its preparation changes. Automated data quality checks at training time can likewise show when data no longer matches what was certified. Where data changes faster than it can practicably be re-certified, as with a frequently updated retrieval corpus or continuously streamed telemetry, how much to re-certify, and how often, is the organization’s decision, within any regulatory or contractual obligations, scaled to the consequence of the SI system’s outputs. The risk that uncertified data reaches the SI system in the meantime may not be fully avoidable. A record of where uncertified data can reach an SI system also shows an attacker where inserted data is least likely to be caught. Protecting that record is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice. Record it, and rely on controls that do not depend on the data being correct: independent constraints on what the SI system may output or command ([Implementation 3.2.2: Define and Independently Enforce Deterministic Operational Constraints](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints)), fail-safe fallback when those constraints are violated ([Implementation 3.2.3: Specify Fail-Safe States and Fallback Behavior](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior)), monitoring for anomalous behavior that can reveal bad data by its effects ([Task 3.4: Monitor for Anomalous SI Behavior](#task-3.4:-monitor-for-anomalous-si-behavior)), cross-checks of high-consequence outputs against an independent source such as a separate sensor or a person, and provenance records that let outputs influenced by a bad batch be traced and reviewed afterward ([Practice 7](#practice-7:-manage-internal-si-supply-chain-and-data-provenance) and [Practice 10](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities)).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Who certifies data, and which changes to a source or its preparation trigger re-certification?  
* Where data changes faster than it can be re-certified, how much is re-certified, how often, and which controls cover the remaining risk?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-218A, Secure Software Development Practices for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models: An SSDF Community Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218A), July 2024, from NIST. Task PW.3.1 asks that data be analyzed for signs of poisoning, bias, homogeneity and tampering before it is used for training, testing, fine-tuning or aligning. Recommendation R2 lists methods, including anomaly detection, bias detection, data cleaning, curation, filtering, sanitization and fact-checking, and consideration C1 suggests a human-in-the-loop to examine the data, which supports the certification by appropriately knowledgeable personnel that this Implementation asks for. PW.3.1 covers data used to build the model; data used only for retrieval falls outside it.  
* **Guidance** [Artificial intelligence and machine learning: Supply chain risks and mitigations](https://media.defense.gov/2026/Mar/04/2003882809/-1/-1/0/AI_ML_SUPPLY_CHAIN_RISKS_AND_MITIGATIONS.PDF), 2025, from the Australian Signals Directorate, co-sealed by national cyber security agencies of Canada, Japan, the Republic of Korea, New Zealand, Singapore, the United Kingdom and the United States (the National Security Agency). The AI data section, under its mitigations, asks that data be reviewed and preprocessed before use, checking that it is as expected and free of obvious errors and correcting issues such as missing features, duplicates or uneven sample distribution. It also asks that externally sourced data be quarantined and tested on isolated systems before migration to internal repositories. These are concrete checks behind the certification this Implementation asks for.  
* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by CISA. Section 2.2, Manage OT Data Security Risks for AI Systems, lists data quality and availability among the data-related challenges, noting the difficulty of capturing safety-related edge cases in industrial settings and that OT operator expertise is necessary to capture that specialized knowledge. This bears on who is appropriately knowledgeable to certify data under this Implementation.

#### Implementation 7.2.2: Verify Data Provenance {#implementation-7.2.2:-verify-data-provenance}

A provenance trail helps the organization show where critical data came from and, where the trail is protected, detect later changes to the data or the trail. Tools such as cryptographic hashing and data lineage tools can be used to maintain an audit trail for tracing critical data from source to final SI system output. Whether a trail is protected from later change, and how strongly, is for the organization to decide, within any regulatory or contractual obligations. Weigh the consequence of the data, how likely the trail is to be needed as evidence, and the risk that someone changes the data or the trail without detection. Some guidance, such as AI Data Security, describes a cryptographically signed, immutable, append-only ledger of data changes as one way to make such changes detectable. [Implementation 10.2.2: Protect Logs from Alteration Where They Serve as Evidence](#implementation-10.2.2:-protect-logs-from-alteration-where-they-serve-as-evidence) describes the options, including how to reconcile them with deletion obligations. 

For critical datasets, the trail can record where the data came from and the path it follows through the SI system. Original versions can be cryptographically signed, with each later revision signed by the person who made it. A hash confirms only that data matches what the source published, and cannot reveal changes made before publication. Data whose origin cannot be established, or whose hash does not match, can be labeled as unverified and limited to lower-consequence uses until it is verified. For retrieval, documents can be checked against the organization’s controlled document management system so that only current, approved versions are indexed.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which datasets count as critical for the provenance trail, and which uses are allowed for unverified data?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control SR-4, Provenance, documents, monitors and maintains valid provenance, defined as the chronology of origin, development, ownership, location and changes, for systems, components and associated data, and its discussion covers monitoring for unauthorized changes to provenance records and their non-repudiation, which is the audit trail this Implementation builds for data used by AI systems.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v2r1, Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v2r1), from NIST. Table D-4 describes Provenance Tracking as identifying and tracking the provenance of data, software or hardware elements, and Integrity Checks as validating the integrity or quality of information, including through cryptographic hashes. Section 3.1.5.2 adds that checksums designed to catch accidental change are not sufficient where modification may be deliberate, and that cryptographically signed hashes are needed to support both integrity checking and provenance tracking.  
* **Guidance** [AI Data Security: Best Practices for Securing Data Used to Train & Operate AI Systems](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/ai-data-security-best-practices-securing-data-used-train-operate-ai-systems), Version 1.0, May 2025, from the National Security Agency’s Artificial Intelligence Security Center with CISA, the FBI and partner agencies. Best practice 1 asks that provenance tracking trace data origins and log the path data follows through an SI system, using a cryptographically signed provenance database that keeps an immutable, append-only ledger of data changes. Best practice 3 asks that original versions of data be signed and that each later revision be signed by the person who made it. These are the mechanisms behind the audit trail this Implementation asks for.  
* **Guidance** [Artificial intelligence and machine learning: Supply chain risks and mitigations](https://media.defense.gov/2026/Mar/04/2003882809/-1/-1/0/AI_ML_SUPPLY_CHAIN_RISKS_AND_MITIGATIONS.PDF), 2025, from the Australian Signals Directorate, co-sealed by national cyber security agencies of Canada, Japan, the Republic of Korea, New Zealand, Singapore, the United Kingdom and the United States (the National Security Agency). The AI data section, under data verification and provenance, notes that checksums, hashes and digital signatures verify integrity only against the source and do not include modifications made to the data before publishing, and that more robust lineage and provenance methods are being developed. This is the limit of the hashing this Implementation relies on.

#### Implementation 7.2.3: Assess the Conditions Under Which Source Data Is Created {#implementation-7.2.3:-assess-the-conditions-under-which-source-data-is-created}

Understanding how source data is created helps the organization find records that were lost or distorted before they reached a repository. Extend provenance validation upstream of ingestion to the point of capture. Data quality certification performed under [Implementation 7.2.1: Implement Data Quality Monitoring](#implementation-7.2.1:-implement-data-quality-monitoring) can only assess data that successfully arrived; it cannot reveal records that were degraded, overwritten, or never transferred during collection. Document the field conditions, tooling, and manual steps involved in creating source data, and identify where those conditions systematically introduce loss or inconsistency. Much of this data was collected for operations rather than for SI systems. For process data, the conditions include historian settings, such as compression, deadband, interpolation and sampling rate, and the substitution of values when an instrument reports bad quality. Each can make the stored record differ from the process it describes. For event and maintenance records, they include who entered each record, the coding scheme in use and its changes over time, and reporting practices, such as work orders closed with a generic code. Recording changes such as sensor recalibrations, deadband changes and tag renames can help trace them to the SI systems and training periods they affect. Potential failure modes include the following. In a multi-stage transfer chain, field personnel move data from local device storage to intermediate media and then to a central or cloud repository, and an incomplete stage can silently drop records. Stored data can be overwritten inadvertently during later collection cycles. Migration between maintenance management systems (for example, CMMS platforms), or limitations within them, can introduce loss or inconsistency. Where a manual step cannot be removed, consider monitoring how completely it is performed, for example the proportion of expected records that reach the central repository. Findings about where records are lost or substituted also show where altered or missing data is least likely to be noticed. Protecting those findings is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice. Where the capture environment is intermittently connected or resource-constrained, coordinate with [Implementation 10.1.4: Asynchronous Telemetry and Inference Logging for Constrained Edges](#implementation-10.1.4:-asynchronous-telemetry-and-inference-logging-for-constrained-edges). Findings should be recorded against the relevant entries in the data inventory maintained under [Implementation 7.1.2: Maintain a Data Inventory](#implementation-7.1.2:-maintain-a-data-inventory), and should inform training delivered under [Implementation 9.1.3: Include Data-Originating Roles in Competency Mapping](#implementation-9.1.3:-include-data-originating-roles-in-competency-mapping).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Where a manual capture step cannot be removed, is its completeness monitored, and how?
* Whose time is used to document capture conditions, given that much of it falls to field and maintenance staff outside the SI project?

**References:**

* **Research** [Kang, J. et al., “A data quality management framework for equipment failure risk estimation: Application to the oil and gas industry”, Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence 136 (2024) 108834](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.engappai.2024.108834). A framework for deciding whether field data is of sufficient quality for an equipment failure risk estimation model, with a case study of electronic boards in downhole drilling tools. Section 3.5 briefly identifies root causes of poor field data, including manual transfer steps that field personnel skip, inadvertent overwriting, and loss or inconsistency from maintenance management system migrations, and suggests training and data collection KPIs as remedies.

#### Implementation 7.2.4: Select and Prepare the Inputs Each SI System Receives {#implementation-7.2.4:-select-and-prepare-the-inputs-each-si-system-receives}

For training, fine-tuning, retrieval and runtime alike, decide which inputs the AI system needs for its task, and how they should be represented, rather than supplying everything that is available. Selecting and engineering inputs has long been part of building machine learning systems (see Kuhn 2020). Examples include using derived quantities that operators already work with, filtering and resampling sensor signals to the rates that matter, and passing only the fields relevant to the decision. This remains relevant where a large model could accept far more. Inputs the task does not need can degrade performance and let a model learn patterns that do not hold in operation. They also add routes by which an adversary or a fault can influence it ([Implementation 3.8.1: SI Attack Surface Mapping (Adversarial Exposure)](#implementation-3.8.1:-si-attack-surface-mapping-\(adversarial-exposure\))), make its behavior harder to explain and test, and expose information that did not need to be exposed. Draw on subject matter experts as well as the data: inputs chosen only by experts can miss useful signal, and inputs chosen only from the data can fit patterns that do not hold (see Kuhn 2020). At runtime, check inputs against what the AI system was trained and tested on, such as ranges, units, rates and formats, and treat anything outside that as untested under [Task 1.3: Implement Evaluation and Test Plans, Including TEVV, Across the SI Lifecycle](#task-1.3:-implement-evaluation-and-test-plans,-including-tevv,-across-the-si-lifecycle). Check also that each input is still current and valid. A sensor value frozen at its last good reading, a drifting or fouled instrument, or an instrument replaced with one of a different range can stay within expected limits while no longer reflecting the process. An SI system given such inputs can produce confident outputs with no sign of anomaly. Where the control system already marks values as bad or substituted, such as through quality codes in a historian or SCADA system, pass that marking to the SI system with the value, or exclude the value, so that a substituted value is not treated as a measurement. Existing checks, such as redundant or voted instruments, mass or energy balances and, in power systems, state estimation, can also help validate inputs. For learned systems, the preparation applied to inputs, such as unit conversion, resampling, filtering and the handling of missing values, should be the same in operation as in training, for example by using the same versioned code for both. A difference between the two can degrade performance without any visible error. Where inputs cannot be meaningfully sanitized, such as images or free text, the available controls may be limited to which sources can supply them and what accompanies them. For agentic AI systems, the same principle applies to what is carried from one step to the next ([Implementation 5.3.4: Limit the Context Carried Forward Between Steps](#implementation-5.3.4:-limit-the-context-carried-forward-between-steps)). The record of which inputs each SI system receives, and the ranges and formats its checks accept, shows an attacker which inputs reach the system and which values pass unchallenged. Protecting that record is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice (see also [Implementation 3.8.1: SI Attack Surface Mapping (Adversarial Exposure)](#implementation-3.8.1:-si-attack-surface-mapping-\(adversarial-exposure\))).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which inputs does each SI system receive, and which subject matter experts take part in choosing them?

**References:**

* **Research** [Kuhn, M. and Johnson, K., Feature Engineering and Selection: A Practical Approach for Predictive Models, CRC Press, 2020](https://doi.org/10.1201/9781315108230). A practitioner’s text on representing and selecting the inputs (predictors) of predictive models, with a free online edition at [https\://feat.engineering](https://feat.engineering). Chapter 1 defines feature engineering as creating representations of data that increase a model’s effectiveness, and Section 1.2.6 sets subject matter experts’ prescriptive choice of inputs against choosing them empirically from the data, which risks overfitting to false patterns and producing complex models without an obvious rational explanation. Section 10.1 recommends reducing the number of predictors as far as possible without compromising predictive performance, noting that even where a model is insensitive to extra predictors, the minimum set that gives acceptable results makes good scientific sense. In the simulation in Section 10.3, adding predictors unrelated to the outcome drastically degraded some of the best-performing models, including neural networks and support vector machines, while others were barely affected. Chapter 9 works through preparing spectroscopy data from bioreactors in pharmaceutical manufacturing (removing baseline drift, standardizing and smoothing), and notes that smoothing too heavily removes the peaks that carry the signal and that the amount of preprocessing can be treated as a parameter to tune.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Release 5.2.0, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final), from NIST. Control SI-10, Information Input Validation, checks the syntax and semantics of system inputs, including character set, length, numerical range and acceptable values, against specified definitions for format and content. This is the control-catalog form of the runtime input checks this Implementation asks for. Its discussion of attacker-supplied inputs being interpreted as control information also applies to content passed to an AI model.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-218A, Secure Software Development Practices for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models: An SSDF Community Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218A), July 2024, from NIST. Task PW.3.1 asks that data be analyzed for signs of poisoning, bias, homogeneity and tampering before it is used for training, testing, fine-tuning or aligning. This Implementation adds the earlier question of which data, and which representation of it, the AI system should be given at all.

### Task 7.3: Manage Version Control and Logging for Internal SI Safety Mechanisms {#task-7.3:-manage-version-control-and-logging-for-internal-si-safety-mechanisms}

Keeping the mechanisms that constrain an SI system under version control helps the organization know which safeguards are in force and notice when they change. Establish rigorous configuration management and logging for the internal “wrappers,” system prompts, and safety filters built around both internal and external AI systems. Treat system prompts that contain sensitive procedures, refusal conditions or credentials as sensitive information, and keep credentials out of prompts where possible. This Task helps ensure that the mechanisms used to constrain AI behavior, including those that relate to other practices, are documented, traceable, reversible, auditable, and protected from unauthorized internal modification. As with interlocks and alarms, guardrails that block legitimate actions are natural candidates for relaxation, and a series of changes that are each reasonable can leave a mechanism weaker than the form that was validated. Review a proposed change against the hazards the mechanism was designed to address, not only against its previous version. Compare the running configuration of each mechanism with its approved version at defined intervals, so that a change made outside change control can be detected. Organizations that already manage the configuration of control system settings and software can extend that practice to prompts, filters, and other safety logic; those without established configuration management can start with the mechanisms around their highest-consequence SI systems.

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Accountable:** Contributes a centralized change log for safety parameters, prompt templates and filter logic that names who authorized each change and the technical justification, with cryptographic signatures on changes to safety logic. This Task does not cover defining who is permitted to make those changes, which [Task 7.4: Define Authorization and Access Controls for SI Modifications](#task-7.4:-define-authorization-and-access-controls-for-si-modifications) covers.  
* **Secure:** Contributes protection of the mechanisms that constrain AI behavior: system prompts containing sensitive procedures or refusal conditions treated as sensitive, and credentials kept out of prompts where possible. This Task does not cover determining what those mechanisms enforce, which [Task 3.2: Implement Independent Guardrails for SI Outputs](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs) covers.  
* **Valid:** Contributes a policy lock that stops streaming data from altering learned thresholds outside change control, so that an SI system that adapts at runtime keeps operating within the thresholds that were tested, whether the data it would have learned from was unrepresentative or deliberately shaped. This Task does not cover deciding when a tuning cycle should be opened, which [Implementation 2.3.4: Recurrent Risk Evaluations](#implementation-2.3.4:-recurrent-risk-evaluations) and [Implementation 3.3.2: Establish Maximum Drift Thresholds](#implementation-3.3.2:-establish-maximum-drift-thresholds) inform.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Secure:** System prompts, filter rules, and the change log describe what the safety mechanisms block, how, and how that has changed over time. An attacker could use them to craft inputs or actions that pass the filters, or to find a recently relaxed rule. [Task 7.3: Manage Version Control and Logging for Internal SI Safety Mechanisms](#task-7.3:-manage-version-control-and-logging-for-internal-si-safety-mechanisms) already treats sensitive system prompts as sensitive. Protecting the filter logic and change log is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Robust versus Valid, Reliable and Secure:** Where a system adapts at runtime because its conditions shift faster than a release cycle, freezing it during operational windows holds it to conditions that may already have moved. Where the streaming data it learns from is unrepresentative, such as during an upset or a sensor fault, or can be shaped by an adversary, the same adaptation moves learned thresholds away from what was tested, without review. One way to balance this is the policy lock in [Implementation 7.3.3: Freeze Adaptation of Online-Learning SI Systems During Operational Windows](#implementation-7.3.3:-freeze-adaptation-of-online-learning-si-systems-during-operational-windows), which confines adaptation to deliberate tuning cycles entered through a physical or out-of-band step; others include using the drift triggers in [Implementation 2.3.4: Recurrent Risk Evaluations](#implementation-2.3.4:-recurrent-risk-evaluations) to decide when such a cycle is opened.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MAP 4.2** (on establishing risk controls for AI system components): This Task makes the internal controls around an AI system, its wrappers, system prompts and filter logic, identifiable by version and traceable through each change; it does not cover deciding what those controls enforce. For that, see for example [Task 3.2: Implement Independent Guardrails for SI Outputs](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs).  
* **MANAGE 4.1** (on post-deployment risk management): This Task covers change management for the safety mechanisms of deployed AI systems, through signed changes, approval and regression testing before release; it does not cover the monitoring that such plans also call for. For that, see for example [Task 3.4: Monitor for Anomalous SI Behavior](#task-3.4:-monitor-for-anomalous-si-behavior).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* At what intervals is the running configuration of each safety mechanism compared with its approved version?
* Who acts when the running configuration of a safety mechanism differs from its approved version, and with what authority to restore it?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-128, Guide for Security-Focused Configuration Management of Information Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-128), August 2011, with updates as of October 2019, from NIST. Section 2.3.10, Configuration Monitoring, describes activities to determine whether systems are configured in accordance with the organization’s agreed-upon baseline configurations. This is the comparison this Task asks for between the running configuration of each safety mechanism and its approved version.

#### Implementation 7.3.1: Maintain a Registry of SI Systems and Changes {#implementation-7.3.1:-maintain-a-registry-of-si-systems-and-changes}

A registry of versions and changes helps the organization know which configuration was in service at a given time, and so trace outputs back to it. The registry should uniquely identify the specific versions of the AI systems and models, versions of prompt templates, and the specific “if/then” safety logic used for output filtering. Document every change to these safety parameters in a centralized change log that identifies the person who authorized the change and the technical justification. The registry and change log describe the safety logic in detail and name who may change it, so they warrant the same protection as the sensitive system prompts in [Task 7.3: Manage Version Control and Logging for Internal SI Safety Mechanisms](#task-7.3:-manage-version-control-and-logging-for-internal-si-safety-mechanisms). Keep earlier versions retrievable, so that an investigation can establish which model, prompt template and safety logic were in force when a given output was produced. Keeping every version carries storage and management overhead, especially for systems that change often. How long to keep them is for the organization to decide, within any regulatory or contractual obligations (see [Task 10.1: Define Decision-Level Logging and Metadata Retention Policies](#task-10.1:-define-decision-level-logging-and-metadata-retention-policies)).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [AI Incident Response Framework, Workstream 2: Preparing Defenders for a Changing Cybersecurity Landscape](https://www.coalitionforsecureai.org/defending-ai-systems-a-new-framework-for-incident-response-in-the-age-of-intelligent-technology/), version 1.0, 27 October 2025, from the Coalition for Secure AI, an OASIS Open Project. Section 3.3.1, Preparation Phase, lists system prompt versioning and configuration management among monitoring considerations, with guidance to maintain an auditable prompt history and to track all model versions and parameters. Section 3.3.3.1 adds that forensic analysis needs to retrieve the system prompt and other parameters used when interacting with a model. Both bear on the registry this Implementation asks for.  
* **Guidance** [Artificial intelligence and machine learning: Supply chain risks and mitigations](https://media.defense.gov/2026/Mar/04/2003882809/-1/-1/0/AI_ML_SUPPLY_CHAIN_RISKS_AND_MITIGATIONS.PDF), 2025, from the Australian Signals Directorate, co-sealed by national cyber security agencies of Canada, Japan, the Republic of Korea, New Zealand, Singapore, the United Kingdom and the United States (the National Security Agency). The machine learning models section, under model verification and provenance, asks that a model registry be kept of the specific model versions that have been verified, tested and approved for use, and that each new version be verified and tested before approval. This is the model side of the registry this Implementation asks for.

#### Implementation 7.3.2: Automate Policy-as-Code {#implementation-7.3.2:-automate-policy-as-code}

Translate safety and operational policies into automated, machine-readable logic rules embedded directly within the deployment workflow (often referred to as Policy-as-Code). Inference requests that possess mission impact should be logged with their full context, including version identifiers of safety filters and any triggered rules (e.g., “Blocked: Safety Boundary Violation”). All changes to underlying safety logic should require cryptographic signatures, appropriate approval oversight, and automated regression testing (informed by [Practice 2: Define SI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service Expectations](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations)) to help ensure updates do not inadvertently degrade system availability. Include in the regression tests cases that the rules are meant to block, drawn from the failure modes mapped under [Implementation 2.3.2: Targeted Failure Mode Mapping](#implementation-2.3.2:-targeted-failure-mode-mapping), so that a change that weakens a safety boundary is detected as well as one that blocks legitimate requests. Record for each rule the policy, regulation or other requirement it implements, so that a change to that source can be traced to the rules it affects, and a triggered rule can be traced back to its source. The rule set, and logs that name each triggered rule, show exactly what is blocked and why. An attacker could use them to shape requests that fall just outside every rule. Protecting them is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**References:**

* **Standard** [ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023, Systems and software engineering: system life cycle processes](https://www.iso.org/standard/81702.html), published jointly by ISO, IEC and IEEE. Clause 6.4.2.3, in its task to maintain traceability of stakeholder needs and requirements, notes that bi-directional traceability is maintained through the life cycle between the needs and requirements and their stakeholders and sources. This is the traceability this Implementation asks for between each machine-readable rule and the requirement it implements.  
* **Guidance** [OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/), Version 2026, December 2025, from the Agentic Security Initiative of the OWASP Gen AI Security Project, a volunteer community project of the Open Worldwide Application Security Project. Entry ASI08, Cascading Failures, includes among its mitigations validating every high-impact tool invocation against a policy-as-code rule before executing it, and separating planning from execution through an external policy engine. This is a runtime form of the machine-readable safety rules this Implementation asks for.

#### Implementation 7.3.3: Freeze Adaptation of Online-Learning SI Systems During Operational Windows {#implementation-7.3.3:-freeze-adaptation-of-online-learning-si-systems-during-operational-windows}

For AI systems utilizing online learning (including reinforcement learning), continuous local fine-tuning, dynamic prompt optimization, real-time retraining, or other forms of adaptation at runtime, where the organization controls the adaptation, programmatically freeze all changes to the system during operational windows.

This may include model weights (the model’s internal, learned parameters) and other online adaptation configuration parameters, such as hyper-parameters (pre-defined configuration settings that control how the model learns or operates). Boundary logic (the programmatic code defining the safe operating limits the system should stay within, as established in [Task 3.2: Implement Independent Guardrails for SI Outputs](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs)) is not an adaptation parameter: the system’s own adaptation should never be able to alter it. Other changes to it, whether during an operational window or not, should be frozen for the window where appropriate and otherwise made only under the change control and version tracking of [Task 7.3: Manage Version Control and Logging for Internal SI Safety Mechanisms](#task-7.3:-manage-version-control-and-logging-for-internal-si-safety-mechanisms), so that operators know when the limits have changed.

Shifting a deployed model from a static runtime state into a tuning cycle should require a physical confirmation step or an out-of-band administrative governance mechanism. This helps prevent streaming production data or unvetted operational telemetry from silently altering the model’s learned behavioral thresholds outside of formal configuration change control channels. Where some adaptation is permitted during operation, define what may change automatically, for example retraining on more recent data while the architecture and hyperparameters stay fixed, and record the justification for allowing it.

The freeze itself can be a software setting, such as a mode that operators can see on their displays. Turning learning back on is what needs the separate step. Otherwise anything able to change that setting, including the SI system itself, another automated process, or someone using a stolen account, could restart learning without anyone noticing. This is similar to the physical key switch found on many industrial controllers, which must be turned by hand before the controller’s program can be changed. Where a separate step is not practical, requiring two people to approve the change, alerting operators when it happens, and logging it reduces this risk but does not remove it.

Where the organization does not control the adaptation, as with an SI service whose provider updates or retrains it upstream, a freeze may not be possible at all. The options then include pinning a fixed model version where the provider offers one, requiring notice of changes under [Implementation 6.1.1: Add SI Disclosure to Existing Procurement Policies](#implementation-6.1.1:-add-si-disclosure-to-existing-procurement-policies), watching for changes in behavior under [Task 3.4: Monitor for Anomalous SI Behavior](#task-3.4:-monitor-for-anomalous-si-behavior), and relying on constraints that hold whatever the model does, under [Implementation 3.2.2: Define and Independently Enforce Deterministic Operational Constraints](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints). The remaining risk of an unannounced change should be recorded.

Examples of operational windows that may warrant a freeze include startup and shutdown, planned switching or maintenance, abnormal or emergency operation, and active incident investigation. During abnormal conditions, an adapting SI system can learn from unrepresentative data, or absorb a developing fault into what it treats as normal. Make the current state, frozen or adapting, visible to operators, and log each transition with the person who authorized it. A schedule or log of when adaptation is enabled tells an attacker when crafted data would be learned. Protecting it is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice, balanced against operators’ need to see the current state. Where freezing would remove the function itself, such as adaptive control that tracks changing plant dynamics, or where a product offers no means to freeze adaptation, bound the adapted parameters with deterministic limits ([Task 3.2: Implement Independent Guardrails for SI Outputs](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs)) and monitor them directly. Record any such gap in the asset list under [Implementation 7.1.1: Create and Maintain a Master SI Asset List](#implementation-7.1.1:-create-and-maintain-a-master-si-asset-list).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which operational windows call for a freeze, and what, if anything, may change automatically outside them? (see the Robust versus Valid, Reliable and Secure tension in [Task 7.3: Manage Version Control and Logging for Internal SI Safety Mechanisms](#task-7.3:-manage-version-control-and-logging-for-internal-si-safety-mechanisms))  
* What separate step turns learning back on, and where none is practical, which compensating controls apply?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025), March 2025, from NIST. Section 2.3.5, Poisoning Attacks in the Real World, describes documented poisoning of a chatbot, an email spam filter and a malware classification service, and observes that in each case attackers crafted poisoned samples after release, relying on the model being continuously updated. This is the adversarial case for the policy lock this Implementation places on online and adaptive learning.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control enhancement CM-3(8), Prevent or Restrict Configuration Changes, prevents or restricts configuration changes under organization-defined circumstances, enforceable through automated mechanisms, which supports a policy lock that freezes model weights and other adaptation parameters during operational windows; treating learned parameters as configuration is this Implementation’s own extension.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Appendix F.7.5, the OT discussion of CM-3(8), Prevent or Restrict Configuration Changes, gives the example of PLC key switches that require physical access to enter programming mode, a precedent for the out-of-band step this Implementation suggests.  
* **Commentary** [Artificial Intelligence Model Risk Management: Observations from a Thematic Review](https://www.mas.gov.sg/publications/monographs-or-information-paper/2024/artificial-intelligence-model-risk-management), Information Paper, December 2024, from the Monetary Authority of Singapore, written for banks. Section 6.5, under Change Management, observes that some banks update models automatically to cope with drift, and that such “dynamic AI” is subject to enhanced controls. These include justifying automatic updating and defining what may be updated automatically, for example retraining on more recent data but not changing model architectures or hyperparameters. This bears on the scope of any adaptation that this Implementation’s policy lock leaves open.

### Task 7.4: Define Authorization and Access Controls for SI Modifications {#task-7.4:-define-authorization-and-access-controls-for-si-modifications}

Controlling who can change an SI system, its data, and its safety mechanisms helps keep changes to the system to those that were reviewed and approved. Establish strict identity-based access controls for individuals authorized to modify internal AI models, systems, AI safety mechanisms, datasets, or configurations. This Task implements and extends the principle of least privilege to help ensure that only qualified personnel can alter the behavior of critical functions, reducing the risk of accidental or malicious internal interference. The same restriction applies where the modifier is an agent: an agent should not hold write access to its own system prompt, permissions or safety mechanisms outside the change process this Task defines (see also [Task 5.3: Implement Principles of Least Agency and Least Privilege for SI Entities](#task-5.3:-implement-principles-of-least-agency-and-least-privilege-for-si-entities)). The controls in this Task determine who may act on the system. Whether a specific proposed action is permitted at the moment of execution is a separate question, addressed in [Task 3.2](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs) and [Implementation 5.2.2](#implementation-5.2.2:-action-level,-context-aware-authorization-policies).

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Secure:** Contributes identity-based, least-privilege restriction on who may modify internal AI models, safety mechanisms, datasets and configurations, reducing both accidental and malicious internal interference. This Task does not cover deciding whether a specific proposed action is permitted at the moment of execution, which [Task 3.2](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs) and [Implementation 5.2.2](#implementation-5.2.2:-action-level,-context-aware-authorization-policies) address.  
* **Reliable:** Contributes regular checks that external SI services interfacing with internal systems have not been unexpectedly altered, such as by a silent vendor update, so that behavior tested earlier is not assumed to continue. This Task does not cover obtaining update disclosures from vendors, which [Implementation 6.2.2: Track Vendor Updates and Third-Party Entity Changes Through Change Management Process](#implementation-6.2.2:-track-vendor-updates-and-third-party-entity-changes-through-change-management-process) covers.  
* **Accountable:** Contributes a record for each change of what was altered, who approved it and the evidence the approval rested on, so that a later investigation can reconstruct why the change was judged safe. This Task does not cover assessing the change’s effect before deployment, which [Task 7.5: Conduct Impact Assessments and Risk Management for SI System and Model Updates](#task-7.5:-conduct-impact-assessments-and-risk-management-for-si-system-and-model-updates) covers.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Secure:** The list of who may modify each SI system, dataset, and safety mechanism identifies the accounts an attacker would most want to compromise. Protection sits with the organization’s identity and access management practice ([Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools)) and its existing information classification and handling practice.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Safe versus Safe:** Where a proposed change can wait, heavier approval keeps an unsafe modification out of service. Where the change corrects a known defect in an SI system or in its safety mechanisms, the same approval keeps that defect in service for longer. Options include holding the SI system in an advisory or fallback mode until the full review is complete, where such a mode has been prepared and tested ([Implementation 3.2.3: Specify Fail-Safe States and Fallback Behavior](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior)). Others include an emergency change path, if the organization has chosen to establish one, reviewed and recorded through the normal process afterward, or pre-approving narrow classes of corrective change, such as reverting to a previous approved version that has been kept deployable ([Implementation 7.5.1: Perform Pre-Update Validation and Re-Calibration](#implementation-7.5.1:-perform-pre-update-validation-and-re-calibration)). Each carries its own considerations. An advisory mode shifts load onto personnel, and a previous version can bring back the faults it was replaced to fix.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MANAGE 4.1** (on post-deployment risk management): This Task covers approval and logging requirements for changes to models, knowledge bases and guardrails, routing behavior-altering changes to re-evaluation; it does not cover the behavioral monitoring by which a change that bypassed approval may be caught. For that, see for example [Task 3.4: Monitor for Anomalous SI Behavior](#task-3.4:-monitor-for-anomalous-si-behavior).  
* **MANAGE 3.1** (on monitoring and responding to third-party risks): This Task covers regular integrity checks that external AI services interfacing with internal systems have not been unexpectedly altered; it does not cover the update disclosures obtained from vendors. For those, see for example [Implementation 6.2.2: Track Vendor Updates and Third-Party Entity Changes Through Change Management Process](#implementation-6.2.2:-track-vendor-updates-and-third-party-entity-changes-through-change-management-process).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Is there an emergency change path or pre-approved classes of corrective change, and how are such changes reviewed afterward? (see the Safe versus Safe tension in [Task 7.4: Define Authorization and Access Controls for SI Modifications](#task-7.4:-define-authorization-and-access-controls-for-si-modifications))
* Does any agent hold write access to its own system prompt, permissions, or safety mechanisms, and if so, under what change process?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control CM-5, Access Restrictions for Change, defines, approves and enforces access restrictions associated with changes, permitting only qualified and authorized individuals to initiate them, and covers operational procedures as well as software. Enhancement CM-5(4), Dual Authorization, calls for two qualified individuals to approve and implement changes to selected components, which suits changes to safety wrappers.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-218A, Secure Software Development Practices for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models: An SSDF Community Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218A), July 2024, from NIST. Task PO.5.1 recommendation R3 asks that training pipelines, model registries and related components be protected according to the principle of least privilege, and recommendation R4 asks that model modifications in the model registry be continuously monitored. These are the development-environment controls that correspond to restricting and recording who may modify an internal AI model, as this Task asks.

#### Implementation 7.4.1: Define and Implement Requirements for Approvals and Logging of Updates and Changes to SI Systems {#implementation-7.4.1:-define-and-implement-requirements-for-approvals-and-logging-of-updates-and-changes-to-si-systems}

Approvals and logging are particularly important for changes to models, knowledge bases, and guardrails, especially for applications operating in a reduced oversight mode, or where automation bias is a known risk and thus where changes in behavior may not be immediately noticed. Record for each change what was altered, who approved it, and the evidence the approval rested on, so that a later potential investigation can reconstruct why the change was judged safe. Where a change alters model behavior rather than configuration alone, treat it as a trigger for re-evaluation under [Implementation 2.3.4: Recurrent Risk Evaluations](#implementation-2.3.4:-recurrent-risk-evaluations), the same treatment a disclosed vendor update receives for an externally sourced component ([Implementation 6.2.2: Track Vendor Updates and Third-Party Entity Changes Through Change Management Process](#implementation-6.2.2:-track-vendor-updates-and-third-party-entity-changes-through-change-management-process)). An internal change reaching production unreviewed is the internally sourced equivalent of a silent vendor update, and would otherwise be caught, if at all, only by [Task 3.4: Monitor for Anomalous SI Behavior](#task-3.4:-monitor-for-anomalous-si-behavior). An update to an SI system that performs, influences, or constrains a protective or safety function should be treated as a change to that function’s settings or configuration, subject to equivalent approval and logging requirements, regardless of how the vendor or developer characterizes the change.

Where changes are deployed through an automated pipeline, the pipeline can be configured so that a change cannot be promoted to production until the required approvals are recorded. Where the organization already runs a management of change process for operational technology or process changes, changes to SI systems that act on those processes can be routed through it rather than through a separate process. The depth of review can scale with consequence. For example, a change to an SI system that acts on a physical process, or to a safety mechanism, may warrant safety review, test evidence from outside production, independent approval and a tested rollback plan, while a change to an advisory tool may need only owner approval and logging. Where few qualified people are available, for example in a small organization or a field office, the person who makes a change may also have to approve it. Where that happens, record it, and how the conflict is offset, such as by a later review by someone outside the change or by closer monitoring after deployment ([Implementation 3.9.6: Keep a Record of Design Decisions and Accepted Risks](#implementation-3.9.6:-keep-a-record-of-design-decisions-and-accepted-risks)). Where the organization chooses to establish one, an emergency path for changes that cannot wait, such as disabling or reverting a capability, can let the change proceed and then be reviewed and recorded through the normal process as soon as practical afterward. Disabling or reverting a capability carries its own considerations, such as losing the function it performed or bringing back faults an earlier version had (see [Practice 4](#practice-4:-define-procedures-for-emergency-avoidance-override,-recovery,-and-situational-awareness) and [Practice 11](#practice-11:-maintain-si-aware-mission-continuity-and-disaster-recovery-planning)). Until that review is complete, temporary measures such as closer monitoring or tighter guardrails can limit the risk of a change that has not yet been reviewed.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Are changes to SI systems that act on a process routed through the existing management of change process?  
* How does the depth of review scale with consequence, and which changes qualify for the emergency path?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control CM-3, Configuration Change Control, determines which changes are configuration-controlled, reviews and approves or disapproves them with explicit consideration of impact analyses, documents change decisions, and retains records of changes, which is the record of what was altered, who approved it and why that this Implementation asks for, applied here to models, knowledge bases and guardrails. Enhancement CM-3(1), Automated Documentation, Notification, and Prohibition of Changes, uses automated mechanisms to prohibit changes until designated approvals are received, which is the pipeline gate this Implementation suggests.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-128, Guide for Security-Focused Configuration Management of Information Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-128), August 2011, with updates as of October 2019, from NIST. Section 3.3.2, on the configuration change control process, states that when time does not allow the established process to be followed, unscheduled changes are still managed and controlled, that procedures allow rapid but controlled change to fix software errors, and that unscheduled changes are reviewed as soon as practical afterward. This is the emergency path this Implementation describes.  
* **Guidance** [Adapting Zero Trust Principles to Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/adapting-zero-trust-principles-operational-technology), 29 April 2026, from CISA, the Department of War and the Department of Energy with partners. The Configuration and Change Management section asks that changes, including updates to zero trust policies, follow a formalized Management of Change process, typically with a multi-disciplinary review board that includes engineering peer review and safety review. This bears on routing changes to SI systems that act on operational technology through that existing process, as this Implementation suggests.

#### Implementation 7.4.2: Implement Regular Integrity Checks for Systems that Interface with External SI Services {#implementation-7.4.2:-implement-regular-integrity-checks-for-systems-that-interface-with-external-si-services}

Because behavior observed in testing may not continue after a provider changes an external SI service, regular checks help an organization know whether its test results still apply. Integrity checks should verify that external AI systems and services have not been unexpectedly altered. This may incorporate TEVV protocols such as those from [Task 2.3: Establish Protocols for and Regularly Perform Systematic and Achievable Testing, Evaluation, Validation, and Verification (TEVV)](#task-2.3:-establish-protocols-for-and-regularly-perform-systematic-and-achievable-testing,-evaluation,-validation,-and-verification-\(tevv\)). Checks can include re-verifying signatures, hashes and declared versions where the service exposes them, and monitoring behavior for change. A provider may modify serving infrastructure without notice, in ways that change model behavior subtly. Contractual terms that require notice of version updates can help, but a provider may not give notice of changes it considers immaterial. Behavioral checks can reuse the validated standard dataset of [Implementation 2.3.1: Baseline SI System Performance](#implementation-2.3.1:-baseline-si-system-performance), run on a schedule and after any notified change, with results compared against those recorded when the service was validated. The validated dataset, and the size of difference that triggers review, tell an attacker how far a service’s behavior can be shifted without detection. Protecting them is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice. An unexplained difference can be treated as a change and reviewed under [Implementation 7.4.1: Define and Implement Requirements for Approvals and Logging of Updates and Changes to SI Systems](#implementation-7.4.1:-define-and-implement-requirements-for-approvals-and-logging-of-updates-and-changes-to-si-systems).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* How often are integrity checks on external SI services run, and what size of difference triggers review?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Establish Risks and Controls for the AI Supply Chain, version 1.0](https://www.coalitionforsecureai.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/risks-and-controls-for-the-ai-supply-chain-v1.pdf), 12 June 2025, from Workstream 1, Software Supply Chain Security for AI Systems, of the Coalition for Secure AI, an OASIS Open Project. Section 3.1.4, AI Infrastructure Supply Chain Security, lists infrastructure configuration drift among the concerns when consuming hosted models: third-party providers may modify serving configurations without notice, changing model behavior in subtle ways that downstream consumers cannot detect. This is the case the integrity checks in this Implementation address.  
* **Guidance** [OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/), Version 2026, December 2025, from the Agentic Security Initiative of the OWASP Gen AI Security Project, a volunteer community project of the Open Worldwide Application Security Project. Entry ASI04, Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities, asks in its continuous validation mitigation that signatures, hashes and SBOMs, including AIBOMs, be re-checked at runtime, and that behavior, privilege use and lineage be monitored for anomalies. These are checks this Implementation can include.  
* **Guidance** [OpenSSF Model Signing (OMS) Specification, Version 1.0](https://github.com/ossf/model-signing-spec), from the AI/ML Working Group of the Open Source Security Foundation, a cross-industry body hosted by the Linux Foundation; checked against commit 91bf841, October 2026\. It defines a detached signature file, distributed with the model, that lists a digest for every file in the model directory, and a verification procedure that by default fails if any file has changed or any unlisted file is present (Sections 8.4 and 8.5). Its README notes that signing verifies only that a model has not changed since it was signed, not its quality or security. This is one way to make the integrity check in this Implementation verifiable for models the organization holds locally.  
* **Commentary** [Artificial Intelligence Model Risk Management: Observations from a Thematic Review](https://www.mas.gov.sg/publications/monographs-or-information-paper/2024/artificial-intelligence-model-risk-management), Information Paper, December 2024, from the Monetary Authority of Singapore, written for banks. Section 6.5, under Change Management, observes that most banks have set up processes for third-party SI providers to notify them of version updates, and a footnote records that a provider may not notify end users of changes it views as immaterial. This is the gap the integrity checks in this Implementation cover.

### Task 7.5: Conduct Impact Assessments and Risk Management for SI System and Model Updates {#task-7.5:-conduct-impact-assessments-and-risk-management-for-si-system-and-model-updates}

Establish procedures for and perform structured risk and performance assessment before deploying any internal updates to AI systems, such as model prompts, configuration changes, data inputs, or safety wrappers. Where increases in risk are identified, if the deployment proceeds then mitigating controls should be identified and implemented. This Task helps check that “minor” internal adjustments do not unintentionally degrade overall system resilience or violate established functional safety benchmarks and requirements (see [Practice 2: Define SI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service Expectations](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations)). Degradation can come from unintended side effects of new behaviors, or from “catastrophic forgetting”, in which an AI system loses previously learned correct behavior after an update or retraining. This Task also applies where a change in operating context alters rules that are encoded in the AI system, such as in its prompts, retrieval corpus or rule base, or in the guardrails or safety wrappers around it, even though nothing in the AI system itself has changed (see [Implementation 1.1.3: Establish Triggers for Re-Validating Requirements on Change of Operating Context](#implementation-1.1.3:-establish-triggers-for-re-validating-requirements-on-change-of-operating-context)).

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Reliable:** Contributes a check, before any internal update to prompts, configuration, data or safety wrappers reaches production, that behavior which was already correct has not been lost, including through catastrophic forgetting, with shadow-mode comparison against the production system. This Task does not cover setting the benchmarks updates are judged against, which [Practice 1](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success) and [Practice 2](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations) set.  
* **Robust:** Contributes a change trigger for replacing a physical component or data feed with an equivalent from a different vendor, scaled to whether the component sits on a safety-critical path, because an AI system may depend on behavior beyond the specification the replacement meets. This Task does not cover verifying the AI system’s tolerance of such variance in the first place, which [Task 2.5: Verify that Learned Behavior Is Robust to Component, Hardware, and Data Schema Variance](#task-2.5:-verify-that-learned-behavior-is-robust-to-component,-hardware,-and-data-schema-variance) covers.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Secure:** Impact assessments and validation results record where an update loses accuracy and which classes of input are routed to an earlier model. An attacker could use them to target the inputs the SI system handles least well. Protecting these records is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Accurate versus Accurate:** Where the classes of input that lose accuracy under an update carry no more consequence than those that gain, an aggregate improvement can be judged on its own terms. Where a class that loses carries higher consequence, such as a type of equipment whose missed faults matter most, the aggregate gain conceals the loss that matters. Options include the fallback in [Implementation 7.5.1: Perform Pre-Update Validation and Re-Calibration](#implementation-7.5.1:-perform-pre-update-validation-and-re-calibration), which routes that class to the previous model where that version has been kept deployable. Others include re-calibrating thresholds, or declining the update.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MEASURE 2.3** (on ensuring realistic measurement): This Task covers measurement of a prospective update in shadow mode, alongside the production system on the same inputs, before switch-over; it does not cover defining the evaluation metrics used. For those, see for example [Task 1.3: Implement Evaluation and Test Plans, Including TEVV, Across the SI Lifecycle](#task-1.3:-implement-evaluation-and-test-plans,-including-tevv,-across-the-si-lifecycle).  
* **MEASURE 2.10** (on measuring privacy): This Task covers a privacy impact assessment before initial deployment and at each significant model or system update, covering data minimization, re-identification and inference; it does not address privacy risk arising between updates, such as from changes in how the system is used.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* How is an update judged when it improves accuracy overall but does worse on a class of inputs where errors matter more? (see the Accurate versus Accurate tension)
* What happens to a needed update when its assessment cannot be completed in time, and who decides?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control CM-4, Impact Analyses, analyzes changes to determine potential security and privacy impacts prior to implementation, and its discussion includes risk assessments to determine whether additional controls are required, which is the pre-deployment assessment and mitigation this Task sets out for model, prompt, data and safety-wrapper updates. Enhancement CM-4(2), Verification of Controls, verifies after a change that impacted controls are implemented correctly, operating as intended and producing the desired outcome.

#### Implementation 7.5.1: Perform Pre-Update Validation and Re-Calibration {#implementation-7.5.1:-perform-pre-update-validation-and-re-calibration}

Validation before an update is deployed helps an organization find regressions, such as worse performance on one class of input, while they can still be addressed. Validation and re-calibration should be performed before deploying any updates to models, system prompts, databases, and other components of AI systems that affect performance and safety. This should be informed by [Practice 1](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success) and [Practice 2](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations). Changes to performance should be documented and, where necessary, mitigating controls should be put in place prior to deployment. Validation data can include recent operating conditions and cases drawn from incident and near-miss reports, such as those received under [Task 8.6: Establish Non-Punitive Reporting for SI-Related Near-Misses](#task-8.6:-establish-non-punitive-reporting-for-si-related-near-misses). Record the version of the validation data with the results. For example, a new model for an AI system that summarizes and prioritizes equipment condition reports for maintenance scheduling might have improved accuracy overall. 

Pre-update validation might reveal an unacceptably higher false negative rate for specific types of equipment that could not be addressed by re-calibrating thresholds. Mitigating controls can then be put in place, such as having the AI system fall back onto the previous model for reports from these types of equipment. Keep the previous version deployable until the update has been validated in operation, so that a fallback of this kind remains available (see also the comparison in [Implementation 7.5.2: Perform Automated “Champion-Challenger” Assessment](#implementation-7.5.2:-perform-automated-“champion-challenger”-assessment)). Where outputs of the SI system feed thresholds, alarms or confidence-based rules, re-calibration means adjusting those settings so that they again match the updated system’s observed error rates. Some guidance, such as Deploying AI Systems Securely, expects a new model version to be within acceptable limits before it is redeployed. Where no mitigating control adequately addresses a safety-relevant regression, withhold the update unless the role that owns the safety function formally accepts the regression. That role needs the information, time, and authority to judge the regression, and to reject it. Record the outcome and the reason for it. Protect the integrity of any reference or historical dataset used for this comparison. A comparison against reference data that is itself poisoned or otherwise compromised is invalid.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* How long is the previous version kept deployable after an update?  
* Where no mitigating control adequately addresses a safety-relevant regression, is the update withheld?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control enhancement CM-3(2), Testing, Validation, and Documentation of Changes, tests, validates and documents changes before their implementation is finalized. Its discussion notes that testing should not interfere with mission operations, that operational systems may need to be taken offline or replicated before testing, and that compensating controls apply where testing on operational systems is not possible. This is the established control form of the pre-update validation this Implementation asks for.  
* **Guidance** [Deploying AI Systems Securely: Best Practices for Deploying Secure and Resilient AI Systems](https://media.defense.gov/2024/Apr/15/2003439257/-1/-1/0/CSI-DEPLOYING-AI-SYSTEMS-SECURELY.PDF), Version 1.0, April 2024, from the National Security Agency’s Artificial Intelligence Security Center with CISA, the FBI and partner agencies. Under Update and patch regularly, it asks that a full evaluation be run when a model is updated to a new or different version, so that accuracy, performance and security tests are within acceptable limits before redeployment. This is the pre-update validation this Implementation asks for, stated for SI systems.  
* **Guidance** [Artificial intelligence and machine learning: Supply chain risks and mitigations](https://media.defense.gov/2026/Mar/04/2003882809/-1/-1/0/AI_ML_SUPPLY_CHAIN_RISKS_AND_MITIGATIONS.PDF), 2025, from the Australian Signals Directorate, co-sealed by national cyber security agencies of Canada, Japan, the Republic of Korea, New Zealand, Singapore, the United Kingdom and the United States (the National Security Agency). Under performance testing of machine learning models, it notes that where an existing standard or historical dataset is compared against live results, steps should be taken to protect its integrity, since any comparison would be invalid if that reference data were also poisoned or compromised. This is the pitfall named at the end of this Implementation.

#### Implementation 7.5.2: Perform Automated “Champion-Challenger” Assessment {#implementation-7.5.2:-perform-automated-“champion-challenger”-assessment}

Seeing how a prospective update behaves on the same live inputs as the production system, before its outputs are used, helps the organization decide whether to switch over. The comparison should be done by concurrently running existing production AI systems (“champion”) alongside the prospective updated AI system (“challenger”) in a “shadow mode” to determine the differences in behavior. The “challenger” system should demonstrate appropriate improvements in performance, as measured in [Practice 1](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success) and [Practice 2](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations), utilizing evaluation metrics that align with [Task 1.3: Implement Evaluation and Test Plans, Including TEVV, Across the SI Lifecycle](#task-1.3:-implement-evaluation-and-test-plans,-including-tevv,-across-the-si-lifecycle), and mitigating controls established, prior to switch-over to the new system. Where actual outcomes become known, compare the outputs of both systems with those outcomes as well as with each other. A difference between the two does not by itself show which one is in error, since the champion’s output is also a prediction. A review of shadow-mode (“silent”) evaluations of medical AI found that far fewer studies verified outputs against ground truth in the setting of use than reported technical performance metrics. This process also supports [Practice 9: Provide Role-Based SI Risk Training that Builds Well-Founded Trust](#practice-9:-provide-role-based-si-risk-training-that-builds-well-founded-trust) in training those interacting with the system, should this be required by any change in the behavior of the new system.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* How long does the challenger run alongside the champion, and what improvement is needed before it replaces it?
* Who provides the compute and reviewer time to run both systems, and what comparison is used where running both is not practical?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [SR 11-7, Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management](https://www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/srletters/2011/sr1107a1.pdf), April 2011, from the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, written for banks. Section V, Model Validation, describes parallel outcomes analysis, in which the original and adjusted models’ forecasts are both tested against realized outcomes, and states that an adjusted model that does not outperform the original needs further change before it replaces it. Its discussion of benchmarking adds that a difference from a benchmark does not by itself mean the model is in error. Both bear on the champion-challenger comparison in this Implementation.  
* **Research** [Tikhomirov, L. et al., “A scoping review of silent trials for medical artificial intelligence”, Nature Health, 2026](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44360-025-00048-z). Reviews 75 studies of “silent” evaluation, in which an ML model runs prospectively in its intended clinical setting without affecting care. It finds that most reported area under the curve and similar technical metrics, and that far fewer verified outputs against ground truth in the setting of use. This bears on what a shadow-mode comparison in this Implementation measures.

#### Implementation 7.5.3: Integrate Privacy Impact Assessments (PIA) into Update Cycles {#implementation-7.5.3:-integrate-privacy-impact-assessments-\(pia\)-into-update-cycles}

Repeating a privacy impact assessment as an SI system is updated helps the organization notice when a change creates new privacy risk. Conduct a PIA before initial deployment, where one was not conducted when the SI system was developed or procured, and for all significant model or system updates to identify risks related to data minimization, re-identification, and inference. Check that updates do not bypass existing privacy controls.
