For agents, privacy risk can also build up within a session, where material carried across steps combines into a disclosure that no single tool call would make; see [Implementation 5.3.4: Limit the Context Carried Forward Between Steps](#implementation-5.3.4:-limit-the-context-carried-forward-between-steps).

Updates that may warrant a PIA include adding data sources or fields to training, fine-tuning or retrieval, extending retention, giving the SI system tools that reach customer or employee records, and changing who can query it. Operational data can be personal data indirectly. For example, interval data from smart meters can indicate when a household is occupied, and camera, badge or location telemetry collected for safety monitoring can reveal the movements of individual workers. For learned systems, the assessment can include whether the updated SI system can reproduce personal data from its training or retrieval data, and whether its outputs or logs now contain information that the previous version’s did not. Record the outcome with the version identifier of the update in the change record under [Implementation 7.4.1: Define and Implement Requirements for Approvals and Logging of Updates and Changes to SI Systems](#implementation-7.4.1:-define-and-implement-requirements-for-approvals-and-logging-of-updates-and-changes-to-si-systems). A privacy finding from the PIA should be resolved or formally accepted before the update is deployed. A finding that the SI system can reproduce personal data also tells an attacker where to attempt extraction. Until it is resolved, protecting it is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which updates count as significant enough to call for a PIA?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control RA-8, Privacy Impact Assessments, calls for a privacy impact assessment before developing or procuring information technology that processes personally identifiable information, and its discussion describes the assessment as a living document that is updated whenever changes to the technology or the organization’s practices alter the privacy risks, which supports repeating it on each significant model or system update. The Personally Identifiable Information Processing and Transparency (PT) family covers the related processing authority and purpose controls.  
* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025), March 2025, from NIST. Section 3.3.2, Information Extraction, describes training data extraction attacks on generative language models and observes that verbatim memorization of sensitive information, such as email addresses, phone numbers and locations, has been seen in more recent transformer models. This bears on checking whether an updated SI system can reproduce personal data.

#### Implementation 7.5.4: Audit Interoperability for Hardware or Data Substrate Substitution {#implementation-7.5.4:-audit-interoperability-for-hardware-or-data-substrate-substitution}

Treating a like-for-like replacement as a change helps the organization check whether a replacement component, data feed, or computing platform that meets its specification changes how an SI system behaves. Establish a change-management trigger within the internal supply chain for when physical operational components or software data feeds (e.g., valves, pumps, switches, or sensors, or API schemas, electronic health record modules, or transaction journals) are replaced with equivalents from a different vendor or manufacturer. A change in the manufacturer or model recorded for the asset in the asset inventory can serve as this trigger. A substitution of this kind is a form of drift that comes from the supply chain rather than from the process the SI system observes (see [Implementation 3.3.2: Establish Maximum Drift Thresholds](#implementation-3.3.2:-establish-maximum-drift-thresholds)). The same trigger applies to the SI system’s own substrate. A change of processor or accelerator, inference runtime or driver, or numerical precision, such as quantization to 8-bit integers, can change its behavior even when the model has not been retrained. For a replaced sensor, historian or protocol gateway, the checks can include units and scaling, sampling rate, timestamp handling, tag mapping, and the encoding of missing or bad-quality values. A difference in any of these can produce inputs that appear valid but were never tested (see also the runtime input checks in [Implementation 7.2.4: Select and Prepare the Inputs Each SI System Receives](#implementation-7.2.4:-select-and-prepare-the-inputs-each-si-system-receives)).

Even if the replacement part complies perfectly with existing engineering specifications, the internal supply chain process should mandate a regression test of any governing AI systems to help ensure the vendor swap does not invalidate undocumented physical dependencies embedded within the AI system’s learned model as discussed in [Task 2.5: Verify that Learned Behavior Is Robust to Component, Hardware, and Data Schema Variance](#task-2.5:-verify-that-learned-behavior-is-robust-to-component,-hardware,-and-data-schema-variance). If mandating full regression testing for every replacement-in-kind substitution is not feasible given the volume of routine component swaps in normal maintenance, organizations can consider the following guidance for action:

* If the substituted component has no plausible link to the AI system, such as an unrelated office HVAC sensor, standard engineering sign-off is sufficient.  
* If the component is one the AI system depends on or influences but outside any safety-critical path, such as a sensor on a non-critical secondary line, flag it for engineering review under [Task 2.5: Verify that Learned Behavior Is Robust to Component, Hardware, and Data Schema Variance](#task-2.5:-verify-that-learned-behavior-is-robust-to-component,-hardware,-and-data-schema-variance) rather than a full regression test.  
* If the component sits within a safety-critical control path, such as a valve actuator on a shutdown system or a sensor feeding a chemical batch temperature loop, require full regression testing before deployment.

Where it is unclear which of these cases a component falls in, full regression testing remains available as the more conservative choice.

Regression testing after a substitution can also confirm that latency and throughput still meet control-loop or operator-response requirements, and that guardrails, logging and monitoring still function. Record the hardware, runtime, numerical precision and data interfaces with the model version in the configuration baseline, so that the tested configuration can be identified and a later discrepancy traced to the substitution.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Who decides which tier a substituted component falls in?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Adapting Zero Trust Principles to Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/adapting-zero-trust-principles-operational-technology), 29 April 2026, from CISA, the Department of War and the Department of Energy with partners. The Configuration and Change Management section asks that all changes follow a formalized Management of Change process, typically with a multi-disciplinary review board covering engineering peer review, safety review, and size, weight, power and material review, followed by formal authorization and documentation. A substitution trigger under this Implementation can route through that existing process.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Appendix F.7.5, the OT discussion of CM-3, Configuration Change Control, states that configuration change control procedures should align with the organization’s management of change practices. This bears on placing the substitution trigger within existing change management rather than beside it.  
* **Guidance** [Foundations for OT Cybersecurity: Asset Inventory Guidance for Owners and Operators](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-08/joint-guide-foundations-for-OT-cybersecurity-asset-inventory-guidance_508c.pdf), 13 August 2025, from CISA with the EPA, NSA, FBI and partner agencies in Australia, Canada, Germany, the Netherlands and New Zealand. It lists manufacturer and model among the high-priority attributes to collect for each asset, and under Continuous Improvement asks that change management processes track OT asset modifications, additions and decommissioning. A change in the recorded manufacturer or model is a point at which the substitution trigger in this Implementation can fire.  
* **Guidance** [OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-genai-llm-top-10-2026/), Version 2026, August 4, 2026, from the OWASP GenAI Security Project, a volunteer community project. LLM04:2026, Supply Chain, notes under compromised conversion, merge and quantization workflows that model weights can be crafted so that the full-precision model evaluates benignly while the quantized artifact behaves as an attacker chooses, so full-precision assurances do not transfer to the deployed quantized artifact. This bears on treating a change of numerical precision as a substitution under this Implementation.

### Task 7.6: Establish Processes for Internal SI Component Deprecation and Decommissioning {#task-7.6:-establish-processes-for-internal-si-component-deprecation-and-decommissioning}

Establish secure, structured protocols for the sunsetting, deprecation, and decommissioning of internally developed AI agents, systems, tools, models, training datasets, and associated software dependencies. This Task helps ensure that when internal AI assets reach end-of-life, they are safely removed from production environments without breaking legacy system dependencies or leaving behind unmonitored attack surfaces. This Task covers the artifacts: the models, datasets, pipelines and tools themselves. Where the organization has system disposal and media sanitization practice, this Task can build on it. The withdrawal of an operating AI system’s authority, the preservation of what it knew, and the decisions recorded for everything that depended on it are in [Practice 13: Establish Procedures for Retiring SI Systems and Withdrawing Their Authority](#practice-13:-establish-procedures-for-retiring-si-systems-and-withdrawing-their-authority).

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Secure:** Contributes destruction or secure archiving of retired models, training pipelines and datasets so that “zombie models” are not exfiltrated. This Task does not cover withdrawing the credentials, triggers and delegated authority of a retiring system, which [Task 13.2: Withdraw All Authority and Confirm the Result](#task-13.2:-withdraw-all-authority-and-confirm-the-result) covers.  
* **Safe:** Contributes destruction or controlled archiving of retired models so that one retired for inappropriate behavior is not accidentally put back into use, and isolation of deprecated systems that cannot yet be removed so that their faults are contained. This Task does not cover deciding when a model should be retired, which [Implementation 13.1.1: Identify Retirement Triggers, Including Those Outside the Organization’s Control](#implementation-13.1.1:-identify-retirement-triggers,-including-those-outside-the-organization’s-control) covers.  
* **Resilient:** Contributes the dependency audit and deprecation timeline that allow downstream IT, OT and ICS systems to be refactored or reverted to deterministic fallbacks before a model is turned off. This Task does not cover recording a decision for each dependent, which [Implementation 13.3.3: Determine and Record What Happens to Everything that Depended on the System](#implementation-13.3.3:-determine-and-record-what-happens-to-everything-that-depended-on-the-system) adds.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Secure and Safe versus Accountable:** Where a retired model is destroyed, nothing remains to be exfiltrated, or to be put back into use by mistake. Where it was retired because it behaved inappropriately, destruction also removes what an investigation or a later claim may need to examine. One way to balance this is the choice [Implementation 7.6.2: Secure Archiving and Destruction of Model and Other SI Artifacts](#implementation-7.6.2:-secure-archiving-and-destruction-of-model-and-other-si-artifacts) already offers between destruction and secure archiving, made artifact by artifact; others include capturing the evidence identified under [Task 13.3: Preserve What Is Needed and Hand Over What Depended on the System](#task-13.3:-preserve-what-is-needed-and-hand-over-what-depended-on-the-system) before anything is destroyed.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **GOVERN 1.7** (on establishing decommissioning processes): This Task covers the artifact side of phasing out safely: dependency mapping before turn-off, secure archiving or destruction, and isolation for what cannot yet be retired; it does not cover withdrawing the authority of an AI system that is still operating. For that, see for example [Task 13.2: Withdraw All Authority and Confirm the Result](#task-13.2:-withdraw-all-authority-and-confirm-the-result).  
* **MANAGE 2.4** (on decommissioning or superseding AI systems): This Task covers disposal of superseded models, including those found to behave inappropriately, so that they are not accidentally resurrected; it does not cover the decision to deactivate or the conditions that prompt it. For that, see for example [Implementation 13.1.1: Identify Retirement Triggers, Including Those Outside the Organization’s Control](#implementation-13.1.1:-identify-retirement-triggers,-including-those-outside-the-organization’s-control).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Is each retired artifact destroyed or archived? (see the Secure and Safe versus Accountable tension in [Task 7.6: Establish Processes for Internal SI Component Deprecation and Decommissioning](#task-7.6:-establish-processes-for-internal-si-component-deprecation-and-decommissioning))
* Who owns retiring an internal artifact whose original developer or team has moved on or left?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-37r2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations: A System Life Cycle Approach for Security and Privacy](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-37r2), from NIST. Task M-7, System Disposal, calls for a disposal strategy when a system is removed from operation, implementation of disposal controls such as media sanitization, configuration management and record retention, updates to inventory and tracking systems, notification of users and application owners hosted on the system, and review of any control inheritance relationships. It applies equally to system elements removed from operation, which is the level at which individual models, datasets and pipelines are retired.

#### Implementation 7.6.1: Internal Dependency Mapping (Orphan System Prevention) {#implementation-7.6.1:-internal-dependency-mapping-\(orphan-system-prevention\)}

Mapping what depends on an SI component before it is turned off helps the organization retire it without leaving dependent systems broken. Before decommissioning an internal AI agent, system, tool, model or API, organizations should audit the internal supply chain to identify, as completely as practical, the downstream IT, OT, or ICS systems that rely on its outputs. Build the map from observation as well as documentation, for example from API gateway logs, use of the component’s credentials and network flow records. These can reveal callers that were never registered. The resulting map shows which systems would fail if a component stopped responding, which an attacker could use to choose a target for disruption. Protecting it is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice, as with the mapping under [Implementation 3.5.1: Map Direct Functional and Algorithmic Dependencies](#implementation-3.5.1:-map-direct-functional-and-algorithmic-dependencies). A deprecation period in which calls are still served but logged and flagged can surface remaining dependents before the component is turned off. Establish strict “deprecation timelines” and notifications to help ensure dependent systems are safely refactored, or reverted to deterministic fallbacks where these exist or can be prepared, before the model is turned off. Where neither is possible in time, [Implementation 7.6.3: Legacy Logic Vulnerability Management](#implementation-7.6.3:-legacy-logic-vulnerability-management) applies. The process of mapping dependencies is common to [Implementation 3.5.1: Map Direct Functional and Algorithmic Dependencies](#implementation-3.5.1:-map-direct-functional-and-algorithmic-dependencies) and, for shared infrastructure, [Implementation 3.5.2: Identify Indirect Shared Infrastructure and Collateral Damage Exposure](#implementation-3.5.2:-identify-indirect-shared-infrastructure-and-collateral-damage-exposure). If that mapping has already been performed and kept current, much of the groundwork for decommissioning will already be in place. [Implementation 13.3.3: Determine and Record What Happens to Everything that Depended on the System](#implementation-13.3.3:-determine-and-record-what-happens-to-everything-that-depended-on-the-system) requires that a decision is recorded for each dependent identified here, including where that decision is to make no provision.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* How long is the deprecation period, and what happens to dependents not refactored by its end?

**References:**

* **Standard** [ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023, Systems and software engineering: system life cycle processes](https://www.iso.org/standard/81702.html), published jointly by ISO, IEC and IEEE. Clause 6.4.14, the disposal process, notes under its task to deactivate a system or system element that interfaces to other systems are considered, and that when a system is modified for upgrades only the impacted system elements are deactivated and removed. This is the systems-engineering form of the dependency audit this Implementation asks for before an internal SI component is turned off.  
* **Guidance** [NIST IR 8179, Criticality Analysis Process Model: Prioritizing Systems and Components](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.IR.8179), April 2018, from NIST. Sub-process B.2 asks that interactions between activities or processes be examined to determine which processes rely on the outputs of others, and that the result be mapped, including what must be completed before another process can begin. This is a structured method for identifying the downstream systems that rely on an SI component’s outputs, as this Implementation asks.

#### Implementation 7.6.2: Secure Archiving and Destruction of Model and Other SI Artifacts {#implementation-7.6.2:-secure-archiving-and-destruction-of-model-and-other-si-artifacts}

Define destruction (cryptographically secure as appropriate) or secure archiving standards for retired models, training pipelines, and datasets. This helps prevent “zombie models” from being accidentally used, resurrected or exfiltrated. This may be particularly important for models that were found to behave inappropriately, do not comply with regulations, are found to contain illegal or otherwise undesirable content, or found to be susceptible to reverse engineering and leakage of confidential or proprietary information. Archived models can be kept as encrypted copies with recorded hashes in a location protected against tampering, with the keys and hash values stored apart from the encrypted copies. Before storage media that held data for SI systems are repurposed or disposed of, they can be sanitized by a method such as cryptographic erase, block erase or overwrite. An archived model can also serve later as a challenger or baseline under [Implementation 7.5.2: Perform Automated “Champion-Challenger” Assessment](#implementation-7.5.2:-perform-automated-“champion-challenger”-assessment). Before destruction or archiving, identify the artifacts and copies concerned, which can include weights and checkpoints, adapters, embeddings and retrieval indexes, prompts, safety-wrapper configurations, and copies held in backups, on edge devices or on developer workstations. An archive intended to allow a model to be examined or run again should keep the runtime, dependency versions and configuration with the weights. The weights alone may not reproduce its behavior. Weights and embeddings can be classified as at least as sensitive as the data they were derived from. Training data can sometimes be extracted from a model, and stored embeddings can be inverted to recover source text.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* How long are archives kept, and are they kept in a form that can be run again?

**References:**

* **Research** [Supervision of Artificial Intelligence in Finance: Challenges, Policies and Practices](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/supervision-of-artificial-intelligence-in-finance_92743dc1-en.html), OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 54, January 2026, from the OECD Directorate for Financial and Enterprise Affairs. Section 2.2 observes that robust governance calls for retaining each model instance rather than only the latest version, because a problem such as biased output can surface after a model is fixed and cannot then be investigated from the latest version alone. This bears on this Implementation’s choice between destruction and secure archiving for models found to behave inappropriately.  
* **Guidance** [Deploying AI Systems Securely: Best Practices for Deploying Secure and Resilient AI Systems](https://media.defense.gov/2024/Apr/15/2003439257/-1/-1/0/CSI-DEPLOYING-AI-SYSTEMS-SECURELY.PDF), Version 1.0, April 2024, from the National Security Agency’s Artificial Intelligence Security Center with CISA, the FBI and partner agencies. Under Validate the AI system before and during use, it asks that hashes and encrypted copies of each release of the model and system be archived in a tamper-proof location, with hash values or keys kept apart from the encrypted copies. This is a concrete form of the secure archiving this Implementation asks for.  
* **Guidance** [AI Data Security: Best Practices for Securing Data Used to Train & Operate AI Systems](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/ai-data-security-best-practices-securing-data-used-train-operate-ai-systems), Version 1.0, May 2025, from the National Security Agency’s Artificial Intelligence Security Center with CISA, the FBI and partner agencies. Best practice 9, Delete data securely, asks that drives used to store and process data for SI systems be erased before they are repurposed or decommissioned, by cryptographic erase, block erase or data overwrite, and points to NIST SP 800-88. This is the media side of the destruction this Implementation asks for.  
* **Guidance** [Supervisory Statement SS1/23, Model risk management principles for banks](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/prudential-regulation/publication/2023/may/model-risk-management-principles-for-banks-ss), May 2023, updated 16 April 2026, from the Prudential Regulation Authority of the Bank of England, which sets its expectations for UK banks with internal model approval. A footnote to Principle 1.2 notes that the rationale for decommissioning a model can inform later model development, and that the decommissioned model may be used as a challenger model itself. This is a further reason to archive rather than destroy.  
* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025), March 2025, from NIST. Section 3.3.2, Information Extraction, describes training data extraction attacks on generative language models and observes that verbatim memorization of sensitive information has been seen in more recent transformer models. This bears on handling retired weights at the sensitivity of their training data.  
* **Guidance** [OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-genai-llm-top-10-2026/), Version 2026, August 4, 2026, from the OWASP GenAI Security Project, a volunteer community project. LLM09:2026, Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, states under Embedding Inversion that stored embeddings can be inverted to recover source text, and that vector-database backups and exported embeddings should be treated as equivalent to a leak of the underlying documents. This bears on archiving or destroying retrieval indexes under this Implementation.

#### Implementation 7.6.3: Legacy Logic Vulnerability Management {#implementation-7.6.3:-legacy-logic-vulnerability-management}

Containing a deprecated SI system that has to stay in service helps the organization keep supporting the functions that depend on the system while limiting the risk the system carries. For AI systems that cannot be immediately decommissioned due to legacy constraints (e.g., dependent systems that cannot be updated), establish an “Extended Isolation Protocol.” This requires appropriate controls, such as redeployment onto isolated systems, additional monitoring, or stricter fail-over conditions, to contain risks associated with continuing to use an otherwise deprecated system. Where the developer or vendor no longer supports the SI system, continued support can come from in-house staff or from an external provider under contract. While such a system remains in service, vulnerability advisories for its runtime, libraries and supporting software should continue to be tracked, and its access to other systems limited to what its remaining dependents need. A list of deprecated SI systems kept in service, and of their unpatched components, points an attacker to the least-supported systems. Protecting it is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Where vendor support has ended, is support continued in house or by an external provider under contract?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control SA-22, Unsupported System Components, asks that components be replaced when support is no longer available or that alternative support be provided. Its discussion allows exceptions for systems providing critical mission capabilities where newer technologies are not available, and notes that the increased risk can be mitigated by prohibiting connection to public or uncontrolled networks or by other forms of isolation. Applied here to deprecated SI systems, this corresponds to the Extended Isolation Protocol.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Appendix F.7.16, the OT discussion of SA-22, notes that OT systems may contain unsupported components that have not been replaced because of operational, safety, availability or lifetime constraints, and asks organizations to identify alternative methods to continue supported operation and to consider additional compensating controls. This is the OT form of the legacy constraint this Implementation addresses.

## Practice 8: Incorporate SI-Aware Incident Analysis and Response Procedures {#practice-8:-incorporate-si-aware-incident-analysis-and-response-procedures}

*Develop and implement protocols for responding to and investigating SI-related failures in operational environments, addressing the challenges posed by SI system behaviors that can be complex, opaque, or non-deterministic.*

This Practice helps an organization investigate and respond to incidents involving SI systems with the clarity that regulators, safety investigators, and incident response teams need, and contributes to keeping such incidents from compromising accountability or the reliable operation of the organization’s systems. Organizations with established incident response, investigation, and reporting arrangements can build on them for SI systems. For example, cybersecurity-focused playbooks for incident response should be expanded to cover the broader SI Risk Surface discussed in [Task 3.8: Scope and Map the Expanded SI Attack Surface and Risk Surface](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface). 

Those investigating and responding to an SI-related incident within the organization may need to judge whether an anomaly is more likely an active exploit or a non-adversarial risk across the Trustworthiness Characteristics, such as drift, an unannounced model update, stale or contaminated retrieved context, dynamic multi-agent feedback loops, or plausible hallucinations in generated logic ([Implementation 8.1.6: Incident Triage Across the Dual Attack/Risk Surface](#implementation-8.1.6:-incident-triage-across-the-dual-attack/risk-surface)). That judgment often has to be made, and acted on, before the cause is known for sure. Containing the situation and understanding it can pull against each other: investigating can delay restoring service, while acting without understanding can let the situation worsen or destroy the evidence needed to stop it recurring. Some steps, such as isolating the SI system, preserving its state, or falling back to an alternative operating mode, can serve both (see [Task 3.4](#task-3.4:-monitor-for-anomalous-si-behavior) and [Practice 11](#practice-11:-maintain-si-aware-mission-continuity-and-disaster-recovery-planning)). Isolating the system or falling back is available only where the organization has prepared for it in advance, and each brings its own considerations, such as losing whatever the SI system was contributing, including protective functions (see [Task 11.2: Define Manual and Alternative Operating Procedures for Long-Term Mission Continuity](#task-11.2:-define-manual-and-alternative-operating-procedures-for-long-term-mission-continuity)).

An apparent operator error may also have been shaped by an SI system’s output, so investigations should consider an SI system whose outputs personnel relied on as a possible contributing factor, and not only as a cause or an attack vector. This Practice focuses on governance and resourcing to satisfy transparency and regulatory requirements. It dovetails with [Practice 2: Define SI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service Expectations](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations), which focuses on technical and functional requirements, and [Practice 11: Maintain SI-Aware Mission Continuity and Disaster Recovery Planning](#practice-11:-maintain-si-aware-mission-continuity-and-disaster-recovery-planning), which focuses on maintaining operations. It also draws on, among others, the records kept under [Practice 10: Implement Multi-Tiered SI System Logging and Audit Capabilities](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities) and the inventory of SI deployments in [Task 7.1: Maintain an Internal Registry of SI Deployments](#task-7.1:-maintain-an-internal-registry-of-si-deployments).

**Search Keywords:** AI incident response, incident investigation, root-cause analysis (RCA), safety investigation, just culture, near-miss reporting, normalization of deviance, non-punitive disclosure, evidence preservation, chain of custody, multi-agent cascade reconstruction, forensic interpretability gap, post-hoc attribution limitations, attack vs. risk surface triage, AI incident response team (AIRT), regulatory notification, de-identified incident sharing, lessons learned, after-action review (AAR)

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Accountable:** Contributes identification of where an SI system’s failures must be reconstructable to the standard that regulators and safety investigators expect, and what to do where a system cannot support that, together with named people who own an incident from first response through to return to service. This Practice does not cover capturing the records an investigation draws on, which [Practice 10: Implement Multi-Tiered SI System Logging and Audit Capabilities](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities) covers.  
* **Transparent:** Contributes disclosure in both directions: notification of SI incidents to regulators and the public, sharing of de-identified failure modes with peer operators, and reporting routes through which personnel can raise near-misses without bearing the cost of doing so. This Practice does not cover obtaining disclosures from vendors in the first place, which [Practice 6: Integrate Visibility of the External Supply Chain of SI into Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management) covers.  
* **Safe:** Contributes a decision on where to use an SI system whose failures cannot be traced to a cause ([Task 8.2: Identify Additional Controls that May Be Required in Scenarios Where Deterministic Root Cause Analysis Is Not Possible](#task-8.2:-identify-additional-controls-that-may-be-required-in-scenarios-where-deterministic-root-cause-analysis-is-not-possible)). Where regulation requires the cause to be found, that requirement governs. Otherwise, the organization records whether other controls close the gap, and sets margins beyond which control passes to manual oversight or to a fallback whose own failures can be traced and that shares as few of the SI system’s sources of error as practical, and with those it does share, such as common sensors, identified. This Practice does not cover enforcing those boundaries while the system runs, which [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior) covers.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Secure:** Disclosing an incident to regulators and the public, and sharing failure modes with peer operators, describes how the organization’s SI systems failed and which control did not hold. An adversary could use that account to repeat an attack here, or to target peers running the same SI system before they have closed the gap. [Implementation 8.6.4: Share De-Identified Incident Records for Collective Learning](#implementation-8.6.4:-share-de-identified-incident-records-for-collective-learning) strips model internals and safety-sensitive data from shared records, and the same considerations can inform what a public disclosure includes, within any legal or regulatory obligation to disclose.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MANAGE 4.3** (on incident response): This Practice covers SI-aware processes for analyzing, responding to and communicating incidents, including to regulators, the public and peer operators; it does not cover sustaining and restoring essential functions during and after an incident. For that, see for example [Practice 11: Maintain SI-Aware Mission Continuity and Disaster Recovery Planning](#practice-11:-maintain-si-aware-mission-continuity-and-disaster-recovery-planning).  
* **GOVERN 4.3** (on establishing SI incident response and information-sharing processes): This Practice covers incident identification across the attack and risk surface, protected near-miss reporting, and de-identified sharing with peer operators; it does not cover the SI testing GOVERN 4.3 also names. For that, see for example [Practice 1](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success) and [Practice 2](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Who decides, during an incident, whether to contain first or investigate first, and do they have the information, authority, and support to act on that decision?  
* Where do the people, time, and budget for investigating SI incidents come from, and what happens when they are not available?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-61r3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-61r3), April 2025, from NIST. Section 2.2 sets out incident response roles beyond the response team, including leadership, legal, public affairs and asset owners, with incident handlers on staff, on contract or available when needed. Subcategory RS.AN-03 asks that analysis establish the sequence of events and the underlying or systemic root causes. Section 1 limits the guide to adverse cybersecurity events, which is the boundary this Practice extends to the non-adversarial part of the SI Risk Surface.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Section 6.4.3 asks that cyber and non-cyber incidents affecting OT be identified and classified, with accidental actions by authorized personnel as a class alongside targeted and untargeted attacks, and suggests engaging external organizations where OT forensic capability is lacking. Section 6.2.4.5 names the choice between returning to normal operations quickly and preserving forensic data as a priority to determine, which bears on the tension in Task 8.3.  
* **Guidance** [NIST AI 600-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1), July 2024, from NIST. Appendix A.1.8, Incident Disclosure, quotes a definition of an “AI incident” whose listed harms include disruption of the management and operation of critical infrastructure, notes that formal channels to report and document SI incidents do not currently exist, and holds that logging, recording and analyzing incidents ease sharing with other “AI Actors.” It bears on this Practice’s regulatory notification and de-identified sharing with peer operators.  
* **Guidance** [AI Incident Response Framework, Workstream 2: Preparing Defenders for a Changing Cybersecurity Landscape](https://www.coalitionforsecureai.org/defending-ai-systems-a-new-framework-for-incident-response-in-the-age-of-intelligent-technology/), version 1.0, 27 October 2025, from the Coalition for Secure AI, an OASIS Open Project. Section 1.3.1 gives an SI incident taxonomy that places performance failures such as model drift beside security vulnerabilities and misuse. Section 3.3.3.1 notes that a model will not in general give the same output from the same input, so raw outputs need preserving to reconstruct an incident. It covers only what is SI-specific, deferring the rest to NIST SP 800-61r3.  
* **Guidance** [DOE-HDBK-1028-2009, Human Performance Improvement Handbook, Volume 1: Concepts and Principles](https://www.energy.gov/ehss/articles/doe-hdbk-1028-2009), June 2009, from the U.S. Department of Energy. The Preface treats human error not as a cause of failure on its own but as the effect or symptom of deeper trouble in the system, systematically connected to people’s tools, tasks and operating environment. Written for DOE facilities, it bears on treating an SI system whose outputs personnel relied on as part of that system when investigating an apparent operator error.

### Task 8.1: Identify Scenarios Requiring Deterministic Root Cause Analysis and Incident Reconstruction {#task-8.1:-identify-scenarios-requiring-deterministic-root-cause-analysis-and-incident-reconstruction}

Knowing in advance which failures must be reconstructable helps an organization choose SI systems that support those investigations and focus forensic effort where it matters most. Define the specific applications, operational thresholds, and safety-critical triggers that mandate a comprehensive, deterministic reconstruction of an AI-driven failure, for both post-event investigation as well as to provide situational awareness for immediate-term incident response. Applications where return to service after an incident depends on showing that its cause has been corrected, as in the checklist of [Implementation 11.4.1: Define a Checklist for Validating System Safety Before Re-Engaging SI Control](#implementation-11.4.1:-define-a-checklist-for-validating-system-safety-before-re-engaging-si-control), are among these. Existing obligations to find a cause, for example incident investigation under process safety management rules or the identification of the causes of protection system misoperations under electric reliability standards, can also indicate where these triggers lie. Incident response criteria should explicitly account for both the AI Attack Surface and the AI Risk Surface ([Task 3.8: Scope and Map the Expanded SI Attack Surface and Risk Surface](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface)), helping ensure triage procedures can differentiate between adversarial cyber exploits and non-adversarial failures.

This Task helps the organization use, for applications that require forensic root cause analysis, AI systems that support such investigations. It also helps prioritize forensic resources for high-impact events and supports meeting the evidentiary standards that regulatory and safety oversight require. Here, deterministic reconstruction means being able to replay what the AI system received and produced, including its inputs, versions and settings, in a forensic investigation setting. This is distinct from explaining why it produced that output. The reconstruction needed can differ by scenario, for example full replay, a record of the inputs and retrieved documents that an output drew on, the full sequence of an agent’s actions and tool calls, or only what the SI system recommended and what the operator did. Reconstruction can be needed after the SI system has been updated or retired, so the model version, prompts, configuration, and other state and information that influenced the output at the time need keeping ([Implementation 10.1.5: Define What Each Operational Record Is For](#implementation-10.1.5:-define-what-each-operational-record-is-for); see also [Practice 13: Establish Procedures for Retiring SI Systems and Withdrawing Their Authority](#practice-13:-establish-procedures-for-retiring-si-systems-and-withdrawing-their-authority)).

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Accountable:** Contributes identification, for each AI application, of where a failure must be reconstructable to the evidentiary standard of regulatory and safety oversight, with systems that cannot support this substituted, compensated or bounded by handover ([Implementation 8.1.1: Evaluate SI Applications](#implementation-8.1.1:-evaluate-si-applications)), and with post-hoc attribution such as SHAP and LIME excluded as forensic proof ([Implementation 8.1.2: Identify SI Systems that May Not Satisfy Root Cause Analysis Requirements](#implementation-8.1.2:-identify-si-systems-that-may-not-satisfy-root-cause-analysis-requirements)). This Task does not cover capturing the inputs, prompts and metadata reconstruction draws on, which [Task 10.1: Define Decision-Level Logging and Metadata Retention Policies](#task-10.1:-define-decision-level-logging-and-metadata-retention-policies) covers.  
* **Secure:** Contributes triage pathways that isolate whether an anomaly originated on the attack surface or in the non-adversarial part of the risk surface ([Implementation 8.1.6: Incident Triage Across the Dual Attack/Risk Surface](#implementation-8.1.6:-incident-triage-across-the-dual-attack/risk-surface)), so that an intrusion is not dismissed as drift. This Task does not cover detecting the anomaly at runtime, which [Task 3.4: Monitor for Anomalous SI Behavior](#task-3.4:-monitor-for-anomalous-si-behavior) covers.  
* **Reliable:** Contributes the other half of the same triage, so that drift, sensor schema variance or a multi-agent cascade is not misclassified as an intrusion and left uncorrected while response effort goes elsewhere. This Task does not cover setting the drift thresholds that define when degradation requires action, which [Implementation 3.3.2: Establish Maximum Drift Thresholds](#implementation-3.3.2:-establish-maximum-drift-thresholds) covers.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Privacy-Enhanced:** Telemetry that spans agent boundaries, capturing inter-agent communications and context window handoffs ([Implementation 8.1.5: Multi-Agent Cascade Reconstruction Capabilities](#implementation-8.1.5:-multi-agent-cascade-reconstruction-capabilities)), can carry personal and sensitive data that passed through those agents. [Implementation 10.1.3: Forensic Integrity and Privacy-Preserving Log Partitioning](#implementation-10.1.3:-forensic-integrity-and-privacy-preserving-log-partitioning) sets out the masking and the logically separated storage that keep such records out of routine operational view.
* **Secure:** The list of SI systems whose failures cannot be reconstructed ([Implementation 8.1.2: Identify SI Systems that May Not Satisfy Root Cause Analysis Requirements](#implementation-8.1.2:-identify-si-systems-that-may-not-satisfy-root-cause-analysis-requirements)), and the triage pathways that decide whether an anomaly is treated as drift or as an attack ([Implementation 8.1.6: Incident Triage Across the Dual Attack/Risk Surface](#implementation-8.1.6:-incident-triage-across-the-dual-attack/risk-surface)), show where an attack would be hardest to trace and how to make one look like a non-adversarial failure. An attacker could use them to choose a target and to disguise an intrusion as drift. Protecting this material is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Accountable versus Accurate:** Where an SI system’s version and settings are already fixed, replaying it costs little. Where replay depends on holding back a newer version, or on disabling sampling in a generative component, it can keep a known defect in service or change output quality. Options include fixing versions and settings to the degree of reconstruction each scenario needs under this Task, and relying on records made at the time of the output ([Task 10.1: Define Decision-Level Logging and Metadata Retention Policies](#task-10.1:-define-decision-level-logging-and-metadata-retention-policies)) where full replay is not needed.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MANAGE 4.3** (on incident response): This Task covers the criteria and triage pathways that let AI-driven failures be tracked and responded to, and the drills that keep reconstruction usable during a live incident; it does not cover communicating incidents outside the organization. For that, see for example [Task 8.4: Define External Reporting and Regulatory Disclosure Protocols Following SI Incidents](#task-8.4:-define-external-reporting-and-regulatory-disclosure-protocols-following-si-incidents).  
* **MEASURE 2.9** (on measuring interpretability and explainability): This Task informs how AI output is interpreted after an incident, by excluding post-hoc attribution such as SHAP and LIME as forensic proof of cause; it does not cover setting how outputs are explained to personnel during operation. For that, see for example [Task 4.6: Ensure that Confidence and Rationale Shown to Personnel Reflect How the SI System Reached Its Output](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which applications and scenarios call for deterministic reconstruction, and how much reconstruction does each need?  
* How far are versions and settings held fixed for replay? (see the Accountable versus Accurate tension in [Task 8.1: Identify Scenarios Requiring Deterministic Root Cause Analysis and Incident Reconstruction](#task-8.1:-identify-scenarios-requiring-deterministic-root-cause-analysis-and-incident-reconstruction))  
* Who decides that an incident meets a reconstruction trigger, and do they have the authority to hold back restoration while evidence is preserved?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-86, Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-86), August 2006, from NIST. Section 2.4.3, Supporting Forensics in the Information System Life Cycle, notes that many incidents can be handled more efficiently and effectively if forensic considerations have been incorporated into the information system life cycle. Its examples include enabling auditing, forwarding audit records to secure centralized log servers and keeping configuration baselines. Written for conventional IT systems, it bears on choosing, before deployment, SI systems that support the investigations this Task identifies.

#### Implementation 8.1.1: Evaluate SI Applications {#implementation-8.1.1:-evaluate-si-applications}

Finding forensic gaps before an incident, rather than during the investigation that follows one, gives the organization time to close them or plan how to compensate. Evaluate AI applications to identify the extent of root cause analysis required to satisfy risk management and regulatory requirements. This evaluation should explicitly screen for process paths where deterministic forensic reconstruction is a safety or operational requirement. For each application, the evaluation can record the facts that decide whether reconstruction is possible: whether the SI system is run locally or hosted by a provider, whether its version can be held fixed, whether it gives the same output for the same input, and what it can log. Where a model was obtained outside procurement, for example downloaded directly, the facts may depend on what the organization itself recorded about it (see [Task 3.7](#task-3.7:-govern-and-mitigate-risks-from-unauthorized,-transient,-and-“shadow-si”-systems) and [Task 7.1](#task-7.1:-maintain-an-internal-registry-of-si-deployments)). Where a proposed AI system cannot satisfy these specific analytical demands, organizations should either substitute systems inherently capable of true root cause analysis, demonstrably close the gap via validated compensating controls, or implement deterministic boundaries so that execution hands over to manual or legacy systems capable of the required analysis, where such systems are available and maintained (see [Task 11.2: Define Manual and Alternative Operating Procedures for Long-Term Mission Continuity](#task-11.2:-define-manual-and-alternative-operating-procedures-for-long-term-mission-continuity)).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Where a proposed SI system cannot meet the reconstruction demands, is it substituted, are compensating controls validated, or does execution hand over to manual or legacy systems?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Release 5.2.0, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final), from NIST. Control enhancement SI-2(7), Root Cause Analysis, added in Release 5.2.0, calls for root cause analysis of issues and failures, and its discussion has organizations choose the analysis method according to incident severity. That is the proportionality this Implementation applies when deciding the extent of root cause analysis each AI application must support. The control does not itself require deterministic reconstruction; whether an AI system can support that is the further question this Implementation screens for.

#### Implementation 8.1.2: Identify SI Systems that May Not Satisfy Root Cause Analysis Requirements {#implementation-8.1.2:-identify-si-systems-that-may-not-satisfy-root-cause-analysis-requirements}

Where an SI system’s behavior cannot be replayed after the event, other evidence and controls planned in advance can help compensate. Identify specific AI system classes that carry inherent forensic gaps that cannot be fully closed by techniques like runtime telemetry. These include large language model components with non-deterministic sampling, agentic systems with ephemeral context, and remote-hosted inference services without preserved telemetry. Retrieval-augmented systems whose document store changes between an incident and its investigation, and systems whose memory or learned parameters change during operation, carry similar gaps unless that state is preserved. Disabling sampling in large language model components does not by itself make them replayable. Batching, parallel floating-point arithmetic and changes to software libraries or hardware can also change their outputs, so whether replay is possible is better tested by re-running recorded inputs on the production configuration than taken from a provider’s description. In addition, some architectures and systems rely on inherent operational randomness that may not be able to be meaningfully replayed. These gaps concern reproducing the model’s output. The record of what action was requested, and whether and on what basis it was permitted, can still be complete and deterministic where it is generated by the enforcement or validation layer ([Implementation 10.1.2: Runtime Telemetry and Artifact Tracking](#implementation-10.1.2:-runtime-telemetry-and-artifact-tracking)).

Post-hoc explainability tools such as those based on SHAP and LIME should not be treated as forensic proof of how or why an incident occurred. Such techniques estimate, after the fact, which inputs most influenced an output, for example by querying the system with perturbed inputs or by computing feature attributions. The result is one hypothesis for what drove the output, not a record of the actual inputs, system state or sequence of events in an incident. Where such systems are identified, technical managers should cross-reference with [Task 8.2: Identify Additional Controls that May Be Required in Scenarios Where Deterministic Root Cause Analysis Is Not Possible](#task-8.2:-identify-additional-controls-that-may-be-required-in-scenarios-where-deterministic-root-cause-analysis-is-not-possible) to implement appropriate safety margins or alternative validation frameworks. What can serve as forensic evidence is a record made at the time of the output, such as the inference receipts and decision-level telemetry in [Implementation 10.1.2: Runtime Telemetry and Artifact Tracking](#implementation-10.1.2:-runtime-telemetry-and-artifact-tracking), the execution traces of symbolic, hybrid and self-interpretable components in [Implementation 4.6.3: Display Execution Traces from Symbolic, Hybrid, and Self-Interpretable Components](#implementation-4.6.3:-display-execution-traces-from-symbolic,-hybrid,-and-self-interpretable-components), and the provenance metadata in [Implementation 12.1.2: Provenance and Traceability](#implementation-12.1.2:-provenance-and-traceability). Explanations that an SI system produces about its own output, including the reasoning text that some language models generate before answering, should likewise not be treated as forensic proof. Such text may not reflect the computation that produced the output ([Task 4.6: Ensure that Confidence and Rationale Shown to Personnel Reflect How the SI System Reached Its Output](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output)).

**References:**

* **Commentary** [Utilities must ask AI vendors these questions to meet critical infrastructure protection standards](https://www.utilitydive.com/news/why-post-hoc-ai-auditing-is-already-obsolete-for-nerc-cip/812008/), by E. Swidey, founder of Thirty Seven Inc., a company offering AI decision-making frameworks, 2026, from Utility Dive, a trade publication covering the electric utility sector. Argues that vendor explainability features typically generate post-hoc rationalizations rather than real-time audit trails, that auditors who catch backdated access logs will apply the same skepticism to reconstructed AI explanations, and that by the time of an audit the model that made a determination may have been retrained. Asks for a contemporaneous record of each determination’s inputs, decision logic and output, tamper-proof logging, and challenge by a separate system before a determination is final. Written about NERC CIP-015-1 monitoring tools; the argument parallels this Implementation wherever forensic reconstruction is a regulatory obligation.  
* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by CISA. Section 4.1 asks that logging be configured so AI decisions can be tracked for compliance and forensic analysis, and notes that explainability tools are designed to help developers understand a model and that it is an open question whether they would be adequate for OT environments.  
* **Guidance** [NIST IR 8312, Four Principles of Explainable Artificial Intelligence](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.IR.8312), September 2021, from NIST. Section 6.2.1 describes LIME, which builds a local interpretable model by querying points near a decision, and SHAP, which assigns per-feature importance using Shapley values. Section 2.3 distinguishes explanation accuracy from decision accuracy. Together they support treating these outputs as explanations of a model’s behavior near an input, not as evidence of how a specific incident occurred.  
* **Research** [A Systematic Review of Industrial IoT Anomaly Detection and the Forensic Interpretability Gap](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics15112240), by M. A. Ben Haha, A. Bohli, N. Haddour and R. Bouallegue, Electronics 15(11), 2240, May 2026, from MDPI. Reviews 48 studies from 2021 to 2025 across wastewater, manufacturing and energy settings and distinguishes post-hoc feature attribution, which explains why the model produced an anomaly score, from forensic diagnosis, which links the anomaly to a physical root cause. Notes that attribution methods such as SHAP and LIME cannot confirm whether a flagged sensor is the cause or a symptom of a failure elsewhere, and that most of the literature it reviewed offers only the former.  
* **Research** [Fooling LIME and SHAP: Adversarial Attacks on Post hoc Explanation Methods](https://doi.org/10.1145/3375627.3375830), by D. Slack, S. Hilgard, E. Jia, S. Singh and H. Lakkaraju, Proceedings of the 2020 AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES ’20). Shows that post-hoc explanation techniques that rely on input perturbations are not reliable: a classifier can be wrapped so that it behaves as before on real inputs but detects the out-of-distribution perturbations these techniques generate and answers them differently, producing an explanation of the wrapper’s choosing. Supports this Implementation’s point that such explanations are not forensic proof, and that they can be manipulated.

#### Implementation 8.1.3: Update Existing Incident Response Policies and Playbooks {#implementation-8.1.3:-update-existing-incident-response-policies-and-playbooks}

Include documenting the state of AI systems at the time of the incident, such as information from [Task 7.1: Maintain an Internal Registry of SI Deployments](#task-7.1:-maintain-an-internal-registry-of-si-deployments). Playbooks should also cover the failure states that an SI system introduces, including how to bypass or replace it. Bypassing or replacing the SI system is available only where the organization has prepared the alternative in advance (see [Task 11.2: Define Manual and Alternative Operating Procedures for Long-Term Mission Continuity](#task-11.2:-define-manual-and-alternative-operating-procedures-for-long-term-mission-continuity)). It brings its own considerations, such as reduced capacity or the loss of a protective function the SI system was performing. Where a containment step would reset an agent’s memory, purge conversation history or revert a model version, the playbook can call for state such as copies of the model weights or version, prompts and retrieval store state to be preserved first, so that containment does not remove what reconstruction needs. Keeping such copies carries storage and handling overhead, and for a hosted system it may need the provider’s cooperation, which can be agreed in advance (see [Task 8.5: Pre-Arrange Specialized Resources for Investigating and Recovering from SI Incidents](#task-8.5:-pre-arrange-specialized-resources-for-investigating-and-recovering-from-si-incidents)). Deciding in advance which SI system state to preserve, and under what conditions, can help responders act quickly when containment is urgent. The playbook should name who preserves the SI system’s state, such as the point of contact for the SI system under [Implementation 8.3.1: Identify Internal Incident Management Points of Contact](#implementation-8.3.1:-identify-internal-incident-management-points-of-contact), or its provider for a purchased-as-a-service system.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Who preserves SI system state, and which state is preserved before containment, under what conditions?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Cybersecurity Incident & Vulnerability Response Playbooks: Operational Procedures for Planning and Conducting Cybersecurity Incident and Vulnerability Response Activities in FCEB Information Systems](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/publications/Federal_Government_Cybersecurity_Incident_and_Vulnerability_Response_Playbooks_508C.pdf), November 2021, from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). In the Incident Response Playbook, the containment considerations include any impact on the collection, preservation, securing and documentation of evidence. The checklist in Appendix B asks responders to weigh the requirement to preserve evidence when choosing a containment strategy, and to make system backups to preserve evidence. Written for federal civilian agencies and cyber incidents, it is a model for the playbook steps that this Implementation extends to SI system state.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-86, Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-86), August 2006, from NIST. Section 5.2.1, Collecting Volatile OS Data, notes that powering off a system, or even disconnecting it from a network, can remove the chance to collect volatile data, and that the criteria for deciding whether to preserve it should ideally be documented in advance. Written about operating system memory, it bears on SI system state, such as agent memory or conversation context, that is held only in a running system.  
* **Guidance** [AI Incident Response Framework, Workstream 2: Preparing Defenders for a Changing Cybersecurity Landscape](https://www.coalitionforsecureai.org/defending-ai-systems-a-new-framework-for-incident-response-in-the-age-of-intelligent-technology/), version 1.0, 27 October 2025, from the Coalition for Secure AI, an OASIS Open Project. Section 3.3.3 lists containment steps for each architecture, such as resetting memory and purging conversation history, and under Evidence Preservation asks for forensic copies before containment, including vector database state and model weights. Section 3.3.3.1 adds that system and user prompts, parameters and raw outputs need to be retrievable by the investigator. These are the SI system state that this Implementation adds to incident playbooks.  
* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by CISA. Section 4.2, Embed Safety and Failsafe Mechanisms, asks that the new failure states an SI system introduces, including how to bypass or replace it, be incorporated into existing functional safety and incident response processes, which is the playbook update this Implementation describes.

#### Implementation 8.1.4: Conduct Incident Reconstruction Drills {#implementation-8.1.4:-conduct-incident-reconstruction-drills}

Such drills should be conducted within digital twins or high fidelity simulators to help ensure that the resulting root cause analysis process and outputs are both accurate and accurately understood by responding personnel. A simulator that omits behavior that responders will meet in real operations can leave gaps in their preparation. Regular drills also detect shifts in the capabilities of underlying systems to enable root cause analysis, particularly where AI functionality is provided by external parties. Where feasible, include those external parties in the drills. Where they cannot take part, a member of the exercise staff can play their role. This is particularly important in applications where such analysis is required in real-time to inform ongoing, time-sensitive incident response activities. Record the findings of each drill in an after action report, and use its recommendations to update the reconstruction procedures and the playbooks in [Implementation 8.1.3: Update Existing Incident Response Policies and Playbooks](#implementation-8.1.3:-update-existing-incident-response-policies-and-playbooks). Drills can work from the records that production systems actually retain, testing whether responders can identify the SI system version in use, reproduce or account for its output, and place it in the timeline alongside historian, alarm and other operational records.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which external parties take part in reconstruction drills, and who plays the role of those that cannot?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-84, Guide to Test, Training, and Exercise Programs for IT Plans and Capabilities](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-84), September 2006, from NIST. Section 2 describes functional exercises, in which personnel validate their operational readiness in a simulated operational environment. Section 5.4 has exercise staff play the roles of internal and external entities that are not participating, and Section 5.5 documents findings and recommendations for enhancing the exercised plan in an after action report. Written for IT plans in general, it gives a structure for the drills this Implementation describes.  
* **Guidance** [Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Real-Time System Operations](https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/our-work/white-papers/whitepaper-ai-and-ml-in-real-time-system-operations.pdf), White Paper Revision 1, November 2024, from the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC). In Chapter 3, Training with High-Fidelity Simulations calls simulators the most effective way to build the skills and mental models for working with SI systems, and warns that a simulator that leaves out behavior operators will meet, such as under- or over-frequency relay action, could introduce gaps in training. Written about operator training, it applies equally to the simulators in which reconstruction drills run.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-61r3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-61r3), April 2025, from NIST. Subcategory ID.IM-02 identifies improvements from security tests and exercises, including those done in coordination with suppliers and relevant third parties, and notes that exercises prepare involved third parties, such as critical service providers and product suppliers, for future incident response. That bears on drills where SI functionality is provided by external parties.

#### Implementation 8.1.5: Multi-Agent Cascade Reconstruction Capabilities {#implementation-8.1.5:-multi-agent-cascade-reconstruction-capabilities}

Records that follow each message and handoff from one agent to the next help investigators trace an error that passed between agents at machine speed. For deployments involving multiple cooperating or nested AI agents, establish logging and telemetry requirements that explicitly span agent boundaries. Where feasible, carry a shared trace identifier through each inter-agent message, tool call and handoff, and synchronize agent clocks with the time source used for operational records, so that events can be joined and ordered across agents after the fact. Where agents share a memory store, record what each agent read from it and when. Where cooperating agents are operated by different organizations, for example a supplier and an operator, agree in advance what each will log, how long the records will be kept and how they will be shared after an incident. Telemetry should capture inter-agent communications, dynamic delegation chains, and context window handoffs. Where an agent produces a confidence or uncertainty estimate, record it at each handoff with the output passed on, since confidence that is acceptable for each agent can be unacceptable once outputs are chained. This tracking is necessary to trace how errors propagate through an ecosystem, helping ensure forensic investigators can accurately distinguish an originating system anomaly from downstream algorithmic amplification. Where feasible, record for each claim an agent passes on whether the agent produced it or received it and, if received, from which agent or source, so that an error inherited from upstream can be distinguished from one that originated at that agent.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Where cooperating agents are operated by different organizations, what does each log, for how long, and how are the records shared after an incident?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/), Version 2026, December 2025, from the Agentic Security Initiative of the OWASP Gen AI Security Project, a volunteer community project of the Open Worldwide Application Security Project. ASI08, Cascading Failures, describes how a single fault propagates across agents, and its mitigation on logging and non-repudiation asks that inter-agent messages, policy decisions and execution outcomes be recorded in tamper-evident, time-stamped logs, with lineage metadata for every propagated action to support forensic traceability. ASI06, Memory and Context Poisoning, covers corruption of the stored and retrieved context that agents pass on.  
* **Guidance** [MITRE ATLAS](https://atlas.mitre.org/), from MITRE, a United States not-for-profit corporation that operates federally funded research and development centers. A matrix of tactics and techniques observed in attacks on SI-enabled systems, organized by the stage of an attack, which helps model how an exploit at one agent can lead to further steps against adjacent systems.  
* **Guidance** [AI Incident Response Framework, Workstream 2: Preparing Defenders for a Changing Cybersecurity Landscape](https://www.coalitionforsecureai.org/defending-ai-systems-a-new-framework-for-incident-response-in-the-age-of-intelligent-technology/), version 1.0, 27 October 2025, from the Coalition for Secure AI, an OASIS Open Project. Section 3.2, Monitoring and Telemetry, lists agentic workflow execution, including tool calls and retries, among AI telemetry types. Among the attributes it recommends are trace\_id and session\_id, which correlate activity across distributed systems for forensic investigation when an incident spans multiple services, and confidence\_score. These are concrete fields for the cross-agent telemetry and the per-handoff confidence this Implementation asks for.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Appendix F.7.17, the OT discussion of SC-45, System Time Synchronization, notes that time synchronization can make root cause analysis more efficient by aligning audit logs from different systems. For enhancement SC-45(1), it suggests an authoritative time source where data is correlated across organizational boundaries, with mechanisms such as GPS or IEEE 1588\. Written for OT devices, it bears on ordering events across agents and against operational records.

#### Implementation 8.1.6: Incident Triage Across the Dual Attack/Risk Surface {#implementation-8.1.6:-incident-triage-across-the-dual-attack/risk-surface}

Explicit triage pathways help incident response teams avoid treating an attack as drift, or drift as an attack. Incorporate explicit triage pathways in incident playbooks to systematically isolate whether an AI anomaly originated on the Attack Surface (e.g., unauthorized access, API key abuse, or malicious prompt injection) or within the non-adversarial part of the Risk Surface (e.g., sensor schema variance, distribution drift, or multi-agent cascade failure). This helps ensure forensic resources are directed toward the true root cause rather than misclassifying systemic algorithmic errors as external cyber intrusions, or vice versa. Before attributing a reported defect to the SI system, triage should also consider whether it arose upstream or downstream of it, for example in source data, ingestion, transformation or mapping, configuration or business rules, post-processing, or human interpretation of the output. Drift can also come from the supply chain, such as an unannounced update to a hosted model or a change in a data feed, and not only from changes in the inputs. Where the origin is unclear, triage can bring together cybersecurity, operations or safety, and the owners of the SI system, keeping both lines of inquiry open until the evidence rules one out.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which functions are brought together for triage when the origin of an anomaly is unclear?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v2r1, Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v2r1), December 2021, from NIST. Section C.2 notes that an advanced persistent threat can take advantage of, or make its behavior appear to result from, other forms of adversity, including human error, structural failure or natural disaster. That is the case in which an intrusion is read as a non-adversarial failure, one of the two misclassifications this Implementation’s triage is meant to catch.

### Task 8.2: Identify Additional Controls that May Be Required in Scenarios Where Deterministic Root Cause Analysis Is Not Possible {#task-8.2:-identify-additional-controls-that-may-be-required-in-scenarios-where-deterministic-root-cause-analysis-is-not-possible}

Planning in advance for SI systems whose failures cannot be traced to a cause helps the organization make informed, defensible decisions about deploying and re-commissioning them. Establish formal risk-based protocols and alternative verification standards for scenarios where a precise root-cause identification is not possible, for example because the SI system is non-deterministic or opaque. Where regulation requires forensic root cause analysis, that requirement governs. Where the need rests on a safety obligation the organization has identified, whether to deploy such a system, and on what compensating controls, is for the organization to decide, within any regulatory or contractual obligations. Substituting a system that supports root cause analysis keeps the investigative path open but may give up capability; compensating controls keep the capability but need to be shown to close the gap. Record the decision and its basis. Some applications and situations may allow a root cause requirement to be relaxed; [Implementation 8.2.1: Identify Applications and Situations for Which Root Cause Analysis Requirements May Be Relaxed](#implementation-8.2.1:-identify-applications-and-situations-for-which-root-cause-analysis-requirements-may-be-relaxed) covers identifying them, and the organization defines and documents a margin when it does so. Compensating controls that depend as little as practical on the SI system, such as the independent guardrails in [Task 3.2: Implement Independent Guardrails for SI Outputs](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs) or a deterministic check of its output of the kind described in [Task 2.2: Establish Requirements for Redundancy in SI-Driven Functions](#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions), can be relied on whether or not the SI system’s failure can be traced. Where the SI system’s failure cannot be traced to a cause, an investigation can still establish why these surrounding controls did or did not contain it. Where an incident involving such a system leaves its cause unknown, re-commissioning may need to rest on re-validation of its behavior, such as the shadow-mode comparison in [Implementation 11.4.2: Implement “Shadow Mode” Validation and Independent Safety Protection Checks for SI Re-Commissioning](#implementation-11.4.2:-implement-“shadow-mode”-validation-and-independent-safety-protection-checks-for-si-re-commissioning), with operation on a fallback in the meantime, where the organization has prepared one (see [Task 11.2: Define Manual and Alternative Operating Procedures for Long-Term Mission Continuity](#task-11.2:-define-manual-and-alternative-operating-procedures-for-long-term-mission-continuity)). Operating on a fallback brings its own considerations, such as reduced capacity and manual skills that may have faded (see [Task 3.6: Mitigate Automation Complacency and Skills Degradation](#task-3.6:-mitigate-automation-complacency-and-skills-degradation)).

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Safe:** Contributes a basis for deciding whether and how to deploy systems whose failures cannot be traced to a cause. Where regulation requires root cause analysis, that requirement governs. Otherwise, the organization records whether compensating controls close the gap, and sets margins beyond which control passes to manual oversight or to a fallback whose own failures can be traced and that shares as few of the SI system’s sources of error as practical, with those it does share identified, such as a verified-safe legacy system ([Implementation 8.2.2: Identify Opaque Systems and Appropriate Safety Margins](#implementation-8.2.2:-identify-opaque-systems-and-appropriate-safety-margins)). This Task does not cover enforcing those margins at runtime, which [Task 3.2: Implement Independent Guardrails for SI Outputs](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs) covers.
