* **Accountable:** Contributes a documented, defensible basis for each decision to deploy or re-commission such a system, including the margin the organization defines and documents when it relaxes a root cause requirement ([Implementation 8.2.1: Identify Applications and Situations for Which Root Cause Analysis Requirements May Be Relaxed](#implementation-8.2.1:-identify-applications-and-situations-for-which-root-cause-analysis-requirements-may-be-relaxed)). This Task does not name who takes that decision, which [Implementation 3.9.1: Establish Accountable Ownership](#implementation-3.9.1:-establish-accountable-ownership) covers.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Secure:** The safety margins set under [Implementation 8.2.2: Identify Opaque Systems and Appropriate Safety Margins](#implementation-8.2.2:-identify-opaque-systems-and-appropriate-safety-margins), and the list of systems they apply to, show how far an SI system can be pushed before control passes to a fallback. An attacker could use them to keep a manipulated system just inside its margins, so that the hand-off never triggers. Protecting them is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Safe versus any characteristic the SI system was deployed to improve, including Safe itself:** Where the SI system seldom approaches its safety margins, wide margins cost little. Where it operates near them, frequent hand-off to deterministic, legacy or manual operation gives up much of the benefit for which the SI system was deployed, which may include safety, and adds to operator workload. Options include setting margins relative to a verified-safe legacy system, where one exists, as in [Implementation 8.2.1: Identify Applications and Situations for Which Root Cause Analysis Requirements May Be Relaxed](#implementation-8.2.1:-identify-applications-and-situations-for-which-root-cause-analysis-requirements-may-be-relaxed), so that each hand-off returns operation to a known baseline.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MANAGE 1.3** (on responding to high-priority risks): This Task covers response options for the risk that a failure cannot be traced to its cause, from substitution through compensating controls to safety margins with handover; it does not cover identifying which systems carry that risk. For that, see for example [Implementation 8.1.2: Identify SI Systems that May Not Satisfy Root Cause Analysis Requirements](#implementation-8.1.2:-identify-si-systems-that-may-not-satisfy-root-cause-analysis-requirements).  
* **MANAGE 1.1** (on authorizing the system): This Task informs the decision whether to deploy or re-commission an AI system whose failures cannot be traced deterministically; it does not cover the broader determination of whether the system achieves its intended purposes. For that, see for example [Practice 1: Establish Requirements for Success](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Where a safety obligation the organization has identified calls for root cause analysis, is the system deployed with compensating controls or substituted?  
* How wide are the safety margins, given the benefit a hand-off gives up? (see the tension in [Task 8.2: Identify Additional Controls that May Be Required in Scenarios Where Deterministic Root Cause Analysis Is Not Possible](#task-8.2:-identify-additional-controls-that-may-be-required-in-scenarios-where-deterministic-root-cause-analysis-is-not-possible))  
* What does the organization operate on while an SI system whose failure has no known cause is re-validated, and what happens if no fallback is prepared?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Section 2.3.7, Safety Systems, describes the safety instrumented system, designed in accordance with IEC 61511, as often independent of all other control systems so that a failure of the basic process control system will not impair its function. Written for process safety, it is a sector example of a compensating control whose effect does not depend on the system it guards against, here an SI system whose failures cannot be traced to a cause.

#### Implementation 8.2.1: Identify Applications and Situations for Which Root Cause Analysis Requirements May Be Relaxed {#implementation-8.2.1:-identify-applications-and-situations-for-which-root-cause-analysis-requirements-may-be-relaxed}

This Implementation helps the organization decide, and record, when a root cause requirement can be relaxed without losing sight of the risk that relaxing it accepts. It applies where [Task 8.1: Identify Scenarios Requiring Deterministic Root Cause Analysis and Incident Reconstruction](#task-8.1:-identify-scenarios-requiring-deterministic-root-cause-analysis-and-incident-reconstruction) has identified a need for forensic root cause analysis. Many applications, SI or otherwise, carry no such requirement, and nothing here creates one. Whether to relax these requirements, and which other risk management controls are enough to do so, is for the organization to decide, within any regulatory or contractual obligations. Relaxing them can let a useful application proceed, and also accepts that some failures will not be traced to a cause. For example, a load-balancing optimization application might typically require forensic root-cause analysis for all actions. It may be acceptable to revise this so that it does not require forensic root-cause analysis for actions that differ by no more than a margin the organization defines and documents from a verified-safe (but sub-optimal) legacy system. For each relaxation, document why the requirement cannot be met, how those controls reduce risk, and the residual risk that is accepted. Inform those who decide on the use of the SI system of the limitation that the relaxation accepts. Revisit each relaxation when the SI system’s scope, level of autonomy or operating context changes.

For advisory uses, a qualified person can review each output before it is acted on. The reviewer needs the expertise, time and independent information to judge the output rather than simply accept it. This review can catch an unacceptable output. It does not show why the SI system produced that output. If an error gets past the reviewer, its root cause may still not be found. Record the review as one of the controls the relaxation relies on. Also record that some errors may not be traced to a cause, and who has accepted that.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which applications or situations have a relaxed root cause requirement, and which other controls does each rely on?  
* For advisory uses, does the relaxation rely on a person reviewing each output before it is acted on? If so, who accepts that some errors may still not be traced to a cause?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Appendix F.4, Tailoring Considerations, holds that each use of compensating controls should involve a risk-based determination of how much residual risk to accept, and asks organizations to document why the baseline control could not be implemented, how the compensating controls provide equivalent capability, and the risk acceptance for any residual risk. Written for security controls in OT, it gives the record this Implementation asks for when a root cause analysis requirement is relaxed.  
* **Guidance** [SR Letter 11-7 Attachment, Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management](https://www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/srletters/2011/sr1107a1.pdf), April 2011, from the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. Section V, Model Validation, notes that banks may at times have a limited ability to use key validation tools such as back-testing. In those cases it asks for more attention to the model’s limitations when considering whether to use it, with senior management fully informed of those limitations. Written for bank models, it is a sector example of accepting a gap in analysis while keeping decision makers informed.

#### Implementation 8.2.2: Identify Opaque Systems and Appropriate Safety Margins {#implementation-8.2.2:-identify-opaque-systems-and-appropriate-safety-margins}

Where an SI system’s failures cannot be traced afterward, safety margins and a planned hand-off help an organization reduce its exposure to failures it could not investigate. Identify opaque systems and the safety margins within which they will operate to acceptably minimize the likelihood of failures for which root-cause analysis cannot be performed. Such margins can take forms such as operating limits set back from equipment ratings or a lower level of autonomy, and can be checked against the most severe conditions recorded in operation. These margins may be relative to other systems, as per [Implementation 8.2.1: Identify Applications and Situations for Which Root Cause Analysis Requirements May Be Relaxed](#implementation-8.2.1:-identify-applications-and-situations-for-which-root-cause-analysis-requirements-may-be-relaxed). Beyond these safety margins, establish appropriate procedures for hand-off to manual oversight or to a system whose own failures can be traced, such as a verified-safe legacy system. That system should share as few of the SI system’s sources of error as practical, and those it does share, such as common sensors, should be identified. Where control passes to manual oversight, personnel who were not actively involved in the task can take longer to take over after a failure, so the margins and the hand-off procedure can allow for that time. [Task 3.6: Mitigate Automation Complacency and Skills Degradation](#task-3.6:-mitigate-automation-complacency-and-skills-degradation) covers keeping those capabilities exercised.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* What form do the safety margins take, and how much time does the hand-off to manual oversight allow?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by CISA. Section 4.1 asks operators to establish safe operating bounds for OT devices that detect AI drift and model changes affecting safety and performance, and to maintain a known good state or thresholds for safe behavior. Section 4.2 asks for failsafe mechanisms that let an SI system fail gracefully, including how to bypass or replace it. These correspond to the margins and the hand-off this Implementation defines.  
* **Research** [The Out-of-the-Loop Performance Problem and Level of Control in Automation](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1518/001872095779064555), by M. R. Endsley and E. O. Kiris, Human Factors 37(2), pages 381 to 394, 1995, from the journal Human Factors. Describes how operators of automated systems are handicapped in taking over manual operations when automation fails, and reports a study in which lower situation awareness went with slower decisions after an expert system failed. The level of operator control moderated that loss. It bears on the time that a hand-off to manual oversight in this Implementation can need.

### Task 8.3: Designate Roles for SI Incident Governance {#task-8.3:-designate-roles-for-si-incident-governance}

Settling incident roles before an incident, rather than during one, helps an organization act quickly when an SI system is involved. How AI incident roles are organized, whether as a standing cross-functional AI Incident Response Team (AIRT), an extension of an existing incident response team or another arrangement, is for the organization to decide, within any regulatory or contractual obligations. Decisions during an AI incident can turn on legal, technical, risk management and communications considerations, which argues for drawing those perspectives in; a separate team can also run in parallel to existing incident command and add coordination cost. Record the arrangement and how each perspective is represented. This Task helps ensure that the high-level management of an incident is supported by a “digital chain of command” capable of making informed decisions regarding liability, public safety, and mission continuity. Where the organization already uses a standardized incident management structure, such as the Incident Command System within the National Incident Management System, the AIRT can work within it, with expertise in the SI systems involved available to the incident commander, so that the digital chain of command does not run in parallel to it. Its decision rights during response should be defined so that they do not overlap with the incident commander’s.

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Accountable:** Contributes a named point of contact for every AI system that can affect the mission, purchased-as-a-service systems included, who keeps its criticality, impacts, fail-over options and dependencies documented before an incident ([Implementation 8.3.1: Identify Internal Incident Management Points of Contact](#implementation-8.3.1:-identify-internal-incident-management-points-of-contact)), and a standing cross-functional team able to decide on liability, public safety and continuity. This Task does not cover establishing ownership of the capability’s governance decisions outside an incident, which [Implementation 3.9.1: Establish Accountable Ownership](#implementation-3.9.1:-establish-accountable-ownership) covers.  
* **Resilient:** Contributes leadership of recovery: evidence-based prioritization to restore the most mission-critical functions first, and oversight of recovery and re-commissioning ([Implementation 8.3.2: Form an SI Incident Governance Team](#implementation-8.3.2:-form-an-si-incident-governance-team)). This Task does not cover setting the restoration priorities or the re-validation tests, which [Task 11.1](#task-11.1:-identify-and-prioritize-si-dependent-essential-functions) and [Task 11.4](#task-11.4:-establish-system-integrity-re-validation-and-re-commissioning-protocols) set out.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Secure:** The documentation that each point of contact keeps under [Implementation 8.3.1: Identify Internal Incident Management Points of Contact](#implementation-8.3.1:-identify-internal-incident-management-points-of-contact), covering mission-criticality, impacts, fail-over options, and dependencies, maps which SI systems matter most and what the organization falls back on. An attacker could use it to choose targets, or to time an attack for when the fallback is also unavailable. Contact lists and decision rights also show whom to impersonate to have an SI system taken offline. Protecting this material is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Resilient versus Accountable:** Where the state of the AI system at the time of the incident is already held independently of it, restoring the most critical functions first costs little evidence. Where restoration means a rollback, restart or model change that overwrites the context, prompts or version in use, or the system is remote-hosted and its state is not the operator’s to keep, restoring first can remove what reconstruction needs. One way to balance this is to make documenting the state of the AI systems at the time of the incident, which [Implementation 8.1.3: Update Existing Incident Response Policies and Playbooks](#implementation-8.1.3:-update-existing-incident-response-policies-and-playbooks) adds to incident playbooks, an early response step; others include relying on records protected under [Task 10.2: Establish Data Integrity and Tamper-Evidence Controls for Telemetry and Logging](#task-10.2:-establish-data-integrity-and-tamper-evidence-controls-for-telemetry-and-logging) so that restoration need not wait.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **GOVERN 2.1** (on establishing roles and responsibilities): This Task covers the incident roles: a point of contact for each AI system and a standing governance team spanning legal, technical, risk and communications; it does not cover roles for AI risk outside an incident. For accountable ownership of the capability, see [Implementation 3.9.1: Establish Accountable Ownership](#implementation-3.9.1:-establish-accountable-ownership).  
* **MANAGE 4.3** (on incident response): This Task covers the people who lead tracking, response and recovery for each AI system, including purchased-as-a-service systems; it does not cover communicating incidents to regulators and the public. For that, see for example [Task 8.4: Define External Reporting and Regulatory Disclosure Protocols Following SI Incidents](#task-8.4:-define-external-reporting-and-regulatory-disclosure-protocols-following-si-incidents).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Are AI incident roles organized as a standing AIRT, an extension of an existing incident response team or another arrangement, and how do they fit any existing incident command structure?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Section 6.4.2, Response Communications, notes that the FEMA National Incident Management System (NIMS) can be used to standardize common terminology and roles for incident response. Its OT-specific guidance assigns roles that could include incident commander and lists a designated incident commander among internal resources. Written for cybersecurity incidents in OT, it bears on placing the AIRT within an existing incident management structure.

#### Implementation 8.3.1: Identify Internal Incident Management Points of Contact {#implementation-8.3.1:-identify-internal-incident-management-points-of-contact}

A named point of contact for each SI system gives incident response teams someone who knows the system’s criticality, dependencies, and fallback options when an incident starts. Identify internal incident management points of contact for every AI system that can affect the organization’s mission, and ensure that they are resourced and well-practiced to foresee, prepare for, and manage incidents relating to their AI system(s). This includes both internally hosted AI systems and purchased-as-a-service systems. For a purchased-as-a-service system, the point of contact should know the division of incident responsibilities agreed with the provider, including information flows and who has authority to act on the organization’s behalf. Before an incident occurs, they maintain documentation of their system’s mission-criticality, organizational impacts, fail-over options, and dependencies. They should also name an alternate who can act when they are unavailable, with contact details kept current in the incident response plan and checked during drills. Who leads prioritization of restoration during an incident, and how restoration is sequenced against preserving what reconstruction needs, is for the organization to decide, within any regulatory or contractual obligations. The point of contact knows the system’s mission-criticality and dependencies best, and is also under the most pressure to restore it quickly (see the tension in [Task 8.3: Designate Roles for SI Incident Governance](#task-8.3:-designate-roles-for-si-incident-governance)). Record who leads and how preservation of SI system state is sequenced with restoration. Where few people are available, for example on a night shift or at a remote site, the point of contact may also have to lead restoration. Where that happens, record it and how the conflict is offset, such as by having a second person confirm that SI system state was preserved before restoration began ([Implementation 3.9.6: Keep a Record of Design Decisions and Accepted Risks](#implementation-3.9.6:-keep-a-record-of-design-decisions-and-accepted-risks)).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Who leads restoration, and how is preservation of SI system state sequenced with it? (see the Resilient versus Accountable tension in [Task 8.3: Designate Roles for SI Incident Governance](#task-8.3:-designate-roles-for-si-incident-governance))  
* Who is the alternate for each point of contact?  
* Where does each point of contact’s time to prepare for and practice incident response come from, alongside their other duties?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-61r3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-61r3), April 2025, from NIST. Section 2.2 notes that asset owners may have valuable insights on response and recovery priorities for their affected assets. Where a provider takes on incident response responsibilities, it asks that these be defined in a contract, with the response team aware of the division, including information flows, coordination and authority to act on behalf of the organization. That bears on the point of contact for a purchased-as-a-service system.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-34r1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-34r1), May 2010, from NIST. Appendix A, Section 2.3 of each sample contingency plan template, asks that at a minimum roles be established for a system owner or business unit point of contact, a recovery coordinator and a technical recovery point of contact. That is a per-system pattern this Implementation extends to SI systems.

#### Implementation 8.3.2: Form an SI Incident Governance Team {#implementation-8.3.2:-form-an-si-incident-governance-team}

A designated team helps an organization make decisions about recovering an SI system and returning it to service deliberately and consistently, including when those decisions must be made without a full explanation of what went wrong. The team oversees the recovery and recommissioning of SI systems following an incident. Who sits on it, such as senior leadership, technical and legal staff with expertise in AI, and operations management, and whether it is a standing body or convened when needed, is for the organization to decide, within any regulatory or contractual obligations. A standing team keeps relationships and knowledge current between incidents, at the cost of members’ time. Drawing in senior leadership gives the team authority over recovery and re-commissioning decisions, and also brings the production pressure to restore service quickly. Record the membership, how the team is convened and the reason for each choice. Where few qualified people are available, for example in a small organization or a field office, the same people may fill several of these seats. Where that happens, record it, and how the team obtains a view independent of the pressure to restore service ([Implementation 3.9.6: Keep a Record of Design Decisions and Accepted Risks](#implementation-3.9.6:-keep-a-record-of-design-decisions-and-accepted-risks)). Agree in advance who is accountable for decisions such as declaring an AI incident, taking an SI system offline and approving external communications, for example in a responsibility matrix.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Who sits on the governance team, and is it a standing body or convened when needed?  
* Who is accountable for declaring an AI incident, taking an SI system offline and approving external communications?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [AI Incident Response Framework, Workstream 2: Preparing Defenders for a Changing Cybersecurity Landscape](https://www.coalitionforsecureai.org/defending-ai-systems-a-new-framework-for-incident-response-in-the-age-of-intelligent-technology/), version 1.0, 27 October 2025, from the Coalition for Secure AI, an OASIS Open Project. Section 1.3.2 asks that AI incident response roles, authorities and decision thresholds be defined during preparation. Section 1.3.3 gives an example responsibility matrix across incident commander, AI/ML engineer, legal and compliance, and communications, for declaring an incident, technical investigation, taking a model offline, external communications and the post-mortem report.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control enhancement IR-4(11), Integrated Incident Response Team, describes a team of experts that assesses, documents and responds to incidents, whose personnel include forensic analysts, systems security and privacy engineers and real-time operations personnel. That is the mix of technical and operations staff this Implementation names.

### Task 8.4: Define External Reporting and Regulatory Disclosure Protocols Following SI Incidents {#task-8.4:-define-external-reporting-and-regulatory-disclosure-protocols-following-si-incidents}

Establish formal procedures and relationships with external organizations for notifying sector-specific regulators and the public following an AI-related anomaly. This Task helps ensure that the organization meets its legal and transparency obligations, helping to maintain community trust and contribute to broader sector-wide knowledge of how SI systems fail, whether through attack or otherwise. Reporting timelines can start before the role of an SI system in an incident is established. The decision to notify should not wait for that role to be proven, and an initial notification can state what is not yet known.

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Transparent:** Contributes notification of AI incidents to sector regulators and the public, with triggers that name AI-driven causes such as model drift or automated decision error so these are reported as completely as a cybersecurity incident ([Implementation 8.4.1: Integrate SI-Specific Triggers into Existing Incident Disclosure and Reporting Protocols](#implementation-8.4.1:-integrate-si-specific-triggers-into-existing-incident-disclosure-and-reporting-protocols)), an automated initial alert where timelines are short, and a detailed impact disclosure after it. This Task does not cover voluntary sharing of failure modes with peer operators, which [Implementation 8.6.4: Share De-Identified Incident Records for Collective Learning](#implementation-8.6.4:-share-de-identified-incident-records-for-collective-learning) covers.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Accurate:** An initial alert automated from triggers is issued before the cause is established, so it may attribute an incident to drift that later proves to be an exploit, or the reverse. [Implementation 8.4.2: Establish Automated Notification and Detailed Impact Disclosure for Sector-Specific Authorities](#implementation-8.4.2:-establish-automated-notification-and-detailed-impact-disclosure-for-sector-specific-authorities) follows it with a detailed impact disclosure prepared by the incident response team, which can correct it once the triage in [Implementation 8.1.6: Incident Triage Across the Dual Attack/Risk Surface](#implementation-8.1.6:-incident-triage-across-the-dual-attack/risk-surface) has run.
* **Secure:** A notification or impact disclosure describes how an SI system failed and which control did not hold. An attacker could use it to repeat the attack here or against peers running the same SI system. What a public disclosure includes, within any legal or regulatory obligation to disclose, can draw on the de-identification considerations in [Implementation 8.6.4: Share De-Identified Incident Records for Collective Learning](#implementation-8.6.4:-share-de-identified-incident-records-for-collective-learning).

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MANAGE 4.3** (on incident response): This Task covers the communication of AI incidents to regulators and the public, with AI-specific triggers, an automated initial alert and a detailed follow-up disclosure; it does not cover the internal processes for responding to and recovering from incidents. For those, see for example [Task 8.1](#task-8.1:-identify-scenarios-requiring-deterministic-root-cause-analysis-and-incident-reconstruction) and [Practice 11](#practice-11:-maintain-si-aware-mission-continuity-and-disaster-recovery-planning).  
* **GOVERN 1.1** (on legal and regulatory): This Task covers AI-specific triggers within the organization’s existing regulatory reporting obligations; it does not cover identifying the legal and regulatory requirements that apply to the AI system more broadly.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Beyond legal and regulatory obligations, whether, when and how is the public notified?  
* When is a notification made, relative to establishing the SI system’s role in the incident?  
* What detail about how the SI system failed is withheld from public disclosure, and on whose judgment?

**References:**

* **Regulation** [Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act](http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), 13 June 2024, from the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union. Article 73(2) has providers of high-risk AI systems report a serious incident once a causal link with the AI system, or the reasonable likelihood of such a link, is established. Article 73(5) allows an initial report that is incomplete, followed by a complete report. It applies only to high-risk AI systems in the EU, and is one model for notifying before an SI system’s role is proven.

#### Implementation 8.4.1: Integrate SI-Specific Triggers into Existing Incident Disclosure and Reporting Protocols {#implementation-8.4.1:-integrate-si-specific-triggers-into-existing-incident-disclosure-and-reporting-protocols}

SI-specific triggers help the organization recognize and report SI-driven events as completely as it would a traditional cybersecurity incident. Add triggers that call out AI-driven causes, such as model drift or automated decision error, to the organization’s existing incident reporting protocols. Scenario B.3 in [Appendix B](#appendix-b:-scenario-to-practice-mapping) describes one such case. Triggers can also include an agent attempting an action outside its authorized scope, even where the attempt was blocked, a guardrail around an SI system failing or being bypassed, and an SI system’s output contributing to a loss of view or control. Personnel should be able to escalate a suspected SI involvement without first confirming it. The decision points and error modes identified in [Implementation 3.1.1: Identify SI System Decision Points and Potential Outcomes of SI System Errors](#implementation-3.1.1:-identify-si-system-decision-points-and-potential-outcomes-of-si-system-errors) are a starting point: for each, identify which of the organization’s existing reporting obligations it could trigger, such as device-malfunction reporting where the SI system is part of a regulated medical device, so that an SI-caused event is recognized as reportable under the obligation that already applies.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which SI-specific triggers are added to the existing reporting protocols?

**References:**

* **Research** [Trends in AI Incidents and Hazards Reported by the Media](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/trends-in-ai-incidents-and-hazards-reported-by-the-media_4f5ff43c-en.html), OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 53, February 2026, from the OECD Directorate for Science, Technology and Innovation, a paper describing preliminary results and research in progress, as published in February 2026\. Box 1.1 defines an AI incident as an event in which the development, use or malfunction of one or more AI systems directly or indirectly leads to listed harms, one of which is disruption of the management and operation of critical infrastructure. Section 1 notes that these definitions were developed alongside the OECD common reporting framework for AI incidents, and they are one vocabulary against which the AI-specific triggers in this Implementation can be written.

#### Implementation 8.4.2: Establish Automated Notification and Detailed Impact Disclosure for Sector-Specific Authorities {#implementation-8.4.2:-establish-automated-notification-and-detailed-impact-disclosure-for-sector-specific-authorities}

Where regulatory timelines require rapid notification, automate the initial alert to relevant sector authorities based on the triggers defined in [Implementation 8.4.1: Integrate SI-Specific Triggers into Existing Incident Disclosure and Reporting Protocols](#implementation-8.4.1:-integrate-si-specific-triggers-into-existing-incident-disclosure-and-reporting-protocols), followed by a more detailed impact disclosure prepared by the incident response team. Where release of the initial alert is automated, define in advance the conditions it covers, and test it. Otherwise, automation can detect a potentially reportable condition, preserve evidence, and assemble and route the initial report, while release to external authorities remains with the role designated under [Task 8.3: Designate Roles for SI Incident Governance](#task-8.3:-designate-roles-for-si-incident-governance). The detailed impact disclosure can include, alongside the content the authority requires, the SI system and version involved, the actions it took or recommended, the physical and service consequences, and, where this is known, whether other operators using the same SI system or vendor may be exposed.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Is release of the initial alert automated, and if so, which conditions does it cover?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control IR-6, Incident Reporting, reports incident information to defined authorities, with the types, content and timeliness of reports reflecting applicable laws and regulations, and enhancement IR-6(1), Automated Reporting, uses automated mechanisms for that reporting, which is the existing form of the automated initial alert to sector authorities this Implementation describes.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-61r3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-61r3), April 2025, from NIST. Subcategory RS.CO-02 asks that law enforcement and regulatory bodies be notified of incidents based on criteria in the incident response plan and management approval, with designated individuals contacting them, and that coordination procedures set what must be reported to whom and when. That bears on keeping release with a designated role where it is not automated.

### Task 8.5: Pre-Arrange Specialized Resources for Investigating and Recovering from SI Incidents {#task-8.5:-pre-arrange-specialized-resources-for-investigating-and-recovering-from-si-incidents}

Identifying specialist help before an incident can shorten investigation and recovery once one occurs. Pre-identify the specialized personnel and budgetary resources needed for complex investigations, such as third-party AI forensic auditors or specialized legal counsel. Whether to go further and pre-arrange that access is for the organization to decide, within any regulatory or contractual obligations: pre-arranged access shortens response when an incident occurs, and costs money whether or not one does. Record the level chosen and the reason for it. The market for third-party AI forensic auditors is currently nascent. Interim approaches include developing internal capability through targeted training, establishing sector-level mutual aid via ISACs and Sector Coordinating Councils, and forming partnerships with academic centers conducting AI safety, reliability, security and forensics research. This Task addresses potential internal skill gaps and helps ensure that the investigation of and recovery from non-deterministic AI failures is adequately funded and supported. In a sector-wide event, such as a flaw in a widely used foundation model, many affected operators may seek the same few specialists at once. Where an SI system is supplied or hosted by a vendor, the access that investigators will need during an incident can be agreed in the procurement terms in advance, such as access to model version histories, inference logs and vendor engineering staff, and whether a third party may examine them. Where a model was obtained outside procurement, for example downloaded directly, no such terms exist. What investigators can learn about its versions then depends on what the organization recorded itself (see [Task 3.7](#task-3.7:-govern-and-mitigate-risks-from-unauthorized,-transient,-and-“shadow-si”-systems) and [Task 7.1](#task-7.1:-maintain-an-internal-registry-of-si-deployments)). [Practice 6: Integrate Visibility of the External Supply Chain of SI into Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management) covers procurement terms more broadly.

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Accountable:** Contributes access, identified and ideally arranged before an incident, to the forensic and legal expertise needed to establish what a non-deterministic AI system did, with interim routes while that market is nascent: internal training, sector mutual aid and academic partnerships. This Task does not cover the records those experts will work from, which [Practice 10: Implement Multi-Tiered SI System Logging and Audit Capabilities](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities) covers.  
* **Resilient:** Contributes priority access to specialized responders through retainer arrangements ([Implementation 8.5.2: Establish Formal Retainer-Style Relationships with Specialized SI Incident Responders and Auditors](#implementation-8.5.2:-establish-formal-retainer-style-relationships-with-specialized-si-incident-responders-and-auditors)), so recovery does not wait on finding help during a live incident. This Task does not cover securing the operational resources that keep the function running in the meantime, which [Task 11.3: Pre-Allocate Operational Resources for Alternative Service Delivery](#task-11.3:-pre-allocate-operational-resources-for-alternative-service-delivery) covers.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Secure:** Bringing in third-party forensic auditors and counsel gives people outside the organization access to logs, prompt history, model details and incident evidence. In the wrong hands, that material shows how the organization’s SI systems work and where they failed. This Task does not address the terms of that access, which are a matter for the retainer agreements ([Implementation 8.5.2: Establish Formal Retainer-Style Relationships with Specialized SI Incident Responders and Auditors](#implementation-8.5.2:-establish-formal-retainer-style-relationships-with-specialized-si-incident-responders-and-auditors)) and the organization’s existing third-party access controls.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **MANAGE 2.1** (on allocating resources): This Task covers the budget and pre-arranged specialist access that investigating and recovering from non-deterministic AI failures need; it does not cover the resources for operating through non-AI alternatives. For that, see for example [Task 11.3: Pre-Allocate Operational Resources for Alternative Service Delivery](#task-11.3:-pre-allocate-operational-resources-for-alternative-service-delivery).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Is access to specialized personnel and budget only pre-identified, or also pre-arranged?  
* Who holds the budget for specialist incident support, and what is the fallback if pre-arranged specialists are unavailable during a sector-wide event?

#### Implementation 8.5.1: Identify Third-Party SI Forensic and Legal Experts for Contingency Access {#implementation-8.5.1:-identify-third-party-si-forensic-and-legal-experts-for-contingency-access}

Identify and pre-qualify external AI forensic specialists and legal counsel experienced in AI-related incidents before one occurs, since this market is still nascent and locating qualified help during an active incident wastes critical response time. Deciding which forensic tasks to keep in house and which to hand to outside specialists can take into account cost, response time, and the sensitivity of the data those specialists would see. Tasks that are needed rarely can be more cost-effective to obtain from an external party. For each identified party, record its capabilities, how to reach it and any relationship with the organization’s SI vendors that could bear on its independence, and confirm periodically that it remains available.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which forensic tasks are kept in house and which are handed to outside specialists?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Section 6.4.3 suggests engaging external organizations to perform forensic analysis where an organization lacks adequate resources or capability to conduct OT forensics, which is the gap this Implementation fills in advance for SI systems.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-86, Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-86), August 2006, from NIST. Section 2.2, Forensic Staffing, notes that many organizations combine their own staff with external parties, using outside parties when specialized assistance is needed and seeking external assistance when expert testimony is needed for legal proceedings. It lists cost, response time and data sensitivity as factors in deciding which parties handle each aspect of forensics, and notes that actions needed rarely might be more cost-effectively performed by an external party.

#### Implementation 8.5.2: Establish Formal Retainer-Style Relationships with Specialized SI Incident Responders and Auditors {#implementation-8.5.2:-establish-formal-retainer-style-relationships-with-specialized-si-incident-responders-and-auditors}

Where budget allows, convert the contacts identified in [Implementation 8.5.1: Identify Third-Party SI Forensic and Legal Experts for Contingency Access](#implementation-8.5.1:-identify-third-party-si-forensic-and-legal-experts-for-contingency-access) into formal retainer agreements, securing priority access to specialized responders rather than competing for their availability during a live incident. The agreement can set out in advance the division of responsibilities, the access the responder will have to logs, prompts and model details, and any restrictions on what the responder may do or share. Where an auditor’s findings will be relied on outside the organization, such as by a regulator, consider how the auditor’s selection, payment and access terms bear on its independence.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Are retainer agreements used, and what responsibilities, access and restrictions do they set?  
* Where an auditor’s findings will be relied on outside the organization, how do its selection, payment and access terms protect its independence?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Section 6.4.2 notes that legal departments can help develop non-disclosure agreements or other contracts for external incident response resources, that developing them before an incident lets response be immediate, and that private companies can be held on retainer for an OT incident.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-61r3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-61r3), April 2025, from NIST. Section 2.2 asks that responsibilities a provider takes on be defined in a contract, including information flows, coordination and authority to act, and restrictions on what the provider can do, such as sharing sanitized incident information with other customers. It also notes that service providers often have privileged access to sensitive data.  
* **Research** [Outsider Oversight: Designing a Third Party Audit Ecosystem for AI Governance](https://doi.org/10.1145/3514094.3534181), by I. D. Raji, P. Xu, C. Honigsberg and D. Ho, Proceedings of the 2022 AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES ’22), from ACM. Section 4.2, Independence, reviews evidence that auditors chosen or paid by the audited party tend to be more lenient, and notes that auditors retained by technology companies are potentially compromised by nondisclosure agreements, financial conflicts and competition for services. Section 4.3 notes that contracted auditors can be given access only on the audited party’s terms. That bears on retainer terms where an auditor’s findings will be relied on outside the organization.

### Task 8.6: Establish Non-Punitive Reporting for SI-Related Near-Misses {#task-8.6:-establish-non-punitive-reporting-for-si-related-near-misses}

Non-punitive reporting helps an organization learn of SI near-misses and gradual degradation, including what its systems do not record, before they become incidents. Establish channels through which personnel can report AI-attributable near-misses, degradation, and anomalous behavior without bearing personal or organizational cost for the disclosure. Where the recipient of a report needs to be independent of the function responsible for the deployment, that channel may sit outside the organization; see [Implementation 8.6.2: Protect Reporter Identity Through an Independent Reporting Route](#implementation-8.6.2:-protect-reporter-identity-through-an-independent-reporting-route). Ensure that those who report through these channels are protected by consistently applied organizational policy, especially where they are not otherwise protected by statute or regulation. Such a policy can state in advance where protection ends, for example by covering honest errors and reports of how an SI system behaved while excluding reckless conduct or willful violation. Where labor representatives exist, the policy can be developed with them. Acknowledging reports, and telling the reporting community what was found and what changed as a result, can help sustain reporting. Where the organization already runs a near-miss or safety reporting program, these channels can extend it to SI rather than replace it.

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Transparent:** Contributes routes by which near-misses, degradation and anomalous behavior that personnel observe become known, including what the system itself did not record, by removing the costs that suppress disclosure: benefit-claiming separated from risk-reporting ([Implementation 8.6.1: Separate Benefit-Claiming from Risk-Reporting](#implementation-8.6.1:-separate-benefit-claiming-from-risk-reporting)), an identity-protecting route that may sit outside the organization ([Implementation 8.6.2: Protect Reporter Identity Through an Independent Reporting Route](#implementation-8.6.2:-protect-reporter-identity-through-an-independent-reporting-route)), and supplier terms that do not penalize vendor disclosure ([Implementation 8.6.3: Ensure Supplier Terms Do Not Penalize Degradation Disclosure](#implementation-8.6.3:-ensure-supplier-terms-do-not-penalize-degradation-disclosure)). This Task does not cover determining what the system records, which [Practice 10: Implement Multi-Tiered SI System Logging and Audit Capabilities](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities) covers.  
* **Reliable:** Contributes a way for gradual degradation to surface, where no single observation seems worth the cost of reporting, and for failure modes shared by peer operators to be ingested back into guardrails and drift thresholds ([Implementation 8.6.4: Share De-Identified Incident Records for Collective Learning](#implementation-8.6.4:-share-de-identified-incident-records-for-collective-learning)). This Task does not cover setting those thresholds, which [Implementation 3.3.2: Establish Maximum Drift Thresholds](#implementation-3.3.2:-establish-maximum-drift-thresholds) covers.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Secure:** Near-miss reports, and the shared records built from them ([Implementation 8.6.4: Share De-Identified Incident Records for Collective Learning](#implementation-8.6.4:-share-de-identified-incident-records-for-collective-learning)), describe weaknesses in SI systems and the controls around them, some not yet fixed. An attacker who obtained them could target those weaknesses before they are addressed. [Implementation 8.6.4: Share De-Identified Incident Records for Collective Learning](#implementation-8.6.4:-share-de-identified-incident-records-for-collective-learning) covers de-identifying shared records and disclosing to the vendor before wider release. Protecting the internal reports is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Accountable versus Transparent:** Where a report concerns how an AI system behaved, protection from personal cost removes the main reason not to make it. Where the same report also discloses the reporter’s own action, such as a check skipped or an override not taken, that protection limits how far individual responsibility can be enforced on what the report reveals. One way to balance this is to state in advance what a report will and will not be used for, which [Implementation 8.6.2: Protect Reporter Identity Through an Independent Reporting Route](#implementation-8.6.2:-protect-reporter-identity-through-an-independent-reporting-route) asks the organization to make clear to potential reporters; others include keeping the report as an information source separate from any inquiry into the same event.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **GOVERN 4.3** (on establishing AI incident response and information-sharing processes): This Task covers incident identification by personnel and sharing with peer operators through de-identified records and a trusted intermediary; it does not cover the AI testing GOVERN 4.3 also names. For that, see for example [Task 1.3: Implement Evaluation and Test Plans, Including TEVV, Across the SI Lifecycle](#task-1.3:-implement-evaluation-and-test-plans,-including-tevv,-across-the-si-lifecycle).  
* **MEASURE 3.3** (on enabling feedback, appeal, and override): This Task supports problem reporting by the personnel who operate and supervise AI systems, protected from the cost of reporting; it does not cover routes for impacted communities outside the organization to report problems, or a process to appeal system outcomes.  
* **MANAGE 3.1** (on monitoring and responding to third-party risks): This Task supports monitoring of third-party AI risk by removing contractual disincentives for vendors to disclose degradation, behavioral change or known limitations; it does not cover applying the controls MANAGE 3.1 calls for. For those, see for example [Practice 6: Integrate Visibility of the External Supply Chain of SI into Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Where does protection for reporters end? (see the Accountable versus Transparent tension in [Task 8.6: Establish Non-Punitive Reporting for SI-Related Near-Misses](#task-8.6:-establish-non-punitive-reporting-for-si-related-near-misses))  
* Where labor representatives exist, is the reporting policy developed with them?  
* Who receives and acts on near-miss reports, and do they have the time, resources, and authority to act on what the reports reveal?

**References:**

* **Working Document** [Shared AI Findings Exchange (SAFE)](https://github.com/OpenSecureAIAlliance/RFCs), a proposed non-regulatory framework at request-for-comments stage as of October 2026, from the SAFE Working Group of the Open Secure AI Alliance. Sets out how AI incidents and near-misses can be shared across organizations, with specific notification timelines, which relates to the de-identified sharing in Implementation 8.6.4.  
* **Research** [Trends in AI Incidents and Hazards Reported by the Media](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/trends-in-ai-incidents-and-hazards-reported-by-the-media_4f5ff43c-en.html), OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 53, February 2026, from the OECD Directorate for Science, Technology and Innovation, a paper describing preliminary results and research in progress, as published in February 2026\. Box 1.1 gives the OECD definitions of an AI incident, an event in which the development, use or malfunction of an AI system leads to harm, and an AI hazard, an event or circumstance that could plausibly lead to one. A near-miss reported under this Task falls within the second, which is broader.  
* **Guidance** [DOE-HDBK-1028-2009, Human Performance Improvement Handbook, Volume 1: Concepts and Principles](https://www.energy.gov/ehss/articles/doe-hdbk-1028-2009), June 2009, from the U.S. Department of Energy. Chapter 4, Culture & Leadership, under Create a Just Culture, balances zero tolerance for reckless conduct against confidence that honest errors will go unpunished. Attachment C, Establishing a Reporting Culture, notes that complete immunity is not feasible because some acts are culpable, and lists feedback to the reporting community as a feature of successful programs. Written for DOE facility operations, it bears on the boundary and feedback this Task adds.

#### Implementation 8.6.1: Separate Benefit-Claiming from Risk-Reporting {#implementation-8.6.1:-separate-benefit-claiming-from-risk-reporting}

Identify, for each AI deployment, which organizational function claims its operational or efficiency benefit, and ensure that function is not the sole route through which risks and degradation associated with that deployment are escalated. A function that benefits from a deployment can be less inclined to question outcomes that favor it. Reports and criticism from people outside that function can supply what it does not raise. This sets a minimum that even a small organization can meet. Where size allows, fuller separation of the people, metrics and channels that claim a deployment’s benefit from those that receive its risk reports contributes stronger assurance.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* How far is the escalation of a deployment’s risks separated from the function that claims its benefit?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [SR Letter 11-7 Attachment, Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management](https://www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/srletters/2011/sr1107a1.pdf), April 2011, from the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. Section IV, under Model Use, notes that challenge from model users may be weak if changes are perceived to have adverse effects on the business line, and that users are less likely to challenge an outcome that results in an advantage for them. It asks banks to solicit criticism from sources independent of the line of business using the model. Written for bank models, it is a sector example of the separation this Implementation asks for.

#### Implementation 8.6.2: Protect Reporter Identity Through an Independent Reporting Route {#implementation-8.6.2:-protect-reporter-identity-through-an-independent-reporting-route}

A route that protects reporter identity helps personnel raise concerns about an SI deployment with less fear for their role or standing. Provide a reporting route that does not require the reporter to disclose their identity to the function responsible for the deployment. Where internal anonymity is impractical, or where the deployment function has influence over the reporter’s role, work or standing, route reporting to an independent recipient outside the organization that can receive it in confidence. The sector-level pooling described in [Task 8.5: Pre-Arrange Specialized Resources for Investigating and Recovering from SI Incidents](#task-8.5:-pre-arrange-specialized-resources-for-investigating-and-recovering-from-si-incidents) may provide such a recipient, but a body that supports investigation is not by that fact an independent or confidential one. Make clear to potential reporters, in advance, how a report will be handled, who will see it, and what it will and will not be used for, so that the route can be used with confidence. In a small workforce, such as a single control room or crew, details in a report such as shift times, unit numbers or wording can identify the reporter. These details can be generalized before a report reaches the deployment function. Where follow-up with the reporter is needed, the recipient can hold the reporter’s identity separately from the report and discard the link once follow-up is complete.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Do reports go to an independent recipient outside the organization, and if so, which one?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [DOE-HDBK-1028-2009, Human Performance Improvement Handbook, Volume 1: Concepts and Principles](https://www.energy.gov/ehss/articles/doe-hdbk-1028-2009), June 2009, from the U.S. Department of Energy. Chapter 4, Culture & Leadership, lists among the attributes of a strong safety culture that a variety of methods are available for personnel to raise safety issues without fear of retribution. It notes that if individuals believe their errors will be punished, information about those errors will likely remain obscure. Written for DOE facility operations, it bears on offering a route besides the deployment function.  
* **Guidance** [Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Real-Time System Operations](https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/our-work/white-papers/whitepaper-ai-and-ml-in-real-time-system-operations.pdf), White Paper Revision 1, November 2024, from the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC). In Chapter 3, under Organizational Level, Vendor Transparency compares disclosure of SI issues to near-miss database systems, which can require well-aligned key performance indicators, anonymity of reporter and vendor, and a third party, such as NASA for the Aviation Safety Reporting System, for the information to keep flowing. That is a precedent for the independent recipient in this Implementation.

#### Implementation 8.6.3: Ensure Supplier Terms Do Not Penalize Degradation Disclosure {#implementation-8.6.3:-ensure-supplier-terms-do-not-penalize-degradation-disclosure}

Because a vendor may learn of problems with its model well before the organization does, supplier terms that encourage disclosure help the organization hear of those problems early. Review procurement terms and service-level agreements, as part of any supplier risk management already in place, to confirm they do not create financial or contractual disincentives for vendors to disclose model degradation, behavioral change, or known limitations. This complements the disclosure requirements in [Implementation 6.1.1: Add SI Disclosure to Existing Procurement Policies](#implementation-6.1.1:-add-si-disclosure-to-existing-procurement-policies) and the hazard reachability attestations in [Implementation 6.1.5: Operational SI Hazard Reachability Disclosures](#implementation-6.1.5:-operational-si-hazard-reachability-disclosures), both of which currently rely on vendor self-report. Terms that ask the vendor to share the results of its ongoing performance monitoring can give such disclosure a routine channel. Terms to check include service credits or penalties triggered by issues that the vendor itself reports, and confidentiality terms that would bar the organization from passing degradation information to a regulator or to a sharing community under [Implementation 8.6.4: Share De-Identified Incident Records for Collective Learning](#implementation-8.6.4:-share-de-identified-incident-records-for-collective-learning).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which procurement and service terms are changed to remove disincentives to vendor disclosure?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by CISA. Section 2.3, Understanding the Role of OT Vendors in AI Integration, advises negotiating contractual agreements under which OT vendors give explicit details on SI features. It asks that, beyond typical vulnerability disclosure, the SI vendor disclose any indication it has found that the SI system can provide improper advice or take inappropriate action. That is the disclosure that supplier terms should not penalize.  
* **Guidance** [Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Real-Time System Operations](https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/our-work/white-papers/whitepaper-ai-and-ml-in-real-time-system-operations.pdf), White Paper Revision 1, November 2024, from the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC). In Chapter 3, under Organizational Level, Vendor Transparency asks SI vendors to share bugs, challenges and biases with their customers, ideally in forums shared across customers or industries. It asks them to align their incentives internally, in how they reward identifying and reporting issues, and externally, in how they respond when that information spreads. Written to vendors, it is the supplier side of the terms this Implementation reviews.  
* **Guidance** [SR Letter 11-7 Attachment, Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management](https://www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/srletters/2011/sr1107a1.pdf), April 2011, from the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. Section V, under Validation of Vendor and Other Third-Party Products, expects vendors to indicate a model’s limitations and where its use may be problematic, and to conduct ongoing performance monitoring and outcomes analysis with disclosure to their clients. Written by bank supervisors for banks, it is a sector example of the routine vendor disclosure these terms can support.

#### Implementation 8.6.4: Share De-Identified Incident Records for Collective Learning {#implementation-8.6.4:-share-de-identified-incident-records-for-collective-learning}

Where reports captured under [Implementation 8.6.2: Protect Reporter Identity Through an Independent Reporting Route](#implementation-8.6.2:-protect-reporter-identity-through-an-independent-reporting-route) reveal failure modes with cross-organizational relevance, contribute a de-identified version to a trusted sharing community. Sharing de-identified records helps peer operators learn from a failure mode before it recurs elsewhere. This differs in purpose from the mandatory regulatory disclosure in [Task 8.4](#task-8.4:-define-external-reporting-and-regulatory-disclosure-protocols-following-si-incidents): sharing here is voluntary, structural knowledge transfer intended to raise collective resilience, and it draws on the reporting channel established in [Implementation 8.6.2: Protect Reporter Identity Through an Independent Reporting Route](#implementation-8.6.2:-protect-reporter-identity-through-an-independent-reporting-route) without replacing it. Specify a minimum useful shared record (the AI system’s role and consequence class, the failure mode, contributing factors, how it was detected, and which control did or did not hold) and a de-identification standard that strips the reporting organization’s identity, proprietary model internals, and customer or safety-sensitive data while preserving the pattern that makes the report useful to peers. Model product and version are not model internals. Retaining them makes the record far more useful to peers running the same model, but they can also help identify the reporting organization or expose a weakness the vendor has not yet addressed. Contracts with the vendor, such as nondisclosure or license terms, may restrict whether model product and version can be shared at all. Where contracts allow it, whether to retain them is the organization’s decision. Disclosing to the vendor first can address the concern about exposing an unaddressed weakness. Because this record derives from information captured under [Implementation 8.6.2: Protect Reporter Identity Through an Independent Reporting Route](#implementation-8.6.2:-protect-reporter-identity-through-an-independent-reporting-route), its de-identification standard should be at least as protective of the original reporter as the originating channel that produced it. Removing the reporting organization’s name may not be enough to de-identify a record. An unusual configuration, a precise time or the size of the operation can identify the organization, particularly in combination with other details. A sharing designation scheme, such as the Traffic Light Protocol, can state how far each record may be passed on. Where a record describes a weakness that could be exploited, consider disclosing it to the affected vendor before wider release. Confirm with counsel which legal protections, if any, apply to shared records. Protections written for sharing cyber threat information may not extend to an SI failure that involves no adversary. Whether to share through a trusted intermediary, such as a sector ISAC or Sector Coordinating Council where one exists or a cross-sector AI incident clearinghouse where none exists, or through bilateral arrangements, is for the organization to decide, within any regulatory or contractual obligations. An intermediary adds distance between the record and its source and reaches more peers; bilateral arrangements give more control over who receives a record. Record the route chosen and why. Define how the organization reciprocally ingests peer reports back into its own MAP and MEASURE activity, for example, updating guardrails or drift thresholds in response to a failure mode others have shared (see, for example, [Task 3.2](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs) and [Implementation 3.3.2](#implementation-3.3.2:-establish-maximum-drift-thresholds)).

Note: [Practice 10: Implement Multi-Tiered SI System Logging and Audit Capabilities](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities) governs what the system records. Whether a person who observes something the system did not record has a viable route to say so is governed by [Task 8.6: Establish Non-Punitive Reporting for SI-Related Near-Misses](#task-8.6:-establish-non-punitive-reporting-for-si-related-near-misses), and the reports captured under [Implementation 8.6.2: Protect Reporter Identity Through an Independent Reporting Route](#implementation-8.6.2:-protect-reporter-identity-through-an-independent-reporting-route) are the input stage for this Implementation. Cross-organizational sharing depends on incidents having been reported within organizations first.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Are de-identified records shared through a trusted intermediary or through bilateral arrangements?  
* Are model product and version retained in shared records, where vendor contracts allow it?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 600-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1), July 2024, from NIST. Suggested action GV-4.3-002, under GOVERN 4.3, asks organizations to identify the minimum set of criteria necessary for generative AI incident reporting and gives a field list: system ID, title, reporter, system or source, data reported, date, description, impacts and stakeholders impacted. It is a starting point for the minimum useful shared record this Implementation asks for, to which the de-identification standard is then applied.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-150, Guide to Cyber Threat Information Sharing](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-150), October 2016, from NIST. Section 3.4.1 asks that the legal team and privacy officers be consulted when developing procedures for protecting sensitive information, and Section 3.4.2 presents the Traffic Light Protocol for expressing sharing designations. Section 4.5.1 warns that aggregation, association or enrichment may enable re-identification. Written for cyber threat information, it bears on the de-identification and handling of the shared record in this Implementation.

## Practice 9: Provide Role-Based SI Risk Training that Builds Well-Founded Trust {#practice-9:-provide-role-based-si-risk-training-that-builds-well-founded-trust}

*Establish a systematic program for SI risk management training tailored to specific operational roles, accountability requirements, and decision-making responsibilities.*

This Practice helps ensure that stakeholders across the organization possess the knowledge, matched to their role, necessary to identify SI risks and to trust SI systems neither more nor less than they warrant. The people who supervise SI systems are also the safety net when those systems fail. Over-trust leads personnel to accept outputs they should have checked. Under-trust leads them to ignore or work around systems that are performing well. Both forms of miscalibrated trust grow from inaccurate mental models of how a particular SI system behaves and fails, and both increase risk for the organization. For example, over-trust can lead personnel to act on improperly vetted and potentially incorrect SI system outputs, and impairs oversight. Similarly, under-trust can lead personnel to override correct SI actions with incorrect manual ones, and can reduce capability, particularly where the SI system was intended to contribute to overall risk management, such as anomaly and intrusion detection. 

What each role needs differs: an operator who may have to take over needs practice in recognizing failure and in manual control, while leadership needs enough understanding to judge what assurances are worth and the trade-offs involved ([Task 9.1: Perform Role-Based SI Risk Competency Mapping](#task-9.1:-perform-role-based-si-risk-competency-mapping)). Training covers automation bias and the other human factors of working with SI systems ([Task 9.2: Deliver Specialized Training on Human-SI Interaction and Automation Bias](#task-9.2:-deliver-specialized-training-on-human-si-interaction-and-automation-bias)), and its effectiveness is checked through assessments, simulations and drills rather than assumed from attendance ([Task 9.3: Establish Audit-Ready Systems for Verifying Workforce Readiness](#task-9.3:-establish-audit-ready-systems-for-verifying-workforce-readiness)). It complements [Task 3.6: Mitigate Automation Complacency and Skills Degradation](#task-3.6:-mitigate-automation-complacency-and-skills-degradation), which addresses the erosion of crucial skills and attention when automated tasks that were previously performed manually still require human oversight and fallback. Organizations with established training, qualification, and exercise programs, such as for operational technology or cybersecurity, can build on them rather than start a separate program.

**Search Keywords:** automation bias, automation complacency, calibrated trust, mental model calibration, AI literacy, human factors, role-based competency matrix, incident simulation training, simulator training, skill fade, skills degradation, manual proficiency, manual control retention, over-trust mitigation, under-trust mitigation, workforce readiness, reporting disincentive awareness, normalization of deviance

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Safe:** Contributes training of people who can recognize when an SI system’s output should not be acted on and who can carry out an override in time, so that the intervention path the system depends on works in practice and not only on paper. This Practice does not cover the override mechanisms and procedures themselves, which [Practice 4: Define Procedures for Emergency Avoidance Override, Recovery, and Situational Awareness](#practice-4:-define-procedures-for-emergency-avoidance-override,-recovery,-and-situational-awareness) covers.  
* **Accountable:** Contributes roles whose SI-related responsibilities are matched by defined and verified competence, with records showing who has been trained and assessed for what. This Practice does not cover assigning those responsibilities or the authority to decide, which [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior) sets out.

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Accountable:** A record that personnel were trained can inadvertently place a persistent failure on an individual when its cause is structural. [Implementation 9.2.3: Recognizing Disincentives to Reporting SI Issues](#implementation-9.2.3:-recognizing-disincentives-to-reporting-si-issues) notes that training alone does not resolve under-reporting where disclosure is individually costly, and that persistent under-reporting is evidence of a structural rather than a training deficiency; [Task 8.6: Establish Non-Punitive Reporting for SI-Related Near-Misses](#task-8.6:-establish-non-punitive-reporting-for-si-related-near-misses) sets out the structural reporting measures.  
* **Secure:** Training material that explains how an SI system’s guardrails work, where they are weak, and which failures personnel are drilled to catch also shows which weaknesses to aim for and which failures are least likely to be noticed. An insider, or an outsider who obtains the material, could use it to get around the guardrails. Limiting that detail to the roles that need it can reduce the exposure. Protecting the material is otherwise a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **GOVERN 2.2** (on training for SI risk management): This Practice covers training matched to each role that uses, supervises, or can override an SI system, or creates the data it consumes, with readiness verified rather than assumed; it does not address training for the organization’s partners, which GOVERN 2.2 also names.  
* **MAP 3.4** (on defining operator proficiency): This Practice covers the definition and assessment of operator proficiency with SI system behavior and limitations, including drills and certification renewal for the most critical roles; it does not cover retaining the manual skills that routine SI reliance erodes. For that, see for example [Task 3.6: Mitigate Automation Complacency and Skills Degradation](#task-3.6:-mitigate-automation-complacency-and-skills-degradation).  
* **GOVERN 4.1** (on establishing a risk-aware culture): This Practice covers training that cultivates critical review of SI outputs and recognition of disincentives to reporting SI degradation; it does not cover establishing reporting structures that keep disclosure from being individually costly, without which trained personnel may still under-report. For that, see for example [Practice 8: Incorporate SI-Aware Incident Analysis and Response Procedures](#practice-8:-incorporate-si-aware-incident-analysis-and-response-procedures).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* How will the organization tell whether personnel trust each SI system more than it warrants (over-trust) or less than it warrants (under-trust), rather than assuming training has corrected it?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 1270, Towards a Standard for Identifying and Managing Bias in Artificial Intelligence](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.1270), March 2022, from NIST. Section 3.3.1 calls the perception that a human, expert or otherwise, can effectively and objectively oversee algorithmic decision systems a problematic assumption, notes that experts are not necessarily trained to govern the use of an SI system they played no role in developing, and describes automation complacency. It states that without significant procedural and cultural support, optimistic expectations of human oversight are not borne out in practice, which bears on this Practice as one part of that support.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. Section 6.2.2, Awareness and Training, asks organizations to identify, document and train all personnel with significant OT roles and responsibilities, with training that covers the physical process being controlled as well as the OT system and is tailored to roles ranging from senior executives and third-party providers to control engineers, operators and maintainers. This is the existing OT training structure into which this Practice adds SI-specific competence by role.  
* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by CISA. Table 2 lists SI dependency, in which operators miss safety-related information the SI misses and lose manual skills, among the SI risks in an OT environment alongside cybersecurity and data quality, and maps it to Section 1.3, “Educate Personnel on AI.” That section adds skill gaps, in which personnel misinterpret SI outputs, and treats training as a mitigation of these risks rather than general awareness.

### Task 9.1: Perform Role-Based SI Risk Competency Mapping {#task-9.1:-perform-role-based-si-risk-competency-mapping}

Identify specific AI-related knowledge and skills required for different organizational roles, from executive level to front-line operations. This Task helps ensure that training is targeted to the specific risks encountered in each role and provides those responsible for mission continuity with relevant, actionable information and practice. Organizations that already analyze training needs by role, for cybersecurity or operational training, can build on that analysis.

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Accountable:** Contributes a mapping from each role that uses, supervises or can override an AI system to the AI literacy and risk awareness that role requires, distinguishing what a front-line operator needs from what an executive needs, so that responsibility assigned to a role comes with defined competence.
