* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-88r2, Guidelines for Media Sanitization](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/88/r2/final), from NIST. Its Appendix C provides a sample Certificate of Sanitization, a record naming what was acted on, by what method, by whom, and how the result was verified. It is the established documented form of the confirmed and retained result this Implementation asks for, and transfers directly to credentials and triggers.  
* **Guidance** [Agentic Identity and Access Management](https://www.coalitionforsecureai.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/agentic-identity-and-access-control.pdf), Workstream 4: Secure Design Patterns for Agentic Systems, from the Coalition for Secure AI. The Decommissioning subsection of Section 3.5 states the actions this Implementation calls for: revoke the identity and invalidate tokens, securely erase private keys, purge or appropriately handle sensitive data consistent with data-protection obligations, and revoke downstream delegated rights. The paper’s Appendix E supplies the corresponding record, an agent registry holding lifecycle state and an agent.decommissioned lifecycle event, which is where the confirmation is retained rather than in the teardown procedure itself.

#### Implementation 13.2.2: Revoke Authority Delegated to Other Entities, and Record What Could Not Be Confirmed {#implementation-13.2.2:-revoke-authority-delegated-to-other-entities,-and-record-what-could-not-be-confirmed}

Tracing authority that a system passed on helps an organization find actions that could continue after the system itself is retired. Where the AI system could delegate authority or create subordinate agents, trace and revoke that authority through every level it reaches. Tracing is more practical where delegation chains were kept visible in credentials and logs, for example through a correlation identifier shared by the events of one workflow, so that a chain can be reconstructed in order of delegation depth. Delegated authority is not limited to tokens. It can include tasks queued or scheduled for later execution, standing instructions or approvals left in workflow systems or with suppliers, and, in OT, schedules or setpoints written into control systems that continue to execute. Queued actions can be cancelled. An instruction that has already been acted on cannot be recalled, and its effects become a matter for [Implementation 13.3.3: Determine and Record What Happens to Everything that Depended on the System](#implementation-13.3.3:-determine-and-record-what-happens-to-everything-that-depended-on-the-system). Where a delegation cannot be confirmed revoked, whether to complete the retirement on a recorded exception or to hold it open is for the organization to decide, within any regulatory or contractual obligations. Completing leaves authority that may still be live, which a compensating control can cover. Holding it open leaves the retirement indefinitely incomplete, often because the means of confirmation has itself failed. Record what could not be confirmed, the decision taken and any compensating control. Under an externally imposed trigger the means of confirming revocation may itself have failed, which is when an unresolvable check is most likely.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Where a delegation cannot be confirmed revoked, is the retirement closed, as a last resort, with a record of what could not be confirmed, or held open, and what compensating control covers any remaining authority? (see the Safe and Accountable versus Secure and Safe itself tension in [Practice 13: Establish Procedures for Retiring SI Systems and Withdrawing Their Authority](#practice-13:-establish-procedures-for-retiring-si-systems-and-withdrawing-their-authority))

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Agentic Identity and Access Management](https://www.coalitionforsecureai.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/agentic-identity-and-access-control.pdf), Workstream 4: Secure Design Patterns for Agentic Systems, from the Coalition for Secure AI. Section 3.5 requires that decommissioning revoke downstream delegated rights, and the paper’s Appendix D describes the mechanism that makes this achievable at retirement: short-lived, tightly scoped delegation tokens, a centralized revocation service supporting near real-time invalidation, and runtime components subscribing to revocation events so that they stop accepting revoked tokens rather than waiting for expiry. The paper’s Appendix E names delegation.revoked as a logged event, which is what allows a revocation to be shown rather than assumed. Its Section 1.2 core principles require delegation chains to remain visible in credentials and logs, and Appendix E gives a query that reconstructs a chain from events sharing a correlation identifier, ordered by delegation depth.

#### Implementation 13.2.3: Reclaim Resources, Not Only Permissions {#implementation-13.2.3:-reclaim-resources,-not-only-permissions}

Identify and reclaim the compute and storage resources associated with the AI system, including containers, sandboxes, scratch storage and cached data. The same applies to network and naming resources registered for the system, such as DNS names, network addresses, endpoints, message queues and storage bucket names. A name released while other systems still trust it may be registered by another party and used to impersonate the retired system. Firewall rules and other boundary permissions opened for the system, for example between IT and OT zones, should also be removed. Resources and boundary permissions of this kind are distinct from the permissions revoked under [Implementation 13.2.1: Revoke Credentials and Disable Triggers, and Confirm the Result](#implementation-13.2.1:-revoke-credentials-and-disable-triggers,-and-confirm-the-result) and are often missed because the retirement record is organized around authorizations. An orphaned execution environment may hold a mounted credential that survives the revocation of everything else, keep running work that nobody is any longer watching, or retain cached data, including personal data, that outlives the retention decisions made for the system’s main stores. What happens to the model, training pipeline and datasets themselves is addressed in [Implementation 7.6.2: Secure Archiving and Destruction of Model and Other SI Artifacts](#implementation-7.6.2:-secure-archiving-and-destruction-of-model-and-other-si-artifacts).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Which network names, addresses and endpoints are released, and which are held for a period so that another party cannot register them?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-88r2, Guidelines for Media Sanitization](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/88/r2/final), from NIST. Section 3.1 sets out the Clear, Purge and Destroy methods and the basis for choosing between them, which is the decision to be made for each storage resource associated with a retired AI system rather than one choice applied to all of them.

### Task 13.3: Preserve What Is Needed and Hand Over What Depended on the System {#task-13.3:-preserve-what-is-needed-and-hand-over-what-depended-on-the-system}

Before an AI system is torn down, capture the evidence that will not survive it, and address what was relying on it. This includes volatile state that exists only while the system is running, the operational function the system was performing for others, and any protective function it was performing that would otherwise disappear without a corresponding record. What is preserved, and for how long, can be set from records retention schedules, sector record-keeping obligations, and any requirement to preserve records, and the record can state what was preserved, where, for how long and in whose custody. Where the facility has a management of change process, retiring an SI function in a process that it covers can be taken through that process. Where a function returns to manual operation or to a fallback mode, such as the one in [Implementation 11.2.2: Develop a Validated “Safe Operating Mode” that Depends Minimally on SI Infrastructure](#implementation-11.2.2:-develop-a-validated-“safe-operating-mode”-that-depends-minimally-on-si-infrastructure), that mode should be in place, and the personnel who will run it confirmed proficient under [Implementation 3.6.1: Baseline Human Competency Retention](#implementation-3.6.1:-baseline-human-competency-retention), before authority is withdrawn under [Task 13.2: Withdraw All Authority and Confirm the Result](#task-13.2:-withdraw-all-authority-and-confirm-the-result).

**Search Keywords:** forensic preservation, volatile state, working memory, control handover, successor system, downstream dependents, deprecation notice, control regression, data migration, records retention schedule, legal hold

**Main Trustworthiness Contributions:**

* **Transparent:** Contributes the capture of state that exists only while the system runs, before the teardown that destroys it, so that an incident-driven retirement does not also destroy the evidence of what prompted it. This Task does not cover the durable logging that survives teardown on its own, which [Practice 10: Implement Multi-Tiered SI System Logging and Audit Capabilities](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities) covers.  
* **Whichever characteristic the retired protective function served:** Contributes the treatment of a retired detection, monitoring, screening or filtering capability as a change to controls as well as an asset disposal, so that a protective function, whether it guarded against intrusion, equipment faults, unsafe outputs or bad input data, is handed over rather than silently discontinued. It draws on, but does not itself maintain, the account of system behavior kept under [Implementation 13.1.2: Maintain a Current Account of System Behavior, Not Only Its Specification](#implementation-13.1.2:-maintain-a-current-account-of-system-behavior,-not-only-its-specification).

**Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider:**

* **Privacy-Enhanced:** Preserving volatile state and learned material before teardown retains content that the retirement was in part intended to remove, and volatile state may contain material never intended to persist at all. [Practice 7: Manage Internal SI Supply Chain and Data Provenance](#practice-7:-manage-internal-si-supply-chain-and-data-provenance) governs how that material is then handled, and the tension is set out at [Practice 13: Establish Procedures for Retiring SI Systems and Withdrawing Their Authority](#practice-13:-establish-procedures-for-retiring-si-systems-and-withdrawing-their-authority).
* **Secure:** The dependents list, captured state, and any record of a coverage gap left by a retired protective capability show what relied on the system and where detection is weaker for a time. An attacker could use them to time an attack for that window or to target a dependent that was left without provision. Protecting them is a matter for the organization’s existing information classification and handling practice.

**Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance:**

* **Accountable versus Safe:** Where the retirement is planned and the capability is not protective, preserving evidence and handing over the function can both be done at an unhurried pace. Where the retirement follows an incident, the same actions compete: capturing volatile state takes time during which a system suspected of causing harm is still running. One way to balance this is to separate isolation from teardown, cutting the system’s authority and reach first under [Task 13.2: Withdraw All Authority and Confirm the Result](#task-13.2:-withdraw-all-authority-and-confirm-the-result) while leaving it running long enough to capture state; others include pre-authorizing the capture so it does not require a decision in the moment.  
* **Safe versus Safe:** Where a successor runs alongside the retiring system in shadow mode, the overlap avoids a gap in the capability without the two competing for control. Where both can act on the same equipment or process, the same overlap can produce conflicting actions, with each system acting as though it held the authority. One way to balance this is to bound the overlap and to give authority over each item of equipment to one system at a time, transferring it at a recorded point; others include keeping the successor in shadow mode until the transfer, using the comparison described for re-commissioning in [Implementation 11.4.2: Implement “Shadow Mode” Validation and Independent Safety Protection Checks for SI Re-Commissioning](#implementation-11.4.2:-implement-“shadow-mode”-validation-and-independent-safety-protection-checks-for-si-re-commissioning).

**Related AI RMF Subcategories Include:**

* **GOVERN 4.2** (on documenting impact): This Task covers the identification of parties that depended on a retired AI system and a recorded decision for each, including where that decision is to make no provision; it does not cover the technical mapping of internal systems consuming its outputs, or the deprecation timeline given to them. For that, see for example [Implementation 7.6.1: Internal Dependency Mapping (Orphan System Prevention)](#implementation-7.6.1:-internal-dependency-mapping-\(orphan-system-prevention\)).  
* **GOVERN 1.7** (on establishing decommissioning processes): This Task covers the requirement that phasing out does not decrease trustworthiness by removing a protective function without handover, and that evidence is captured before teardown makes it unrecoverable; it does not cover the withdrawal of authority. For that, see for example [Task 13.2: Withdraw All Authority and Confirm the Result](#task-13.2:-withdraw-all-authority-and-confirm-the-result).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* What is preserved, for how long and in whose custody, given retention schedules, preservation requirements, and any obligation to purge? (see the Privacy-Enhanced and Secure versus Transparent tension in [Practice 13: Establish Procedures for Retiring SI Systems and Withdrawing Their Authority](#practice-13:-establish-procedures-for-retiring-si-systems-and-withdrawing-their-authority))  
* Is the retirement of an SI function taken through the facility’s management of change process?  
* How long may a successor overlap the retiring system, and when does authority over each item of equipment pass to it? (see the Safe versus Safe tension in [Task 13.3: Preserve What Is Needed and Hand Over What Depended on the System](#task-13.3:-preserve-what-is-needed-and-hand-over-what-depended-on-the-system))  
* Who runs the manual or fallback mode after retirement, and what training, time, and authority do they need to do it?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-86, Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-86), August 2006, from NIST. Section 3.1.3, Incident Response Considerations, has the containment decision made with the incident response team, on the basis of containment policy and the assessed risk, so that the chosen strategy mitigates risk while maintaining the integrity of potential evidence whenever possible. It also asks organizations to consider in advance the impact of containment strategies on operations. This bears on the Accountable versus Safe tension in this Task.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), September 2020, from NIST. Control SI-12, Information Management and Retention, has information within and output from a system retained in accordance with applicable laws, regulations, policies and operational requirements. Its discussion notes that these requirements can extend beyond system disposal and suggests coordinating with records management personnel. This bears on setting what this Task preserves from retention obligations rather than from what happens to be available.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), September 2023, from NIST. In the OT overlay, Appendix F.7.5, the OT Discussion for control CM-3, Configuration Change Control, asks that configuration change control procedures align with the organization’s management of change practices. This bears on taking the retirement of an SI function in a covered process through an existing management of change process.

#### Implementation 13.3.1: Capture Volatile State Before Teardown {#implementation-13.3.1:-capture-volatile-state-before-teardown}

Capturing state that exists only while a system runs helps an organization understand what went wrong after the system is gone. Where retirement follows an incident or a suspected failure, capture working memory, in-flight state and intermediate reasoning artifacts before the execution environment is destroyed. For an SI system, this can include the contents of agent memory, conversation history, and the state of a retrieval index or vector database as it stood at the time. Some containment steps, such as resetting memory or purging conversation history, destroy this state. At a planned retirement, capture may still be worthwhile where a problem could surface only after the system is gone, such as a question about its past decisions. Weigh this against the cost of capture and against any obligation to purge sensitive data at retirement. Record the decision either way. Durable logs and stored records are addressed under [Practice 10: Implement Multi-Tiered SI System Logging and Audit Capabilities](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities). This Implementation concerns the state that exists only while the system is running and that teardown destroys permanently. What is kept alongside durable records so that they remain interpretable once the system is gone is considered under [Task 10.1: Define Decision-Level Logging and Metadata Retention Policies](#task-10.1:-define-decision-level-logging-and-metadata-retention-policies). This step should precede teardown and resource reclamation, because those actions can make the state unrecoverable. Where the system is suspected of causing harm, its authority and reach can be withdrawn first under [Task 13.2: Withdraw All Authority and Confirm the Result](#task-13.2:-withdraw-all-authority-and-confirm-the-result), leaving it running long enough for the capture (see the Accountable versus Safe tension in [Task 13.3: Preserve What Is Needed and Hand Over What Depended on the System](#task-13.3:-preserve-what-is-needed-and-hand-over-what-depended-on-the-system)). Where immediate containment rules out capture, follow the pre-established safety response and record what could not be preserved. Some isolation steps, such as disconnecting the system from a network, can themselves destroy volatile state, so the criteria for capture and its order relative to isolation can be decided in advance. Where feasible, capture state with tools independent of the SI system rather than by asking the system to report it, since a compromised system can return false information to the tools that query it. Captured state is itself a record and may hold sensitive or personal material: assign it an accountable owner, access restrictions, a retention basis and period, and a disposition event, as for other SI artifacts governed under [Practice 7: Manage Internal SI Supply Chain and Data Provenance](#practice-7:-manage-internal-si-supply-chain-and-data-provenance). Captured state may be readable only with the software and configuration of the system being retired, so retain or record what is needed to interpret it.

Where an investigation is possible, collect the most volatile state first, compute a hash of each capture so that its integrity can later be shown, and record its chain of custody. The state to capture can also include current adaptive parameters or thresholds where they may differ from those documented, the prompt and configuration versions active at the time, and logs held with short retention by a supplier.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* Is volatile state captured at planned retirements as well as after an incident or suspected failure?  
* Is capture pre-authorized, and does it come before or after isolation? (see the Accountable versus Safe tension in [Task 13.3: Preserve What Is Needed and Hand Over What Depended on the System](#task-13.3:-preserve-what-is-needed-and-hand-over-what-depended-on-the-system))  
* Who owns captured state, and what are its access restrictions, retention basis and disposition?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-61r3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-61r3), April 2025, from NIST. In Table 3, recommendation R1 under RS.AN-07 is to collect and retain incident evidence in accordance with evidence preservation procedures and data retention policies, considering the cost of retaining both the data and the hardware and software needed to access it in the future. This bears on keeping captured state readable after the system that produced it is gone.  
* **Guidance** [AI Incident Response Framework, Workstream 2: Preparing Defenders for a Changing Cybersecurity Landscape](https://www.coalitionforsecureai.org/defending-ai-systems-a-new-framework-for-incident-response-in-the-age-of-intelligent-technology/), version 1.0, 27 October 2025, from the Coalition for Secure AI, an OASIS Open Project. Section 3.3.3 asks for containment to be implemented without destroying evidence, and lists forensic copies before containment and vector database state preservation as evidence preservation steps. It also notes that containment for an SI system with memory can mean resetting memory and purging conversation history. This bears on the order of capture and containment in this Implementation.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-86, Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-86), August 2006, from NIST. Section 5.2.1, Collecting Volatile OS Data, notes that volatile data can be collected only from a live system, that powering off or even disconnecting a system from a network can end the opportunity to collect it, and that the criteria for deciding whether to preserve it should be documented in advance. Section 5.2.1.1 warns that a fully compromised system can return false data to the tools that query it. Written for operating systems, it bears on the order and the means of capture in this Implementation.

#### Implementation 13.3.2: Treat the Retirement of a Protective SI Capability as a Change to Controls {#implementation-13.3.2:-treat-the-retirement-of-a-protective-si-capability-as-a-change-to-controls}

Treating the retirement of a protective SI capability as a change to controls helps an organization keep the protection in place, or know where a gap remains. Where an AI system performs a detection, monitoring, screening or filtering function, its retirement removes a control and should be processed as a control change as well as an asset disposal. Establish what the system was detecting, including behavior it had learned to detect that is not documented elsewhere, and what will perform that function afterward. Before the capability is withdrawn, verify through defined testing that the successor or compensating control covers what is required, for example by running the two in parallel and comparing their outputs, and retain the evidence. Where equivalent coverage cannot be established first, record the residual risk, the interim compensating measures, the role with authority to accept that risk, and a date for review. Some frameworks and obligations, such as SP 800-37, limit the delegation of risk acceptance. A replacement that begins without this information starts without the accumulated basis of the one it replaces, and the resulting gap may not be visible from either system’s records. The operators and analysts who acted on the retired system’s alerts should be told that the absence of an alert no longer carries the meaning it did. Where a successor takes over, its alerts can differ in which events they flag, how often they occur and how often they are false, and the people receiving them should be told what will change. Documents that cite the capability as a control, such as a system security plan, a safety case or hazard analysis, or compliance evidence provided to a regulator, should be updated to record its removal and what replaces it.

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* What testing shows that a successor or compensating control provides the required coverage, and who accepts any gap until it does?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-37r2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations: A System Life Cycle Approach for Security and Privacy](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-37r2), from NIST. Task M-7, System Disposal, calls for any control inheritance relationships to be reviewed and assessed for impact when a system is removed from operation. Where other systems inherit controls from the disposed system, this review shows what protection they lose. A detection, monitoring or filtering AI system can play that role whether or not it is formally recorded as a control provider, and this Implementation extends the review to behavior it had learned to detect that is documented nowhere else. Their Task R-4 and Appendix D also state that the explicit acceptance of risk is the responsibility of the authorizing official and cannot be delegated.

#### Implementation 13.3.3: Determine and Record What Happens to Everything that Depended on the System {#implementation-13.3.3:-determine-and-record-what-happens-to-everything-that-depended-on-the-system}

Deciding what happens to each thing that relied on a system helps an organization retire it without leaving others to fail unnoticed. Identify the processes, systems and people that relied on the AI system’s output, and record for each whether it will be migrated to an alternative, formally notified and wound down, or left without provision. The list of dependents can be built from observed calls and access logs as well as from design and integration records, over a period long enough to include infrequent uses such as monthly reporting, seasonal operations or rarely triggered emergency functions. Abandonment may be a legitimate decision, but it should be a recorded one. Where the SI system has authorized or initiated actions that are still pending in downstream systems, record how those actions will be completed, reversed or handed over, and the point from which new actions are no longer authorized, since withdrawing authority for new actions does not by itself resolve commitments already made. Human operators and downstream automation may have adapted to the retired system’s particular behavior, so the effect of removal is not limited to the function it formally provided. Where the dependents are internal systems consuming the AI system’s outputs, the mapping and the deprecation timeline are in [Implementation 7.6.1: Internal Dependency Mapping (Orphan System Prevention)](#implementation-7.6.1:-internal-dependency-mapping-\(orphan-system-prevention\)); what this Implementation adds is that a decision is recorded for each dependent, including where that decision is to make no provision. Dependents can also be outside the organization. Where known external parties rely on the SI system’s outputs for consequential decisions, the record can include whether and how they will be notified, the effective date, and any alternative or transition arrangement, subject to applicable legal and contractual obligations.

After retirement, a dependent that was missed can fail without an obvious error, for example a dashboard that continues to display the last values it received as though they were current, or a controller that holds the last setpoint it was sent. Monitoring dependents for failed calls, missing inputs and stale values for a period after retirement can help reveal dependents the record missed, so that each receives a recorded decision. Where a dependent is a control system that received setpoints or recommendations from the SI system, its behavior on loss of that input should be defined before retirement, as set out in [Implementation 3.2.3: Specify Fail-Safe States and Fallback Behavior](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior).

**Decisions for the Organization:**

* For each dependent, is it migrated, notified and wound down, or left without provision?  
* Which external parties are notified, with what notice and transition arrangement, within any legal and contractual obligations?  
* For how long are dependents monitored after retirement for failed calls, missing inputs and stale values?

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 600-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1), July 2024, from NIST. Suggested action GV-1.7-002, under GOVERN 1.7, lists factors to consider when decommissioning a generative AI system, including data retention, data leakage after decommissioning, dependencies between upstream, downstream and other systems, and users’ emotional entanglement. Suggested action MG-2.4-001, under MANAGE 2.4, asks for communication plans for deactivation that cover reasons, workarounds, user access removal and alternative processes. Together they cover the dependents and the notification this Implementation asks to be decided and recorded.

# Glossary and Terminology Crosswalk {#glossary-and-terminology-crosswalk}

This glossary defines terms as they are used in this profile. Particularly in fast-moving fields, there is rarely a single definition that serves every use; the [NIST Computer Security Resource Center glossary](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary) often lists several definitions of the same term, drawn from different NIST publications and catering to different contexts and audiences.

This profile is written for a wide range of readers across the critical infrastructure ecosystem, including those with backgrounds in OT and automation; governance, regulation, and policy; electrical, electronic, mechanical, structural, and civil engineering; and the breadth of machine learning, SI, and computer science. Familiarity with definitions will range from formal to colloquial.

The definitions chosen in this profile aim to be as accurate and understandable as possible across this wide audience. As a result, many of these will not exactly match those used in particular sectors or in other documents, including other NIST documents, that were written for different contexts and audiences. For most terms, the glossary therefore also gives a brief terminology crosswalk, relating the definition to other wordings and to definitions used elsewhere.

Readers of this profile are welcome to adopt these definitions, or to note where their own usage differs, as appropriate for their own contexts and audiences.

Within each entry, the terminology crosswalk appears under one or more of the following headings:

* **Also called** lists other wordings the reader may meet in this and related documents.  
* **Collides with** notes where a sector, field or framework uses the term differently and a misreading would change what someone does.  
* **References** lists selected NIST publications and other sources with similar or related definitions, and notes any differences.

Entries may also include:

* **Forms include**, which lists specific kinds of the thing the term names.  
* **Contrast**, which names related terms that are easily confused with this one.  
* **See**, which points to where the term is used in this profile, and **See also**, which points to related entries.

The 13 trustworthiness characteristics are defined in the Trustworthiness Characteristics table and [Appendix A](#appendix-a:-trustworthiness-characteristics) rather than here.

\> To the Reviewer:  
\> These entries are being updated in line with EO 14434, and several await more detailed guidance.  
\> We welcome suggestions and contributions, particularly for terms whose different meanings across sectors may not be obvious.

## Action-level authorization {#action-level-authorization}

The decision, made at the moment of execution, whether a specific proposed action by an identified entity is permitted, given its parameters, the entity’s current task scope and the operational state. It is distinct from access authorization, which decides whether an entity may interact with a system at all, and from authentication, which establishes which entity is acting. An entity that is authenticated and has access to a system is not thereby authorized for each action it can request, and an authorized action is not thereby safe to execute.

**Also called:** action authorization, per-action authorization, per-request authorization.

**Contrast:** access authorization; authentication; **safety wrapper**.

**Collides with:** “authorization” in general access control usage, where it usually means the permissions granted to a user or other principal; and an authorization to operate, a management decision about a whole system.

**See:** [Task 5.1](#task-5.1:-establish-identities-and-authentication-for-si-entities), [Implementation 5.2.2](#implementation-5.2.2:-action-level,-context-aware-authorization-policies), [Task 7.4](#task-7.4:-define-authorization-and-access-controls-for-si-modifications), [Task 3.2](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs), [Implementation 3.2.3](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior); **zero trust**.

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-207), from NIST. Section 2.1, Tenets of Zero Trust, includes that authentication and authorization to one resource will not automatically grant access to a different resource; this entry applies the same principle to individual actions within an authenticated session.

## Agentic AI system {#agentic-ai-system}

A system that consists of, or incorporates, one or more **AI agents**. A single agent is the simplest case. Systems of several agents that co-ordinate with one another, break a goal down into tasks and delegate them, and operate over extended periods are what the term most often refers to, and they add risks beyond those of each agent: errors and compromised context can pass from one agent to another, delegation chains and dependencies can form that no one documented, and one agent’s resilience can mask another’s failure.

**Also called:** agentic AI, agentic system; multi-agent system (for the several-agent case).

**See:** [Practice 3](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior), [Practice 5](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools), [Task 3.3](#task-3.3:-establish-failure-notification-requirements), [Implementation 3.8.3](#implementation-3.8.3:-dynamic-risk-surface-coupling-analysis), [Implementation 4.4.2](#implementation-4.4.2:-adapting-existing-alarm-management-for-complex,-adaptive-or-otherwise-unpredictable-systems), [Implementation 8.1.5](#implementation-8.1.5:-multi-agent-cascade-reconstruction-capabilities), [Implementation 13.2.2](#implementation-13.2.2:-revoke-authority-delegated-to-other-entities,-and-record-what-could-not-be-confirmed).

**See also:** **AI agent**.

**References:**

* **Research** [The Agentic AI Landscape and Its Conceptual Foundations](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/the-agentic-ai-landscape-and-its-conceptual-foundations_396cf758-en.html), OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 56, February 2026, from the OECD Directorate for Science, Technology and Innovation. Section 3.2 describes agentic AI as generally involving multiple co-ordinated agents, task decomposition and delegation, and extended operation; this profile also counts a system with a single agent, so the OECD’s agentic AI is the main case of the term here rather than the whole of it.

## AI agent {#ai-agent}

An AI system that is given a goal and some authority to act, and that pursues the goal by deciding on and carrying out a series of steps itself, rather than only producing an output for a person to act on. Communicating on the organization’s behalf counts as acting where no person reviews the output first, for example disclosing information to, or making commitments to, a customer. Those steps may include gathering information, using software tools or other systems, and changing data, configurations or physical equipment, without a person approving each one. How much it can do on its own depends on the permissions and limits it is given. Many current AI agents are built on large language models, but a planner or reinforcement-learning system that decides which steps to take toward a goal is an AI agent in the same sense. A controller that applies a fixed, pre-engineered response to its inputs is automated rather than agentic; the profile treats such logic as non-AI when it serves as a fallback or interlock ([Task 2.2](#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions)).

**Also called:** agent (where the context is clear).

**Contrast:** **agentic AI system**, which may consist of one AI agent or many.

**Collides with:** “agent” in endpoint-security and IT-management usage, meaning installed monitoring or management software, “threat agent”, meaning an attacker, and “conversational agent”, a common name for a chatbot, which may converse with a user without acting for the organization. Some definitions for AI agent also count any AI system whose output drives actions without human intervention as an agent, even where its sequence of steps is fixed in advance. This profile’s emphasis on OT and ICS in critical infrastructure requires careful deconfliction with the term “automation.” Therefore, this profile keeps the term AI agent for systems that decide their own steps, at the level of abstraction being considered, to reduce confusion with concepts that the OT community would consider “automation,” such as fixed, pre-engineered control logic that OT relies on as an independent fallback or interlock. Its controls on authority and access, such as those in [Practice 5](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools), apply equally to fixed-sequence systems whose actions are driven by an AI system’s output, and to conversational systems whose responses reach people outside the organization without review.

**See:** [Practice 3](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior), [Practice 5](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools), [Task 5.3](#task-5.3:-implement-principles-of-least-agency-and-least-privilege-for-si-entities), [Implementation 5.3.3](#implementation-5.3.3:-separate-privilege-via-encapsulated-downstream-agents-and-tools), [Implementation 5.3.2](#implementation-5.3.2:-task-bounded-and-revocable-agent-authority).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025), from NIST. Appendix A defines “agent”, broadly consistent with this entry; this profile also stresses the authority and permissions the agent is given.  
* **Guidance** Artificial Intelligence Executive Oversight Group AI Lexicon (the Shared Artificial Intelligence (AI) Lexicon), February 2026, from the Artificial Intelligence Executive Oversight Group, a public-private partnership formed by the U.S. Department of the Treasury with the FBIIC and FSSCC. The entries “Agentic AI” and “AI Agent” define AI systems that make decisions and take actions to achieve goals without direct human intervention, consistent with this entry; neither mentions the permissions or limits that this profile treats as setting how much an agent can do.  
* **Standard** [ISO/IEC 22989:2022, Information technology: Artificial intelligence: Artificial intelligence concepts and terminology](https://www.iso.org/standard/74296.html), from ISO and IEC. Clause 3.1.1 defines “AI agent” as an automated entity that senses and responds to its environment and takes actions to achieve its goals; like this entry, it is not limited to language-model agents, but it says nothing about delegated authority.  
* **Research** [The Agentic AI Landscape and Its Conceptual Foundations](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/the-agentic-ai-landscape-and-its-conceptual-foundations_396cf758-en.html), OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers No. 56, February 2026, from the OECD Directorate for Science, Technology and Innovation, a paper that describes itself as preliminary results and research in progress. Section 3.1 surveys definitions of AI agents and finds that most share objectives, actions and a degree of autonomy, which this entry follows.

## Alarm flood {#alarm-flood}

More alarms, alerts or other notifications arriving than the people responsible can recognize, assess and act on, so that important signals are missed, delayed or cancelled without being understood. The profile treats AI as a new source of floods: in domains with no alarm-management experience, by breaking the assumptions behind established alarm management (for example, one fault reported in many slightly different ways), and through a correlated surge, when one external event makes many AI systems request attention at once.

**Also called:** alert flood, alert/alarm flood.

**See also:** alert fatigue (also alarm fatigue), the desensitization that repeated floods produce; **oversight capacity**.

**Collides with:** process-industry alarm management (ISA-18.2, EEMUA 191), where an alarm is specifically an indication to the operator of an abnormal condition **requiring a response**, and floods are judged against recommended alarm-rate targets, such as those cited in [Task 4.4](#task-4.4:-attention-governance-and-alert/alarm-flood-mitigation). The profile uses “alarm”, “alert” and “notification” interchangeably.

**See:** [Task 4.4](#task-4.4:-attention-governance-and-alert/alarm-flood-mitigation); [Implementation 4.4.1](#implementation-4.4.1:-recognizing-novel-si-driven-alert-floods-in-unfamiliar-domains); [Implementation 4.4.2](#implementation-4.4.2:-adapting-existing-alarm-management-for-complex,-adaptive-or-otherwise-unpredictable-systems); [Implementation 4.4.3](#implementation-4.4.3:-managing-correlated-multi-system-attention-surges); [Implementation 4.4.4](#implementation-4.4.4:-applying-consolidation-and-low-cognitive-load-design-techniques); [Task 3.3](#task-3.3:-establish-failure-notification-requirements); [Implementation 3.3.1](#implementation-3.3.1:-context-specific-failure-modes); [Implementation 3.2.4](#implementation-3.2.4:-define-further-logging-and-communication-actions).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), from NIST. Appendix B defines “alarm”, but not alarm flood.  
* **Guidance** Health and Safety Executive (2000), [Better alarm handling](https://www.hse.gov.uk/pubns/chis6.pdf), Chemicals Sheet No 6, from Great Britain’s workplace health and safety regulator. States long-term average alarm-rate targets for process plant.  
* **Guidance** [EEMUA Publication 191, Alarm Systems: A Guide to Design, Management and Procurement](https://www.eemua.org/products/publications/print/eemua-publication-191), from the Engineering Equipment and Materials Users’ Association.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), from NIST. Table 21, under “Spoofed reporting message”, names alarm floods as an adversary tactic to distract defenders and operators from the actual source of a problem; this profile treats floods mainly as an effect of AI, and the NIST passage adds the adversarial case.  
* **Guidance** [The Joint Commission (2013) Sentinel Event Alert 50: Medical device alarm safety in hospitals](https://www.jointcommission.org/en-us/knowledge-library/newsletters/sentinel-event-alert/issue-50), 8 April 2013, from the US non-profit that accredits healthcare organizations. Describes “alarm fatigue”: alarm signals reaching several hundred per patient per day, most needing no clinical intervention, leading clinicians to become desensitized and to silence or reset alarms; a healthcare counterpart to process-industry alarm floods.  
* **Commentary** [Understanding and Applying the ANSI/ISA 18.2 Alarm Management Standard](https://www.isa.org/getmedia/55b4210e-6cb2-4de4-89f8-2b5b6b46d954/PAS-Understanding-ISA-18-2.pdf), 2010, from PAS, a commercial supplier of alarm management software and services. Summarizes ANSI/ISA-18.2-2009, quoting its definition of an alarm as an indication of an abnormal condition requiring a response, and its recommended alarm-rate and alarm-flood metrics, which it notes are approximate and not on their own an indicator of acceptability.

## Artificial intelligence (AI) {#artificial-intelligence-\(ai\)}

\> To the Reviewer: This entry is a placeholder pending more detailed guidance regarding compatibility with EO 14434\.

In this profile, AI and SI (Super Intelligence) refer to the same systems: a machine-based system that can, for a given set of human-defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations or decisions influencing real or virtual environments, adapted from 15 U.S.C. § 9401\. This deliberately includes reasoning, planning, optimization and statistical systems, deep learning neural networks, large language models and hybrid systems, and so covers automated and agentic systems, not only machine learning or chatbots.

The body text says “SI” following Executive Order 14434, while cited works, proper names, quotations, identifiers, terms of art and keyword lists keep “AI”. Where the profile calls a fallback, verifier or interlock “non-AI”, it means manual or legacy procedures, or deterministic logic whose behavior is fully specified and verified in advance, even if that logic would otherwise fall within this definition.

**Also called:** SI, Super Intelligence.

**Collides with:** everyday and executive usage, where AI means generative AI or chatbots, and OT usage, where rule-based or model-predictive control is called “advanced control”, not AI.

**See:** Section 1 (Introduction), Section 1.2 (Scope), footnote 1\.

**References:**

* **Standard** [ISO/IEC 22989:2022, Information technology: Artificial intelligence: Artificial intelligence concepts and terminology](https://www.iso.org/standard/74296.html), from ISO and IEC. Clause 3.1.4 defines “AI system” as an engineered system that generates outputs such as content, forecasts, recommendations or decisions for a given set of human-defined objectives, close to 15 U.S.C. § 9401; clause 3.1.3 reserves “artificial intelligence” for the research discipline, unlike this profile.  
* **Regulation** [Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act](http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), 13 June 2024, from the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union. Article 3(1) defines “AI system” as a machine-based system that infers from its input how to generate outputs for explicit or implicit objectives; Recital 12 explains that the definition does not cover systems based on rules defined solely by natural persons to execute operations automatically, a narrower scope than this profile’s.  
* **Guidance** Artificial Intelligence Executive Oversight Group AI Lexicon (the Shared Artificial Intelligence (AI) Lexicon), February 2026, from the Artificial Intelligence Executive Oversight Group, a public-private partnership formed by the U.S. Department of the Treasury with the FBIIC and FSSCC. Its “Artificial intelligence (AI)” entry quotes 15 U.S.C. § 9401, the source this profile adapts; its separate “AI system” entry, from 40 U.S.C. chapter 113, excludes common commercial products with embedded AI, which this profile’s scope deliberately includes.  
* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-1), from NIST. The Executive Summary defines an AI system as an engineered or machine-based system that can, for a given set of objectives, generate outputs such as predictions, recommendations or decisions influencing real or virtual environments, adapted from the OECD and ISO/IEC 22989; unlike 15 U.S.C. § 9401, it omits “human-defined”.

## As practical {#as-practical}

Used in this profile, as in “as independent as practical” or “shares as little as practical”, for measures that are a matter of degree. How far to go is set by the consequence of a shared failure, weighed against the resources available, and whatever dependency or gap remains is a decision that someone with the authority to accept that level of risk accepts and records.

**Also called:** as independent as practical, shares as little as practical, as far as practical.

**See:** How Far to Go; [Implementation 3.9.6](#implementation-3.9.6:-keep-a-record-of-design-decisions-and-accepted-risks).

## Attack surface {#attack-surface}

The set of points where an attacker can try to enter, affect or extract data from a system, a component or its environment. For an AI system this includes the routes by which adversarial input can reach inference logic, such as prompts, retrieved content, training and fine-tuning data, tools and APIs, and the model itself. It is part of the risk surface. The profile names it separately because security practitioners know the term, and because adversarial and non-adversarial causes call for different responses. It is mapped in [Implementation 3.8.1](#implementation-3.8.1:-si-attack-surface-mapping-\(adversarial-exposure\)). The added monitors, fallbacks and watchdogs that this profile recommends can enlarge it.

**See:** [Task 3.8](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface), [Implementation 3.8.1](#implementation-3.8.1:-si-attack-surface-mapping-\(adversarial-exposure\)), [Practice 5](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools), [Task 8.1](#task-8.1:-identify-scenarios-requiring-deterministic-root-cause-analysis-and-incident-reconstruction), [Implementation 8.1.6](#implementation-8.1.6:-incident-triage-across-the-dual-attack/risk-surface).

**See also:** Risk surface.

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Appendix A defines attack surface as the points on a boundary where an attacker can try to enter, cause an effect on, or extract data.  
* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025), March 2025, from NIST. Sections 2 and 3 catalog attacks on predictive and generative AI systems by attacker goal and capability.

## Automation bias {#automation-bias}

The tendency of people to trust an automated system’s output more than it warrants: accepting it without enough checking, or delaying stepping in when it is wrong. It is related to, but distinct from, **automation complacency**, where a system that usually works leads people to monitor it less or lets manual skills fade.

**Also called:** over-trust, over-reliance.

**Note:** Both words are also used for automation complacency, which NIST SP 1270 defines as over-reliance, so should be read in context.

**Collides with:** “bias” in its fairness or measurement senses. In this profile, automation bias is a human error source handled under Bias Managed.

**See:** [Task 3.6](#task-3.6:-mitigate-automation-complacency-and-skills-degradation), [Implementation 3.6.3](#implementation-3.6.3:-cognitive-engagement-by-design), [Task 4.6](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output), [Task 9.2](#task-9.2:-deliver-specialized-training-on-human-si-interaction-and-automation-bias), [Implementation 9.2.1](#implementation-9.2.1:-include-role-specific-training-on-si-failure-modes), [Task 12.2](#task-12.2:-implement-multi-layered-validation-of-machine-authored-logic).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 1270, Towards a Standard for Identifying and Managing Bias in Artificial Intelligence](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.1270), from NIST. The Glossary defines the related term “automation complacency”.  
* **Regulation** [Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act](http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), 13 June 2024, from the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union. Article 14(4)(b) names “automation bias” as the possible tendency of automatically relying or over-relying on a high-risk AI system’s output, and provides that people assigned oversight be enabled to remain aware of it; close to this entry, though it does not separate out automation complacency.  
* **Guidance** [NIST AI 600-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1), from NIST. Section 2.7, Human-AI Configuration, describes automation bias as excessive deference to automated systems and notes it can exacerbate confabulation risk; NIST frames it for generative AI, while this profile applies it to any automated output.

## Break-glass {#break-glass}

A pre-established emergency procedure by which authorized personnel, including external emergency responders where provided for, can quickly override AI-driven actions, modeled on the audited emergency override of access control. It is tiered rather than all-or-nothing, because simply cutting off the AI system can leave the process unsafe.

**Collides with:** IAM and OT “break-glass accounts”, which grant emergency access but do not by themselves stop AI actions or hand over control.

**See:** [Task 3.9](#task-3.9:-assess-and-document-organizational-readiness-for-each-si-enabled-capability), [Practice 4](#practice-4:-define-procedures-for-emergency-avoidance-override,-recovery,-and-situational-awareness), [Task 4.1](#task-4.1:-establish-“break-glass”-intervention-procedures), [Implementation 4.1.1](#implementation-4.1.1:-ensure-that-si-systems-can-be-reliably-overridden), [Implementation 4.1.2](#implementation-4.1.2:-establish-tiered-intervention-procedures,-training,-and-authorization).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control enhancement AC-3(10), Audited Override of Access Control Mechanisms, is the audited emergency override this entry says break-glass is modeled on; the NIST control overrides access control, not AI-driven actions.  
* **Guidance** [Adapting Zero Trust Principles to Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/adapting-zero-trust-principles-operational-technology), 29 April 2026, from CISA, the Department of War and the Department of Energy with partners. The ICAM for OT section calls emergency access non-negotiable and describes break-glass accounts with limited lifespans and stringent auditing; this is the IAM sense the entry lists under “Collides with”, granting access rather than stopping AI actions.

## Cold start {#cold-start}

The disorientation of people who take over from an AI system without current awareness of system state, recent automated decisions or accumulated work.

**Collides with:** ML “cold start” (no prior data) and power-plant cold start or grid black start.

**See:** [Task 4.2](#task-4.2:-ensure-that-personnel-are-able-to-gain-and-maintain-situational-awareness), [Implementation 11.2.3](#implementation-11.2.3:-human-factors-and-cognitive-transition-protocols-for-control-handoffs).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance led by the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Section 1.3, Educate Personnel on AI, warns that relying too much on AI can reduce human oversight and situational awareness and erode the manual skills needed during AI failures; it does not address handover itself, but describes conditions that make a cold start more likely.

## Common-cause failure {#common-cause-failure}

The failure of two or more systems, components or safeguards because of a single shared cause, such as a common power or cooling supply, network path, hypervisor, software library, training dataset or operating condition. Redundancy only protects against failures that do not share a cause, so the profile asks that functionally independent systems and safeguards be checked for what they share, rather than assumed to fail independently.

**Also called:** common mode failure (in the SP 800-160v2r1 material the profile cites); correlated failure modes ([Implementation 3.2.5](#implementation-3.2.5:-artifact-verification)); common-cause analysis (the activity of looking for shared causes).

**See:** [Task 3.5](#task-3.5:-define-and-control-risks-to-adjacent-and-related-systems); [Implementation 3.5.2](#implementation-3.5.2:-identify-indirect-shared-infrastructure-and-collateral-damage-exposure); [Task 2.2](#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions); [Implementation 3.2.5](#implementation-3.2.5:-artifact-verification); **diversity (in redundancy)**.

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v1r1, Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v1r1), from NIST. Principle E.26, Redundancy, defines common mode failure as a single event that results in the same or equivalent elements failing in the same manner, and identifies diversity as a means to address it; this profile’s term also covers shared dependencies such as power, data or hosting.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), from NIST. The OT Discussion for control enhancement SR-3(1), Diverse Supply Base, uses “common cause failures” in this profile’s sense and notes that limited supply options can prevent diversity.

## Compensating control {#compensating-control}

A control put in place to cover a gap where a recommended measure cannot be applied, for example where a legacy device cannot hold a unique identity, a vendor cannot supply a complete AIBOM, or an AI system cannot support the root cause analysis an application calls for. The profile asks that the gap and the control covering it be documented, and in some places that the control be shown to close the gap.

**Collides with:** “compensating controls” in the NIST Risk Management Framework, controls “employed in lieu of the controls in the baselines described in NIST Special Publication 800-53B that provide equivalent or comparable protection for a system or organization” (NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5). Because this profile also uses the term for partial measures proportional to the gap ([Implementation 6.1.2](#implementation-6.1.2:-require-sibom-for-mission-critical-applications)), a measure it calls a compensating control may not qualify as one in an RMF assessment.

**See:** [Implementation 3.2.2](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints); [Implementation 5.1.1](#implementation-5.1.1:-audit-for-and-replace-shared-credentials,-service-accounts,-secrets,-passwords,-and-api-keys); [Implementation 5.2.3](#implementation-5.2.3:-determine-the-appropriate-level-of-agent,-asset,-and-permission-granularity); [Implementation 6.1.1](#implementation-6.1.1:-add-si-disclosure-to-existing-procurement-policies); [Implementation 6.1.2](#implementation-6.1.2:-require-sibom-for-mission-critical-applications); [Implementation 8.1.1](#implementation-8.1.1:-evaluate-si-applications); [Task 8.2](#task-8.2:-identify-additional-controls-that-may-be-required-in-scenarios-where-deterministic-root-cause-analysis-is-not-possible); [Implementation 8.2.1](#implementation-8.2.1:-identify-applications-and-situations-for-which-root-cause-analysis-requirements-may-be-relaxed); [Practice 13](#practice-13:-establish-procedures-for-retiring-si-systems-and-withdrawing-their-authority).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Appendix A defines “compensating controls” as controls used in place of those in a baseline that provide equivalent or comparable protection; this profile also uses the term for partial measures proportional to the gap (Implementation 6.1.2).  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-37r2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-37r2), from NIST. Their Glossary gives a closely similar definition: controls “implemented in lieu of the controls in the baselines described in NIST Special Publication 800-53” that provide equivalent or comparable protection.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), from NIST. Section F.4, Tailoring Considerations, describes compensating controls for OT that cannot support certain baseline controls, and says organizations should document why the baseline control could not be implemented, how the compensating controls provide equivalent security capabilities, and the risk acceptance for any residual risk; close to this entry’s documentation ask.

## Confidence score {#confidence-score}

A number produced by an AI system indicating how certain it is about an output. It is not necessarily a reliable probability that the output is correct. [Implementation 3.2.2](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints) recommends that safety constraints not depend on such values, and [Task 4.6](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output) that any confidence shown to personnel be derived from how the AI system reached its output.

**Also called:** self-reported certainty.

**Note:** Where shown to personnel, the profile speaks of confidence metrics, indications or bands, which [Task 4.6](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output) asks to be derived from the decision process rather than taken from the raw score.

**Collides with:** the statistical confidence interval or confidence level, which is a different concept.

**See:** [Implementation 3.1.3](#implementation-3.1.3:-define-acceptable-risk-thresholds-and-associated-control-responses), [Implementation 3.2.2](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints), [Implementation 3.3.3](#implementation-3.3.3:-actionable-operator-decision-&-escalation-pathways), [Implementation 4.2.3](#implementation-4.2.3:-human-centered-interfaces-for-si-uncertainty-and-actionable-triggers), [Task 4.6](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output), [Implementation 4.6.2](#implementation-4.6.2:-derive-confidence-and-rationale-for-learned-components-from-their-decision-processes).

## Critical infrastructure {#critical-infrastructure}

Systems and assets, physical or virtual, so vital that their incapacity or destruction would have a debilitating impact on security, the economy, public health or safety, or any combination of these. This profile is framed around the 16 critical infrastructure sectors defined in National Security Memorandum 22 (NSM-22), and its Practices apply more broadly to any high-consequence application.

**Collides with:** “CI”, which has several established meanings among the profile’s readers: counterintelligence, in cleared industry, insider threat and security programs; configuration item, in configuration and change management (NIST SP 800-128); continuous integration, as in CI/CD pipelines, in software development; and confidence interval, in statistics. This profile spells out critical infrastructure in body text and keeps CI in some titles; the acronym SICI is a name rather than an abbreviation to be expanded.

**See also:** High-consequence application.

## Data poisoning {#data-poisoning}

Deliberately corrupting data that an AI system learns from or draws on, so that it behaves as an attacker intends. In this profile it covers training and fine-tuning data, data that an adaptive or online-learning system keeps learning from in operation, and content a system retrieves or holds in its context or memory, such as a document planted in a retrieval knowledge base.

**Also called:** training data poisoning, knowledge base poisoning, memory and context poisoning, context window poisoning.

**See:** [Implementation 3.8.1](#implementation-3.8.1:-si-attack-surface-mapping-\(adversarial-exposure\)); [Task 7.2](#task-7.2:-validate,-select,-and-prepare-data-for-si-systems); [Implementation 7.2.1](#implementation-7.2.1:-implement-data-quality-monitoring); [Implementation 7.3.3](#implementation-7.3.3:-freeze-adaptation-of-online-learning-si-systems-during-operational-windows); [Implementation 8.1.5](#implementation-8.1.5:-multi-agent-cascade-reconstruction-capabilities).

**See also:** model poisoning, where the model itself is altered, for example through a compromised vendor update ([Implementation 6.1.1](#implementation-6.1.1:-add-si-disclosure-to-existing-procurement-policies)).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025), from NIST. Appendix A defines “data poisoning” as an adversary controlling part of the training data, and Section 3.4.2 treats knowledge base poisoning separately as an attack on RAG systems; this profile uses the one term for all of these.  
* **Guidance** [OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/), Version 2026, December 2025, from the Agentic Security Initiative of the OWASP Gen AI Security Project, a volunteer community project. ASI06, Memory & Context Poisoning, describes adversaries corrupting or seeding the context an agent retains, retrieves or reuses, such as summaries, embeddings and RAG stores, so that its later reasoning, planning or tool use becomes biased or unsafe; this matches the entry’s “memory and context poisoning”.  
* **Guidance** Artificial Intelligence Executive Oversight Group AI Lexicon (the Shared Artificial Intelligence (AI) Lexicon), February 2026, from the Artificial Intelligence Executive Oversight Group, a public-private partnership formed by the U.S. Department of the Treasury with the FBIIC and FSSCC. The entry “Data poisoning” limits the term to corrupting training data, as does NIST AI 100-2; financial services readers using the lexicon may read it more narrowly than this profile, which also covers retrieved content and memory.

## Design basis {#design-basis}

The conditions an item is deliberately designed to withstand, chosen with regard to their likelihood, their consequences, and the resources available, such as the severity of flood, the size of a surge, or the capability of an adversary. Conditions beyond the design basis are possible but judged too unlikely to design for; they are still examined so that the organization understands what would happen, and plans for it where it can.

**Collides with:** the regulatory sense in nuclear safety, where design bases are defined in 10 CFR 50.2 as “the specific functions to be performed by a structure, system, or component of a facility, and the specific values or ranges of values chosen for controlling parameters as reference bounds for design”, and where the design-basis threat has a specific regulatory meaning (10 CFR 73.1). This profile uses the term in its general engineering sense and does not invoke those requirements.

**See:** How Far to Go; [Appendix A](#appendix-a:-trustworthiness-characteristics), A.3.1; [Implementation 4.4.3](#implementation-4.4.3:-managing-correlated-multi-system-attention-surges); [Task 11.2](#task-11.2:-define-manual-and-alternative-operating-procedures-for-long-term-mission-continuity).

**References:**

* **Regulation** [10 CFR 50.2, Definitions](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-10/chapter-I/part-50/subpart-A/section-50.2), from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Defines design bases as the specific functions a structure, system, or component must perform and the values or ranges chosen as reference bounds for design.
* **Regulation** [10 CFR 73.1, Purpose and scope](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-10/chapter-I/part-73/subpart-A/section-73.1), from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Sets out the design basis threats against which safeguards systems are designed.
* **Guidance** [NRC glossary, “Beyond design-basis accidents”](https://www.nrc.gov/education-regulatory-research/glossary/beyond-design-basis-accidents), from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Describes accident sequences that are possible but were not fully considered in the design process because they were judged too unlikely, and that are analyzed to understand the capability of a design.
* **Guidance** [NRC glossary, “Design-basis accident”](https://www.nrc.gov/education-regulatory-research/glossary/design-basis-accident) and [“Design-basis threat (DBT)”](https://www.nrc.gov/education-regulatory-research/glossary/design-basis-threat-dbt), from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v1r1, Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v1r1), from NIST. Appendix D.3, Security Design Order of Precedence, speaks of the system design basis for loss potential, reduced to an acceptable level within the constraints of cost, schedule, and performance.
* **Guidance** [USGS, “The 100-Year Flood”](https://www.usgs.gov/water-science-school/science/100-year-flood), from the U.S. Geological Survey. Explains return periods, such as a flood with a 1 percent chance of being equaled or exceeded in any year.
* **Guidance** [UK National Risk Register 2023](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-risk-register-2023), from the UK Government. Plans against a reasonable worst-case scenario for each risk.

## Digital twin {#digital-twin}

A detailed virtual replica of physical equipment or a process, kept up to date with data from the real system. The profile uses digital twins mainly as places to test AI systems, rehearse incidents and train staff where doing so on live equipment would be unsafe, and as simulated environments in which to train AI models across their full operating range. It notes that a twin cannot reproduce every real-world condition, and that twin predictions should be compared with live telemetry to detect divergence. A digital twin that uses learned or symbolic models for forecasting or “what-if” planning is also an AI application in its own right, and is in scope.

**Also called:** high-fidelity digital twin, twin.

**See:** Section 1.2 (Scope); [Implementation 1.3.1](#implementation-1.3.1:-define-tevv-scope-and-requirements-per-si-system); [Implementation 1.3.2](#implementation-1.3.2:-categorization-of-testing-environments); [Implementation 1.4.1](#implementation-1.4.1:-maintenance-&-operations); [Implementation 2.3.3](#implementation-2.3.3:-use-digital-twins-to-regularly-test-si-system-behavior); [Implementation 2.5.1](#implementation-2.5.1:-train-across-the-full-operating-range); [Implementation 8.1.4](#implementation-8.1.4:-conduct-incident-reconstruction-drills); [Implementation 9.2.2](#implementation-9.2.2:-implement-realistic-incident-simulation-training); [Task 11.5](#task-11.5:-execute-periodic-mission-continuity-simulations-and-stress-tests); [Implementation 11.5.2](#implementation-11.5.2:-execute-high-fidelity-simulation-drills-involving-total-si-infrastructure-loss-and-recovery); [Implementation 12.3.1](#implementation-12.3.1:-isolated-execution-testing-\(sandboxing\)).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), from NIST. Appendix E.2.8, Digital Twins, describes their use in OT as an anomaly detection tool that compares real-time sensor inputs against a baseline model.

## Diversity (in redundancy) {#diversity-\(in-redundancy\)}

Building redundant paths from implementations that differ from one another, for example in model architecture, training data, supplier, hosting or technology, so that a single fault, attack or other common cause is less likely to disable every path at once. Diversity can be more apparent than real: secondary models that share a foundation model, training data or hosting provider may fail together. Diversity among AI models alone, which [Implementation 2.2.1](#implementation-2.2.1:-maintain-backup-systems-proportionate-to-consequence) calls heterogeneous AI redundancy, does less against a cause in the operating environment, such as distribution drift that reaches every model built on similar data; a backup that differs in technology, or a physical interlock, holds under the same drift, provided its behavior does not rest on the same training data or on other potentially correlated sources of error. Some shared design assumptions are usually unavoidable; those that remain warrant particularly careful verification, since a flaw in one would reach every path. Such a backup may itself use AI techniques, such as rule-based reasoning or planning.

**Also called:** heterogeneity, heterogeneous redundancy, heterogeneous AI redundancy; design diversity and supply chain diversity are forms of it.

**See:** [Task 2.2](#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions); [Implementation 2.2.1](#implementation-2.2.1:-maintain-backup-systems-proportionate-to-consequence); [Implementation 3.2.5](#implementation-3.2.5:-artifact-verification); **redundancy gradient**; **common-cause failure**.

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v2r1, Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v2r1), from NIST. Table D-2 defines the Diversity technique, and Table D-4 its Design Diversity and Supply Chain Diversity approaches; the NIST technique emphasizes threats that exploit common vulnerabilities, while this profile applies it equally to non-adversarial failures. **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Controls SC-29, Heterogeneity, and SA-17(9), Design Diversity.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v1r1, Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v1r1), from NIST. Principle E.11, Diversity (Dynamicity), states that a design incorporating diversity helps to avoid common mode failures and introduces unpredictability to adversaries, and lists variation in structure, behavior, interfaces, data and control flow, and technology and component selection; unlike the 800-160v2r1 technique, it is not limited to threats.

## Drift {#drift}

In this profile, the difference between the data or conditions an SI system was trained or designed for and those it meets in use, arising from changes in, for example, its inputs, the operating environment, the equipment, the population served or the task. The term names the difference itself, not a trend: drift can be gradual or sudden, and it does not necessarily grow, since it can grow and then shrink again, as with seasonal factors. Drift can degrade performance while the SI system itself is unchanged, so change management alone does not reveal it; it is detected by comparing operation against baselines.

**Also called:** distribution drift, distribution shift, data drift, operational drift. In this profile, “model drift” and “behavioral drift” usually refer to the resulting change in a model’s performance or behavior.

**Contrast:** calibration drift, in which an instrument’s reading moves away from the true value ([Implementation 2.3.3](#implementation-2.3.3:-use-digital-twins-to-regularly-test-si-system-behavior), [Implementation 7.2.4](#implementation-7.2.4:-select-and-prepare-the-inputs-each-si-system-receives)). It is a property of the sensor rather than of the SI system, but it can be one cause of drift in the SI system’s inputs. Also configuration drift, in which a system’s running configuration departs from its approved baseline ([Implementation 12.3.3](#implementation-12.3.3:-monitoring-for-latent-failures)). Unlike drift in this entry’s sense, it is a change to the system itself, and it is found by comparing the configuration against that baseline.

**Collides with:** “concept drift”, which has two incompatible senses. NIST SP 1270 uses it for “Use of a system outside the planned domain of application”, with no element of change over time, which is closer to this entry or to an out-of-distribution input. In machine learning, concept drift is a change in the relationship between a system’s inputs and the correct output, so that “the decision boundary moves” even though the input data have not changed (ISO/IEC 22989:2022). Gama and colleagues describe this second sense as “an online supervised learning scenario when the relation between the input data and the target variable changes over time”, which can happen with or without a change in the input distribution, and suddenly, gradually or in recurring patterns. Monitoring of input statistics alone may not detect concept drift in that second sense.

**See:** [Implementation 2.3.4](#implementation-2.3.4:-recurrent-risk-evaluations), [Implementation 3.3.2](#implementation-3.3.2:-establish-maximum-drift-thresholds), [Task 3.4](#task-3.4:-monitor-for-anomalous-si-behavior), [Task 6.2](#task-6.2:-align-si-and-existing-ci-asset-lifecycle-management), [Task 10.3](#task-10.3:-implement-systematic-audit-review-and-performance-trend-analysis).

**See also:** Out-of-distribution input; Diversity (in redundancy); Training cutoff.

**References:**

* **Standard** [ISO/IEC 22989:2022, Information technology: Artificial intelligence: Artificial intelligence concepts and terminology](https://www.iso.org/standard/74296.html), from ISO and IEC. Clause 5.11.9.1, Retraining, distinguishes data drift, in which “the accuracy of the model’s predictions decays over time due to changes in the statistical characteristics of the production data”, from concept drift, in which “the decision boundary moves”; this entry’s drift corresponds to the first, without assuming that the difference only grows.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 1270, Towards a Standard for Identifying and Managing Bias in Artificial Intelligence](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.1270), March 2022, from NIST.
