Section 5, Glossary, defines “concept drift” as “Use of a system outside the planned domain of application, and a common cause of performance gaps between laboratory settings and the real world”; this is the first sense under Collides with.  
* **Research** [Gama, J., Žliobaitė, I., Bifet, A., Pechenizkiy, M. and Bouchachia, A., “A Survey on Concept Drift Adaptation”, ACM Computing Surveys 46(4), Article 44, 2014](https://doi.org/10.1145/2523813). Defines concept drift as a change over time in the relation between input data and target variable, distinguishes “real concept drift”, a change in the output given the input, from “virtual drift”, a change in the input distribution alone, and describes drift that is sudden, incremental, gradual or reoccurring. A change in the task or population served, which this entry includes, can produce either kind.

## Embedded AI {#embedded-ai}

An AI capability built into a larger software product, service or device, where the people operating it may not realize it is there or what kind of AI it is. AI features may also be added to existing software during routine updates.

**Collides with:** embedded systems engineering, where “embedded” means computing built into a device or cyber-physical system, such as a controller. This profile uses the word in both senses, so readers may miss AI features inside SaaS and enterprise software.

**See:** Section 1.2 (Scope), [Implementation 6.1.1](#implementation-6.1.1:-add-si-disclosure-to-existing-procurement-policies), [Implementation 6.2.1](#implementation-6.2.1:-register-externally-sourced-si-components-in-asset-management-systems), [Task 7.1](#task-7.1:-maintain-an-internal-registry-of-si-deployments), [Implementation 13.1.4](#implementation-13.1.4:-establish-what-retirement-the-product-itself-supports).

**References:**

* **Standard** [ISO/IEC 22989:2022, Information technology: Artificial intelligence: Artificial intelligence concepts and terminology](https://www.iso.org/standard/74296.html), from ISO and IEC. Clause 5.14.1 describes AI as a component in embedded systems such as the internet of things and cyber-physical systems; this is the embedded-systems sense the entry lists under “Collides with”, not AI hidden inside software products.  
* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance led by the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Section 2.3, Understanding the Role of OT Vendors in AI Integration, advises demanding transparency from OT vendors on how AI is embedded in their products, including contractual detail on AI features and the option to disable them; this addresses the entry’s concern that operators may not know AI is present.

## Fail loudly {#fail-loudly}

To make a failure or degradation immediately and explicitly known to people, even if the system keeps running, perhaps in a degraded capacity. Failing loudly concerns notification and is separate from moving to a **fail-safe state**, although an unacknowledged loud failure may be set to force that move. How loudly to fail is weighed against the limited attention of the people receiving the alarms.

**Contrast:** quiet failure, where autonomous recovery or the resilience of other agents masks a degradation ([Task 3.3](#task-3.3:-establish-failure-notification-requirements)).

**Collides with:** “failover” in IT continuity usage, the capability to “switch over automatically (typically without human intervention or warning) to a redundant or standby system” (NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5). A silent switch to a backup or fallback controller, such as one forced by a watchdog ([Implementation 2.2.2](#implementation-2.2.2:-deploy-“watchdog”-controllers)), is a form of the quiet failure described under Contrast.

**See:** [Task 3.3](#task-3.3:-establish-failure-notification-requirements), [Implementation 3.3.1](#implementation-3.3.1:-context-specific-failure-modes), [Task 4.4](#task-4.4:-attention-governance-and-alert/alarm-flood-mitigation).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. The Discussion for control SI-17, Fail-Safe Procedures, includes alerting operator personnel as part of fail-safe procedures; this profile separates the notification (failing loudly) from the move to a fail-safe state.

## Fail-safe state {#fail-safe-state}

A predefined state (or states), chosen for the specific application, that the controlled process moves to when an AI output violates its constraints, an AI action is refused, the AI system becomes unavailable or degraded, or a person overrides or disengages it. It may hold last-known-safe setpoints, revert to conservative baselines or hand control to an independent deterministic controller. It does not necessarily mean shutting down, which can itself be the hazard, and where an action is refused part-way through a sequence it accounts for the steps already taken.

Despite the name, a fail-safe state is rarely free of risk. It is chosen because it is expected to be safer than continuing in the condition that triggered it. The fail-safe state carries hazards of its own, such as lost production or service, reduced capability, or more demand on the people who take over. Those hazards are best identified and planned for when the state is chosen.

**Also called:** safe state, known-safe state, fallback state, safe fallback state, pre-defined safe state.

**Note:** The same caveat applies to each. This profile uses “fallback behavior” for the wider set of responses, including for requests that do not act on the physical process.

**Contrast:** fallback behavior, the wider set of responses to a failure or refusal, which may also keep the SI-enabled function running in a degraded mode rather than moving the process to a defined state ([Implementation 3.2.3](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior)).

**Collides with:** functional safety, where fail-safe can mean the de-energized state; the profile uses that sense where it refers to E-stops ([Implementation 4.1.2](#implementation-4.1.2:-establish-tiered-intervention-procedures,-training,-and-authorization)) and to a process that can be stopped safely ([Practice 4](#practice-4:-define-procedures-for-emergency-avoidance-override,-recovery,-and-situational-awareness)). Also security usage, where IETF RFC 4949 gives “fail-safe” two senses that it calls “opposing design alternatives”: a synonym for fail-secure, which preserves a secure state though some resource may be damaged, and “A mode of termination of system functions that prevents damage to specified system resources and system entities” when a failure occurs, though the failure might still compromise security. CNSSI 4009 (2015) adopts only the second. Both senses describe ways of terminating system functions; a fail-safe state in this profile may keep the process running.

**See:** [Implementation 3.2.3](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior), [Task 3.2](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs), [Implementation 5.2.2](#implementation-5.2.2:-action-level,-context-aware-authorization-policies), [Implementation 2.2.2](#implementation-2.2.2:-deploy-“watchdog”-controllers), [Task 3.3](#task-3.3:-establish-failure-notification-requirements).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), from NIST. Section 5.3.1 describes fail-to-a-known-state (fail-safe) design as placing equipment or the process in a safe state that prevents injury or property damage and avoids cascading events or secondary hazards, and says organizations should define thresholds for operating with reduced capabilities; this entry adds that the state actually reached may fall short of that aim.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control SC-24, Fail in Known State, has organizations define the known state and the state information preserved in failure; this profile’s fail-safe state is the application-specific known state, extended to refused AI actions part-way through a sequence.  
* **Guidance** [NIST IR 8183r1, Cybersecurity Framework Version 1.1 Manufacturing Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.IR.8183r1), October 2020, from NIST. Appendix B, Glossary, defines “Fail to Known State”, in which a system that fails because of a disruption event fails to a predetermined state, and says that “Failure in a known safe state helps to prevent systems from failing to a state that may cause injury to individuals or destruction to property.” It adds preserving system state information so that the system can restart with less disruption.

## Fine-tuning {#fine-tuning}

Further training an existing AI model, such as a foundation model, on an organization’s own or task-specific data to adapt it to a particular task or domain. Fine-tuning changes the model itself, unlike **retrieval-augmented generation**, which changes what the model is given with each request. The profile asks that the source and authorization of fine-tuning data be documented, and that fine-tuned versions, such as adapters, be tracked in the AI asset list with their lineage back to the base model.

**Also called:** local fine-tuning; continuous local fine-tuning (when done during operation).

**See:** [Implementation 7.1.1](#implementation-7.1.1:-create-and-maintain-a-master-si-asset-list); [Implementation 7.1.2](#implementation-7.1.2:-maintain-a-data-inventory); [Task 7.2](#task-7.2:-validate,-select,-and-prepare-data-for-si-systems); [Implementation 7.3.3](#implementation-7.3.3:-freeze-adaptation-of-online-learning-si-systems-during-operational-windows).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025), from NIST. Appendix A defines “fine-tuning” in the same sense.

## Foundation model {#foundation-model}

A large AI model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many different tasks, for example by fine-tuning. Large language models are one kind. Many AI products are built on the same few foundation models, so one model’s flaws or retirement can affect many systems at once.

**See:** [Implementation 2.2.1](#implementation-2.2.1:-maintain-backup-systems-proportionate-to-consequence), [Implementation 7.1.1](#implementation-7.1.1:-create-and-maintain-a-master-si-asset-list), [Implementation 13.1.1](#implementation-13.1.1:-identify-retirement-triggers,-including-those-outside-the-organization’s-control).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025), from NIST. Appendix A defines “foundation model”, consistent with this entry, adding that such models are trained by self-supervised learning; its definition opens “In generative AI”, a limit this entry does not share.  
* **Guidance** Artificial Intelligence Executive Oversight Group AI Lexicon (the Shared Artificial Intelligence (AI) Lexicon), February 2026, from the Artificial Intelligence Executive Oversight Group, a public-private partnership formed by the U.S. Department of the Treasury with the FBIIC and FSSCC. The entry “Foundation models” describes large machine learning models trained on vast amounts of unlabeled data and adaptable to many downstream tasks, with large language models as a common subset; consistent with this entry, though it says unsupervised where NIST AI 100-2 says self-supervised learning.  
* **Regulation** [Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act](http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), 13 June 2024, from the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union. Article 3(63) defines “general-purpose AI model”, the closest EU term to this profile’s foundation model, as a model that displays significant generality and can be integrated into a variety of downstream systems or applications; this matches the entry’s concern that one model’s flaws can reach many systems.

## General-purpose AI assistant {#general-purpose-ai-assistant}

An AI tool, such as a chatbot, built for a wide range of tasks and not designed or vetted for a specific critical infrastructure use. The profile covers these when they generate configuration files, automation code or operational procedures, or summarize operationally relevant material, even with no direct connection to a control loop. Lighter controls may suit purely informational output, but once that output informs an operational decision or a deployed configuration, full guardrail rigor applies.

**Also called:** general-purpose LLM-based assistant.

**See:** Section 1.2 (Scope), [Implementation 3.1.1](#implementation-3.1.1:-identify-si-system-decision-points-and-potential-outcomes-of-si-system-errors), [Task 3.2](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs).

**References:**

* **Regulation** [Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act](http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), 13 June 2024, from the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union. Article 3(66) defines “general-purpose AI system” as an AI system based on a general-purpose AI model that can serve a variety of purposes; this profile’s term is narrower, meaning assistant tools not vetted for a specific critical infrastructure use.  
* **Guidance** Artificial Intelligence Executive Oversight Group AI Lexicon (the Shared Artificial Intelligence (AI) Lexicon), February 2026, from the Artificial Intelligence Executive Oversight Group, a public-private partnership formed by the U.S. Department of the Treasury with the FBIIC and FSSCC. The entry “General purpose AI” defines AI designed for a broad array of tasks rather than for a specific domain, consistent with this entry’s “not designed or vetted for a specific CI use”.

## Generative AI {#generative-ai}

An AI system, or a capability of one, that produces new content, such as text, code, images, audio, configurations or plans, that is related to the data it learned from, in response to a prompt or other instruction. In this profile the term describes what a system does, not how it is built. A system described colloquially as an LLM (see Large language model) usually includes generative output, and it may combine generative components with symbolic, rule-based and hand-written ones, such as guardrails. The profile’s concerns about generated content apply to the generated output, whichever component produced it: it can be fluent and plausible yet wrong (see Hallucination), and it should be checked before it is relied on or acted upon.

**Contrast:** Predictive or discriminative AI, which classifies inputs or forecasts values rather than producing new content. Many critical infrastructure systems combine the two, for example a predictive anomaly detector with a generative assistant that summarizes its alerts.

**Collides with:** Everyday usage in which “AI” means generative AI, especially chatbots. In this profile, AI (and SI) covers predictive, generative and control systems alike (see AI).

**See:** Section 1.2 (Scope); [Appendix B](#appendix-b:-scenario-to-practice-mapping) (B.5).

**See also:** Large language model; Hallucination; Foundation model.

**References:**

* **Research** [Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations (NIST AI 100-2e2025)](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025), March 2025, from NIST. The opening of Section 3 describes GenAI as a branch of AI that develops models that can generate content with similar properties to their training data, and its taxonomy divides attacks into predictive and generative AI; the Glossary defines discriminative methods.  
* **Guidance** [Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (NIST AI 600-1)](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1), July 2024, from NIST. A cross-sectoral AI RMF profile for generative AI; Section 2 lists risks unique to or exacerbated by it, including confabulation.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-218A, Secure Software Development Practices for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models: An SSDF Community Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218A), July 2024, from NIST. Appendix A, Glossary, defines “generative artificial intelligence”, citing Executive Order 14110, as “The class of AI models that emulate the structure and characteristics of input data in order to generate derived synthetic content”; this entry describes the same capability, for systems as well as models.

## Graceful degradation {#graceful-degradation}

Continuing to provide essential service at reduced capability when part of a system, such as an AI component, is not performing as expected, rather than failing abruptly. In [Task 2.2](#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions) it means the SI-enabled function continuing in a reduced or derated mode, as distinct from transferring to a fail-safe state or manual control; in NIST SP 800-82r3 it also covers shedding automation in stages down to manual operation.

**Also called:** degraded mode, derated operation.

**See:** Trustworthiness Characteristics table (Resilient), [Practice 2](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations), [Task 2.2](#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions), [Implementation 1.3.1](#implementation-1.3.1:-define-tevv-scope-and-requirements-per-si-system), [Practice 11](#practice-11:-maintain-si-aware-mission-continuity-and-disaster-recovery-planning).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), from NIST. The Executive Summary, under maintaining functionality during adverse conditions, describes graceful degradation as moving from normal operation with full automation, through emergency operation with operators more involved, to manual operation with no automation; consistent with this entry.  
* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-1), from NIST. Section 3.3, Secure and Resilient, describes AI systems as resilient if, among other things, they can maintain their functions and structure in the face of change and degrade safely and gracefully when necessary (adapted from ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022); consistent with this entry.

## Guardrail {#guardrail}

A loose term for a control that constrains what an SI system can do. Guardrails can sit within the SI component, such as instructions it is given or behaviors trained into it, or around it, such as filters on its inputs and outputs or limits on the rate at which it acts, and they may or may not be independent of it or themselves AI-based. This profile uses the term across that range: for the process-informed limits of [Implementation 2.1.2](#implementation-2.1.2:-develop-process-informed-guardrails), for the guardrails built into SI products or set by their vendors ([Implementation 5.3.3](#implementation-5.3.3:-separate-privilege-via-encapsulated-downstream-agents-and-tools), [Implementation 6.1.2](#implementation-6.1.2:-require-sibom-for-mission-critical-applications), [Implementation 6.2.2](#implementation-6.2.2:-track-vendor-updates-and-third-party-entity-changes-through-change-management-process)), and for the independent, deterministic checks of [Task 3.2](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs), which it calls safety wrappers. Where independence matters, the profile says “safety wrapper” or “independent guardrail”.

**Collides with:** “guardrails” in AI security and vendor usage, which are often assumed to provide protection whatever their independence; a guardrail that is not independent of the SI system does not by itself meet [Task 3.2](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs).

**See:** Safety wrapper; [Implementation 2.1.2](#implementation-2.1.2:-develop-process-informed-guardrails); [Implementation 5.3.3](#implementation-5.3.3:-separate-privilege-via-encapsulated-downstream-agents-and-tools); [Implementation 6.1.2](#implementation-6.1.2:-require-sibom-for-mission-critical-applications); [Implementation 6.2.2](#implementation-6.2.2:-track-vendor-updates-and-third-party-entity-changes-through-change-management-process).

## Hallucination {#hallucination}

Output from an AI system that sounds plausible and confident but is false or not supported by its inputs or sources. The profile is most concerned with the “plausible hallucination”, which reads as correct to a non-expert, for example a maintenance step that looks valid but would damage equipment. NIST AI 600-1 calls this risk *confabulation*.

**Also called:** confabulation, plausible hallucination.

**See:** [Implementation 2.4.3](#implementation-2.4.3:-technical-accuracy-and-“plausible-hallucination”-audits), [Implementation 3.8.2](#implementation-3.8.2:-system-wide-risk-surface-mapping-\(non-adversarial-trustworthiness-exposure\)), [Task 4.6](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output), [Implementation 12.2.2](#implementation-12.2.2:-subject-matter-expert-\(sme\)-review-of-procedures).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 600-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1), from NIST. Section 2.2, Confabulation, defines the risk and notes “hallucination” as a colloquial term for it.  
* **Guidance** Artificial Intelligence Executive Oversight Group AI Lexicon (the Shared Artificial Intelligence (AI) Lexicon), February 2026, from the Artificial Intelligence Executive Oversight Group, a public-private partnership formed by the U.S. Department of the Treasury with the FBIIC and FSSCC. The entry “Hallucination” defines output that is erroneous or flawed but in the form of a convincing narrative or presentation, and notes it can occur even when the underlying data is free of defects; this matches the entry’s “plausible hallucination”.  
* **Guidance** [OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-genai-llm-top-10-2026/), Version 2026, August 4, 2026, from the OWASP GenAI Security Project, a volunteer community project. LLM07:2026, Misinformation, lists hallucination among the causes of incorrect output that appears credible enough to be trusted and acted on by people, workflows or agents; this matches the profile’s concern with outputs that read as correct.

## Hazard reachability {#hazard-reachability}

Whether a known limitation or vulnerability of an AI component can actually lead to harm in a particular deployment, given the controls around it. A hazard shown to be unreachable is described as *contained* or operationally unreachable (VEX status “Not Affected”). The profile handles software flaws through standard VEX and model behaviors through contextual hazard reachability ([Implementation 6.1.5](#implementation-6.1.5:-operational-si-hazard-reachability-disclosures)). Reachability can change when autonomy is widened, agents are chained or the operating environment moves, even if the record still shows the hazard as contained.

**Also called:** contextual hazard reachability (for model behaviors specifically).

**Collides with:** “containment” in incident response, meaning preventing an incident from expanding, which the profile also uses ([Implementation 5.1.1](#implementation-5.1.1:-audit-for-and-replace-shared-credentials,-service-accounts,-secrets,-passwords,-and-api-keys)); and “containment” of consequence or blast radius ([Task 3.5](#task-3.5:-define-and-control-risks-to-adjacent-and-related-systems)).

**See:** [Task 3.8](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface), [Implementation 3.8.3](#implementation-3.8.3:-dynamic-risk-surface-coupling-analysis), [Implementation 6.1.5](#implementation-6.1.5:-operational-si-hazard-reachability-disclosures), [Task 4.4](#task-4.4:-attention-governance-and-alert/alarm-flood-mitigation).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-61r3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-61r3), from NIST. The notes to subcategory RS.MI-01 define containment as preventing the expansion of an incident, a different sense from “contained” here.  
* **Guidance** [Minimum Requirements for Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange (VEX)](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/minimum-requirements-vulnerability-exploitability-exchange-vex), April 2023, from CISA. Section 2.7.1.1.3 lists justifications for “not\_affected”, such as vulnerable code not in the execute path, not controllable by an attacker, or blocked by inline mitigations; the software-vulnerability analogue of a hazard shown to be contained in a deployment.

## Human oversight {#human-oversight}

An umbrella term for arrangements by which people remain responsible for an AI system’s behavior in operation. It denotes a category, not a single control, and comprises four distinct objects defined below: oversight mode, oversight capacity, oversight threshold and oversight authority. [Task 3.9](#task-3.9:-assess-and-document-organizational-readiness-for-each-si-enabled-capability) refers to oversight authority as decision authority.

**See:** [Implementation 1.3.1](#implementation-1.3.1:-define-tevv-scope-and-requirements-per-si-system), [Task 3.9](#task-3.9:-assess-and-document-organizational-readiness-for-each-si-enabled-capability), [Practice 4](#practice-4:-define-procedures-for-emergency-avoidance-override,-recovery,-and-situational-awareness), [Task 4.4](#task-4.4:-attention-governance-and-alert/alarm-flood-mitigation), [Task 4.5](#task-4.5:-define-operational-regimes-for-human-on-the-loop-and-human-out-of-the-loop-operation).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-1), from NIST. Subcategory MAP 3.5 is that processes for human oversight are defined, assessed and documented, and GOVERN 3.2 that policies and procedures define and differentiate roles and responsibilities for human-AI configurations and oversight; neither separates oversight into the four objects this profile defines.  
* **Regulation** [Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act](http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), 13 June 2024, from the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union. Article 14 sets out human oversight of high-risk AI systems, with measures commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use, including the ability to override the output and to interrupt the system so that it comes to a halt in a safe state; it applies only to systems the Act classes as high-risk.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 1270, Towards a Standard for Identifying and Managing Bias in Artificial Intelligence](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.1270), from NIST. Section 3.3.1, under “Human-in-the-loop”, calls the perception that a human can effectively and objectively oversee algorithmic decision systems a problematic assumption, notes that human-in-the-loop practices are not intended to serve as a form of oversight, and says optimistic expectations of human oversight are not borne out without significant procedural and cultural support.

ISO/IEC DIS 42105, Guidance for Human Oversight of AI Systems, and ISO/IEC TS 8200:2024, Controllability of Automated Systems, are also under consideration.

### Oversight mode {#oversight-mode}

The regime governing how a person participates in an AI system’s decisions: human-in-the-loop (approval required before action), human-on-the-loop (action proceeds, with intervention capability retained), or human-out-of-the-loop (autonomous execution with retrospective review). The three are ordered from most to least direct human participation; “more restrictive” and “reduced” in this profile refer to that order. [Task 4.5](#task-4.5:-define-operational-regimes-for-human-on-the-loop-and-human-out-of-the-loop-operation) defines the boundaries between them.

**Also called:** oversight regime, operational regime.

**Collides with:** “human-in-the-loop” in modeling and simulation, “A model that requires human interaction” (DoD 5000.59-M, DoD Modeling and Simulation (M\&S) Glossary, January 1998), such as a simulation with human participants; that sense would also cover what this profile calls human-on-the-loop.

**See:** [Task 4.5](#task-4.5:-define-operational-regimes-for-human-on-the-loop-and-human-out-of-the-loop-operation), [Implementation 1.3.1](#implementation-1.3.1:-define-tevv-scope-and-requirements-per-si-system), [Implementation 3.2.5](#implementation-3.2.5:-artifact-verification), [Implementation 4.5.2](#implementation-4.5.2:-establish-deterministic-boundary-constraints-for-automated-regimes).

**See also:** **human oversight**, **oversight authority**.

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance led by the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Section 4.1 discusses human-in-the-loop decision-making for SI-enabled OT, and Section 4.2 failsafe mechanisms, including how to bypass or replace an AI system.  
* **Standard** [ISO/IEC 22989:2022, Information technology: Artificial intelligence: Artificial intelligence concepts and terminology](https://www.iso.org/standard/74296.html), from ISO and IEC. Clause 5.13, Table 1, sets out levels of automation from 0 (no automation) to 6 (autonomy), with level 3, conditional automation, relying on an external agent ready to take over when necessary; these describe the system’s automation, whereas oversight mode describes the person’s participation.  
* **Guidance** Artificial Intelligence Executive Oversight Group AI Lexicon (the Shared Artificial Intelligence (AI) Lexicon), February 2026, from the Artificial Intelligence Executive Oversight Group, a public-private partnership formed by the U.S. Department of the Treasury with the FBIIC and FSSCC. The entry “Human-in-the-Loop (HITL)” defines a risk-control approach in which a human is integrated within the AI’s decision-making process; it does not distinguish approval before action from intervention after, which this profile’s three modes separate.

### Oversight capacity {#oversight-capacity}

The finite human attention available to exercise oversight, measured across all AI systems drawing on the same pool of people rather than per system. Capacity is exhaustible, is consumed concurrently by every system an operator supervises, and can be saturated by a correlated event even where each system’s individual demand is manageable. Applied to a single review step ([Implementation 3.2.5](#implementation-3.2.5:-artifact-verification)), it also means the time and competence the reviewer has to examine what is in front of them.

**Also called:** operator triage capacity, oversight pool.

**See:** [Implementation 1.3.1](#implementation-1.3.1:-define-tevv-scope-and-requirements-per-si-system), [Task 4.4](#task-4.4:-attention-governance-and-alert/alarm-flood-mitigation), [Implementation 4.4.3](#implementation-4.4.3:-managing-correlated-multi-system-attention-surges).

**See also:** **human oversight**, **alarm flood**.

**References:**

* **Guidance** [EEMUA Publication 191, Alarm Systems: A Guide to Design, Management and Procurement](https://www.eemua.org/products/publications/print/eemua-publication-191), from the Engineering Equipment and Materials Users’ Association. The process-industry guide to alarm system design, which frames alarm load against what an operator can handle.  
* **Guidance** Health and Safety Executive (2000), [Better alarm handling](https://www.hse.gov.uk/pubns/chis6.pdf), Chemicals Sheet No 6, from Great Britain’s workplace health and safety regulator. States alarm-rate targets for process plant operators.  
* **Research** [Simon, H. (1971), “Designing Organizations for an Information-Rich World”](https://gwern.net/doc/design/1971-simon.pdf). Argues that in an information-rich world attention is the scarce resource, and that the design principle “that attention is scarce and must be preserved” differs from “the more information the better”; this profile applies the same point to the human attention available to oversee AI systems.

### Oversight threshold {#oversight-threshold}

The point beyond which a given oversight mode ceases to be effective: where the interval between an anomaly and an irreversible consequence is shorter than what human intervention can be relied upon to achieve, or where the judgment the person would have to make cannot reliably be made in the time available. [Implementation 4.5.1](#implementation-4.5.1:-define-engineering-time-constant-thresholds) defines how these are established.

**See:** [Task 4.5](#task-4.5:-define-operational-regimes-for-human-on-the-loop-and-human-out-of-the-loop-operation), [Implementation 4.5.1](#implementation-4.5.1:-define-engineering-time-constant-thresholds), [Implementation 3.8.3](#implementation-3.8.3:-dynamic-risk-surface-coupling-analysis).

**See also:** **human oversight**.

**References:**

* **Standard** ISA-84 / IEC 61511, Functional Safety: Safety Instrumented Systems for the Process Industry Sector, from the International Society of Automation and the International Electrotechnical Commission. The process-industry standard for automated protective layers that act where human response cannot be relied on.  
* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance led by the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Section 4.1, under Human-in-the-Loop Decision-Making, cautions that with active AI systems directly influencing control, problems can escalate before operators become aware of them, and suggests safety thresholds and intervention points; this is the condition the oversight threshold names, without a time-constant test.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v1r1, Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v1r1), from NIST. Principle E.4, Commensurate Response, matches the aggressiveness of a response action to the immediacy needed to control each loss scenario, and notes that the severity of the problem and the time available for an effective response dictate the strategy; a related principle, since the oversight threshold also turns on the time available to respond.

### Oversight authority {#oversight-authority}

The authority, held by a named role, to accept the risk of operating an SI-enabled capability in a given oversight mode, to change that mode, and to restrict, suspend, roll back or reduce the capability’s delegated authority. Distinct from the ability to intervene in a particular action: authority persists in regimes where real-time intervention is infeasible.

**Contrast:** the authorizing official of the NIST Risk Management Framework, a “Senior (federal) official or executive with the authority to formally assume responsibility for operating an information system at an acceptable level of risk” (NIST SP 800-39). That authority covers operating the system as a whole. Oversight authority is held for one SI-enabled capability in a given oversight mode. Some frameworks and obligations, such as SP 800-37, limit the delegation of risk acceptance. Which role holds oversight authority depends on the obligations that apply to the organization.

**See:** [Implementation 3.9.2](#implementation-3.9.2:-define-decision-authority-and-reassessment-triggers), [Task 4.5](#task-4.5:-define-operational-regimes-for-human-on-the-loop-and-human-out-of-the-loop-operation).

**See also:** **human oversight**, **operating envelope**.

**References:**

* **Regulation** [Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Artificial Intelligence Act](http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), 13 June 2024, from the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union. Article 26(2) provides that deployers of high-risk AI systems assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support; it names authority as a condition of oversight but does not define its scope as this profile does.  
* **Standard** [ISO/IEC 22989:2022, Information technology: Artificial intelligence: Artificial intelligence concepts and terminology](https://www.iso.org/standard/74296.html), from ISO and IEC. Clause 5.15.5, AI controllability, identifies determining which agents can control which components of an AI system as a key aspect of controllability; oversight authority is narrower, the named authority to set and change the oversight mode and revoke the operating envelope.

## Industrial control system (ICS) {#industrial-control-system-\(ics\)}

A control system that monitors and manipulates physical processes, such as supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems, distributed control systems (DCS) and programmable logic controllers (PLCs), made up of control components that act together to achieve an industrial objective. ICS are a subset of operational technology (OT), which also includes systems such as building automation and physical access control.

**Also called:** industrial automation and control system (IACS).

**Note:** IACS is the ISA/IEC 62443 term.

**Collides with:** in emergency management and public safety, ICS more commonly means the Incident Command System, the standardized incident management structure within the National Incident Management System (NIMS). This profile does not use ICS in that sense.

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), from NIST. Appendix B defines “industrial control system” and “operational technology”.

## Inference receipt {#inference-receipt}

A record created each time an AI system providing decision support or diagnostics from structured data produces an output, capturing the data elements it used, the thresholds in effect and the versioned configuration. Where the system applies encoded rules or is self-interpretable, the receipt can also record the rules or branches applied. It lets the output be traced and checked later.

**Contrast:** audit trail, “A chronological record that reconstructs and examines the sequence of activities surrounding or leading to a specific operation, procedure, or event in a security-relevant transaction from inception to result” (NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5). An audit trail records what was done and in what order; an inference receipt records what a single output was based on, so existing audit logging does not necessarily provide it.

**See:** [Implementation 4.6.3](#implementation-4.6.3:-display-execution-traces-from-symbolic,-hybrid,-and-self-interpretable-components), [Task 10.1](#task-10.1:-define-decision-level-logging-and-metadata-retention-policies), [Implementation 10.1.2](#implementation-10.1.2:-runtime-telemetry-and-artifact-tracking).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Agentic Identity and Access Management](https://www.coalitionforsecureai.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/agentic-identity-and-access-control.pdf), Workstream 4: Secure Design Patterns for Agentic Systems, version 1.0, 20 March 2026, from the Coalition for Secure AI, an OASIS Open Project. Appendix E’s logging schema lists what logs should capture for each significant agent action, including the decision and reason, scopes used, policy version and attestation information; it logs authorization decisions rather than the data and thresholds behind an output.  
* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance led by the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Section 4.1, in its example of monitoring a predictive maintenance system, recommends an audit trail logging all AI system operating data, including timestamps, inputs and outputs, for analysis of AI behavior; an inference receipt adds the thresholds, versioned configuration and rules applied, so the output can be checked as well as traced.

## Intercept point {#intercept-point}

A place in the path between an AI system’s output and its effect where that output can be monitored, checked, blocked or overridden by something other than the AI system. One path may have several: in the profile’s example of an AI system recommending setpoints, they include the setpoint interface, the local controller and existing emergency shutoff mechanisms. Intercept points are where **safety wrappers** and override procedures can act. A wrapper may check or block outputs at some of them, and at others act through an existing mechanism, for example by triggering an emergency shutoff where that is practical and permitted by policy and regulation. It should not gate commands from protective functions such as emergency stops ([Implementation 3.2.2](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints)), except where a simple stop would itself be unsafe, as in a dynamically unstable process; there, a stop request may go to logic that carries out a safe shutdown sequence.

**Also called:** AI output intercept point, operational intercept point.

**See:** [Implementation 3.2.1](#implementation-3.2.1:-identify-si-output-intercept-points); [Task 3.2](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs); [Implementation 4.1.1](#implementation-4.1.1:-ensure-that-si-systems-can-be-reliably-overridden); Appendix C.1.

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance led by the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Section 4.1, under Human-in-the-Loop Decision-Making, recommends that where AI is actively updating control logic, safety thresholds, alternative sensor output or state changes be used to add human-in-the-loop intervention points; intercept points in this profile also include automated checks, not only human ones.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v1r1, Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v1r1), from NIST. Principle E.19, Mediated Access, states that all access to and operations on system elements are mediated, and separates the access mediation decision from its enforcement; an intercept point is a place where such mediation can be applied to an AI system’s output before it takes effect.

## Interlock {#interlock}

A mechanism that blocks an action, or forces a protective action, unless defined conditions are met. In this profile it mostly means a physical or hardware safety interlock at the process boundary that holds regardless of what an AI system commands, at the high-consequence end of the **redundancy gradient**. The profile also uses it for logic conditions on a trigger, such as the “state-aware interlocks” that stop a watchdog from forcing a failover during a sensitive process transition, and for automated “policy interlocks” in non-physical processes.

**Also called:** safety interlock, physical interlock, hardware interlock.

**See also:** safety instrumented system (SIS), the engineered system that takes a process to a safe state, which an AI system should not be able to affect ([Implementation 3.5.3](#implementation-3.5.3:-impact-compartmentalization-\(sandboxing\))).

**See:** [Task 2.2](#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions); [Implementation 2.2.1](#implementation-2.2.1:-maintain-backup-systems-proportionate-to-consequence); [Implementation 2.2.2](#implementation-2.2.2:-deploy-“watchdog”-controllers); [Implementation 2.3.4](#implementation-2.3.4:-recurrent-risk-evaluations); [Implementation 3.1.1](#implementation-3.1.1:-identify-si-system-decision-points-and-potential-outcomes-of-si-system-errors); [Implementation 3.2.1](#implementation-3.2.1:-identify-si-output-intercept-points); [Implementation 3.2.2](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints); [Task 4.5](#task-4.5:-define-operational-regimes-for-human-on-the-loop-and-human-out-of-the-loop-operation); [Implementation 11.2.3](#implementation-11.2.3:-human-factors-and-cognitive-transition-protocols-for-control-handoffs).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-82r3, Guide to Operational Technology (OT) Security](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-82r3), from NIST. Appendix B defines “safety instrumented system”, giving “safety interlock system” as another name; it does not define “interlock” on its own. Section 2.3.7, Safety Systems, describes an SIS as often independent of other control systems, so that a failure of the basic process control system will not impair it, and notes integrated control and safety systems that do communicate with the control system; relevant to the entry’s point that interlocks hold regardless of what an AI system commands.

## Knowledge graph {#knowledge-graph}

In this profile, the YAML file distributed with the Markdown version of the document. It lists every Practice, Task and Implementation by item number, with the cross-references between them, their trustworthiness characteristics, AI RMF subcategories, references and [Appendix B](#appendix-b:-scenario-to-practice-mapping) incidents, so that an LLM-based assistant can check that it has seen every item and follow the links between them. It is generated from the Markdown by a script and adds no content; where the two differ, the document governs.

**Collides with:** the general data-management sense, a database of entities and relationships used as a knowledge source in its own right.

**See:** Section 1.4; [Section 2](#2:-the-profile); [Appendix E](#appendix-e:-suggested-ways-to-use-this-document-with-an-llm-based-assistant) (E.1).

## Known-safe {#known-safe}

Describes a state, setting, mode of operation or controller whose behavior has been established in advance, through analysis, testing or operating history, to be acceptably safe under the conditions it was assessed for. “Known” refers to that prior assessment, not to a guarantee: a known-safe state is safe only as far as the assessment holds, and may not be if conditions have moved outside what was assessed. **Last-known-safe** setpoints are the most recent values assessed or observed to be safe. They are a sensible default when an AI system’s output is blocked or lost, but they reflect conditions at the time they were recorded, which may since have changed.

**Contrast:** known-good, which this profile uses for a configuration, procedure or artifact version that has been verified to work and is kept for rollback ([Task 12.3](#task-12.3:-manage-operational-continuity-and-resilience-for-generated-artifacts), [Implementation 12.3.2](#implementation-12.3.2:-version-control-and-rollback-procedures)). A known-good configuration restores function; a known-safe state limits harm. One need not be the other.

**See also:** fail-safe state.

**See:** [Practice 2](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations), [Task 3.2](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs), [Implementation 3.2.3](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior), [Implementation 4.1.2](#implementation-4.1.2:-establish-tiered-intervention-procedures,-training,-and-authorization).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control SC-24, Fail in Known State, has organizations define the known state a system fails to and the state information it preserves.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v1r1, Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v1r1), from NIST. Appendix B, Glossary, defines “safety” as “Expectation that a system does not, under defined conditions, lead to a state in which human life, health, property, or the environment is endangered”; like this entry, it ties safety to defined conditions.  
* **Guidance** [NIST IR 8183r1, Cybersecurity Framework Version 1.1 Manufacturing Profile](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.IR.8183r1), October 2020, from NIST. Appendix B, Glossary, defines “Fail to Known State” as failing to a predetermined state, and says that “Failure in a known safe state helps to prevent systems from failing to a state that may cause injury to individuals or destruction to property.” As in this entry, the state is established in advance.  
* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance led by the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Section 4.1 asks operators to establish and maintain a known good state, or thresholds for safe behavior, against which departures can be recognized.

## Large language model (LLM) {#large-language-model-\(llm\)}

In this profile, an LLM is the whole system that the general public colloquially refers to (e.g., “Which LLM are you using to summarize your emails?”), not only the model at its core. Such a system typically combines one or more large statistical language models with other components: additional models, symbolic and rule-based components, retrieval of external data, tool and agent interfaces, hand-written instructions and code, and guardrails that filter inputs and outputs. Its behavior comes from all of these together, and these components may be changed by the provider without notice. An LLM-based assistant, chatbot, or coding agent is such a system, with associated additional tools and functionality, used to help a person with the associated tasks.

In computer science, “large language model” refers more narrowly to the model alone. In current practice, this is usually a large statistical model of language, implemented as a deep learning neural network, though not every definition requires it. The model is not limited to generating text, and a system built around it need not be generative. Where this profile means the model alone, it says so.

**Also called:** LLM-based assistant, LLM-based system.

**Collides with:** the computer-science sense described above, in which “the LLM” is only the trained model. Statements that hold for the model alone, about its training data, size or architecture, do not necessarily hold for the system, and controls that act on the model do not by themselves govern the rest of the system.

**See also:** foundation model, general-purpose AI assistant, safety wrapper.

**See:** Section 1.2 (Scope), Section 1.4, [Implementation 1.4.2](#implementation-1.4.2:-administrative-&-support), [Implementation 3.7.1](#implementation-3.7.1:-si-attestation), [Appendix E](#appendix-e:-suggested-ways-to-use-this-document-with-an-llm-based-assistant).

**References:**

* **Guidance** Artificial Intelligence Executive Oversight Group AI Lexicon (the Shared Artificial Intelligence (AI) Lexicon), February 2026, from the Artificial Intelligence Executive Oversight Group, a public-private partnership formed by the U.S. Department of the Treasury with the FBIIC and FSSCC. The entry “Large language model” describes machine learning trained on large amounts of data through self-supervised learning to recognize patterns and respond to user requests in natural language, and the “Foundation models” entry calls LLMs a common subset of foundation models. This is the model-centered sense; this profile uses the term for the wider system.

## Least agency {#least-agency}

The principle that an AI system’s ability to initiate actions or invoke tools should be limited to what its defined function strictly requires, and that it should not use access unnecessarily even where access exists. It extends to what an AI system carries forward between steps, such as context and memory, as well as what it can initiate. It differs from least privilege, which limits the resources and authorizations the system is granted; least agency also limits how much the system decides and does on its own within them.

**Contrast:** excessive agency.

**See:** [Task 5.3](#task-5.3:-implement-principles-of-least-agency-and-least-privilege-for-si-entities), [Implementation 5.3.1](#implementation-5.3.1:-determine-the-practical-minimum-necessary-permissions-for-a-specific-task-and-apply-them-to-the-si-system), [Implementation 5.3.3](#implementation-5.3.3:-separate-privilege-via-encapsulated-downstream-agents-and-tools), [Implementation 5.3.4](#implementation-5.3.4:-limit-the-context-carried-forward-between-steps), [Practice 5](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Appendix A defines the related principle “least privilege”, which limits the access and authorizations granted; least agency limits what the system initiates.  
* **Guidance** [OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/), Version 2026, December 2025, from the Agentic Security Initiative of the OWASP Gen AI Security Project, a volunteer community project. The opening letter describes “Least-Agency” as extending least privilege and excessive agency, advising organizations to avoid unnecessary autonomy, and ASI02 mitigation 1 pairs least agency with least privilege for tools; consistent with this entry.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v1r1, Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v1r1), from NIST. Principle E.14, Least Functionality, states that each system element has the capability to accomplish its required functions but no more; least agency applies this to what an AI system can initiate.

## Operating envelope {#operating-envelope}

The defined range of conditions, such as input and output ranges, setpoint limits, latency limits, physical tolerances and dependencies, within which an AI system is specified and validated to operate.

**Also called:** operating window, boundary envelope.

**Note:** [Practice 3](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior) and [Task 3.2](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs) also speak of the process’s “safe operating envelope”: the limits the physical process must stay within, which guardrails enforce regardless of the AI system. That is the process-safety sense below, and where both are meant the document specifies so.

**Collides with:** aviation flight envelope; process-safety safe operating limits.

**See:** [Implementation 1.1.2](#implementation-1.1.2:-structured-requirements-mapping), [Implementation 1.3.1](#implementation-1.3.1:-define-tevv-scope-and-requirements-per-si-system), [Implementation 2.5.1](#implementation-2.5.1:-train-across-the-full-operating-range); for the process sense, [Practice 3](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior) and [Task 3.2](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs); [Implementation 3.2.2](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints) combines both senses as “safe operating limits.”

**References:**

* **Regulation** [DoD Manual 5000.101, “Operational Test and Evaluation and Live Fire Test and Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence-Enabled and Autonomous Systems,” December 9, 2024](https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodm/5000101p.pdf), a policy issuance of the United States Department of Defense. Paragraph 3.3.a.(3)(d) evaluates how predictable a system is across its operating envelope, including when it exits the expected performance envelope, and paragraph 4.1.b.(1) asks test plans to account for conditions that may take it outside its expected parameters and quantified bounds; it uses the term without defining it.

## Operational enforceability {#operational-enforceability}

The demonstrated ability to turn a governance decision about an SI-enabled capability, such as restricting, suspending, rolling back or reducing its delegated authority, into an actual change in what the system does. [Implementation 3.9.5](#implementation-3.9.5:-demonstrate-operational-enforceability) tests whether that change is effective, timely relative to consequence, verifiable without relying solely on the capability’s own report, durable and sufficient in scope.

**See:** [Task 3.9](#task-3.9:-assess-and-document-organizational-readiness-for-each-si-enabled-capability), [Implementation 3.9.4](#implementation-3.9.4:-assess-operational-capability), [Implementation 3.9.5](#implementation-3.9.5:-demonstrate-operational-enforceability).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-1), from NIST. Subcategory MANAGE 2.4 is that mechanisms are in place and applied, and responsibilities are assigned and understood, to supersede, disengage or deactivate AI systems whose performance or outcomes are inconsistent with intended use; operational enforceability is the tested ability of such mechanisms to change what the system actually does, timely and verifiably.  
* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance led by the United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Section 2.3 advises specifying, in arrangements with OT vendors, conditions under which AI features can be disabled or enabled, with control given to the operator; relevant to enforceability where the capability is embedded in a vendor product.

## Organizational readiness {#organizational-readiness}

A determination, made for one SI-enabled capability in its operating context, that the accountability, authority, escalation paths, operational capability and enforceability needed to govern it are actually in place and can be exercised, so that a governance decision, once made, takes effect in the running system. It is made before deployment and again after any material change, and it is not a general organizational maturity assessment.

**Collides with:** “workforce readiness” ([Task 9.3](#task-9.3:-establish-audit-ready-systems-for-verifying-workforce-readiness)), which is the training competence of personnel.

**See:** [Task 3.9](#task-3.9:-assess-and-document-organizational-readiness-for-each-si-enabled-capability), [Implementation 3.9.2](#implementation-3.9.2:-define-decision-authority-and-reassessment-triggers), [Implementation 3.9.5](#implementation-3.9.5:-demonstrate-operational-enforceability).

**See also:** **operational enforceability**.

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-1), from NIST. Subcategory MANAGE 1.1 is that a determination is made as to whether the AI system achieves its intended purposes and stated objectives and whether its development or deployment should proceed; organizational readiness is a narrower determination, whether the governance needed for that capability is actually in place.

## Out-of-band {#out-of-band}

Operating through a separate, independent path from the system being monitored or controlled, so that a failure or compromise of that system does not reach it.

**Collides with:** IT out-of-band management and authentication, which is the same idea in a narrower sense.

**See:** [Task 4.3](#task-4.3:-establish-independent-\(“out-of-band”\)-communication,-monitoring,-alerting,-and-control-capabilities), [Implementation 2.2.2](#implementation-2.2.2:-deploy-“watchdog”-controllers), [Implementation 3.2.2](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints), [Implementation 4.3.2](#implementation-4.3.2:-implement-si-independent-channels), [Task 7.3](#task-7.3:-manage-version-control-and-logging-for-internal-si-safety-mechanisms).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control SC-37, Out-of-Band Channels, describes channels such as local non-network access, physically separate network paths and non-electronic paths, distinct from those carrying routine operational traffic, so that compromise of in-band channels does not affect them; this profile extends the idea from channels to monitoring and control paths.

## Out-of-distribution input {#out-of-distribution-input}

An input or operating condition unlike those an AI system was trained or designed for, where its behavior is less predictable.

**Also called:** novel input, unhistorical conditions.

**Note:** Related to drift (see Drift), the overall difference between the data a system was trained or designed for and the data it meets in use; out-of-distribution describes the individual input or condition.

**Collides with:** “concept drift” in NIST SP 1270, defined as “Use of a system outside the planned domain of application”, which is close to this entry and has no element of change over time. In machine learning the same term means something different (see Drift).

**See:** [Implementation 3.3.3](#implementation-3.3.3:-actionable-operator-decision-&-escalation-pathways), [Implementation 4.2.3](#implementation-4.2.3:-human-centered-interfaces-for-si-uncertainty-and-actionable-triggers), [Task 9.2](#task-9.2:-deliver-specialized-training-on-human-si-interaction-and-automation-bias).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025), from NIST. Appendix A defines “out-of-distribution” data in terms of how it was collected relative to the training data; this profile also covers conditions a non-learned system was not designed for.  
* **Standard** [ISO/IEC 22989:2022, Information technology: Artificial intelligence: Artificial intelligence concepts and terminology](https://www.iso.org/standard/74296.html), from ISO and IEC. Clause 5.15.2, AI robustness, describes robustness as comparable performance on atypical data or on inputs dissimilar to those the system was trained on; it names the property that out-of-distribution inputs test, without defining the inputs themselves.

## Post-hoc explanation {#post-hoc-explanation}

An explanation of an AI output generated afterward, typically by a separate tool that probes how outputs change with inputs (for example SHAP or LIME). Its output is a hypothesis about why the model may have behaved as it did, not a record of what it did.

**Also called:** post-hoc attribution, post-hoc statistical explanation.

**Contrast:** introspective explanation, drawn from the process that produced the output ([Task 4.6](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output)). A surrogate model distilled from a learned model is a post-hoc explanation when it is used to explain that model, and an introspective one only when it is deployed in its place ([Implementation 4.6.4](#implementation-4.6.4:-distill-learned-models-into-interpretable-models-that-can-be-verified)).

**See:** [Task 1.4](#task-1.4:-establish-the-si-system’s-domain-knowledge-and-linguistic-alignment-requirements), [Implementation 4.6.2](#implementation-4.6.2:-derive-confidence-and-rationale-for-learned-components-from-their-decision-processes), [Implementation 8.1.2](#implementation-8.1.2:-identify-si-systems-that-may-not-satisfy-root-cause-analysis-requirements), [Implementation 10.1.2](#implementation-10.1.2:-runtime-telemetry-and-artifact-tracking), [Task 12.1](#task-12.1:-establish-governance-and-accountability-for-si-generated-execution-artifacts), [Implementation 12.1.2](#implementation-12.1.2:-provenance-and-traceability).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST IR 8312, Four Principles of Explainable Artificial Intelligence](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.IR.8312), from NIST. Section 6 defines post-hoc explanations as explanations, often generated by other software tools, that describe, explain or model an algorithm to give an idea of how it works, contrasting them with self-interpretable models; Section 6.2 divides them into local and global explanations.  
* **Guidance** [NIST IR 8367, Psychological Foundations of Explainability and Interpretability in Artificial Intelligence](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.IR.8367), from NIST. Section 3.2.1 says LIME replaces a causal description of a model with a simpler model whose results are only correlated with it, that SHAP shares its strengths and weaknesses, and that both are prone to unknown error outside the local neighborhood of a prediction; this supports the entry’s point that the output is a hypothesis.

## Prompt compromise {#prompt-compromise}

Loss of integrity or confidentiality of the instructions an AI system works from, such as its system prompt, standing instructions or the context it is given. Integrity is lost when the instructions are altered, whether by prompt injection, a changed system prompt, an insider or a compromised update. Confidentiality is lost when instructions that are legitimate but sensitive are leaked. System prompts can contain internal procedures, the conditions under which the system refuses, or credentials, and a leak can help an attacker get around controls.

**Forms include:** prompt injection; system prompt leakage, also called prompt extraction when it is done deliberately.

**See:** [Implementation 5.1.1](#implementation-5.1.1:-audit-for-and-replace-shared-credentials,-service-accounts,-secrets,-passwords,-and-api-keys), [Implementation 5.3.3](#implementation-5.3.3:-separate-privilege-via-encapsulated-downstream-agents-and-tools), [Task 7.3](#task-7.3:-manage-version-control-and-logging-for-internal-si-safety-mechanisms).

**See also:** Prompt injection.

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025), March 2025, from NIST. Section 3.1.1 describes system prompts and notes that, because they may be security-relevant, a prompt extraction attack may try to steal them; the Glossary defines prompt extraction.  
* **Guidance** [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025](https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/), from the OWASP GenAI Security Project. LLM07:2025, System Prompt Leakage, describes system prompts that contain sensitive information not intended to be discovered, and advises against relying on the system prompt to keep secrets or enforce controls.

\> To the Reviewer: The 2025 OWASP list is cited here because its LLM07 item is the clearest source; the draft elsewhere cites the 2026 list in which LLM08:2026, Hidden Context Exposure, appears to cover the same ground. We would welcome views on which to cite.

## Prompt injection {#prompt-injection}

An attack in which instructions placed in an AI system’s input, either typed directly or hidden in content the system reads (indirect prompt injection), cause it to ignore its intended instructions or take unintended actions.

**See also:** Prompt compromise, the broader term, which also covers prompts altered by other routes and sensitive prompts that are leaked.

**See:** [Implementation 3.8.1](#implementation-3.8.1:-si-attack-surface-mapping-\(adversarial-exposure\)), [Implementation 3.2.2](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints), [Implementation 5.3.3](#implementation-5.3.3:-separate-privilege-via-encapsulated-downstream-agents-and-tools).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025), from NIST. Appendix A defines “prompt injection”, with direct and indirect forms, consistent with this entry.  
* **Guidance** [OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-genai-llm-top-10-2026/), Version 2026, August 4, 2026, from the OWASP GenAI Security Project, a volunteer community project. LLM01:2026, Prompt Injection, lists direct and indirect forms, including injection through retrieved content and low-privilege but trusted channels, and states that no reliable prevention mechanism exists today, so defense is architectural; consistent with this profile’s use of controls outside the model.

## Protective AI capability {#protective-ai-capability}

An SI system that performs a detection, monitoring, screening or filtering function, and so provides a protective function for other systems, acting as a control for them whether or not it is formally recorded as one. Retiring it removes that control, so the profile treats its retirement as a change to controls as well as an asset disposal. That includes establishing what it had learned to detect that is not documented elsewhere, and what will perform the function afterward.

**Contrast:** protective functions in general, which need not be implemented with AI. Those named in [Implementation 3.2.2](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints), such as protective relay trips, safety instrumented system shutdowns and emergency stops, are usually conventional, and a safety wrapper does not gate their commands. Where SI logic takes the place of a simple stop as a protective function, [Implementation 3.2.2](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints) expects it to be far less complex than the SI system it backs up, independent of it, and verified to the standard of a protective function.

**See:** [Implementation 13.3.2](#implementation-13.3.2:-treat-the-retirement-of-a-protective-si-capability-as-a-change-to-controls); [Task 13.3](#task-13.3:-preserve-what-is-needed-and-hand-over-what-depended-on-the-system).

## Redundancy gradient {#redundancy-gradient}

The profile’s scheme for matching how independent a backup is to how severe the consequences of failure would be. For lower- and moderate-consequence functions where a non-AI fallback is not technically feasible, the backup may be a secondary AI model with a different architecture, training data and hosting (see **diversity (in redundancy)**). For high-consequence or cyber-physical functions, it escalates to include independent deterministic algorithms or out-of-band, non-AI physical safety **interlocks**, which may be paired with an AI backup. The degree of independence is set by the severity of consequences rather than from what is convenient to build.

**Collides with:** “deterministic” in its computing sense, a deterministic algorithm being “An algorithm that, given the same inputs, always produces the same outputs” (NIST SP 800-90A Rev. 1). Being deterministic does not make a component non-AI: classical planning and logical inference are often deterministic, and a trained model may or may not be, depending on how inference is run. What the redundancy gradient relies on is a fallback that shares as little as practical with the SI system, particularly its training data, and fully specified and verified in advance, including any design assumptions it shares with the SI system.

**See:** [Implementation 2.2.1](#implementation-2.2.1:-maintain-backup-systems-proportionate-to-consequence); [Task 2.2](#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions); [Implementation 3.1.3](#implementation-3.1.3:-define-acceptable-risk-thresholds-and-associated-control-responses).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v1r1, Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v1r1), from NIST. Principle E.6, Commensurate Trustworthiness, makes the trustworthiness required of an element commensurate with the most significant adverse effect of its failure, and E.26, Redundancy, notes that redundant solutions are susceptible to common mode failure, with diversity as a means to address it; the gradient applies this scaling to how independent a backup must be.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v2r1, Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v2r1), from NIST. Structural design principle D.5.2.6, Maintain Redundancy, says Redundancy for cyber resiliency should be applied in conjunction with Diversity and considered at multiple layers, and warns that trends to convergence can undermine it; the gradient adds a rule tying the degree of independence to consequence.

## Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) {#retrieval-augmented-generation-\(rag\)}

An AI system design in which, for each request, the model is given information retrieved from a separate store, such as a document collection, database or vector store, and uses it to produce its output. The system’s behavior therefore depends on what is in that store as well as on the model, and changing the store changes the behavior without any change to the model.

**Also called:** retrieval augmentation, retrieval-augmented system; the store is called a knowledge base or retrieval-augmented data repository.

**Collides with:** “knowledge base” in symbolic AI ([Implementation 4.6.3](#implementation-4.6.3:-display-execution-traces-from-symbolic,-hybrid,-and-self-interpretable-components)), where it means the encoded rules a system reasons with, not documents it retrieves.

**See:** [Practice 6](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management); [Implementation 6.1.2](#implementation-6.1.2:-require-sibom-for-mission-critical-applications); [Implementation 7.1.2](#implementation-7.1.2:-maintain-a-data-inventory); [Task 7.2](#task-7.2:-validate,-select,-and-prepare-data-for-si-systems); [Implementation 7.4.1](#implementation-7.4.1:-define-and-implement-requirements-for-approvals-and-logging-of-updates-and-changes-to-si-systems).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025), from NIST. Appendix A defines “retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)” in the same sense.  
* **Guidance** [OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-genai-llm-top-10-2026/), Version 2026, August 4, 2026, from the OWASP GenAI Security Project, a volunteer community project. LLM09:2026, Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, names RAG as the most familiar case of similarity search deciding what the model sees, and states that the embedding layer then becomes part of the application’s trust boundary; consistent with the entry’s point that the store, not only the model, shapes behavior.

## Risk surface {#risk-surface}

The full set of ways in which an AI system can cause physical, operational or administrative harm, across all the trustworthiness characteristics, whether an attacker is involved or not. It includes the attack surface. The profile often names both, as in “attack and risk surface”, for emphasis and for readers who know only one of the terms. It can grow or shrink over time as the environment, the data or the degree of autonomy changes, which [Implementation 3.8.3](#implementation-3.8.3:-dynamic-risk-surface-coupling-analysis) tracks. [Implementation 3.8.2](#implementation-3.8.2:-system-wide-risk-surface-mapping-\(non-adversarial-trustworthiness-exposure\)) maps its non-adversarial part, and [Implementation 8.1.6](#implementation-8.1.6:-incident-triage-across-the-dual-attack/risk-surface) triages incidents between the adversarial and non-adversarial parts.

**Collides with:** Usage that treats the two as separate, with “risk surface” meaning only harm that involves no attacker.

**See:** [Task 3.8](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface), [Implementation 3.8.2](#implementation-3.8.2:-system-wide-risk-surface-mapping-\(non-adversarial-trustworthiness-exposure\)), [Implementation 3.8.3](#implementation-3.8.3:-dynamic-risk-surface-coupling-analysis), [Implementation 8.1.6](#implementation-8.1.6:-incident-triage-across-the-dual-attack/risk-surface), [Practice 8](#practice-8:-incorporate-si-aware-incident-analysis-and-response-procedures), [Task 8.1](#task-8.1:-identify-scenarios-requiring-deterministic-root-cause-analysis-and-incident-reconstruction), [Task 10.1](#task-10.1:-define-decision-level-logging-and-metadata-retention-policies), [Practice 10](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities).

**See also:** Attack surface.

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Principles for the Secure Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2025-12/joint-guidance-principles-for-the-secure-integration-of-artificial-intelligence-in-operational-technology-508c.pdf), December 2025, joint guidance from nine national cybersecurity agencies across seven countries, led by CISA. Section 2.1 asks operators to weigh the impact of expanding the environment’s risk surface, including the security infrastructure needed to protect the expanded attack surface.

## Root cause analysis {#root-cause-analysis}

In this profile, establishing why a particular incident, failure or SI output occurred, so that its cause can be corrected and the correction shown.
