For an SI system this usually rests on reconstructing what the system received and produced, including its inputs, versions and settings; a post-hoc explanation offers a hypothesis about the cause, not a record of it ([Implementation 8.1.2](#implementation-8.1.2:-identify-si-systems-that-may-not-satisfy-root-cause-analysis-requirements)). [Task 8.1](#task-8.1:-identify-scenarios-requiring-deterministic-root-cause-analysis-and-incident-reconstruction) identifies where root cause analysis must rest on deterministic reconstruction, and [Task 8.2](#task-8.2:-identify-additional-controls-that-may-be-required-in-scenarios-where-deterministic-root-cause-analysis-is-not-possible) the additional controls that may be needed where that is not possible.

**Collides with:** “root cause analysis” in risk management, a “systems approach for the identification of underlying causes associated with a particular set of risks” (NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1), which looks for the causes of a set of risks rather than reconstructing a specific incident.

**See:** [Practice 8](#practice-8:-incorporate-si-aware-incident-analysis-and-response-procedures), [Task 8.1](#task-8.1:-identify-scenarios-requiring-deterministic-root-cause-analysis-and-incident-reconstruction), [Task 8.2](#task-8.2:-identify-additional-controls-that-may-be-required-in-scenarios-where-deterministic-root-cause-analysis-is-not-possible), [Implementation 8.1.2](#implementation-8.1.2:-identify-si-systems-that-may-not-satisfy-root-cause-analysis-requirements), [Implementation 8.2.1](#implementation-8.2.1:-identify-applications-and-situations-for-which-root-cause-analysis-requirements-may-be-relaxed), [Implementation 11.4.1](#implementation-11.4.1:-define-a-checklist-for-validating-system-safety-before-re-engaging-si-control).

## Safety wrapper {#safety-wrapper}

A hard-coded, deterministic control, as independent of the AI system as practical and not itself AI-based, that checks AI outputs or commands against defined constraints and limits or blocks them, engages fallback controllers, notifies operators and logs the event when a constraint would be violated. Where it guards a physical process, it applies whichever upstream source issued the command, such as an SI recommendation, an automated agent, a remote operator session or another upstream system, except for commands from protective functions, which the wrapper does not gate, and authorized overrides; for SI systems that generate information rather than commands, the constraint may instead be one of completeness or fidelity ([Implementation 3.2.2](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints)). In either case the constraints do not depend on the AI system’s own confidence values. It can only bound the hazards that were identified and written as constraints.

**Also called:** independent guardrail, boundary logic, safety/policy wrapper. “Validation control” is used in [Implementation 3.4.3](#implementation-3.4.3:-monitor-validation-control-integrity) for safety wrappers and watchdog controllers together.

**Forms include:** command validation proxy, guarded proxy ([Implementation 5.3.3](#implementation-5.3.3:-separate-privilege-via-encapsulated-downstream-agents-and-tools)).

**Contrast:** “enforcement layer”, which this profile uses for whatever enforces a check at the point of action: a safety wrapper, the action-level authorization of [Implementation 5.2.2](#implementation-5.2.2:-action-level,-context-aware-authorization-policies), or a guarded proxy ([Implementation 5.3.3](#implementation-5.3.3:-separate-privilege-via-encapsulated-downstream-agents-and-tools)), as in [Task 10.1](#task-10.1:-define-decision-level-logging-and-metadata-retention-policies), [Implementation 10.1.2](#implementation-10.1.2:-runtime-telemetry-and-artifact-tracking) and Appendix C.1. Records of what was permitted should come from it rather than from the SI system ([Implementation 10.1.2](#implementation-10.1.2:-runtime-telemetry-and-artifact-tracking)).

**Collides with:** “guardrails” in AI security writing, which can be checks at any layer of the AI system, including ones that judge prompts or generated content; these are not necessarily independent of the AI system. The profile itself also uses “guardrail” for the process-informed rate limits of [Implementation 2.1.2](#implementation-2.1.2:-develop-process-informed-guardrails), which may be deterministic and may be internal to the AI component rather than independent of it.

**See:** [Task 3.2](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs), [Implementation 3.2.2](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints), [Implementation 3.2.3](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior), [Implementation 3.4.3](#implementation-3.4.3:-monitor-validation-control-integrity), [Implementation 4.5.2](#implementation-4.5.2:-establish-deterministic-boundary-constraints-for-automated-regimes), [Implementation 5.3.3](#implementation-5.3.3:-separate-privilege-via-encapsulated-downstream-agents-and-tools), [Implementation 6.1.1](#implementation-6.1.1:-add-si-disclosure-to-existing-procurement-policies), [Task 7.3](#task-7.3:-manage-version-control-and-logging-for-internal-si-safety-mechanisms), [Task 7.5](#task-7.5:-conduct-impact-assessments-and-risk-management-for-si-system-and-model-updates).

**References:**

* **Research** Vassilev, A., [“Robust AI Security and Alignment: A Sisyphean Endeavor?”](https://doi.org/10.1109/MSEC.2026.3678214), IEEE Security & Privacy, May/June 2026\. Discusses guardrails and other checks at any layer of an LLM-based system, which need not be independent of it.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-53r5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53r5), from NIST. Control AC-25, Reference Monitor, calls for a reference monitor that is tamperproof, always invoked, and small enough to be subject to analysis and testing; a security analogue of the safety wrapper, which is likewise independent of what it checks and does not trust a command because of its source.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-207), from NIST. Section 3, Logical Components of Zero Trust Architecture, describes the policy enforcement point, which enables, monitors and terminates connections between a subject and an enterprise resource. It is a security analogue of the safety wrapper’s position between an SI system’s output and its effect, though it enforces access decisions rather than safety constraints.  
* **Guidance** Artificial Intelligence Executive Oversight Group AI Lexicon (the Shared Artificial Intelligence (AI) Lexicon), February 2026, from the Artificial Intelligence Executive Oversight Group, a public-private partnership formed by the U.S. Department of the Treasury with the FBIIC and FSSCC. The entry “Guardrails” defines layered safeguards against bad information and behavior in an AI system, which may sit at the data, model, application and infrastructure levels; this is the broader sense the entry’s Collides with note describes, with no requirement of independence from the AI system.

## Shadow mode {#shadow-mode}

Running an AI system on live inputs while its outputs are recorded but not acted on, so its behavior can be compared with the system or process actually in control.

**Also called:** passive shadow mode, silent trial, silent evaluation (in clinical AI).

**Contrast:** **silent update**, an unreviewed change to a model, which is unrelated.

**Collides with:** **shadow AI** in this profile; the “shadow model” of adversarial machine learning, a model built to imitate a target model in privacy attacks.

**See:** [Implementation 1.3.2](#implementation-1.3.2:-categorization-of-testing-environments), [Implementation 2.3.3](#implementation-2.3.3:-use-digital-twins-to-regularly-test-si-system-behavior), [Task 7.5](#task-7.5:-conduct-impact-assessments-and-risk-management-for-si-system-and-model-updates), [Implementation 7.5.2](#implementation-7.5.2:-perform-automated-“champion-challenger”-assessment), [Implementation 11.4.2](#implementation-11.4.2:-implement-“shadow-mode”-validation-and-independent-safety-protection-checks-for-si-re-commissioning).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025), from NIST. Appendix A defines “shadow model” as a model that imitates the behavior of the target model, used to train attack models in privacy attacks; this is the contrasting sense the entry’s Collides with note mentions, not a testing technique.

## Shadow SI {#shadow-si}

SI tools, models or services used within an organization’s operations without having gone through its procurement, approval or inventory processes. This includes personal LLM-based assistants and other tools brought in by staff or contractors, and models downloaded and run locally without approval. Because shadow SI sits outside credential directories and asset lists, it may bypass identity and other risk management controls; identity and access controls can detect and deny it when it tries to authenticate ([Practice 5](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools)).

**Also called:** shadow AI

**Collides with:** **shadow mode**, a testing technique in this profile.

**See:** [Task 3.7](#task-3.7:-govern-and-mitigate-risks-from-unauthorized,-transient,-and-“shadow-si”-systems), [Practice 5](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools), [Practice 7](#practice-7:-manage-internal-si-supply-chain-and-data-provenance).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [AI Shared Responsibility Framework, version 1.0](https://www.coalitionforsecureai.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/CoSAI-Shared-Responsibility-Framework.pdf), Workstream 2: Preparing Defenders for a Changing Cybersecurity Landscape, 26 May 2026, from the Coalition for Secure AI, an OASIS Open Project. Section 2.1 names shadow AI proliferation, unsanctioned AI usage that no single group monitors, as a pain point, and Appendix A.1.2.3, AI Tool Usage Governance, lists shadow AI detection and management, including discovery of ungoverned AI tool usage; consistent with this entry.  
* **Research** [NIST AI 800-4, Challenges to the Monitoring of Deployed AI Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.800-4), from NIST. Section 3.1.2 reports staff using AI services on personal accounts despite having authorized tools, as a monitoring visibility problem; it describes the practice without naming it shadow AI.

## SI Bill of Materials (SIBOM) {#si-bill-of-materials-\(sibom\)}

A record, ideally machine-readable and, for acquired systems, supplied by the vendor for each model release, of the models an AI system uses, its main training data sources, the data it retrieves at runtime and the software it depends on at training and run time; the profile also uses it to carry vendor attestations, such as representation of similar environments in the training data. It extends the idea of a software bill of materials (SBOM), but there is no vulnerability database for model behavior equivalent to the one an SBOM is checked against. Formal specifications are still being developed.

**Also called:** AI Bill of Materials, AIBOM, SBOM for AI, AI-SBOM; AI BOM (SPDX), ML-BOM (CycloneDX).

**See:** [Implementation 6.1.2](#implementation-6.1.2:-require-sibom-for-mission-critical-applications), [Implementation 6.1.5](#implementation-6.1.5:-operational-si-hazard-reachability-disclosures), [Implementation 7.1.3](#implementation-7.1.3:-integrate-automated-internal-software-and-si-bill-of-material-management).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Mitigating Artificial Intelligence (AI) Risk: Safety and Security Guidelines for Critical Infrastructure Owners and Operators](https://www.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/2024-04/24_0426_dhs_ai-ci-safety-security-guidelines-508c.pdf), April 2024, from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. Map guideline e lists AI system bills of materials (AIBOMs), with SBOMs and data and model cards, among vendor documents for supply chain review, and footnote 26 describes an AIBOM as containing SBOM-like information for AI systems; it notes that the software security and AI communities are working toward harmonized AIBOM guidance, consistent with this entry’s note that formal specifications are still being developed.  
* **Guidance** G7 Cybersecurity Working Group, A Shared G7 Vision on Software Bill of Materials for AI, 2025, a food-for-thought paper. Section 3 sets out properties of an “SBOM for AI”, including machine-readable format and capture of datasets used across the lifecycle, and example minimum elements covering models, learning, datasets, safety and security characteristics, licensing and infrastructure; its element list is broader than this entry’s.  
* **Guidance** [2026 Minimum Elements for a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/2026-minimum-elements-software-bill-materials-sbom), 29 July 2026, from CISA and co-authoring organizations. The section SBOM for AI Software Systems says AI systems may have components the minimum elements do not capture, such as model and data cards, notes ongoing discussions about SBOM for AI data fields, and does not itself add elements for AI; its footnote points to the G7 joint guidance Software Bill of Materials for AI – Minimum Elements.

## Silent update {#silent-update}

A change to an AI model or its behavior that a vendor applies without the operator being told or having reviewed it, usually also without the operator taking any action, for example a cloud-side model change. An internal change that reaches production unreviewed is the internally sourced equivalent.

**Also called:** unannounced update.

**Contrast:** cloud-side model change, which describes where a change is made rather than whether the operator is told; both a cloud-side change and an on-premises one can be announced or silent ([Implementation 6.1.1](#implementation-6.1.1:-add-si-disclosure-to-existing-procurement-policies)).

**Collides with:** “update” in software security usage, defined as “A patch, upgrade, or other modification to code that corrects security and/or functionality problems in software” (NIST SP 800-213 and NIST IR 8259A). A change-management process built on that sense may not treat a change to a model or to the instructions it is given as an update, although such a change can alter behavior without any change to code.

**See:** [Implementation 6.1.1](#implementation-6.1.1:-add-si-disclosure-to-existing-procurement-policies), [Implementation 6.2.2](#implementation-6.2.2:-track-vendor-updates-and-third-party-entity-changes-through-change-management-process), [Implementation 7.4.1](#implementation-7.4.1:-define-and-implement-requirements-for-approvals-and-logging-of-updates-and-changes-to-si-systems).

## State-at-Handoff {#state-at-handoff}

A summary shown to people taking control from an AI system: recent AI actions, active trends, accumulated task queues, unacknowledged alerts and open physical or policy constraints.

**Also called:** state-at-handoff display.

**See:** [Task 11.2](#task-11.2:-define-manual-and-alternative-operating-procedures-for-long-term-mission-continuity), [Implementation 11.2.3](#implementation-11.2.3:-human-factors-and-cognitive-transition-protocols-for-control-handoffs).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [FAA AC 120-71B, *Standard Operating Procedures and Pilot Monitoring Duties for Flight Deck Crewmembers*](https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/advisory_circulars/index.cfm/go/document.information/documentID/1030486), 10 January 2017, from the United States Federal Aviation Administration. Paragraph 6.4, items 4 and 7, says transfer of pilot flying and pilot monitoring roles should include a short brief of aircraft state, and that a pilot returning from a break should be briefed on aircraft and systems states and current ATC instructions; the aviation analogue of a state-at-handoff summary, between people rather than from an AI system.

## Super Intelligence (SI) {#super-intelligence-\(si\)}

The term this profile uses, following Executive Order 14434, for the systems defined as artificial intelligence in 15 U.S.C. § 9401\. In this profile SI and AI refer to the same systems, and the definition and scope are those set out under **artificial intelligence (AI)**. The order defines SI by reference to that statutory definition, and provides for a new definition to be proposed. Cited works, proper names, quotations, identifiers, established terms of art and keyword lists keep “AI”.

**Also called:** AI, artificial intelligence.

**Collides with:** AI research usage, where “superintelligence” means hypothetical systems whose capabilities exceed those of humans; this profile does not use the term in that sense, and covers the same everyday systems as before, including rule-based, optimization and embedded systems. Other abbreviations that read as SI or contain it: the SI family of security controls (System and Information Integrity) in NIST SP 800-53, cited in this profile as SI-6, SI-10, SI-17 and others; the International System of Units (SI); safety instrumented system (SIS) in process safety; and the identifiers ASI01 to ASI10 in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications.

**See:** footnote 1; Section 1 (Introduction).

**See also:** **artificial intelligence (AI)**.

**References:**

* **Regulation** [Executive Order 14434, Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/02/2026-20321/inaugurating-the-era-of-super-intelligence), signed 29 September 2026, published in the Federal Register 2 October 2026\. Section 2 directs executive departments and agencies to use “Super Intelligence” and “SI” in place of “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI” in non-statutory documents, and does not require previously issued documents to be altered. Section 3(a) defines the terms by reference to 15 U.S.C. § 9401(3); Section 3(b) provides for proposed legislative language for a Federal definition.

## Symbolic AI {#symbolic-ai}

AI that reasons with explicitly represented knowledge, such as rules, logic, constraints or a knowledge base, rather than with patterns learned from data. It is often deterministic, but need not be: planning, search and probabilistic reasoning can involve randomness or uncertainty. Separately, the profile relies on some logic as a fallback, verifier or interlock and describes it in the text as non-AI (for example [Task 2.2](#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions), [Implementation 2.2.2](#implementation-2.2.2:-deploy-“watchdog”-controllers)); what matters there is that its behavior is fully specified and verified in advance and independent of the SI system, not whether its technique is symbolic or deterministic. The rationale it displays can be a trace of the steps it actually applied, which shows how it reached its output but not that its rules are correct. In a hybrid system, such a trace explains only the symbolic part.

**Also called:** symbolic reasoning, logic-based, rule-based.

**See:** [Task 4.6](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output), [Implementation 2.5.1](#implementation-2.5.1:-train-across-the-full-operating-range), [Implementation 4.6.3](#implementation-4.6.3:-display-execution-traces-from-symbolic,-hybrid,-and-self-interpretable-components), [Implementation 10.1.2](#implementation-10.1.2:-runtime-telemetry-and-artifact-tracking).

**References:**

* **Standard** [ISO/IEC 22989:2022, Information technology: Artificial intelligence: Artificial intelligence concepts and terminology](https://www.iso.org/standard/74296.html), from ISO and IEC. Clause 3.1.33 defines “symbolic AI”, contrasted with subsymbolic AI in 3.1.34, and Clause 5.9 notes that modern AI systems typically combine both, as hybrid AI; consistent with this entry.  
* **Guidance** Artificial Intelligence Executive Oversight Group AI Lexicon (the Shared Artificial Intelligence (AI) Lexicon), February 2026, from the Artificial Intelligence Executive Oversight Group, a public-private partnership formed by the U.S. Department of the Treasury with the FBIIC and FSSCC. The entry “Traditional AI”, also called symbolic or rule-based AI, describes AI that performs preset tasks using predetermined algorithms and rules; it ties the term to narrow tasks, which this profile does not.

## Task-bounded authority {#task-bounded-authority}

Authority for an AI agent to act that is limited to a specific task, operational mode or time window, expires automatically and can be revoked quickly, instead of being held as standing privileges. When an agent passes work to downstream tools or sub-agents, their authority is scoped to that task as well. Where the authority cannot be checked in real time, for example at a partitioned or remote site, the profile recommends reverting to pre-engineered local fallback behavior rather than continuing on unverified standing authority.

**Also called:** task-bounded and revocable agent authority.

**See:** [Implementation 5.3.2](#implementation-5.3.2:-task-bounded-and-revocable-agent-authority); [Task 5.3](#task-5.3:-implement-principles-of-least-agency-and-least-privilege-for-si-entities); least agency; Appendix C.1.

**See also:** withdrawal of authority.

**References:**

* **Guidance** [Agentic Identity and Access Management](https://www.coalitionforsecureai.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/agentic-identity-and-access-control.pdf), Workstream 4: Secure Design Patterns for Agentic Systems, version 1.0, 20 March 2026, from the Coalition for Secure AI, an OASIS Open Project. Section 1.2 sets out eliminating standing privilege in favor of short-lived, task- and context-bounded entitlements, and Section 3.4 says scope should narrow at each delegation hop and revocation should cascade downstream; consistent with this entry.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v1r1, Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v1r1), from NIST. Principle E.15, Least Persistence, states that system elements and other resources are available, accessible and able to fulfill their design intent only for the time for which they are needed; task-bounded authority applies this to an agent’s authority to act.

## Testing, evaluation, validation and verification (TEVV) {#testing,-evaluation,-validation-and-verification-\(tevv\)}

The planned activities that produce evidence of how an AI system or one of its components performs against its requirements and previous baselines, at each stage of its lifecycle. This is the AI RMF’s umbrella term, which the AI RMF orders as test, evaluation, verification and validation. “Validation” and “verification” are used here in their general sense.

**Collides with:** “model validation” in financial-sector model risk management, “the set of processes and activities intended to verify that models are performing as expected, in line with their design objectives and business uses” (Federal Reserve SR 11-7, Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management), which spans both verification (against design objectives) and validation (against intended use) in the general senses used here.

**See:** [Task 1.3](#task-1.3:-implement-evaluation-and-test-plans,-including-tevv,-across-the-si-lifecycle) (the anchor, which sets criteria for every lifecycle stage), [Implementation 1.3.1](#implementation-1.3.1:-define-tevv-scope-and-requirements-per-si-system), [Implementation 1.3.2](#implementation-1.3.2:-categorization-of-testing-environments), [Implementation 1.3.4](#implementation-1.3.4:-generate-and-maintain-audit-ready-tevv-evidence), and [Task 2.3](#task-2.3:-establish-protocols-for-and-regularly-perform-systematic-and-achievable-testing,-evaluation,-validation,-and-verification-\(tevv\)), which extends TEVV to anomalous and edge-case conditions.

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-1), from NIST. Appendix A describes TEVV tasks performed throughout the AI lifecycle, for design, development, deployment and operations, and says those carrying out verification and validation should ideally be distinct from those performing test and evaluation; the AI RMF term this entry adopts.  
* **Standard** [ISO/IEC 22989:2022, Information technology: Artificial intelligence: Artificial intelligence concepts and terminology](https://www.iso.org/standard/74296.html), from ISO and IEC. Clauses 3.5.17 and 3.5.18 define “verification” (specified requirements have been fulfilled) and “validation” (the requirements for a specific intended use or application have been fulfilled); these are the general senses the entry says it uses.

## Training cutoff {#training-cutoff}

The most recent date covered by the data a model was trained on. Information that changed after it, such as revised guidance, procedures, or regulations, is not reflected in the model unless supplied at run time, for example through retrieval, so the model may reproduce a superseded version.

**Also called:** knowledge cutoff, training data cutoff.

**See:** [Implementation 1.1.3](#implementation-1.1.3:-establish-triggers-for-re-validating-requirements-on-change-of-operating-context), [Implementation 6.1.1](#implementation-6.1.1:-add-si-disclosure-to-existing-procurement-policies), [Practice 6](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management), [Appendix B](#appendix-b:-scenario-to-practice-mapping) (B.5).

**See also:** Drift; Foundation model.

## Watchdog controller {#watchdog-controller}

An independent, non-AI monitor, implemented in simple deterministic hardware or software, that checks an AI system’s health, latency, setpoint stability and outputs, and starts a safe fallback sequence when they fall outside set limits. It judges whether the AI system as a whole is still performing as required, where a **safety wrapper** checks each command against defined constraints.

**Also called:** enforcement application.

**Collides with:** the embedded-systems watchdog timer, which only detects a system that has stopped responding.

**See:** [Task 2.2](#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions), [Implementation 2.2.2](#implementation-2.2.2:-deploy-“watchdog”-controllers), [Implementation 2.3.4](#implementation-2.3.4:-recurrent-risk-evaluations), [Implementation 3.4.3](#implementation-3.4.3:-monitor-validation-control-integrity).

**References:**

* **Incident Report** [IRGC-Affiliated Cyber Actors Exploit PLCs in Multiple Sectors, Including US Water and Wastewater Systems Facilities, AA23-335A](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-335a), originally published 1 December 2023 and updated 18 December 2024, from CISA and partners. Recommends watchdog timers to enable quick detection of unresponsive systems; this is the narrower embedded-systems sense the entry’s Collides with note distinguishes from a watchdog controller.

## Withdrawal of authority {#withdrawal-of-authority}

In this profile, the removal of every means by which a retired AI system can still act: its credentials, tokens and keys, scheduled and event-driven triggers and registered interfaces, authority it delegated to other entities, and the compute resources that may still hold any of these. Each removal is confirmed rather than assumed, and for any delegation that cannot be confirmed revoked, what could not be confirmed is recorded, together with the decision to complete the retirement on a recorded exception or hold it open, and any compensating control.

**Collides with:** rescinding an authorization to operate, a management decision that does not by itself remove a system’s credentials or triggers.

**See:** [Practice 13](#practice-13:-establish-procedures-for-retiring-si-systems-and-withdrawing-their-authority), [Task 13.2](#task-13.2:-withdraw-all-authority-and-confirm-the-result), [Implementation 13.2.1](#implementation-13.2.1:-revoke-credentials-and-disable-triggers,-and-confirm-the-result), [Implementation 13.2.2](#implementation-13.2.2:-revoke-authority-delegated-to-other-entities,-and-record-what-could-not-be-confirmed).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-37r2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-37r2), from NIST. Appendix F describes authorization rescission, in which an authorizing official rescinds a previous authorization decision. It does not address removing a system’s credentials or triggers, which this profile’s term covers.  
* **Guidance** [Agentic Identity and Access Management](https://www.coalitionforsecureai.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/agentic-identity-and-access-control.pdf), Workstream 4: Secure Design Patterns for Agentic Systems, version 1.0, 20 March 2026, from the Coalition for Secure AI, an OASIS Open Project. Section 3.5 sets out decommissioning as revoking the agent’s identity and invalidating tokens, erasing private keys, handling sensitive data and revoking downstream delegated rights; it covers credentials and delegation, while this profile adds triggers, compute and confirmation of each removal.

## Zero trust {#zero-trust}

A cybersecurity approach in which no implicit trust is granted to users, devices or services based solely on their network location, ownership or prior authorization, and access to each resource is authenticated and authorized separately. This profile applies the underlying principle, that trust is verified at each boundary rather than assumed, to AI risk more generally. The extension is in what is not assumed: in cybersecurity, chiefly that a requester is who it claims to be and is permitted to act; here, also that a legitimate, uncompromised AI system is behaving as intended. An AI system’s outputs, actions and inputs therefore warrant verification where they cross into other systems, physical processes and human decisions, whether a departure from expected behavior arises from compromise, malfunction or a change in operating conditions. For example, an AI agent holding valid credentials is still authorized action by action ([Implementation 5.2.2](#implementation-5.2.2:-action-level,-context-aware-authorization-policies)), and guardrails independent of the AI system check its outputs before they reach a physical process ([Task 3.2](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs)).

**See:** Section 1.2 (Scope); [Task 3.2](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs); [Practice 5](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools); [Implementation 5.2.2](#implementation-5.2.2:-action-level,-context-aware-authorization-policies).

**References:**

* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-207), from NIST. Section 2.1, Tenets of Zero Trust, sets out the principles this entry extends.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v2r1, Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v2r1), from NIST. Appendix A, Glossary, defines “zero trust architecture”, whose zero trust security model “eliminates implicit trust in any one element, component, node, or service and instead requires continuous verification of the operational picture via real-time information from multiple sources to determine access and other system responses”; nearer this profile’s extension than SP 800-207, since what is verified includes the operational picture, not only the requester.  
* **Guidance** [Adapting Zero Trust Principles to Operational Technology](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/adapting-zero-trust-principles-operational-technology), April 2026, from CISA, the Department of War, the Department of Energy and partners. Applies zero trust principles to operational technology.  
* **Guidance** The Future of Agentic Security: From Chatbots to Autonomous Swarms, version 1.0, 16 March 2026, from the Coalition for Secure AI. In its scenario “The Agent That Asked for Help”, it proposes a semantic policy enforcement point extending the zero trust PEP model to the intent of agent requests, and lists applying zero trust posture assessment to a peer agent’s internal state as an unsolved research problem; close to this profile’s point that a legitimate AI system is not assumed to behave as intended.

# Appendix A: Trustworthiness Characteristics {#appendix-a:-trustworthiness-characteristics}

This appendix helps readers apply the Trustworthiness Characteristics consistently, and recognize where they pull against each other. The Trustworthiness Characteristics table introduces the 13 Trustworthiness Characteristics that this profile works with, and why each matters in critical infrastructure. This appendix adds the source definition of each characteristic and where this profile departs from it (A.1), how the grouping relates to the AI RMF’s own (A.2), distinctions between characteristics that readers often merge (A.3), the tensions between characteristics that recur across this Guidebook (A.4), and what the characteristics do not reach (A.5).

The terms and their definitions are drawn from the NIST AI RMF (1.0), which in turn draws several of them from ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022. The grouping, the emphasis placed on each characteristic, and the glosses in the Trustworthiness Characteristics table are this profile’s. Quotations below keep the source’s wording, including “AI”.

\> To the Reviewer:  
\> This appendix is new in this draft. We would particularly welcome comment on the departures from the source definitions in A.1, on whether the distinctions in A.3 help or add confusion, and on tensions you have had to balance in practice that A.4 does not describe.

## A.1 Source Definitions {#a.1-source-definitions}

Each entry below gives the definition the characteristic starts from and, where this profile uses the term more narrowly, more widely or with a different emphasis, what changes and why. Unless otherwise noted, the source is Section 3 of the AI RMF.

### A.1.1 Valid {#a.1.1-valid}

**Source definition:** Validation is the “confirmation, through the provision of objective evidence, that the requirements for a specific intended use or application have been fulfilled” (Section 3.1, citing ISO 9000:2015).

**How this profile uses it:** As in the source. The Trustworthiness Characteristics table emphasizes that validity is established for a particular deployment, so evidence from one system, place or time does not carry over to another without checking.

### A.1.2 Accurate {#a.1.2-accurate}

**Source definition:** “closeness of results of observations, computations, or estimates to the true values or the values accepted as being true” (Section 3.1, citing ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022).

**How this profile uses it:** As in the source. The Trustworthiness Characteristics table adds that the reference itself has to be chosen, and that accuracy is rarely captured by one number (A.3.4).

### A.1.3 Bias Managed {#a.1.3-bias-managed}

**Source definition:** “NIST has identified three major categories of AI bias to be considered and managed: systemic, computational and statistical, and human-cognitive. Each of these can occur in the absence of prejudice, partiality, or discriminatory intent” (Section 3.7, drawing on NIST SP 1270).

**How this profile uses it:** Separated from Fair, and without “harmful”: the AI RMF characteristic is “Fair – with Harmful Bias Managed”. This profile covers systematic error that degrades performance without harming anyone, which is common in critical infrastructure. The AI RMF itself notes that “bias is not always a negative phenomenon”. Managed means deliberately handled, not eliminated: a bias accepted for stated reasons is managed.

### A.1.4 Reliable {#a.1.4-reliable}

**Source definition:** “ability of an item to perform as required, without failure, for a given time interval, under given conditions” (Section 3.1, citing ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). The AI RMF adds that reliability is a goal for correctness “under the conditions of expected use and over a given period of time”.

**How this profile uses it:** The Trustworthiness Characteristics table says “in expected conditions and use”, so that use, and not only conditions, sets the boundary. For an SI system, and above all a general-purpose assistant, a common departure is being used for something it was not meant for, in conditions that are otherwise normal.

### A.1.5 Robust {#a.1.5-robust}

**Source definition:** “ability of a system to maintain its level of performance under a variety of circumstances” (Section 3.1, citing ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). The AI RMF adds that the system “should perform in ways that minimize potential harms to people if it is operating in an unexpected setting”.

**How this profile uses it:** As in the source, including the AI RMF’s addition, which the Trustworthiness Characteristics table carries as “limits harm” without restricting it to harm to people.

### A.1.6 Resilient {#a.1.6-resilient}

**Source definition:** Systems “may be said to be resilient if they can withstand unexpected adverse events or unexpected changes in their environment or use – or if they can maintain their functions and structure in the face of internal and external change and degrade safely and gracefully when this is necessary” (Section 3.3, adapted from ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022). The AI RMF also describes resilience as “the ability to return to normal function after an unexpected adverse event”.

**How this profile uses it:** As in the source. The Trustworthiness Characteristics table emphasizes graceful degradation and the ability to resume operation, because for many SI systems the point at which a fallback is needed is not obvious in advance.

### A.1.7 Safe {#a.1.7-safe}

**Source definition:** Systems should “not under defined conditions, lead to a state in which human life, health, property, or the environment is endangered” (Section 3.2, citing ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022).

**How this profile uses it:** As in the source, including “under defined conditions” (A.3.3). The Trustworthiness Characteristics table adds that harm can reach the process through a person acting on an SI system’s recommendation, not only through the SI system acting itself.

### A.1.8 Secure {#a.1.8-secure}

**Source definition:** “AI systems that can maintain confidentiality, integrity, and availability through protection mechanisms that prevent unauthorized access and use may be said to be secure” (Section 3.3).

**How this profile uses it:** The gloss in the Trustworthiness Characteristics table, “withstands attack”, is closer to ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022, which defines security as “resistance to intentional, unauthorized act(s) designed to cause harm or damage to a system”. An attack can change what a system does through its inputs without any unauthorized access. SI systems can be especially exposed, because inputs that look ordinary, such as subtly altered images or instructions hidden in a document, can redirect them, so a definition centered on access control alone would miss such attacks.

### A.1.9 Transparent {#a.1.9-transparent}

**Source definition:** “Transparency reflects the extent to which information about an AI system and its outputs is available to individuals interacting with such a system” (Section 3.4).

**How this profile uses it:** Separated from Accountable (A.2). The gloss in the Trustworthiness Characteristics table, “the information exists and can be obtained”, stresses that the information has to have been captured in the first place.

### A.1.10 Explainable & Interpretable {#a.1.10-explainable-&-interpretable}

**Source definition:** “Explainability refers to a representation of the mechanisms underlying AI systems’ operation, whereas interpretability refers to the meaning of AI systems’ output in the context of their designed functional purposes” (Section 3.5).

**How this profile uses it:** As in the source. The AI RMF points to NIST IR 8312 and NIST IR 8367 for more. IR 8312’s principle of explanation accuracy, that “An explanation correctly reflects the reason for generating the output and/or accurately reflects the system’s process”, underlies [Task 4.6: Ensure that Confidence and Rationale Shown to Personnel Reflect How the SI System Reached Its Output](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output), which adds that an explanation constructed after the fact may not reflect how the output was actually produced.

### A.1.11 Accountable {#a.1.11-accountable}

**Source definition:** The AI RMF does not define accountability on its own; it states that “Accountability presupposes transparency” (Section 3.4). ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022 defines accountable as “answerable for actions, decisions, and performance”, and notes that “Accountability relates to an allocated responsibility”.

**How this profile uses it:** Separated from Transparent (A.2). The gloss in the Trustworthiness Characteristics table, “responsibility is named and can be enforced”, is consistent with the ISO note. Allocating responsibility in advance is good practice for any system (see Nissenbaum 1996). For SI systems it matters more, because behavior is learned from data, models, and instructions that many parties contribute across the lifecycle, so even where an output can be explained, each party’s part in it can be hard to separate after the event (see Cooper 2022). As the Trustworthiness Characteristics table notes, those responsible should also be appropriately empowered and identified in advance: they need the visibility, time, resources, access, support, and authority to act. [Implementations 3.9.3](#implementation-3.9.3:-establish-escalation-to-empowered-authority) to 3.9.5 test whether that holds for a particular capability.

### A.1.12 Privacy-Enhanced {#a.1.12-privacy-enhanced}

**Source definition:** “Privacy refers generally to the norms and practices that help to safeguard human autonomy, identity, and dignity” (Section 3.6). The AI RMF lists “anonymity, confidentiality, and control” among privacy values, and notes that “AI systems can also present new risks to privacy by allowing inference to identify individuals or previously private information about individuals”.

**How this profile uses it:** Extended to inferences about an organization’s operations, such as staffing or production, and to sensitive operational and proprietary data. The AI RMF’s inclusion of confidentiality among privacy values partly supports this extension. Inferences about staffing fall within the NIST Privacy Framework, which defines an individual as “A single person or a group of persons, including at a societal level”. Operational and proprietary data go further. The Privacy Framework treats privacy risk as problems that individuals experience, and places loss of confidentiality under cybersecurity risk. The ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022 definition of privacy likewise concerns the private life or affairs of an individual. The Trustworthiness Characteristics table treats them together because the same mechanism, inference from records that are each harmless, can expose both.

### A.1.13 Fair {#a.1.13-fair}

**Source definition:** “Fairness in AI includes concerns for equality and equity by addressing issues such as harmful bias and discrimination” (Section 3.7).

**How this profile uses it:** Separated from Bias Managed. The Trustworthiness Characteristics table extends it to uneven performance across equipment, conditions, locations and customers as well as populations, since such variation can breach service obligations an operator has. What level of variation is acceptable is a determination for the operator.

## A.2 Grouping, and Crosswalk to the AI RMF {#a.2-grouping,-and-crosswalk-to-the-ai-rmf}

The AI RMF presents its characteristics in seven groups, and describes Valid and Reliable as “a necessary condition of trustworthiness” and Accountable and Transparent as relating “to all other characteristics” (Figure 4). This profile keeps those relationships. It separates some of the AI RMF’s pairs into single characteristics, and arranges the 13 under five questions:

* Does it do the correct thing? (Valid, Accurate, Bias Managed)  
* Does it keep doing the correct thing, particularly as conditions change? (Reliable, Robust, Resilient)  
* Does it avoid unintentional or deliberate harm? (Safe, Secure)  
* Does it allow its behavior to be observed, understood, and accounted for? (Transparent, Explainable & Interpretable, Accountable)  
* Does it meet its obligations to those who depend on it? (Privacy-Enhanced, Fair)

The questions are a reading aid. They do not claim that characteristics under the same question never pull against each other; several of the tensions in A.4 are between members of one group.

| This profile | AI RMF (1.0) characteristic |
| :---- | :---- |
| Valid, Accurate, Reliable, Robust | Valid and Reliable (Section 3.1), within which accuracy and robustness are discussed |
| Safe | Safe (Section 3.2) |
| Secure, Resilient | Secure and Resilient (Section 3.3) |
| Transparent, Accountable | Accountable and Transparent (Section 3.4) |
| Explainable & Interpretable | Explainable and Interpretable (Section 3.5) |
| Privacy-Enhanced | Privacy-Enhanced (Section 3.6), extended as described in A.1 |
| Bias Managed, Fair | Fair – with Harmful Bias Managed (Section 3.7) |

The pairs are separated for one main reason: evidence for one member is not evidence for the other. A validation report for normal operation says little about behavior outside it, and a record that an SI system’s actions were logged does not show who is responsible for them. The AI RMF draws several of these distinctions itself. It states that “Systems in which harmful biases are mitigated are not necessarily fair”, that security and resilience “are related but distinct characteristics”, and that transparency, explainability and interpretability “are distinct characteristics that support each other”.

Transparent, Explainable & Interpretable, and Accountable are arranged as a chain. Transparency asks whether the information exists and can be obtained. Explainability and interpretability ask whether it carries meaning: in the AI RMF’s words, “how” a decision was made and “why”. Accountability asks whether responsibility attaches to it. Each depends on the one before it, as the AI RMF notes for the first and last (“Accountability presupposes transparency”), but each can fail on its own.

## A.3 Distinctions Between Characteristics {#a.3-distinctions-between-characteristics}

### A.3.1 Valid, and the conditions it has to hold across {#a.3.1-valid,-and-the-conditions-it-has-to-hold-across}

Valid is the overall claim that an SI system is the right one for this use. Reliable, Robust and Resilient describe the conditions across which that claim has to hold:

* **Reliable** concerns performance over time at the conditions and use that were specified. It is measured against the specification, so it is a question of conformance.  
* **Robust** concerns performance across a variety of conditions and uses, including ones not anticipated. It is measured against the system’s own performance in normal operation, so it is a question of whether that performance holds as conditions vary.  
* **Resilient** concerns what happens when performance cannot hold: whether the system keeps its functions and structure, degrades gracefully, and can return to normal operation.

One way to see the three together is through the design basis: the conditions a system is deliberately designed to withstand, chosen with regard to their likelihood, their consequences, and the resources available (see *How Far to Go*). Reliable concerns performance as specified in the expected conditions and use. Robust concerns how far that performance holds as conditions depart from what was expected. Resilient concerns what the system does when that performance cannot hold: maintaining at least a minimally acceptable level of its essential functions, and recovering afterward (see NIST SP 800-160v2r1). The design basis sets how far out the system is designed to do so. Some fields draw these lines explicitly: for nuclear power plants, for example, ground motion above an operating basis earthquake requires the plant to shut down and be inspected, while structures needed for safe shutdown are designed to remain functional through a larger safe-shutdown earthquake (see 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S). Conditions beyond the design basis are not designed for; they are still examined, so that the organization understands what would happen and plans for it where it can. For an SI system, these boundaries are often harder to locate than for engineered equipment, because its behavior was learned from examples rather than specified, and the conditions it was trained on may not match those it meets in use.

Defining validity fixes what counts as expected, and so decides whether a given departure is a question of reliability, robustness or resilience. The three are still listed separately because each needs its own evidence. A system can also be stable, well characterized and reliable, and still not good enough for the task. Stability is not the same as adequacy, and in critical infrastructure a stable but inadequate system is a familiar problem.

What Valid adds beyond the other three is the question of transfer: whether evidence gathered for one deployment applies to another. An SI system validated at one plant, for one patient population or under one set of organizational conventions may be wrong at the next, even if nothing about the SI system has changed.

### A.3.2 Accurate and Reliable {#a.3.2-accurate-and-reliable}

Accuracy is a property of outputs: how closely they agree with a reference. Reliability is the property of continuing to perform as required. Accuracy is often one of the things required, and reliability is that requirement continuing to be met. The words “as required” in the definition of reliability matter. Without them, a system that was consistently wrong would count as reliable.

### A.3.3 Safe, and why Secure is not scoped to conditions {#a.3.3-safe,-and-why-secure-is-not-scoped-to-conditions}

Safe is defined “under defined conditions”, because a hazard analysis has a scope: it identifies the conditions it considered. Secure carries no such qualifier in this profile. Moving a system outside its expected conditions is often what an adversary is trying to do, so scoping a security claim to expected conditions would assume away the threat. For SI systems the cheapest way to do this is often through the inputs: a sensor reading, a maintenance record or a document an assistant is asked to summarize, rather than a change to the plant.

### A.3.4 Bias Managed, Fair, and the choice of reference {#a.3.4-bias-managed,-fair,-and-the-choice-of-reference}

Bias concerns where systematic error comes from. Fairness concerns who is affected by the outcome. The two are independent in both directions. A model whose errors lean toward summer conditions has a bias with no fairness dimension, and a model with no detectable bias can still feed an allocation policy whose outcome is uneven across those it serves.

In critical infrastructure, bias can enter through the history of how data was collected. Records may be dominated by normal operation, with few abnormal events, or by the best-instrumented assets, so that legacy or poorly instrumented equipment is under-represented. Bias can also enter through background and domain knowledge built into an SI system, such as rules, physics models or engineered features, which may be wrong, incomplete or out of date, for example a plant model from commissioning or features designed for equipment since replaced.

Some bias is designed into the method. In machine learning, bias also has a second, technical sense, often called inductive bias: “any basis for choosing one generalization over another, other than strict consistency with the observed training instances” (see Mitchell 1980). Mitchell showed that a learner without such bias is no better than one that stores its training examples and looks them up, so inductive bias is what makes generalization possible. Examples include an assumption that what happens next resembles what came before, a preference for simpler rules among those that fit the data equally well (see [Implementation 4.6.4: Distill Learned Models into Interpretable Models that Can Be Verified](#implementation-4.6.4:-distill-learned-models-into-interpretable-models-that-can-be-verified)), and knowledge of the domain or of how the result will be used. Inductive bias is not a defect. Managing it means choosing it deliberately and checking it against the process, in line with Mitchell’s recommendation to make biases “just as explicit” as the observations a system learns from. Engineers know the same idea from a correlation used outside the range it was fitted for. The difference for many learned models is that the range is not stated anywhere: the assumptions sit in the method, not on a datasheet. A related failure is shortcut learning, where a model relies on a feature that happens to predict the answer in the training data but is not the one that matters (see Geirhos 2020).

The choice of reference brings a similar risk for Accurate. SI systems are often used where a task is too complex to specify simply, and the same complexity makes a faithful reference hard to construct. NIST SP 1270 notes that development teams often use proxies for what cannot be measured directly, and that proxies “can create many risks”. A system tuned to whichever reference was easiest to obtain can improve on the measure while getting worse at the task. This is often called Goodhart’s law, after the observation that “any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes” (see Manheim 2019). Two of the variants Manheim and Garrabrant distinguish are close to concerns elsewhere in this appendix: optimizing a measure can push the system into conditions where the old relationship between measure and goal no longer holds, which is a question of robustness, and an adversary can exploit the gap between them, which is a question of security. Examples include a failure predictor graded against work orders, which record what was noticed rather than what failed, and a summarizer graded on whether it reads well rather than on whether it kept what mattered. A related tension arises where one technical metric is used to rank risks whose consequences differ ([Task 3.1: Identify Risk Trade-offs](#task-3.1:-identify-risk-trade-offs)).

## A.4 Tensions Between Characteristics {#a.4-tensions-between-characteristics}

The AI RMF notes that “tradeoffs are usually involved” in addressing trustworthiness characteristics, and that analysis can show where tradeoffs exist but does “not answer questions about how to navigate the tradeoff”, which depends on “the values at play in the relevant context”. It names some itself: between accuracy and robustness (Section 3.1), between interpretability and privacy, between predictive accuracy and interpretability, and, under conditions such as data sparsity, between privacy-enhancing techniques and accuracy (Section 3). Section 3.6 adds that “Privacy-related risks may influence security, bias, and transparency and come with tradeoffs with these other characteristics”. The AI RMF Playbook asks organizations to articulate and analyze tradeoffs across trustworthiness characteristics for the context of use, and to document them (MAP 1.5), and to document the basis for decisions made on them (MANAGE 4.2). NIST AI 100-2e2025, Section 4.1.1, describes further trade-offs, including between explainability and adversarial robustness.

In this Guidebook, tensions are recorded in the Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance field of individual Practices and Tasks, most with the conditions under which the characteristics move together and those under which they pull apart, and many with one or more possible ways to balance them. How far to go on a measure that is a matter of degree, and how available resources enter these choices, is discussed in *How Far to Go*. A tension stated without its conditions is a half-truth: the same two characteristics often move together in one setting and against each other in another. This section describes the patterns that recur across those entries and points to examples. It is not a complete list, and the entries themselves remain the place to look for a specific item.

**A characteristic against itself.** The most common tension in this Guidebook is between a characteristic and itself, most often Safe against Safe: the same measure that guards against one hazard delays or suppresses the response to another. A fixed ceiling on automated commands can suppress correct action during a fast-moving abnormal condition ([Task 2.1: Establish SI Usage Thresholds and Rate Control Mechanisms](#task-2.1:-establish-si-usage-thresholds-and-rate-control-mechanisms)). A lower detection threshold catches more events but, for rare conditions, multiplies false alarms ([Task 3.1: Identify Risk Trade-offs](#task-3.1:-identify-risk-trade-offs)). Bounding an SI system’s authority can slow a protective action ([Task 5.3: Implement Principles of Least Agency and Least Privilege for SI Entities](#task-5.3:-implement-principles-of-least-agency-and-least-privilege-for-si-entities)), refusing an action part-way through a sequence can leave the process in a hazardous state ([Task 5.2: Determine and Implement Specific Access Requirements](#task-5.2:-determine-and-implement-specific-access-requirements)), and paced handover protects against taking control without context while delaying the takeover ([Task 11.2: Define Manual and Alternative Operating Procedures for Long-Term Mission Continuity](#task-11.2:-define-manual-and-alternative-operating-procedures-for-long-term-mission-continuity)). Other entries with Safe on both sides concern verification steps that become routine ([Task 3.6: Mitigate Automation Complacency and Skills Degradation](#task-3.6:-mitigate-automation-complacency-and-skills-degradation)), hazards whose containment can lapse as autonomy widens ([Task 3.8: Scope and Map the Expanded SI Attack Surface and Risk Surface](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface)), safety margins, where wide margins can give up the benefits the SI system was deployed for, which may include safety ([Task 8.2: Identify Additional Controls that May Be Required in Scenarios Where Deterministic Root Cause Analysis Is Not Possible](#task-8.2:-identify-additional-controls-that-may-be-required-in-scenarios-where-deterministic-root-cause-analysis-is-not-possible)), training that can overshoot into under-trust ([Task 9.2: Deliver Specialized Training on Human-SI Interaction and Automation Bias](#task-9.2:-deliver-specialized-training-on-human-si-interaction-and-automation-bias)), and overlap between a retiring system and its successor ([Task 13.3: Preserve What Is Needed and Hand Over What Depended on the System](#task-13.3:-preserve-what-is-needed-and-hand-over-what-depended-on-the-system)). The same form appears for Accurate, where tuning to a fixed measure improves the measure and not the task ([Task 2.4: Perform Linguistic and Domain-Context Robustness Testing](#task-2.4:-perform-linguistic-and-domain-context-robustness-testing)) and an aggregate gain conceals a loss in a high-consequence class ([Task 7.5: Conduct Impact Assessments and Risk Management for SI System and Model Updates](#task-7.5:-conduct-impact-assessments-and-risk-management-for-si-system-and-model-updates)), and for Resilient, where heterogeneous redundancy does less against drift that affects every model built on similar data ([Task 2.2: Establish Requirements for Redundancy in SI-Driven Functions](#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions)).

**Holding a change against the fix it carries.** Change control, review and approval guard against a change that quietly degrades a characteristic. Where the change is itself an urgent fix, the same review keeps the fault in service ([Practice 7](#practice-7:-manage-internal-si-supply-chain-and-data-provenance), [Implementation 6.1.1](#implementation-6.1.1:-add-si-disclosure-to-existing-procurement-policies), [Task 7.4](#task-7.4:-define-authorization-and-access-controls-for-si-modifications)). Holding back a newer version to allow exact replay after an incident is a variant ([Task 8.1: Identify Scenarios Requiring Deterministic Root Cause Analysis and Incident Reconstruction](#task-8.1:-identify-scenarios-requiring-deterministic-root-cause-analysis-and-incident-reconstruction)).

**Stopping against continuing.** Where a process can be stopped safely, a trip and graceful degradation point the same way. Where stopping is itself hazardous, or the fallback is under-resourced, Safe and Resilient separate ([Practice 4](#practice-4:-define-procedures-for-emergency-avoidance-override,-recovery,-and-situational-awareness), [Task 2.2](#task-2.2:-establish-requirements-for-redundancy-in-si-driven-functions), [Practice 11](#practice-11:-maintain-si-aware-mission-continuity-and-disaster-recovery-planning)). Pressure to return an SI system to service before re-commissioning evidence is complete, because manual operation is consuming resources, is a related form ([Task 11.4: Establish System Integrity Re-Validation and Re-Commissioning Protocols](#task-11.4:-establish-system-integrity-re-validation-and-re-commissioning-protocols)). Waiting for full verification of a new artifact during urgent recovery is a form of the same tension ([Practice 12: Independently Verify SI-Generated Operational Logic and Artifacts Across Their Lifecycle](#practice-12:-independently-verify-si-generated-operational-logic-and-artifacts-across-their-lifecycle)).

**Scope against coverage.** Drawing requirements or boundaries tightly makes acceptance and evidence clear, and can leave behavior outside them uncharacterized or block the behavior that made the SI system worth adopting ([Practice 1](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success), [Practice 3](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior), [Task 3.2](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs)). Filtering anomalous records improves the data an SI system learns from, and can remove the abnormal conditions it most needs to recognize ([Task 7.2: Validate, Select, and Prepare Data for SI Systems](#task-7.2:-validate,-select,-and-prepare-data-for-si-systems)). Tuning for the best average can make a system more fragile at the edges ([Task 1.2](#task-1.2:-create-quantitative-baselines-for-existing-systems-in-both-normal-and-challenging-conditions), [Practice 2](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations)), while training across a whole specification range can spend learning capacity on conditions a given installation will not meet ([Task 2.5: Verify that Learned Behavior Is Robust to Component, Hardware, and Data Schema Variance](#task-2.5:-verify-that-learned-behavior-is-robust-to-component,-hardware,-and-data-schema-variance)), and safeguards that keep a function performing across a wider range can make the point at which the fallback should engage harder to see ([Practice 2: Define SI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service Expectations](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations)). Evidence from the live system is the evidence that applies to it, but gathering it may disrupt a process that cannot tolerate disruption ([Task 1.3](#task-1.3:-implement-evaluation-and-test-plans,-including-tevv,-across-the-si-lifecycle), [Task 2.3](#task-2.3:-establish-protocols-for-and-regularly-perform-systematic-and-achievable-testing,-evaluation,-validation,-and-verification-\(tevv\))). Freezing a system that adapts at runtime holds it to conditions that may have moved, while letting it adapt exposes it to unrepresentative or adversarial data ([Task 7.3: Manage Version Control and Logging for Internal SI Safety Mechanisms](#task-7.3:-manage-version-control-and-logging-for-internal-si-safety-mechanisms)).

**Keeping a record against protecting it.** The record needed to reconstruct a decision can be the protected data itself ([Practice 10](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities), [Task 10.1](#task-10.1:-define-decision-level-logging-and-metadata-retention-policies), [Practice 13](#practice-13:-establish-procedures-for-retiring-si-systems-and-withdrawing-their-authority)), can add latency to a real-time control path ([Practice 10: Implement Multi-Tiered SI System Logging and Audit Capabilities](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities)), or can be lost when restoring service or destroying a retired model ([Task 8.3](#task-8.3:-designate-roles-for-si-incident-governance), [Task 7.6](#task-7.6:-establish-processes-for-internal-si-component-deprecation-and-decommissioning), [Task 13.2](#task-13.2:-withdraw-all-authority-and-confirm-the-result)). Documenting boundary logic for operators and auditors can also tell an adversary where its thresholds sit ([Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior)), and autonomous recovery that goes unannounced can remove the signal that a safety margin is being consumed ([Task 3.3: Establish Failure Notification Requirements](#task-3.3:-establish-failure-notification-requirements)). After an incident, capturing volatile state takes time while a system suspected of causing harm is still running ([Task 13.3: Preserve What Is Needed and Hand Over What Depended on the System](#task-13.3:-preserve-what-is-needed-and-hand-over-what-depended-on-the-system)). Protecting those who report near-misses encourages reports while limiting how far individual responsibility can be enforced on what they reveal ([Task 8.6: Establish Non-Punitive Reporting for SI-Related Near-Misses](#task-8.6:-establish-non-punitive-reporting-for-si-related-near-misses)).

**People in the loop.** Keeping a person in the loop contributes to both Accountable and Safe only if the person can act in time ([Task 4.5: Define Operational Regimes for Human-on-the-Loop and Human-Out-of-the-Loop Operation](#task-4.5:-define-operational-regimes-for-human-on-the-loop-and-human-out-of-the-loop-operation)). More rationale can help a person who works with an SI system daily and overload an emergency responder under time pressure ([Task 4.2: Ensure that Personnel Are Able to Gain and Maintain Situational Awareness](#task-4.2:-ensure-that-personnel-are-able-to-gain-and-maintain-situational-awareness)), and consolidating alerts reduces load while risking delay to a single urgent one ([Task 4.4: Attention Governance and Alert/Alarm Flood Mitigation](#task-4.4:-attention-governance-and-alert/alarm-flood-mitigation)).

**Accuracy against explanation.** Whether accuracy and explanation pull apart depends on whether the knowledge a decision rests on can be stated as rules, constraints or a self-interpretable model ([Task 1.4](#task-1.4:-establish-the-si-system’s-domain-knowledge-and-linguistic-alignment-requirements), [Task 4.6](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output)).

**Confinement against need.** Confining an SI agent to its role bounds an attack or an error, and stops legitimate work, including recovery, when a need arises outside what was anticipated ([Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools)). Related tensions arise for break-glass intervention ([Task 4.1: Establish “Break-Glass” Intervention Procedures](#task-4.1:-establish-“break-glass”-intervention-procedures)), authority on a partitioned site ([Task 5.3: Implement Principles of Least Agency and Least Privilege for SI Entities](#task-5.3:-implement-principles-of-least-agency-and-least-privilege-for-si-entities)), automatic suspension on detection ([Task 5.4: Implement Continuous Monitoring of SI Entities Against Access and Action Boundaries and Expectations](#task-5.4:-implement-continuous-monitoring-of-si-entities-against-access-and-action-boundaries-and-expectations)), and fine-grained identity on constrained devices ([Task 5.1: Establish Identities and Authentication for SI Entities](#task-5.1:-establish-identities-and-authentication-for-si-entities)). They also arise for restrictions on unvetted tools that move use out of view ([Task 3.7: Govern and Mitigate Risks from Unauthorized, Transient, and “Shadow SI” Systems](#task-3.7:-govern-and-mitigate-risks-from-unauthorized,-transient,-and-“shadow-si”-systems)), limits on what leaves for a vendor who monitors the system ([Task 6.3: Identify and Control Dataflows Across the SI Supply Chain](#task-6.3:-identify-and-control-dataflows-across-the-si-supply-chain)), hard limits on a shared resource during an upset ([Task 3.5: Define and Control Risks to Adjacent and Related Systems](#task-3.5:-define-and-control-risks-to-adjacent-and-related-systems)), and restrictions that cannot be lifted quickly when the restricted capability is keeping a service running ([Task 3.9: Assess and Document Organizational Readiness for Each SI-Enabled Capability](#task-3.9:-assess-and-document-organizational-readiness-for-each-si-enabled-capability)). The reverse also occurs: an independent fallback channel that carries control keeps operation possible and adds a route into the process, for an intruder and for a mistaken command alike ([Task 4.3: Establish Independent (“Out-of-Band”) Communication, Monitoring, Alerting, and Control Capabilities](#task-4.3:-establish-independent-\(“out-of-band”\)-communication,-monitoring,-alerting,-and-control-capabilities)).

**Requirements against choice.** Requiring full supplier disclosure costs little when several suppliers can meet it. When few can, it can narrow the choice to a small number of large vendors, or rule out a less transparent system that would improve on the one in service in other respects ([Practice 6: Integrate Visibility of the External Supply Chain of SI into Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management)).

**Drift against interference.** Where one observation could be drift or interference, the reliability response of recalibrating and the security response of preserving state and investigating point in opposite directions ([Task 3.4: Monitor for Anomalous SI Behavior](#task-3.4:-monitor-for-anomalous-si-behavior)).

The tensions the AI RMF names are not all represented in these entries. Accurate against Robust appears in several ([Task 1.2](#task-1.2:-create-quantitative-baselines-for-existing-systems-in-both-normal-and-challenging-conditions), [Practice 2](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations), [Task 2.5](#task-2.5:-verify-that-learned-behavior-is-robust-to-component,-hardware,-and-data-schema-variance)), and accuracy against interpretability in two ([Task 1.4](#task-1.4:-establish-the-si-system’s-domain-knowledge-and-linguistic-alignment-requirements), [Task 4.6](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output)). Privacy against accuracy appears only as part of a wider tension ([Task 5.3: Implement Principles of Least Agency and Least Privilege for SI Entities](#task-5.3:-implement-principles-of-least-agency-and-least-privilege-for-si-entities)), and privacy against interpretability does not appear as such. Privacy against transparency, which Section 3.6 names, appears in three entries ([Practice 10](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities), [Task 10.1](#task-10.1:-define-decision-level-logging-and-metadata-retention-policies), [Practice 13](#practice-13:-establish-procedures-for-retiring-si-systems-and-withdrawing-their-authority)).

## A.5 What These Characteristics Do Not Reach {#a.5-what-these-characteristics-do-not-reach}

The characteristics are framed around the SI system in its deployment. Several Practices depend just as much on people and on the organization. Whether an operator can re-engage in time to act ([Task 4.5: Define Operational Regimes for Human-on-the-Loop and Human-Out-of-the-Loop Operation](#task-4.5:-define-operational-regimes-for-human-on-the-loop-and-human-out-of-the-loop-operation)), whether training leaves trust matched to what the system warrants ([Practice 9: Provide Role-Based SI Risk Training that Builds Well-Founded Trust](#practice-9:-provide-role-based-si-risk-training-that-builds-well-founded-trust)), and whether the governance and oversight planned for a specific SI-enabled capability can actually be carried out ([Task 3.9: Assess and Document Organizational Readiness for Each SI-Enabled Capability](#task-3.9:-assess-and-document-organizational-readiness-for-each-si-enabled-capability)) are questions about people, plant and organization that no characteristic in the Trustworthiness Characteristics table fully covers. Human factors research has long described how people misuse automation through overreliance, disuse it, often because of false alarms, and how designers and managers can abuse it by automating functions “without due regard for the consequences for human performance” (see Parasuraman 1997). Accountable, which concerns who is responsible, and Valid, which concerns the deployment as a whole, come closest. This profile records these questions in the relevant Practices and Tasks rather than adding characteristics for them.

\> To the Reviewer:

\> We would welcome views on whether the characteristics should reach further into human and organizational performance, or whether the Practices are the right place for it.

## A.6 Appendix A References {#a.6-appendix-a-references}

* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-1), January 2023, from NIST. Section 3, AI Risks and Trustworthiness, defines the characteristics this appendix starts from, in Sections 3.1 to 3.7, and its introduction to Section 3 and Figure 4 describe how they relate and the tradeoffs between them.  
* **Guidance** [NIST AI RMF Playbook](https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/playbook/), from NIST. The suggested actions under MAP 1.5 ask organizations to articulate and analyze tradeoffs across trustworthiness characteristics for the proposed context of use and to document them, and those under MANAGE 4.2 to document the basis for decisions made on tradeoffs.  
* **Standard** [ISO/IEC TS 5723:2022, Trustworthiness: Vocabulary](https://www.iso.org/standard/81608.html), from ISO and IEC. Section 3.2 defines trustworthiness characteristics including accountability, accuracy, reliability, resilience, robustness, safety and security, several of which the AI RMF cites, and Section 3.3.1 defines accountable.  
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 1270, Towards a Standard for Identifying and Managing Bias in Artificial Intelligence](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.1270), March 2022, from NIST. Section 2.1.2 describes the three categories of bias that the AI RMF names, and Section 3.2.1, TEVV Challenges, describes the risks of using proxies for concepts that cannot be measured directly.  
* **Guidance** [NIST AI 100-2e2025, Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-2e2025), March 2025, from NIST. Section 4.1.1 documents trade-offs among the attributes of trustworthy SI, including between explainability and adversarial robustness, between privacy and fairness, and between accuracy and adversarial robustness.  
* **Research** [Shortcut Learning in Deep Neural Networks](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-020-00257-z), by R. Geirhos, J.-H. Jacobsen, C. Michaelis, R. Zemel, W. Brendel, M. Bethge and F. A. Wichmann, Nature Machine Intelligence, 2020\. Section 3 defines shortcuts as decision rules that perform well on test data like the training data but fail on out-of-distribution tests.  
* **Guidance** [NIST IR 8312, Four Principles of Explainable Artificial Intelligence](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.IR.8312), September 2021, from NIST. Section 2.3, Explanation Accuracy, states the principle that an explanation correctly reflects the reason for generating the output or the system’s process, as distinct from the accuracy of the decision itself. The AI RMF points to it for explainability.  
* **Guidance** [NIST IR 8367, Psychological Foundations of Explainability and Interpretability in Artificial Intelligence](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.IR.8367), from NIST. Section 3.2.4 distinguishes techniques that help a developer infer how an algorithm works from interpretability, which it describes as meaning in context for the end user. The AI RMF points to it for explainability and interpretability.  
* **Guidance** [NIST Privacy Framework: A Tool for Improving Privacy through Enterprise Risk Management, Version 1.0](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.CSWP.01162020), January 2020, from NIST. Section 1.2.1 and Figure 2 distinguish privacy risks, arising from data processing, from cybersecurity risks, arising from loss of confidentiality, integrity or availability, and Appendix B defines privacy risk in terms of problems individuals experience and an individual as a single person or a group of persons. The AI RMF points to it for privacy.  
* **Research** [Mitchell, T. M., “The Need for Biases in Learning Generalizations”, Rutgers University technical report CBM-TR-117, May 1980](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/usr/mitchell/ftp/pubs/NeedForBias_1980.pdf). Defines bias in learning as any basis for choosing one generalization over another other than consistency with the training instances, shows in Section 3 that an unbiased learner can do no better than rote lookup, and in Section 4 classifies useful biases, including knowledge of the domain, of the intended use and of the source of the training data, and a bias toward simplicity.  
* **Research** [Manheim, D. and Garrabrant, S., “Categorizing Variants of Goodhart’s Law”, arXiv:1803.04585, 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.04585). Describes failures that occur when optimization on a proxy measure causes it to stop tracking the intended goal, and distinguishes regressional, extremal, causal and adversarial variants.  
* **Research** [Parasuraman, R. and Riley, V., “Humans and Automation: Use, Misuse, Disuse, Abuse”, Human Factors, 39(2), 1997, pages 230 to 253](https://doi.org/10.1518/001872097778543886).
