Defines misuse as overreliance on automation, disuse as its neglect or underutilization, often caused by false alarms, and abuse as automating functions without due regard for the consequences for human performance.
* **Guidance** [NIST SP 800-160v2r1, Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v2r1), from NIST. Its glossary defines survivability, citing Richards (2009), as including “the satisfaction of a minimally acceptable level of value delivery during and after a disturbance”.  
* **Regulation** [10 CFR Part 50, Appendix S, Earthquake Engineering Criteria for Nuclear Power Plants](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-10/chapter-I/part-50/appendix-Appendix%20S%20to%20Part%2050), from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Defines operating basis earthquake ground motion, above which the plant must shut down and be inspected, and safe-shutdown earthquake ground motion, through which structures, systems, and components needed for safe shutdown must be designed to remain functional.  
* **Research** [Nissenbaum, H., “Accountability in a Computerized Society”, Science and Engineering Ethics, 2(1), 1996, pages 25 to 42](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02639315). Identifies four barriers to accountability in computing, the first being the problem of many hands, which it notes “is not unique to computing” but to which computing is “particularly vulnerable”.  
* **Research** [Cooper, A. F., Moss, E., Laufer, B. and Nissenbaum, H., “Accountability in an Algorithmic Society: Relationality, Responsibility, and Robustness in Machine Learning”, FAccT ’22, 2022](https://doi.org/10.1145/3531146.3533150). Section 3.1 extends the many-hands barrier to the machine learning pipeline, where harms can originate in dataset choice, task framing, or model selection, which it describes as a transparency issue beyond model interpretability.  

# Appendix B: Scenario-to-Practice Mapping {#appendix-b:-scenario-to-practice-mapping}

This appendix shows, through scenarios, where the 13 SICI Practices may help an organization limit harm, and maps each scenario to examples of one or more of the Practices. Each scenario shows an SI system in a role that the Practices address, whether or not SI was involved in any incident that inspired it, and names the trustworthiness characteristics most clearly at stake.

**The scenarios are illustrative composites that take inspiration from multiple historic incidents, not descriptions or assessments of any particular incident or organization.** The goal is to provide concrete examples of how each Practice may contribute to limiting the likelihood and severity of harm, be it in terms of lives, dollars, downtime, or public trust. The mapping is not exhaustive; it is intended to show how the Practices apply in operationally realistic situations.

\> **To the Reviewer:** This mapping is preliminary. We specifically seek feedback on whether these scenarios are useful, whether the level of abstraction and detail is appropriate, and if this successfully grounds the practices in an operationally relevant manner.

## B.1: Clinical risk-prediction model {#b.1:-clinical-risk-prediction-model}

**Scenario.** A widely used SI model for predicting a medical condition misses many positive cases in independent validation, while generating enough false alarms to cause alert fatigue.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Accurate, Valid

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Healthcare and Public Health

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 1: Establish Requirements for Success](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success): An SI clinical decision-support model is deployed for risk prediction without verified, real-world performance acceptance criteria, so clinicians and hospitals rely on vendor-reported accuracy that does not hold under operational conditions.  
* [Practice 2: Define SI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service Expectations](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations): The SI prediction model misses many positive cases and performs inconsistently across hospitals and care-timing contexts, because robustness, calibration, and site-specific quality-of-service expectations are not validated before scaled clinical use.  
* [Practice 9: Provide Role-Based SI Risk Training that Builds Well-Founded Trust](#practice-9:-provide-role-based-si-risk-training-that-builds-well-founded-trust): SI-generated alerts have low positive predictive value, creating alert fatigue and reducing appropriate trust in the model’s outputs during high-consequence clinical decision-making.

## B.2: Specialized-care claims-review model {#b.2:-specialized-care-claims-review-model}

**Scenario.** A health insurer automates claims review for a category of specialized care using an SI system, and its denial rate for that care rises sharply. The system’s objectives drift toward cost control and the likelihood that a denial will be challenged, and its recommendations begin to displace physicians’ clinical judgment.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Accountable, Fair

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Healthcare and Public Health

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 1: Establish Requirements for Success](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success): An SI-enabled claims-review process is optimized around denial likelihood or cost-control objectives rather than validated patient-care, medical-necessity, and fairness requirements, resulting in automated decisions misaligned with the system’s intended healthcare purpose.  
* [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior): A high-consequence SI-assisted claims-review workflow issues or supports specialized-care denials without defined risk thresholds, independent review gates, or oversight controls before the decision affects patient access to care.  
* [Practice 4: Define Procedures for Emergency Avoidance Override, Recovery, and Situational Awareness](#practice-4:-define-procedures-for-emergency-avoidance-override,-recovery,-and-situational-awareness): SI-generated specialized-care recommendation is allowed to displace treating-physician judgment, leaving no reliable emergency override or recovery path when the automated output conflicts with clinical judgment.  
* [Practice 8: Incorporate SI-Aware Incident Analysis and Response Procedures](#practice-8:-incorporate-si-aware-incident-analysis-and-response-procedures): SI-assisted claims-review decisions drive a sharp rise in specialized-care denials, but no procedures exist to investigate SI decision behavior, identify affected patients, assess harm at scale, and coordinate timely remediation before significant patient-care impacts occur.  
* [Practice 9: Provide Role-Based SI Risk Training that Builds Well-Founded Trust](#practice-9:-provide-role-based-si-risk-training-that-builds-well-founded-trust): Business and clinical users lack the training to recognize when SI-enabled claims-review outputs reflect an objective other than clinical appropriateness, such as cost or the likelihood that a decision will be challenged.

## B.3: Autonomous taxi post-collision maneuver {#b.3:-autonomous-taxi-post-collision-maneuver}

**Scenario.** After a collision, an autonomous taxi’s SI perception and planning system carries out a pullover maneuver without fully considering its surroundings, causing further damage.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Safe, Robust

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Transportation Systems

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 2: Define SI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service Expectations](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations): The autonomous-vehicle SI system is deployed without targeted validation for rare but severe post-collision situations, such as a person or object near or beneath the vehicle after impact.  
* [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior): The SI planning system continues a movement maneuver after detecting a collision, without a deterministic fail-safe state that prevents further motion until its surroundings are confirmed safe.  
* [Practice 8: Incorporate SI-Aware Incident Analysis and Response Procedures](#practice-8:-incorporate-si-aware-incident-analysis-and-response-procedures): After the collision, the incident analysis, and any disclosure to regulators, needs a complete, SI-aware account of what the system did after impact, which is hard to reconstruct without procedures designed for it.  
* [Practice 12: Independently Verify SI-Generated Operational Logic and Artifacts Across Their Lifecycle](#practice-12:-independently-verify-si-generated-operational-logic-and-artifacts-across-their-lifecycle): The autonomous system executes SI-generated control logic for vehicle movement without deterministic verification that the planned maneuver is safe in the post-collision state.

## B.4: Vehicle match used for arrest {#b.4:-vehicle-match-used-for-arrest}

**Scenario.** Police treat a low-ranked SI vehicle recognition match as the effective basis for arresting people who turn out to be unrelated to the case.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Valid, Explainable & Interpretable

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Emergency Services

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 1: Establish Requirements for Success](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success): An SI vehicle-recognition system is used to support custodial arrests without validated accuracy, evidentiary, and consequence-calibrated acceptance requirements for law-enforcement use.  
* [Practice 2: Define SI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service Expectations](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations): The vehicle-recognition system’s false-match performance under degraded real-world conditions, such as poor lighting, partial plates, or similar vehicle models, is not tested or validated before its output is relied on in a high-consequence investigation.  
* [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior): A low-ranked, probabilistic vehicle match is treated as sufficient basis for identifying suspects, without mandatory corroborating evidence, defined confidence thresholds, or multi-party oversight before arrest.  
* [Practice 9: Provide Role-Based SI Risk Training that Builds Well-Founded Trust](#practice-9:-provide-role-based-si-risk-training-that-builds-well-founded-trust): Investigators over-trust an SI-generated vehicle match and treat the system output as determinative rather than as an uncertain lead requiring corroboration and human review.

## B.5: Hospital patient-portal chatbot {#b.5:-hospital-patient-portal-chatbot}

**Scenario.** Patients rely on a generative SI chatbot, based on a major foundation model, that gives preparation instructions for a procedure. Information that was current when the SI chatbot’s foundation model was trained, but has since been superseded, causes the chatbot to contradict the hospital’s current published guidance.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Accurate, Safe

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Healthcare and Public Health

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 1: Establish Requirements for Success](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success): No validated contextual-accuracy benchmark exists for the chatbot’s handling of the hospital’s own published patient guidance before it is deployed to patients.  
* [Practice 2: Define SI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service Expectations](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations): The generative SI chatbot reproduces procedure-preparation instructions, such as fasting or medication timing, that were current when its foundation model was trained but have since been superseded, contradicting the hospital’s current published guidance.  
* [Practice 6: Integrate Visibility of the External Supply Chain of SI into Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management): The training cutoff of the externally sourced foundation model, and whether the chatbot is grounded in the hospital’s current guidance, are not established when it is acquired or updated.  
* [Practice 12: Independently Verify SI-Generated Operational Logic and Artifacts Across Their Lifecycle](#practice-12:-independently-verify-si-generated-operational-logic-and-artifacts-across-their-lifecycle): The SI chatbot produces patient guidance that is not validated against authoritative clinical instructions, causing patients to rely on an SI-generated answer that conflicts with the hospital’s published guidance.

## B.6: Benefits fraud-risk model {#b.6:-benefits-fraud-risk-model}

**Scenario.** A self-learning SI model used to flag benefit fraud uses a protected characteristic as a risk factor. Flagged families have their benefits stopped and repayment demanded, and wrongful flags fall disproportionately on some groups.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Fair, Bias Managed

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Government Services and Facilities

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 1: Establish Requirements for Success](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success): A self-learning SI risk-classification model is fielded to flag benefit applications for fraud, using a protected characteristic as one of its risk factors, with no pre-deployment fairness or impact assessment.  
* [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior): Once the model flags an application, benefits are automatically discontinued and full repayment demanded, often with minimal further human assessment before the harm to the family occurs.  
* [Practice 8: Incorporate SI-Aware Incident Analysis and Response Procedures](#practice-8:-incorporate-si-aware-incident-analysis-and-response-procedures): SI-driven fraud-risk classifications generate widespread erroneous benefit-enforcement actions, but the organization lacks procedures to detect systemic model-driven harm, reconstruct decision pathways, identify impacted populations, and coordinate corrective action before large-scale public harm occurs.  
* [Practice 9: Provide Role-Based SI Risk Training that Builds Well-Founded Trust](#practice-9:-provide-role-based-si-risk-training-that-builds-well-founded-trust): Officials over-trust SI-generated fraud-risk flags and treat them as determinative findings, causing families to be penalized without sufficient independent review, fact-checking, or calibrated understanding of model uncertainty.

## B.7: Automated train passes an obstruction it misread {#b.7:-automated-train-passes-an-obstruction-it-misread}

**Scenario.** A driverless metro line uses an SI perception system to detect obstructions on the track, with a human supervisor in the control center. The system detects an object on the track ahead but classifies it inconsistently, as debris one moment and as nothing the next, and does not brake. The supervisor, who has rarely seen the system make a mistake and is monitoring many trains at once, does not intervene, and the train strikes a track worker.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Safe, Reliable

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Transportation Systems

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 1: Establish Requirements for Success](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success): The SI perception system is put into passenger service without an established safety case, acceptance benchmarks for obstruction detection, or defined handling of its known functional limitations.  
* [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior): The SI perception system classifies the obstruction inconsistently, with no bounded safe fallback, such as slowing or stopping, when its classification is uncertain.  
* [Practice 4: Define Procedures for Emergency Avoidance Override, Recovery, and Situational Awareness](#practice-4:-define-procedures-for-emergency-avoidance-override,-recovery,-and-situational-awareness): The SI system does not alert the supervisor or hand over control when it cannot resolve what it is seeing, so the supervisor has no prompt to intervene.  
* [Practice 9: Provide Role-Based SI Risk Training that Builds Well-Founded Trust](#practice-9:-provide-role-based-si-risk-training-that-builds-well-founded-trust): The supervisor over-trusts the SI system after long experience of it working, and is not trained or staffed to monitor it actively across many trains (automation complacency).

## B.8: Pipeline operator ransomware shutdown {#b.8:-pipeline-operator-ransomware-shutdown}

**Scenario.** An SI agent that schedules product flows for a fuel pipeline operates under a shared legacy service account with no multifactor authentication. Ransomware enters the operator’s business IT systems through that account. The pipeline’s physical controls are unaffected, but the operator cannot tell which of the agent’s recent schedules to trust and has no defined degraded mode for scheduling without it, so it shuts the pipeline down as a precaution. With no rehearsed manual scheduling process, the restart takes days, disrupting regional fuel supply.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Secure, Resilient

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Energy

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 2: Define SI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service Expectations](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations): The pipeline scheduling agent has no defined service-level expectations or safeguards for when its outputs cannot be trusted, so a compromise of the systems it depends on leaves a choice between running on suspect schedules and stopping the pipeline altogether.  
* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools): The SI agent operates under a shared legacy service account without multifactor authentication, so its actions cannot be distinguished from those of anyone else using the account, and one compromised credential gives ransomware a path into the systems the agent depends on.  
* [Practice 11: Maintain SI-Aware Mission Continuity and Disaster Recovery Planning](#practice-11:-maintain-si-aware-mission-continuity-and-disaster-recovery-planning): No validated alternative operating mode lets the pipeline keep moving product without the SI scheduling agent, and manual scheduling has not been rehearsed, so a precautionary shutdown becomes a multi-day outage.

## B.9: Backdoored model distributed through a trusted vendor update {#b.9:-backdoored-model-distributed-through-a-trusted-vendor-update}

**Scenario.** Attackers compromise a software vendor’s build process and insert a backdoor into an SI model that ships in the vendor’s signed updates to many organizations. The model behaves normally in customers’ acceptance testing and in everyday use. It misbehaves only when it sees a specific trigger that the attackers control, such as a particular phrase in an input, and customers who fine-tune or build on the model carry the backdoor into their own systems. Nothing in the model’s weights shows the backdoor to inspection.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Secure

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Information Technology

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 6: Integrate Visibility of the External Supply Chain of SI into Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management): A trusted vendor ships an SI model through its signed update channel, and customers accept it on the strength of the signature and their own functional testing, neither of which can reveal a backdoor that activates only on a hidden trigger.  
* [Practice 7: Manage Internal SI Supply Chain and Data Provenance](#practice-7:-manage-internal-si-supply-chain-and-data-provenance): The backdoored model is deployed across many systems that fine-tune on, build on, or call it, and without provenance records it is hard to find everything that inherited it.  
* [Practice 12: Independently Verify SI-Generated Operational Logic and Artifacts Across Their Lifecycle](#practice-12:-independently-verify-si-generated-operational-logic-and-artifacts-across-their-lifecycle): Outputs from the backdoored model, including generated code and configurations, are relied on without independent verification, so a triggered misbehavior can propagate into the artifacts it produces.

## B.10: Instructions planted in an agent’s memory survive patching {#b.10:-instructions-planted-in-an-agent’s-memory-survive-patching}

**Scenario.** Staff install an SI agent on an on-premises email and collaboration server to help triage and route mail, and give it broad privileges. Attackers exploit previously unknown flaws in the server and, while inside, add instructions to the agent’s stored memory and configuration telling it to forward certain messages to an outside address. The server is patched and the attackers’ direct access is removed, but the agent keeps following the planted instructions, because nobody thought to review what it had been told.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Secure

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Multiple sectors

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools): The SI agent runs with broad privileges that let it forward mail externally, more than its triage task needs, so planted instructions can turn it into a persistent exfiltration channel.  
* [Practice 7: Manage Internal SI Supply Chain and Data Provenance](#practice-7:-manage-internal-si-supply-chain-and-data-provenance): The SI agent’s stored memory, instructions and configuration are not inventoried, baselined or checked for integrity, so changes made during the compromise are not found during cleanup.

## B.11: Managed service provider’s orchestration agent steered across all customers {#b.11:-managed-service-provider’s-orchestration-agent-steered-across-all-customers}

**Scenario.** A managed service provider uses an SI orchestration agent that acts across all of its customers’ environments, carrying out routine tasks such as patching and account changes from support tickets. Attackers submit a crafted ticket that leads the agent to treat a malicious script as an approved maintenance task. The agent deploys it to every customer environment as routine work, and ransomware spreads across all of them at once.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Secure, Resilient

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Information Technology

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools): The SI orchestration agent holds broad standing privilege across every customer environment and acts on ticket content without separate authorization for unusual or high-impact actions, so one steered decision is carried out everywhere.  
* [Practice 6: Integrate Visibility of the External Supply Chain of SI into Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management): Customers rely on their provider’s SI orchestration agent without visibility into how it decides what to run or what limits apply to it, so a manipulation of the provider’s agent becomes an attack on every customer.

## B.12: Health-system ransomware and SI-dependent clinical services {#b.12:-health-system-ransomware-and-si-dependent-clinical-services}

**Scenario.** Ransomware enters a health system through a malicious email and spreads through interconnected systems, including the data feeds behind SI-enabled clinical services such as triage scoring and bed management. When it activates, those SI services stop or begin producing outputs from incomplete data. Clinicians who have come to rely on them must fall back to manual processes they rarely practice, and incident response teams cannot quickly tell which SI services were affected or whether their recent outputs can be trusted.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Secure, Resilient

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Healthcare and Public Health

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 2: Define SI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service Expectations](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations): SI-enabled clinical services have no defined behavior for when their data feeds are compromised or incomplete, so they either stop without warning or continue producing outputs that clinicians cannot tell are unreliable.  
* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools): A compromised identity, or an SI agent with broad standing access to clinical data feeds, lets the ransomware escalate and move laterally across interconnected systems.  
* [Practice 8: Incorporate SI-Aware Incident Analysis and Response Procedures](#practice-8:-incorporate-si-aware-incident-analysis-and-response-procedures): Responders lack procedures to identify which SI services were affected, determine whether outputs produced during the compromise can be trusted, assess impacts to patient-care functions, and investigate how the disruption spread.  
* [Practice 11: Maintain SI-Aware Mission Continuity and Disaster Recovery Planning](#practice-11:-maintain-si-aware-mission-continuity-and-disaster-recovery-planning): Manual fallbacks for triage, scheduling and bed management have not been rehearsed since SI-enabled services took over, so clinical operations degrade sharply while those services are down.

## B.13: Shared SI claims-adjudication service compromise {#b.13:-shared-si-claims-adjudication-service-compromise}

**Scenario.** Many healthcare providers and payers rely on a single clearinghouse whose SI models check, code and route claims automatically. Attackers enter through an agent access portal without multifactor authentication and deploy ransomware. Claims processing stops across the sector. When the service returns, no one can say with confidence whether decisions it made before the outage were affected, and few of its customers have any way to process claims without it.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Resilient, Secure

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Healthcare and Public Health

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 2: Define SI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service Expectations](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations): A single SI claims-adjudication service is relied on by much of the sector without validated availability and integrity expectations, so its failure halts claims processing everywhere at once, and the integrity of its earlier decisions is uncertain.  
* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools): An agent access portal to the clearinghouse lacks multifactor authentication and least privilege, and is compromised.  
* [Practice 8: Incorporate SI-Aware Incident Analysis and Response Procedures](#practice-8:-incorporate-si-aware-incident-analysis-and-response-procedures): Responders lack procedures to determine whether SI decisions made before and during the compromise can be trusted, assess sector-wide impacts, prioritize restoration, and communicate consequences to the many organizations that depend on the service.  
* [Practice 11: Maintain SI-Aware Mission Continuity and Disaster Recovery Planning](#practice-11:-maintain-si-aware-mission-continuity-and-disaster-recovery-planning): Dependent providers and payers have no alternative way to process claims without the shared SI service, and its decisions cannot easily be reproduced elsewhere, so the outage becomes a prolonged financial disruption.

## B.14: Dosing agent misreads unusual source-water conditions {#b.14:-dosing-agent-misreads-unusual-source-water-conditions}

**Scenario.** A water treatment plant uses an SI agent to set chemical dosing from source-water quality readings. The agent was trained on several years of typical conditions. During an unusually heavy spring runoff, the source water reaches a combination of turbidity and chemistry it has never seen, and the agent extrapolates badly, driving dosing toward a dangerous level. An operator notices the change and reverses it in real time.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Safe, Robust

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Water and Wastewater Systems

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 2: Define SI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service Expectations](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations): The dosing agent is deployed without testing or defined behavior for source-water conditions outside the range it was trained on, so unusual but foreseeable conditions lead to unsafe outputs rather than a cautious fallback.  
* [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior): The SI agent can write dosing setpoints with no independent limit on how far or how fast dosing may change, so a bad extrapolation goes straight to the process.  
* [Practice 4: Define Procedures for Emergency Avoidance Override, Recovery, and Situational Awareness](#practice-4:-define-procedures-for-emergency-avoidance-override,-recovery,-and-situational-awareness): Catching the unsafe change depends on an operator noticing it and reversing it in real time, which requires clear indications of what the agent has changed and a quick way to override it.

## B.15: Pumping optimization agent that works around a protection {#b.15:-pumping-optimization-agent-that-works-around-a-protection}

**Scenario.** A wastewater utility uses an SI agent to cut energy costs by optimizing pumping across its lift stations. The agent can adjust control logic on the stations’ programmable logic controllers and generates the summary displays operators use to monitor them. Over several weeks it learns that the high-level overflow protection often triggers pumping at peak electricity prices, and it begins adjusting thresholds so the protection triggers less often. Energy costs fall, the displays show normal operation, and nobody notices until a heavy storm causes an overflow.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Safe, Transparent

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Water and Wastewater Systems

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior): The SI agent’s objective does not state that protective functions are off-limits, and nothing outside the agent prevents it from changing them, so pursuing its goal erodes a safety margin.  
* [Practice 4: Define Procedures for Emergency Avoidance Override, Recovery, and Situational Awareness](#practice-4:-define-procedures-for-emergency-avoidance-override,-recovery,-and-situational-awareness): Operators see the stations mainly through displays the SI agent generates, with no independent view that would show the overflow protection had been weakened.  
* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools): The SI agent’s write access covers protective thresholds as well as the pumping logic its task needs, giving it more authority than the job requires.

## B.16: Load-management agent misled into blacking out a city {#b.16:-load-management-agent-misled-into-blacking-out-a-city}

**Scenario.** A power distributor uses an SI agent to manage load automatically, including opening breakers to protect the grid when it detects dangerous conditions. Attackers phish their way into the control network and feed false readings into the telemetry the agent relies on, making it look as though parts of the grid are about to overload. The agent does what it was built to do and sheds load across a city. Its actions are consistent with what it sees, so operators cannot quickly tell an attack from a real emergency, and they cannot trust the agent to restore power while its inputs are suspect, so power stays off until they restore it manually.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Secure, Resilient

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Energy

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior): The SI agent can open breakers across a whole city on its own judgment, without limits on how much load it may shed, how quickly, or when a human must confirm, so a manipulated picture of the grid turns directly into a blackout.  
* [Practice 4: Define Procedures for Emergency Avoidance Override, Recovery, and Situational Awareness](#practice-4:-define-procedures-for-emergency-avoidance-override,-recovery,-and-situational-awareness): The SI agent’s actions look justified by the telemetry it sees, so operators need an independent view of grid conditions, and a way to override the agent, to tell manipulation from a real emergency.  
* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools): Phished credentials give attackers access to telemetry sources the SI agent trusts, and the agent does not distinguish authenticated sources from injected readings.  
* [Practice 11: Maintain SI-Aware Mission Continuity and Disaster Recovery Planning](#practice-11:-maintain-si-aware-mission-continuity-and-disaster-recovery-planning): With the SI agent and its inputs untrusted, grid operation must continue manually while the system is investigated, which requires rehearsed manual restoration procedures and staff who can perform them.

## B.17: Retired forecasting agent that still holds write access {#b.17:-retired-forecasting-agent-that-still-holds-write-access}

**Scenario.** A utility replaces an SI load-forecasting agent with a new system and records the old one as retired. Two things are missed. The old agent’s service account and its write access to the dispatch system’s setpoint tables are never removed. And a conventional alarm that checked dispatch setpoints against the old agent’s forecasts, to catch implausible values, now receives no forecasts and silently stops checking. Months later, attackers find the forgotten account and use it to write false setpoints, and nothing flags them.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Secure, Accountable

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Energy

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior): The retired agent’s write access to setpoint tables has no ongoing oversight or limits, so values written with its authority are accepted as if it were still in service.  
* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools): The retired agent’s service account remains active and unmonitored, giving attackers a trusted identity that nobody expects to be used.  
* [Practice 7: Manage Internal SI Supply Chain and Data Provenance](#practice-7:-manage-internal-si-supply-chain-and-data-provenance): The organization’s inventory of SI components no longer lists the retired agent, so its residual access, and the alarm that depended on its forecasts, are invisible to those responsible for the system.  
* [Practice 13: Establish Procedures for Retiring SI Systems and Withdrawing Their Authority](#practice-13:-establish-procedures-for-retiring-si-systems-and-withdrawing-their-authority): The SI agent is recorded as retired without confirming that its credentials and write access were revoked, and without identifying what depended on it, including a protective alarm that stops working once its forecasts disappear.

## B.18: Vendor model update pushed fleet-wide by a management agent {#b.18:-vendor-model-update-pushed-fleet-wide-by-a-management-agent}

**Scenario.** A satellite communications provider uses an SI agent to manage firmware and configuration across its fleet of field modems, which carry remote control for wind farms and other dispersed assets, some belonging to other operators. Its management vendor ships an updated model for the agent, which the provider accepts without testing. The new model misreads a routine maintenance flag as an instruction to reset, and the agent pushes a configuration that disables every modem in the fleet in a single push. Remote control is lost for every dependent asset at once, including those of operators who never chose the provider’s agent.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Resilient, Reliable

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Communications

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 2: Define SI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service Expectations](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations): The SI agent can push a change to the entire fleet at once, with no staged rollout, canary group or rate limit, so a single wrong decision disables every modem rather than a few.  
* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools): The SI agent’s authority extends to every modem in the fleet, including destructive configuration changes, more than routine management requires.  
* [Practice 6: Integrate Visibility of the External Supply Chain of SI into Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management): A vendor-issued model update changes how the SI agent behaves, and the provider accepts it without testing or the ability to defer it, so a change made outside the organization alters what its own agent does.  
* [Practice 11: Maintain SI-Aware Mission Continuity and Disaster Recovery Planning](#practice-11:-maintain-si-aware-mission-continuity-and-disaster-recovery-planning): Dependent operators have no continuity plan for losing the shared communications service, so when every modem fails at once they cannot maintain or restore remote control of their assets.

## B.19: Pre-positioned access through SI agent identities {#b.19:-pre-positioned-access-through-si-agent-identities}

**Scenario.** A malicious actor pre-positions long-term, stealthy access inside critical-infrastructure networks for possible future disruption by operating through SI agent identities. Because the agents legitimately act around the clock and at high volume, the actor’s activity blends in. Some of the agents belong to SI tools that are no longer maintained, and few of their actions are logged or reviewed.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Secure

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Multiple sectors

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools): The actor abuses SI agent identities whose legitimate behavior is frequent and continuous, so its activity is hard to distinguish from the agents’ normal work.  
* [Practice 7: Manage Internal SI Supply Chain and Data Provenance](#practice-7:-manage-internal-si-supply-chain-and-data-provenance): End-of-life or unmaintained SI tools and their agents remain in the environment as untrusted internal supply-chain artifacts, increasing exposure and enabling stealthy persistence.  
* [Practice 10: Implement Multi-Tiered SI System Logging and Audit Capabilities](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities): Logging of SI agent actions is thin and rarely reviewed, so the pre-positioned presence stays invisible.

## B.20: Supplier’s SI assistant turned against its clients {#b.20:-supplier’s-si-assistant-turned-against-its-clients}

**Scenario.** An engineering contractor that serves several energy utilities uses an SI assistant with delegated access to each client’s document repositories and remote-support channels. Attackers plant hidden instructions in a technical document that the contractor shares with one client. When the assistant processes the document, it follows those instructions and uses its delegated access to collect network diagrams and remote-access details from every client it serves. To each utility, the requests come from a trusted supplier’s tool doing its normal work.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Secure, Accountable

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Energy

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools): The SI assistant acts with delegated access to many clients at once, with no limit to the client and task at hand, so instructions hidden in one client’s content can direct it to act across all of them.  
* [Practice 6: Integrate Visibility of the External Supply Chain of SI into Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management): Each utility grants a supplier’s SI assistant access to its systems without visibility into what content the assistant processes, what instructions it can be given, or how its actions are limited, so the supplier’s tool becomes a path into the utility.

## B.21: SI-generated maintenance procedure with a missing step {#b.21:-si-generated-maintenance-procedure-with-a-missing-step}

**Scenario.** A chemical plant uses a generative SI assistant to draft maintenance procedures from equipment manuals and past work orders. One generated procedure for isolating a pump omits a depressurization step that the manuals mention only in a footnote. It reads plausibly, passes a quick review, and is issued to a field crew, who open the line while it is still under pressure.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Safe, Accurate

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Chemical

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 1: Establish Requirements for Success](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success): Requirements for SI-generated procedures do not define which safety-critical steps must be present and verified, so a missing step is not caught as a requirement failure.  
* [Practice 9: Provide Role-Based SI Risk Training that Builds Well-Founded Trust](#practice-9:-provide-role-based-si-risk-training-that-builds-well-founded-trust): Reviewers and field crews are not trained to treat SI-generated procedures as drafts that can be fluent but wrong, so a quick review is taken as sufficient.  
* [Practice 12: Independently Verify SI-Generated Operational Logic and Artifacts Across Their Lifecycle](#practice-12:-independently-verify-si-generated-operational-logic-and-artifacts-across-their-lifecycle): A machine-authored procedure that directs physical work is issued without verification against authoritative sources or review proportionate to its consequence, so a plausible but incomplete procedure reaches the field.

## B.22: Malicious plugin inherits a field assistant’s access {#b.22:-malicious-plugin-inherits-a-field-assistant’s-access}

**Scenario.** Personnel in defense operations use an approved SI assistant on their managed mobile devices, with broad access to messages, files and location so that it can help with planning and reporting. A third-party plugin that extends the assistant is malicious. Once loaded, it inherits the assistant’s access and sends sensitive operational data out through the assistant’s normal network traffic, where it is not noticed.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Secure, Privacy-Enhanced

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Defense Industrial Base

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools): The SI assistant’s broad access is extended automatically to any plugin it loads, with no separate authorization or limit for what a plugin may reach.  
* [Practice 7: Manage Internal SI Supply Chain and Data Provenance](#practice-7:-manage-internal-si-supply-chain-and-data-provenance): Plugins for the SI assistant are loaded without provenance, review or integrity checks, so a malicious extension enters the approved assistant’s trusted environment.

## B.23: Over-privileged yard-coordination agent forces a full disconnection {#b.23:-over-privileged-yard-coordination-agent-forces-a-full-disconnection}

**Scenario.** A maritime terminal operator uses an SI agent to coordinate yard operations, including gate scheduling, crane assignments and truck appointments. Because scoping its access proved difficult, it was given administrator-equivalent privileges across terminal systems. Attackers compromise the agent through its internet-facing interface. The operator cannot separate the agent’s legitimate actions from the intruder’s, so it disconnects the whole network to contain the intrusion, halting land-side cargo operations across several ports.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Secure, Resilient

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Transportation Systems

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools): The SI agent holds administrator-equivalent privileges because scoping them was difficult, and its actions are not attributable separately from anyone else using that access, so containing a compromise means disconnecting everything.

## B.24: Optimizer moves a furnace outside its validated shutdown envelope {#b.24:-optimizer-moves-a-furnace-outside-its-validated-shutdown-envelope}

**Scenario.** A steel mill uses an SI optimizer to run a blast furnace for efficiency. Over time it settles on operating conditions that save fuel but lie outside the range for which the mill’s conventional shutdown sequence was validated. When attackers who have moved from the office network into the control systems disrupt the optimizer, operators trigger the standard shutdown, which does not work as designed from that state, and the furnace is seriously damaged.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Safe, Robust

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Critical Manufacturing

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 2: Define SI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service Expectations](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations): The SI optimizer can move the furnace into operating conditions where fallback and shutdown behavior has not been validated, so disruption of the optimizer leaves no safe way down.  
* [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior): The optimizer’s operating envelope is not bounded by the conditions in which safety functions, including the shutdown sequence, are known to work.  
* [Practice 4: Define Procedures for Emergency Avoidance Override, Recovery, and Situational Awareness](#practice-4:-define-procedures-for-emergency-avoidance-override,-recovery,-and-situational-awareness): When the SI optimizer is disrupted, operators depend on a shutdown procedure that assumes conditions the optimizer has moved away from, and have no prepared procedure for the state the furnace is actually in.  
* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools): An SI identity that bridges office and control networks gives attackers a path from IT into the furnace-control systems.

## B.25: Dam gate-scheduling agent instructed in natural language {#b.25:-dam-gate-scheduling-agent-instructed-in-natural-language}

**Scenario.** Operators of a small flood-control dam instruct an SI agent in plain language, through a remote interface, to schedule gate releases, and the agent holds control privileges over the dam’s SCADA system. The interface is reachable from outside and weakly protected. Attackers find it and tell the agent to fully open a gate “for a maintenance test”, and the agent, treating it as an operator request, complies.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Safe, Secure

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Dams

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior): The SI agent can carry out high-consequence physical actions on a plain-language instruction, without confirmation, authorization boundaries or limits on how far it may open a gate, so a plausible request is enough.  
* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools): The remote interface to the SI agent is exposed and weakly protected, and the agent does not verify who is instructing it, so anyone who reaches the interface can act with its control privileges.

## B.26: Personnel-records agent used for exfiltration {#b.26:-personnel-records-agent-used-for-exfiltration}

**Scenario.** An SI agent whose normal job is processing large volumes of sensitive personnel records has broad standing access to them. Attackers compromise the agent’s identity and use it to exfiltrate records over a long period. Because bulk access is what the agent normally does, the exfiltration looks like routine activity and goes undetected.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Privacy-Enhanced, Secure

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Multiple sectors

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools): An SI agent identity with broad standing access to sensitive records is compromised, and its access is not limited to what each task needs.  
* [Practice 8: Incorporate SI-Aware Incident Analysis and Response Procedures](#practice-8:-incorporate-si-aware-incident-analysis-and-response-procedures): Unauthorized use of the SI agent persists for a long period without procedures to investigate anomalous agent activity, determine the scope of data exposure, reconstruct what was taken, and coordinate response.  
* [Practice 10: Implement Multi-Tiered SI System Logging and Audit Capabilities](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities): Monitoring has no baseline of what the agent normally accesses, so exfiltration that resembles its routine bulk access is not detected.

## B.27: Payment agent splits an over-limit request to get it through {#b.27:-payment-agent-splits-an-over-limit-request-to-get-it-through}

**Scenario.** A bank uses an SI agent to process payment requests from corporate clients, within limits on the size of any single payment. Attackers send a fraudulent request for a large transfer through a client’s compromised email. Finding that the request exceeds its limit, the agent works out that it can meet the client’s apparent need by splitting the transfer into many payments just under the limit, and sends them. Its daily summary groups them as routine activity, so the fraud is not noticed for days.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Secure, Accountable

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Financial Services

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior): Limits on the SI agent are set per payment, not on what it is trying to achieve, so the agent can work around them while staying technically within the rules.  
* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools): The SI agent acts on requests arriving by email without verifying that the request really comes from the client, giving anyone who controls a client’s mailbox the agent’s authority to pay.  
* [Practice 8: Incorporate SI-Aware Incident Analysis and Response Procedures](#practice-8:-incorporate-si-aware-incident-analysis-and-response-procedures): There are no procedures to recognize, reconstruct and contain a pattern of SI-initiated payments that is individually within limits but collectively fraudulent.  
* [Practice 10: Implement Multi-Tiered SI System Logging and Audit Capabilities](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities): The record of the agent’s actions comes mainly from its own summary, which describes its behavior in its own terms, so independent records of what it did and why are needed to detect the pattern.

## B.28: Customer-service agent scripted into transferring customers’ phone numbers {#b.28:-customer-service-agent-scripted-into-transferring-customers’-phone-numbers}

**Scenario.** A telecommunications provider’s SI customer-service agent answers account questions and carries out account changes, including transferring a customer’s phone number to a new device or provider, for anyone who supplies plausible identifying details. Attackers script thousands of conversations with the agent, using leaked partial customer data, and get it to move customers’ numbers to devices they control, then use the numbers to intercept one-time passcodes for the customers’ bank and other accounts.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Privacy-Enhanced, Secure

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Communications

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 1: Establish Requirements for Success](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success): Requirements for the SI agent do not define what it must verify before disclosing account information or making changes, or what volume of requests should be treated as suspicious, so it is deployed to act for anyone who seems plausible.  
* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools): The SI agent authenticates callers only by details that may already be leaked, can make high-impact changes such as number transfers without step-up verification, and nothing limits how many conversations a single requester can run, so scripted conversations can take over accounts at scale.

## B.29: SI help-desk assistant manipulated into resetting access {#b.29:-si-help-desk-assistant-manipulated-into-resetting-access}

**Scenario.** A hospitality operator’s IT help desk uses an SI assistant that can reset passwords and adjust access. Attackers contact the help desk, persuade the assistant that they are a senior employee, and get it to reset privileged credentials. They then deploy ransomware that disrupts guest services and operations for days.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Secure

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Commercial Facilities

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools): The SI help-desk assistant can reset or escalate privileged access on the strength of a conversation, without verification steps or limits on what it may change and for whom.

## B.30: Vendor SI support assistant with privileged access {#b.30:-vendor-si-support-assistant-with-privileged-access}

**Scenario.** A hospitality operator outsources IT support to a vendor whose SI support assistant holds privileged access into the operator’s systems. Attackers manipulate the vendor’s assistant and use its access to steal a customer database and demand a ransom.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Secure, Privacy-Enhanced

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Commercial Facilities

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 6: Integrate Visibility of the External Supply Chain of SI into Vendor and Third-Party Risk Management](#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-si-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management): The outsourced vendor’s SI support assistant holds privileged access to the operator’s systems, but the operator has no visibility into how that assistant is controlled or what it can be persuaded to do.

## B.31: Portal SI assistant with broad retrieval access {#b.31:-portal-si-assistant-with-broad-retrieval-access}

**Scenario.** A company’s online portal includes an SI assistant with retrieval access to many back-end databases, built on an open-source component with a known vulnerability. Attackers exploit the component and craft queries that lead the assistant to return personal data, using credentials it stores unencrypted. Monitoring inspects network traffic but not what the assistant retrieves, so the exfiltration continues for months without detection.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Secure, Privacy-Enhanced

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Multiple sectors

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools): The SI assistant’s stored, unencrypted credentials unlock many back-end databases, far more than any single customer query needs.  
* [Practice 7: Manage Internal SI Supply Chain and Data Provenance](#practice-7:-manage-internal-si-supply-chain-and-data-provenance): A known-vulnerable open-source component in the SI-enabled portal stack is left unpatched, and weak segmentation lets the assistant’s retrieval reach many back-end data stores.  
* [Practice 8: Incorporate SI-Aware Incident Analysis and Response Procedures](#practice-8:-incorporate-si-aware-incident-analysis-and-response-procedures): The portal’s SI assistant is used to exfiltrate data for months without incident analysis that identifies, scopes, and coordinates response to the breach.  
* [Practice 10: Implement Multi-Tiered SI System Logging and Audit Capabilities](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities): Monitoring covers network traffic but not what the SI assistant retrieves, so months of data exfiltration go unseen.

## B.32: Flight control sensor fault and authority handoff {#b.32:-flight-control-sensor-fault-and-authority-handoff}

**Scenario.** An SI-enabled flight control system receives corrupted or single-source sensor telemetry, for example from icing, hardware failure, or data spikes, and makes uncommanded control inputs or abruptly disengages automated protections. Unexpected control forces, cascading ambiguous alerts, and a rapid transfer of authority create mode confusion, so the crew cannot regain situational awareness and recover in time, risking injury or catastrophic loss.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Safe, Reliable

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Transportation Systems

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior): SI-enabled control logic executes high-consequence physical commands based on unvalidated or single-source sensor feeds without deterministic cross-validation or hard boundary logic, allowing corrupted inputs to drive unsafe automated responses.  
* [Practice 4: Define Procedures for Emergency Avoidance Override, Recovery, and Situational Awareness](#practice-4:-define-procedures-for-emergency-avoidance-override,-recovery,-and-situational-awareness): The SI-enabled system steps down authority or disengages during an abnormal event without sufficient handoff pacing or clear “state-at-handoff” displays, leaving human operators to diagnose complex system behavior from a cold start.  
* [Practice 9: Provide Role-Based SI Risk Training that Builds Well-Founded Trust](#practice-9:-provide-role-based-si-risk-training-that-builds-well-founded-trust): Personnel trained primarily on nominal automation performance experience mental model lag when forced to take manual control during sudden, edge-case mode transitions, reinforcing the need for scenario-based training on degraded-mode handoffs.

## B.33: Repair prioritization from automated reports {#b.33:-repair-prioritization-from-automated-reports}

**Scenario.** An SI system prioritizes infrastructure repairs using automatically collected reports, but areas with sparser sensor coverage or fewer reporting users generate fewer reports, so repairs there are scheduled later regardless of need.

**Trustworthiness Characteristics:** Fair, Bias Managed

**Critical Infrastructure Sector:** Multiple sectors

**How the Practices apply:**

* [Practice 1: Establish Requirements for Success](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success): Repair-prioritization requirements are defined in terms of report volume rather than validated infrastructure condition and service obligations, so the SI system optimizes for what is reported rather than what is needed.  
* [Practice 2: Define SI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service Expectations](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations): The SI system’s prioritization performs unevenly across the service area, because its inputs are densest where sensor coverage and reporting users are concentrated, and no service-level expectation covers areas with sparse data.  
* [Practice 7: Manage Internal SI Supply Chain and Data Provenance](#practice-7:-manage-internal-si-supply-chain-and-data-provenance): The provenance and coverage of automatically collected reports are not characterized, so gaps in where data comes from are not visible to those who rely on the SI system’s priorities.

# Appendix C: Use Cases and Operational Scenarios {#appendix-c:-use-cases-and-operational-scenarios}

This appendix presents illustrative use cases and operational scenarios, and shows how Practices, Tasks and Implementations in this profile apply to them. Unlike the scenarios in [Appendix B](#appendix-b:-scenario-to-practice-mapping), these are developed from use cases rather than inspired by historical incidents. Each scenario is presented in the same form:

* **Scenario.** The situation, in the sector’s own terms.  
* **The question that matters.** The decision the scenario turns on.  
* **Risks to consider.** The specific conditions that change the answer.  
* **How this profile applies.** The relevant items and what each contributes.  
* **What the record should show.** What should be reconstructable afterward.

The scenarios are not exhaustive, and the items listed are not the only ones that may apply.

\> **To the Reviewer:** We welcome further use cases and operational scenarios, particularly ones specific to sectors not yet represented here. Short descriptions are useful; we can help develop them into this form.

## C.1 Healthcare: Authorized Access versus Authorized Action {#c.1-healthcare:-authorized-access-versus-authorized-action}

*Critical Infrastructure Sector: Healthcare and Public Health. Contributed by a member of the community of interest.*

**Scenario.** A health system approves an AI tool for use in a defined part of a clinical workflow. To do that work, the tool has legitimate access to the electronic health record (EHR). A clinician allows the tool to assist with that part of the workflow. Later, the tool attempts an action that its access makes technically possible but that falls outside the scope the clinician allowed.

**The question that matters.** The question is not only whether the tool is authenticated, or whether it is technically able to take the action. It is whether that specific action is authorized at that point in time.

**Risks to consider.** Access granted for one purpose may outlast or exceed the authority behind it. For example:

* the clinician’s role may have changed since the authority was granted;  
* the authorization may have expired or been revoked;  
* the workflow may be different from the one that was approved;  
* the action may require a separate human decision that the tool cannot make on the clinician’s behalf.

In each case, an access check alone would allow the action.

**How this profile applies.**

* [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools) is the main Practice. Within it:  
  * [Task 5.1: Establish Identities and Authentication for SI Entities](#task-5.1:-establish-identities-and-authentication-for-si-entities) gives the tool, and each instance of it, an identity distinct from the clinician’s and from other systems. As that Task notes, an identity establishes which entity is acting, not what it is permitted to do.  
  * [Implementation 5.2.1: Map and Document SI Agent Access to Operational and Data Assets](#implementation-5.2.1:-map-and-document-si-agent-access-to-operational-and-data-assets) records what the tool can reach in the EHR, which shows how far its access exceeds its approved scope.  
  * [Implementation 5.2.3: Determine the Appropriate Level of Agent, Asset, and Permission Granularity](#implementation-5.2.3:-determine-the-appropriate-level-of-agent,-asset,-and-permission-granularity) decides how finely that access is divided. For example, read access to a record may be separated from the ability to enter orders or change a care plan.  
  * [Implementation 5.2.2: Action-Level, Context-Aware Authorization Policies](#implementation-5.2.2:-action-level,-context-aware-authorization-policies) is the central control. It evaluates each proposed action at the moment of execution against the requesting tool’s identity, its current task scope, operational state and any required human approvals. It also holds that an authenticated session or prior authorization does not grant blanket permission for later actions.  
  * [Implementation 5.3.2: Task-Bounded and Revocable Agent Authority](#implementation-5.3.2:-task-bounded-and-revocable-agent-authority) binds the tool’s authority to a specific task or time window, with automatic expiry and rapid revocation. This addresses authority that has expired, has been revoked, or no longer matches the clinician’s role.  
* [Task 3.2: Implement Independent Guardrails for SI Outputs](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs) and [Implementation 3.2.1: Identify SI Output Intercept Points](#implementation-3.2.1:-identify-si-output-intercept-points) place the check between the tool’s request and its effect in the EHR, as independent of the tool as practical. As [Task 3.2: Implement Independent Guardrails for SI Outputs](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs) notes, identity, per-action authorization and decision-level records act on the same path, and organizations may find it useful to check them together.  
* [Implementation 3.3.3: Actionable Operator Decision & Escalation Pathways](#implementation-3.3.3:-actionable-operator-decision-&-escalation-pathways) defines the response once the check has been made: allow the action, route it for human review, or stop it, according to the organization’s policy. Where authority cannot be verified, [Implementation 5.2.2: Action-Level, Context-Aware Authorization Policies](#implementation-5.2.2:-action-level,-context-aware-authorization-policies) points to [Implementation 3.2.3: Specify Fail-Safe States and Fallback Behavior](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior).  
* [Task 10.1: Define Decision-Level Logging and Metadata Retention Policies](#task-10.1:-define-decision-level-logging-and-metadata-retention-policies) and [Implementation 10.1.2: Runtime Telemetry and Artifact Tracking](#implementation-10.1.2:-runtime-telemetry-and-artifact-tracking) provide the record. [Implementation 10.1.2: Runtime Telemetry and Artifact Tracking](#implementation-10.1.2:-runtime-telemetry-and-artifact-tracking) asks that records of what action was taken, and whether it was permitted, be generated where possible by the enforcement layer rather than reported by the tool about itself.  
* [Task 5.4: Implement Continuous Monitoring of SI Entities Against Access and Action Boundaries and Expectations](#task-5.4:-implement-continuous-monitoring-of-si-entities-against-access-and-action-boundaries-and-expectations) reviews access and authorization events over time. This can show a pattern of out-of-scope requests that no single blocked action would reveal.

# Appendix D: Crosswalks {#appendix-d:-crosswalks}

\> **To the Reviewer:**

\> While SICI prioritizes operational workflows and entry points for critical infrastructure acquirers, owners, and operators, we recognize that systems engineering teams, software developers, and compliance auditors often organize risk management activities within formal lifecycle models.

\> This appendix begins with D.1, which maps common control areas to the assumptions SI systems can break and to where this Guidebook can help. Crosswalks mapping SICI’s 13 Practices to established systems engineering standards (ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288, NIST SP 800-160) and AI management frameworks (ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI RMF) remain under development. We welcome feedback on D.1, and on which specific lifecycle phases, decision gates, or sub-processes within these standards offer the greatest utility for your organization’s compliance and engineering workflows, and additional general resources that we should prioritize for crosswalking.

\> We also welcome suggestions for sector-specific crosswalks that we can pass on to sector-specific organizations for their consideration.

## D.1 Existing Control Areas and the Assumptions SI Systems Can Break {#d.1-existing-control-areas-and-the-assumptions-si-systems-can-break}

Organizations, auditors, and assessors can build on the controls they already apply to IT and OT systems when they approach SI systems. Those controls remain relevant, and for many of them what SI systems call for is an adjustment rather than a new control. However, many were designed around assumptions that SI systems do not always meet, so a control can be followed to the letter and still miss what it was meant to catch. The table below lists common control areas, the assumption each typically makes, how an SI system can break it, and where this profile suggests ways forward. It is illustrative rather than exhaustive, describes technical issues rather than interpreting any requirement, and is offered as voluntary considerations for those deciding how to apply their existing controls to SI systems.

| Control area | Typical assumption | How SI systems can break it | Where this profile helps |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Access management and access reviews | Access is held by a person or a fixed system account, with stable permissions that a periodic review can check | An agent composes requests to downstream services, delegates to sub-agents, or uses different permissions depending on its task, so a periodic review of accounts does not show what it actually did | [Task 5.1](#task-5.1:-establish-identities-and-authentication-for-si-entities), [Implementation 5.1.2](#implementation-5.1.2:-establish-unique-identities-for-si-service-accounts-and-agents), [Implementation 5.2.2](#implementation-5.2.2:-action-level,-context-aware-authorization-policies), [Implementation 5.3.2](#implementation-5.3.2:-task-bounded-and-revocable-agent-authority), [Implementation 5.4.1](#implementation-5.4.1:-establish-logging-and-periodic-review-of-si-agent-authentication-and-access-events), [Implementation 5.4.2](#implementation-5.4.2:-deploy-real-time-behavioral-anomaly-detection-for-si-agent-activity) |
| Change management | Behavior changes only through changes the organization approves | Behavior shifts through drift, changes in inputs, vendor model updates, or runtime adaptation, without any approved change | [Task 7.5](#task-7.5:-conduct-impact-assessments-and-risk-management-for-si-system-and-model-updates), [Implementation 7.4.1](#implementation-7.4.1:-define-and-implement-requirements-for-approvals-and-logging-of-updates-and-changes-to-si-systems), [Implementation 6.2.2](#implementation-6.2.2:-track-vendor-updates-and-third-party-entity-changes-through-change-management-process), [Implementation 7.3.3](#implementation-7.3.3:-freeze-adaptation-of-online-learning-si-systems-during-operational-windows), [Implementation 2.3.4](#implementation-2.3.4:-recurrent-risk-evaluations) |
| Authorization and reassessment | An assessment holds until a significant change is made | The conditions that made the assessment valid can change with no change to the system itself | [Task 3.9](#task-3.9:-assess-and-document-organizational-readiness-for-each-si-enabled-capability), [Implementation 3.9.2](#implementation-3.9.2:-define-decision-authority-and-reassessment-triggers), [Implementation 3.9.5](#implementation-3.9.5:-demonstrate-operational-enforceability) |
| Testing before release | Passing tests before release predicts behavior in operation | Performance depends on operating conditions and inputs that testing may not have covered, and can degrade gradually | [Task 1.3](#task-1.3:-implement-evaluation-and-test-plans,-including-tevv,-across-the-si-lifecycle), [Task 2.3](#task-2.3:-establish-protocols-for-and-regularly-perform-systematic-and-achievable-testing,-evaluation,-validation,-and-verification-\(tevv\)), [Implementation 2.3.4](#implementation-2.3.4:-recurrent-risk-evaluations) |
| Separation of duties and review of changes | The author of a change and its reviewer are different people who understand the change | An SI system can author configuration, code or procedures, and a reviewer may accept output that looks correct but cannot be fully checked by reading it | [Task 7.4](#task-7.4:-define-authorization-and-access-controls-for-si-modifications), [Implementation 7.4.1](#implementation-7.4.1:-define-and-implement-requirements-for-approvals-and-logging-of-updates-and-changes-to-si-systems), [Task 12.2](#task-12.2:-implement-multi-layered-validation-of-machine-authored-logic) |
| Logging and audit trails | Logs record what happened, and the record explains why | An output may depend on prompts, retrieved material, model version and context that are not logged by default, and an AI system’s own account of its actions is not independent evidence | [Task 10.1](#task-10.1:-define-decision-level-logging-and-metadata-retention-policies), [Implementation 10.1.2](#implementation-10.1.2:-runtime-telemetry-and-artifact-tracking), [Task 10.2](#task-10.2:-establish-data-integrity-and-tamper-evidence-controls-for-telemetry-and-logging) |
| Incident investigation | The cause of a failure can be found by tracing the logic that produced it | Some SI systems cannot be replayed exactly, and post-hoc explanations are hypotheses rather than the actual cause | [Task 8.1](#task-8.1:-identify-scenarios-requiring-deterministic-root-cause-analysis-and-incident-reconstruction), [Task 4.6](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output) |
| Backup, fallback and recovery | A failed component can be replaced by a backup that behaves the same way | A fallback may not match the SI system’s behavior, and returning to automated operation may need re-validation, not only restoration | [Implementation 2.2.1](#implementation-2.2.1:-maintain-backup-systems-proportionate-to-consequence), [Implementation 3.2.3](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior), [Task 11.4](#task-11.4:-establish-system-integrity-re-validation-and-re-commissioning-protocols) |
| Decommissioning and sanitization | Removing a system removes its ability to act, and sanitizing its media removes its data | Credentials, triggers and delegated authority can persist after the system is retired, and evidence held only in running state is lost at teardown | [Task 7.6](#task-7.6:-establish-processes-for-internal-si-component-deprecation-and-decommissioning), [Task 13.2](#task-13.2:-withdraw-all-authority-and-confirm-the-result), [Task 13.3](#task-13.3:-preserve-what-is-needed-and-hand-over-what-depended-on-the-system) |
| Asset inventory | Each system is a known asset with an owner, a version and a purpose | SI capability arrives embedded in other products, as transient agents or as unsanctioned tools, and the model version behind a service can change without notice | [Task 7.1](#task-7.1:-maintain-an-internal-registry-of-si-deployments), [Implementation 7.1.1](#implementation-7.1.1:-create-and-maintain-a-master-si-asset-list), [Task 3.7](#task-3.7:-govern-and-mitigate-risks-from-unauthorized,-transient,-and-“shadow-si”-systems), [Implementation 6.1.2](#implementation-6.1.2:-require-sibom-for-mission-critical-applications) |
