| Configuration management | A system’s behavior is set by configuration that can be baselined and compared | Behavior also depends on prompts, retrieved material, learned parameters and safety filters, which may not be under configuration control | [Task 7.3](#task-7.3:-manage-version-control-and-logging-for-internal-si-safety-mechanisms), [Implementation 7.3.3](#implementation-7.3.3:-freeze-adaptation-of-online-learning-si-systems-during-operational-windows), [Task 7.5](#task-7.5:-conduct-impact-assessments-and-risk-management-for-si-system-and-model-updates) |
| Records and retention | The records worth keeping are known in advance, and retaining them preserves the evidence | What explains an SI system’s action may be its prompt, context or model version, which are not records by default; some evidence exists only while the system runs | [Task 10.1](#task-10.1:-define-decision-level-logging-and-metadata-retention-policies), [Implementation 10.1.3](#implementation-10.1.3:-forensic-integrity-and-privacy-preserving-log-partitioning), [Implementation 7.6.2](#implementation-7.6.2:-secure-archiving-and-destruction-of-model-and-other-si-artifacts), [Task 13.3](#task-13.3:-preserve-what-is-needed-and-hand-over-what-depended-on-the-system) |
| Independence of redundant systems | Redundant systems fail independently because they are separate | Separate SI systems can share a foundation model, training data, provider or hosting, and so fail together | [Implementation 2.2.1](#implementation-2.2.1:-maintain-backup-systems-proportionate-to-consequence), [Implementation 3.5.2](#implementation-3.5.2:-identify-indirect-shared-infrastructure-and-collateral-damage-exposure), [Task 3.5](#task-3.5:-define-and-control-risks-to-adjacent-and-related-systems) |
| Monitoring and alerting | Monitoring thresholds catch the failures that matter, and alerts reach someone who can act | An SI system can fail plausibly, with outputs that look normal, and can generate more alerts than people can handle | [Task 3.4](#task-3.4:-monitor-for-anomalous-si-behavior), [Task 3.3](#task-3.3:-establish-failure-notification-requirements), [Task 4.4](#task-4.4:-attention-governance-and-alert/alarm-flood-mitigation), [Implementation 5.4.2](#implementation-5.4.2:-deploy-real-time-behavioral-anomaly-detection-for-si-agent-activity) |
| Third-party and supplier assurance | A supplier’s attestations and documentation describe the product that is delivered | Model updates, retraining and changes in upstream providers can alter behavior after assurance was given | [Task 6.1](#task-6.1:-develop-policies-for-si-supply-chain-requirements), [Task 6.2](#task-6.2:-align-si-and-existing-ci-asset-lifecycle-management), [Implementation 6.1.2](#implementation-6.1.2:-require-sibom-for-mission-critical-applications), [Implementation 6.1.5](#implementation-6.1.5:-operational-si-hazard-reachability-disclosures), [Implementation 6.2.2](#implementation-6.2.2:-track-vendor-updates-and-third-party-entity-changes-through-change-management-process) |
| Training and awareness | Trained staff will recognize when a system is wrong | Staff may over-trust fluent or confident outputs, and manual skills can decay when an SI system takes over the work | [Task 9.2](#task-9.2:-deliver-specialized-training-on-human-si-interaction-and-automation-bias), [Task 3.6](#task-3.6:-mitigate-automation-complacency-and-skills-degradation), [Task 4.6](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output) |
| Incident reporting | Reportable incidents are recognizable events with a clear cause | SI-related failures can be gradual, ambiguous or near-misses, and those who notice them may face disincentives to report | [Task 8.4](#task-8.4:-define-external-reporting-and-regulatory-disclosure-protocols-following-si-incidents), [Task 8.6](#task-8.6:-establish-non-punitive-reporting-for-si-related-near-misses) |

### D.1.1 Worked Example: Access Reviews {#d.1.1-worked-example:-access-reviews}

A periodic user access review typically checks that each account belongs to a current person or system, and that its permissions still match that role. The review assumes that access is held by an identifiable account, that its permissions are stable between reviews, and that reviewing the account reviews what can be done through it.

An AI agent can break each of these assumptions. It may act through a service account shared with other functions, or through credentials issued for a single task. It may compose requests to several downstream services, delegate work to sub-agents or tools that hold their own permissions, and use different permissions depending on the task it is given. A review of the agent’s account can then show permissions that look appropriate, while not showing what the agent actually did with them, or what it could reach through the systems it called.

The control’s intent, that access matches need and is reviewed, still applies. This profile suggests ways of meeting it for AI agents: giving each agent its own identity ([Implementation 5.1.2: Establish Unique Identities for SI Service Accounts and Agents](#implementation-5.1.2:-establish-unique-identities-for-si-service-accounts-and-agents)), bounding its authority to a task and making it revocable ([Implementation 5.3.2: Task-Bounded and Revocable Agent Authority](#implementation-5.3.2:-task-bounded-and-revocable-agent-authority)), authorizing individual actions at the time they are taken ([Implementation 5.2.2: Action-Level, Context-Aware Authorization Policies](#implementation-5.2.2:-action-level,-context-aware-authorization-policies)), and reviewing what agents actually did as well as what they were permitted to do ([Implementation 5.4.1](#implementation-5.4.1:-establish-logging-and-periodic-review-of-si-agent-authentication-and-access-events), [Implementation 5.4.2](#implementation-5.4.2:-deploy-real-time-behavioral-anomaly-detection-for-si-agent-activity)). Which of these an organization needs depends on what its agents can reach and the consequences of misuse.

### D.1.2 Using the table {#d.1.2-using-the-table}

The table is a starting point for conversations between those who own existing controls and those who build and operate SI systems. For a given control area, it can help identify whether the control’s assumption holds for a particular SI system and, where it does not, which items in this profile may help meet the control’s intent. Where an organization concludes that an item does not apply, recording the reasoning supports later review. Where an existing control or supervisory obligation already meets an item’s intent, recording that mapping, and any remaining difference, can avoid standing up a second governance process for the same system.

# Appendix E: Suggested Ways to Use this Document with an LLM-Based Assistant {#appendix-e:-suggested-ways-to-use-this-document-with-an-llm-based-assistant}

\> **To the Reviewer:** The use cases, prompts, and cautions in this appendix are based on the authors’ own trials and on early feedback. We would welcome prompts that have worked well for you, results that surprised you, problems you have encountered, and use cases we have not listed. We would particularly welcome reports from sector-specific or more economical LLM-based assistants.

An LLM-based assistant can help readers find the parts of this document that apply to their situation, and this appendix helps them get more reliable answers from one. It expands on the guidance in Section 1.4, Using this Guidebook. It suggests ways to use an LLM-based assistant with this document, gives example prompts, and describes problems to watch for.

**The uses and prompts in this appendix are illustrative examples, offered as starting points. They have not been systematically tested, results will vary between assistants and between versions of the same assistant, and we make no guarantee about the answers any assistant gives. Check what an assistant tells you against this profile, and above all against the sources it cites.**

This profile is intended to lead readers to the sources it cites, not to replace them. Each reference entry says which part of a source applies and why, so that a reader, or an assistant, can go to that source and read it. The prompts below ask the assistant to name those sources and, where it can, to check its answers against them.

Nothing in this appendix changes the status of the profile. The profile is guidance to inform professional judgment, not a checklist or a set of requirements. An assistant’s reading of it does not change that either.

## E.1 Before You Start {#e.1-before-you-start}

### E.1.1 Give the assistant the whole document {#e.1.1-give-the-assistant-the-whole-document}

Use the Markdown assistant-ready version, which is meant for this purpose. The HTML web edition is meant for reading. This document is long. Some assistants read only part of a long file, or summarize parts of it without saying so. Others may process it in pieces. Ask the assistant to confirm that it has read all 13 Practices and the appendices.

### E.1.2 Provide the knowledge graph too {#e.1.2-provide-the-knowledge-graph-too}

This document is distributed together with a knowledge graph in YAML format. Give the assistant both files. The knowledge graph lists every Practice, Task and Implementation by item number, together with the cross-references between them, their trustworthiness characteristics, AI RMF subcategories, references and [Appendix B](#appendix-b:-scenario-to-practice-mapping) scenarios. It helps an assistant check that it has seen every item and find items that refer to one another. The knowledge graph is generated from this document and adds nothing to it. Where the two differ, the document governs. If you received this document without the knowledge graph, you can obtain it from the same source as the latest version.

### E.1.3 Provide the references where you can {#e.1.3-provide-the-references-where-you-can}

Many of the sources this profile cites are freely available. If you can give the assistant copies of the ones that matter to your question, or an assistant that can retrieve them, it can check what a source says rather than relying on the profile’s description of it. Tell the assistant which sources it has.

### E.1.4 Describe your situation {#e.1.4-describe-your-situation}

This profile is deliberately sector-agnostic. How useful the answers are depends mostly on what the assistant is told about your organization, for example:

* your sector and role;  
* the SI system: what it does, what it is connected to, and who acts on its outputs;  
* the regulatory and contractual obligations that apply;  
* the policies and risk management processes you already have;  
* the people and resources available.

You can describe this in the conversation, supply it as documents where your organization’s policy permits, or ask the assistant to question you before it makes recommendations. Some of this information may be sensitive. Consider what the assistant is permitted to receive and where that information will go.

### E.1.5 Set expectations at the start {#e.1.5-set-expectations-at-the-start}

A short opening instruction can reduce the problems described in E.3. For example:

> Please read the attached profile in full, including all 13 Practices and the appendices, and tell me if you could not, or if you read only part of it. Use the attached knowledge graph to check cross-references. In your answers, cite the item numbers you are drawing on, such as “Task 3.2” or “Implementation 5.2.2.” Where a point rests on a reference the profile cites, name the reference and the part of it the profile points to. If you have the reference itself, check the point against it and tell me whether you did; if you have only the profile’s description, say so. Keep the profile’s own wording, such as “should” and “consider,” rather than turning it into requirements. Mark clearly which points are your own suggestions rather than the profile’s. Tell me when you are applying an item to a situation it was not written for. Before you make recommendations, ask me any questions you need about my organization. If you are unsure what the profile says on a point, re-read the relevant entry rather than answering from memory, and quote it.

## E.2 Use Cases and Example Prompts {#e.2-use-cases-and-example-prompts}

Text in square brackets is a placeholder for your own details.

### E.2.1 Which Practices and Tasks apply {#e.2.1-which-practices-and-tasks-apply}

> We are \[organization type, size and sector\]. We are \[piloting / procuring / operating\] \[description of the SI system, what it reads, what it writes or influences, and who approves its outputs\]. We are regulated by \[regulator or framework\], and our team is \[size and expertise\]. Which Practices and Tasks apply to us, and which should we look at first given our resources? Explain why for each, and name the references cited there that we should read first.

The order in which the profile presents its Practices does not indicate priority. If an assistant proposes an order, that order is its judgment, so ask it to say what it based the order on.

### E.2.2 What a Task would involve, and which References to read {#e.2.2-what-a-task-would-involve,-and-which-references-to-read}

> What would \[Task N.M\] involve for us in practice, given \[situation\]? Which of the References listed under it, or under its Implementations, should we read first, and for what? For each, say which part of the source the profile points to and what we should expect to find there. If you can open the source, tell me whether it says what the profile describes.

References can appear at the Practice, Task or Implementation level. Ask the assistant to say where each reference it names is listed.

### E.2.3 Which items address a specific risk {#e.2.3-which-items-address-a-specific-risk}

> Which Practices, Tasks and Implementations address the risk that \[specific risk, e.g., “an assistant-generated configuration introduces an unsafe change that our reviewers don’t catch”\]? Include items that point to one another, and say which items address the risk directly and which only in part. For each, name the references the profile cites on this point.

### E.2.4 Learning from an incident {#e.2.4-learning-from-an-incident}

> \[Description of the incident: what happened, what the SI system did, how people responded, and what the effects were.\] Which items in this profile might have prevented or limited this? For each, explain what it would have changed, and name the references cited there that would help us understand this kind of failure. Also tell me whether any scenario in [Appendix B](#appendix-b:-scenario-to-practice-mapping) is similar.

This can be useful input to a lessons-learned or after-action review. It works for incidents reported elsewhere as well as your own.

**Incident details are often among the most sensitive information an organization holds.** They may reveal vulnerabilities that have not yet been fixed, personal information, or matters subject to legal privilege, investigation, or reporting obligations. Before describing an incident to an assistant, check what your organization’s policy permits that assistant to receive, and where the information will be stored and used (see NIST SP 1353). Where in doubt, describe the incident in general terms, with identifying details removed, or use an incident reported publicly.

### E.2.5 Trustworthiness tensions {#e.2.5-trustworthiness-tensions}

> For \[use case\], which trustworthiness characteristics may be in tension, and where does this profile discuss those tensions? Quote the relevant entries, cite their item numbers, and name any references cited there that discuss the trade-off.

Tensions are discussed in the “Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance” field of individual entries, and Appendix A.4 describes the patterns that recur across them.

### E.2.6 Finding current or related references {#e.2.6-finding-current-or-related-references}

> Using the description this profile gives for \[reference\], find the current version, any successor document, and any closely related guidance for \[sector\]. Tell me which you were able to confirm and which you could not.

This use requires an assistant that can search. References in this profile describe what part of a source applies, partly so that revised or superseded documents can be traced. An assistant that cannot search may still answer from memory. That memory reflects what was available up to the assistant’s training cutoff, and may be out of date.

### E.2.7 Comparing with your existing controls {#e.2.7-comparing-with-your-existing-controls}

> Here is a summary of our existing \[policy / procedure / control set\] for \[system or process\]. Which items in this profile does it already address, which does it address only in part, and which does it not address? Base your comparison on what our documents actually say, and tell me where you are inferring. For the items it does not address, name the references the profile cites, so that we can read the source guidance.

This is not a compliance assessment, because the profile has no conformance requirements. It can help identify where to look more closely. Internal policies and procedures may also be sensitive; the cautions in E.1 and E.2.4 apply.

### E.2.8 Preparing supplier questions or a leadership briefing {#e.2.8-preparing-supplier-questions-or-a-leadership-briefing}

**Supplier questions:**

> Based on the Practices and Tasks that apply to \[system\], draft questions we could ask our supplier about \[topic, e.g., how model updates are delivered and disclosed\]. For each question, cite the item and the reference it draws on.

**Leadership briefing:**

> Draft a one-page briefing for \[audience\] on which Practices are most relevant to \[system\] and why. Use the profile’s own wording, and cite item numbers and the references behind the key points, so that readers can check it.

Check drafts like these against the cited items, and the sources behind them, before sending them. Problems described in E.3 are easy to miss in polished prose.

### E.2.9 Evaluating a project against the trustworthiness characteristics {#e.2.9-evaluating-a-project-against-the-trustworthiness-characteristics}

Where E.2.7 starts from your controls, this starts from the trustworthiness characteristics. It works as three prompts in sequence, each building on the answers before it.

**Step 1, evaluate:**

> I’m evaluating \[project\] against the trustworthiness characteristics in this profile. \[The project documents are attached / Here is a description of the project.\] \[The reference documents in this folder are available to you.\] For each characteristic, summarize what the project does well and where it may fall short, and cite the Practices, Tasks and Implementations that bear on it. Base the evaluation on what the project documents actually say, and tell me where you are inferring.

**Step 2, recommend:**

> Based on your evaluation, what should the \[project\] team do about the issues you found, and where can they look for more information? For each recommendation, name the references this profile cites that the team should read, and where in each to look. Say which points you checked against the source itself and which rest only on the profile’s description of it.

**Step 3, summarize:**

> Based on your evaluation and recommendations so far, write a two-page executive summary (no more than about 900 words) of what the \[project\] team should do next, for \[audience\] who have not read your earlier answers. Put the most important actions first, and say briefly where the team can find more information on each. Don’t add new analysis beyond what you have already done.

Telling the assistant which reference documents it has, as in the bracketed sentence, lets it check its pointers against them. The project documents in a use like this are often sensitive; the cautions in E.1 and E.2.4 apply. As with E.2.7, this is not a conformance assessment.

## E.3 Things to Watch For {#e.3-things-to-watch-for}

### E.3.1 Partial reading {#e.3.1-partial-reading}

An assistant may read only part of the document, or skim long entries, without saying so in its answer. Ask what it read in full and what it skipped. If it lists only a few Practices for a broad question, ask whether it considered the others. This may occur even with assistants that have large context windows.

### E.3.2 Losing the document as the conversation goes on {#e.3.2-losing-the-document-as-the-conversation-goes-on}

An assistant that read the whole document at the start may not keep all of it in view as a conversation grows longer. It may then answer from a partial memory of an entry, or reconstruct the missing parts, rather than read the text again. Its early answers can be accurate while later ones are not, so a check at the start of a conversation does not guarantee later answers. For important points later in a conversation, ask the assistant to quote the entry it is relying on, or to re-read it before answering. For a new question, consider starting a new conversation with the document attached again.

### E.3.3 Filling in from similar documents {#e.3.3-filling-in-from-similar-documents}

An assistant may draw on other documents it knows: other profiles, earlier drafts of this one, or general guidance on the same topic. It may then present that material as if it came from this profile. Familiar-sounding text is not evidence that a point is in this document. Ask the assistant to quote the passage and cite its item number, and check it against the text.

### E.3.4 The profile’s description taken for the source {#e.3.4-the-profile’s-description-taken-for-the-source}

Each reference entry in this profile describes, in a sentence or two, the part of a source that applies. An assistant without the source may present that description as what the source says, or stretch it into more than the description supports. The description is a pointer to the source, not a substitute for it. Ask the assistant whether it read the source or only the profile’s description, and read the source yourself for anything that matters.

### E.3.5 Guidance presented as requirements {#e.3.5-guidance-presented-as-requirements}

This was the most common problem we observed. Assistants often turn “should” into “must” or “requires,” or describe the profile as mandating something. The profile does not create requirements. Any requirements that apply to your organization come from your regulators, contracts and policies. Wording such as “required by NIST” should not appear in material based on this profile.

### E.3.6 Items stretched beyond their context {#e.3.6-items-stretched-beyond-their-context}

Instead of inventing content, assistants more often apply an item written for one situation to a different one without saying so. For example, an Implementation about reviewing SI-generated configurations before deployment may be applied to operators approving live recommendations. The underlying principle may still be useful, but the extension is the assistant’s, not the profile’s. Ask it to flag such extensions.

### E.3.7 Correct content under the wrong item number {#e.3.7-correct-content-under-the-wrong-item-number}

An assistant may describe an item accurately but cite the wrong number, for example by attributing an Implementation’s content to its parent Task. When a point matters, check the cited entry.

### E.3.8 Content that is not in the document {#e.3.8-content-that-is-not-in-the-document}

An assistant may add standards, figures, examples or regulatory claims that do not come from this profile. These may be useful, but they should be labeled as the assistant’s own and checked separately.

### E.3.9 Unfinished sources presented as settled {#e.3.9-unfinished-sources-presented-as-settled}

References labeled Working Document are drafts, requests for comments, concept papers and similar work still under way. They are cited deliberately, but an assistant may present them as established guidance, or describe what they will eventually require. When an answer relies on a reference, ask the assistant for its label and its status as of this draft. Before acting on a Working Document, check whether it has since been published, revised or withdrawn.

### E.3.10 Incomplete parts of this draft {#e.3.10-incomplete-parts-of-this-draft}

Some fields are still in progress in this draft, and an assistant may not notice. Ask it to say when the profile is silent on a point, rather than filling the gap.

### E.3.11 The assistant is itself an SI system {#e.3.11-the-assistant-is-itself-an-si-system}

The assistant you use may be within the scope of this profile. Manage its risks accordingly, particularly if its outputs will inform configurations, procedures or operational decisions. Parts of the profile that are often most relevant include:

* [Practice 12: Independently Verify SI-Generated Operational Logic and Artifacts Across Their Lifecycle](#practice-12:-independently-verify-si-generated-operational-logic-and-artifacts-across-their-lifecycle), for configurations, scripts and procedures an assistant drafts, and [Task 12.1: Establish Governance and Accountability for SI-Generated Execution Artifacts](#task-12.1:-establish-governance-and-accountability-for-si-generated-execution-artifacts), for keeping track of what a draft is later used for.  
* [Implementation 3.1.1: Identify SI System Decision Points and Potential Outcomes of SI System Errors](#implementation-3.1.1:-identify-si-system-decision-points-and-potential-outcomes-of-si-system-errors), on how an assistant with no connection to operational systems can still introduce errors into them through the people who act on its output, and [Task 3.2: Implement Independent Guardrails for SI Outputs](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs), on scaling checks to how directly an output reaches a physical process.  
* [Task 6.3: Identify and Control Dataflows Across the SI Supply Chain](#task-6.3:-identify-and-control-dataflows-across-the-si-supply-chain), for what information is sent to an assistant hosted by another organization.  
* [Task 3.7: Govern and Mitigate Risks from Unauthorized, Transient, and “Shadow SI” Systems](#task-3.7:-govern-and-mitigate-risks-from-unauthorized,-transient,-and-“shadow-si”-systems), for assistants used without approval, and [Implementation 5.1.2: Establish Unique Identities for SI Service Accounts and Agents](#implementation-5.1.2:-establish-unique-identities-for-si-service-accounts-and-agents), for assistants that act on someone’s behalf.  
* [Task 9.2: Deliver Specialized Training on Human-SI Interaction and Automation Bias](#task-9.2:-deliver-specialized-training-on-human-si-interaction-and-automation-bias), since a fluent, well-organized answer can be trusted more than it warrants.

## E.4 Checking an Answer {#e.4-checking-an-answer}

The following steps take a few minutes and can catch many of the problems above:

1. Pick the three or four items the answer relies on most. Read those entries in the document in full.  
2. For the points that matter most, go to the references those entries cite and read the part they point to.  
3. Ask the assistant to list which statements in its answer come from the profile, which from a source it read, and which are its own suggestions.  
4. Ask it to repeat any “must” or “required” in the profile’s own wording.  
5. Ask what it did not read, and whether any other Practices might apply.  
6. For anything that will be shared or acted on, check the important points against the document and its sources.

# Appendix F: Consolidated References {#appendix-f:-consolidated-references}

This appendix lists sources cited in the body of this profile (Sections 1 and 2), once each, with the places where it is cited. Each Practice, Task and Implementation has its own References field, which says which part of a source applies to that item and why; Section 1.5 does the same for the Introduction. Use this list to see where a source is drawn on across the document, or to find the full citation of a source mentioned in passing. Sources are grouped by kind and, within each group, listed by document number or title. References are neither requirements nor endorsements, and are not exhaustive.

## NIST publications {#nist-publications}

# Additional Information for the Reviewer {#additional-information-for-the-reviewer}

\>This appendix supports the review of this discussion document and will not appear in the published profile.

## Document Design Criteria: {#document-design-criteria:}

The guidelines in this section are internal design suggestions for document authors that guide them when writing the practices, tasks, and implementations, not operational controls for critical infrastructure. They are not compulsory although deviating from these should be done with care. Note that as this document is still very much a draft and work in progress, with text at different levels of refinement, it’s likely that some parts are inadvertently out of compliance with these criteria. Feel free to note this if you see cases where this is particularly important.

### Overall: {#overall:}

1. **“Do no harm.”** This criterion serves as an internal writing constraint to protect operators from the dangers of blind compliance, misinformed blanket regulations, or rigid management mandates. Every practice, task, and implementation should be drafted so that qualified professional and engineering judgment is baked into the requirement itself. To achieve this, avoid broad or generalized statements, instead bounding commands with conditional triggers and engineering qualifiers (e.g., “where technically feasible” or “commensurate with process safety thresholds”). Furthermore, text should leverage deliberate semantic scoping so that if a control is truly inapplicable or physically unsafe for a specific environment, an operator can explicitly satisfy the mandate “to the letter” by formally declaring that specific operational path out of scope, although boundaries should be constructed tightly to prevent loopholes.  
2. **Modular and Entry-Point Agnostic.** Every practice, task, and implementation is designed under the assumption that the reader has reviewed the foundational frontmatter, but not necessarily any other specific row in the framework. While rows work synergistically, an individual reading a single item in isolation should find sufficient context to understand its immediate risk-management utility. If a hard dependency or critical relationship exists with another practice, the row should explicitly route the reader to that section to ensure a seamless “random-access” reading experience.  
3. **Refer to other standards/guidance/resources as much as possible.** Use as few words as necessary to help the reader to understand if this relates to them and to help them scope and interpret those references, especially if it’s a long reference and only part of it is relevant.  
4. **Understandable to the target audience.** Target audiences are described more below.  
5. **Actionable and useful.** At each level of abstraction, there should be a clear line between the practice/task/implementation and something that can actually be done and will improve risk management, particularly given the resource restrictions and legacy infrastructure and policies often present in CI.  
6. **Achievable and provides a gradient.** While our goal is to cover the ideal and industry best practice alongside what a ‘minimum viable’ looks like for resource-constrained environments, we are still evaluating how to best standardize these definitions across different critical infrastructure sectors . This criterion is currently treated as an exploratory objective to determine if tiered implementations prevent compliance fatigue, or if they inject unnecessary complexity into cross-sector governance.  
7. **Risk-proportional.** Practices, tasks, and implementations should help the reader understand the significance of a risk (or lack thereof) to help them allocate limited time, attention, and other resources.  
8. **Acknowledge the tradespace.** Risk management involves managing all relevant risks. Reducing risk in one area might increase risk in others and there may already be existing legacy trade-offs that organizations are used to (or may have mandated) that might be difficult to adjust. We should give stakeholders space to make this trade-off, even if they are obliged to follow a given practice/task/implementation.  
9. **General to all forms of AI that could be in scope.** The terminology we use should be relatable to the various audiences but also leave open room for novel approaches that don’t fit into existing (or commonly understood) approaches. For example, whatever we say should make sense for a neural network approach, as well as a traditional logic-based approach or a neuro-symbolic approach. Actually, I expect some of what we would say would be implicitly comparing/contrasting these. (If we find something that is narrow but really impactful, we need to make that scope clear.)  
10. **Verifiable, measurable, and audit-ready.** Outcomes of these practices, tasks, and implementations should be naturally measurable, and compatible with the “Measure” function of the AI RMF, to allow leadership to track risk mitigation progress and enable regulatory oversight and forensic investigation.

### Practices: {#practices:}

1. **Management/Governance audience.** This might be the only column that a non-technical manager might read and decide to tell the folks under them to do.  
2. **Clear connection to the organization’s goals.** It should be clear to a management audience what the incentive is to pay attention to this practice. This should reference the business/organizational goals and governance, rather than purely technical goals.  
3. **Industry/Sector keywords.** This should tie AI risk management concepts to industry and sector keywords so a non-AI, non-technical person who is just scanning keywords is likely to have an accurate intuition as to the type of risk and mitigation we’re talking about, and the point in the process lifecycle at which it applies.  
4. **Defensively non-technical.** Where possible, language should either be general enough, or appropriately explained, so that interpretation is accurate regardless of if this document is being read in a technical, sector-specific, or colloquial context.  
5. **Clear Ownership with Explicit Routing.** Each practice should allow the reader to identify which internal team or department is best suited to lead the objective. Rather than treating the Practice as an isolated silo, its standalone tasks and implementations serve as navigational signposts, guiding the lead department to the cross-functional collaborators they need to coordinate with next.

### Tasks: {#tasks:}

1. **Technical Management audience.** Note that this could be hands-on-keyboard technical, but it could also be technical policy.  
2. **Discrete, assignable steps.**  
3. **Each should be easily identifiable with achieving some aspect of the practice.**  
4. **May be executed independently.**

### Implementations: {#implementations:}

1. **Should point to specific ways of implementing a task.** Avoid actually going into technical/sequencing details beyond what is necessary to help the reader contextualize what we’re pointing at.  
2. **Should provide necessary, scoped context.** Avoid just pointing at a document and saying “Read this …” especially if the document is very long, involved, and/or from an area that the reader is unlikely to be familiar with. There should be just enough words to tell the reader which aspect of that document they need to pay attention to.  
3. **Ideally should include a minimal implementation.** This should give the reader a good idea of what some minimal steps are to reduce their risk, at minimal expense (and, by implication, when they shouldn’t bother if they don’t even have the resources to do that \- that they might be better off spending their resources on something else that has a greater impact).  
4. **Ideally should include an “ideal” implementation.** This should give the reader a good idea of what a “reasonable” attempt looks like, beyond which it might be worth looking at other measures should be taken to achieve a balanced risk management strategy. These paired structures are experimental; rows may leverage general illustrative examples if a strict resource split proves artificial or unhelpful for a given task.  
5. **Should concretely acknowledge the tradespace.** At least some hints as to specific things that might be traded off, particularly when it comes to mismatched lifecycles (20-30 years for typical CI assets, vs possibly \<1 year for many AI systems) and the need to scale across distributed infrastructure with limited resources.  
6. **Should try to be broadly relatable.** With 16 critical infrastructure sectors, it is likely impossible to come up with singular implementations that are directly relatable to all of them but language should be structured, where possible, to allow folks in sectors that are adjacent to still understand how the crux of the implementation might relate to them. This might require a fleshed out “primary” implementation and some minimal “secondary” ones that relate to the same idea but cover another group of sectors.

## Ideas and References Already in Progress: {#ideas-and-references-already-in-progress:}

We’ve identified a number of promising ideas, structural changes, and candidate references that we’re actively working through internally, but haven’t yet incorporated into the document itself. We’re sharing this list so that if you were about to suggest one of these, you’ll know it’s already on our radar, and so you can help us prioritize, refine, or strengthen it.

For each item below, we’d especially value:

* **Prioritization:** If you could only see three of these addressed in the next revision, which would they be?  
* **Better or additional references:** Especially ones with a brief note on which part of the reference applies and where.  
* **Placement:** Where in the document (which Practice/Task/Implementation) a given idea or reference would be most useful as an illustrative example.  
* **Sector-specific angles:** Whether an idea needs to be adapted, split, or caveated differently for your sector.

This list is not exhaustive, and its presence here doesn’t guarantee inclusion in the next draft. It reflects our current thinking, not a commitment. If something below turns out to be off-base or lower priority than we think, please tell us that too.

### Cross-Cutting Themes {#cross-cutting-themes}

These don’t sit neatly under a single Practice, with each touching several. We’ve noted the Practices most relevant to each so you can jump to related content if useful.

**Enrichment of Search Keywords and references.** Search Keywords are given for each Practice and for some Tasks, and many items do not yet have references. We welcome suggestions for both, particularly references with a note on which part applies and where.

**Autonomy isn’t one-dimensional.** We want to avoid framing AI autonomy as a single linear “level,” since real systems vary across multiple independent dimensions. *Relates to: [Practices 3](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior), 4\. Feedback welcome on: whether a multi-dimensional framing would be clearer for your sector, and what those dimensions should be.*

**Theoretical vs. actual capability.** Distinguishing what a system is formally capable of from what it reliably does in practice. *Relates to: [Practices 1](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success), 2, 3\. Feedback welcome on: where this distinction most needs to be made explicit.*

**Cost as a risk-management input.** Considering a “cost of controls” framing so that overinvestment in one control doesn’t crowd out resources for higher-value ones elsewhere. *Relates to: [Practice 1](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success): Establish Requirements for Success, but potentially applicable wherever a gradient of implementations is offered. Feedback welcome on: whether this deserves standalone treatment or should be folded into the existing gradient/“minimum viable” language.*

**“Living off the land.”** Noting that intended, legitimate functionality (not just malicious code) can still be used to cause harm, both from adversarial action (human or AI), and from legitimate, known, but misbehaving, internal or external AI systems. *Relates to: [Practices 2](#practice-2:-define-si-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations), 3, 5\. Feedback welcome on: whether this needs its own treatment or is better folded into existing guardrail/access-control language.*

**Predictive/monitoring use cases** (e.g., environmental or hazard forecasting) as possible additions to the Scope section’s example list. *Feedback welcome on: sector-appropriate variants beyond a single illustrative case.*

**Document format changes.** This document has outgrown its original tabular format as presented in the PDF version. As we are also ensuring that the same information is also available in the Markdown, we are investigating other ways of presenting views into this same information that can be automatically (and deterministically) generated that may be easier (for both people and AI assistants) to digest, be it in print or interactively. We welcome suggestions.

### Practice-Specific Items {#practice-specific-items}

#### Practice 1: Establish requirements for success (Establish requirements for success) {#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success-\(establish-requirements-for-success\)}

**Understanding what the system is actually optimizing for.** Ensuring requirements-setting explicitly accounts for possible gaps between a stated objective and what a system optimizes toward in practice.

#### Practice 2: Define AI Robustness, Resilience, and Quality of Service expectations (Robustness, resilience, and QoS) {#practice-2:-define-ai-robustness,-resilience,-and-quality-of-service-expectations-\(robustness,-resilience,-and-qos\)}

**Specification gaming.** Addressing cases where a system optimizes for a stated metric in ways that violate the intent behind it.

**Financial, resource and contractual risk across the SI lifecycle, including compute cost volatility.** Both unpredictable usage spikes and vendor pricing and contract changes over time as an operational risk category.

#### Practice 3: Define risks, policies, and oversight for automated AI and agentic behavior (Risks, policies, and oversight for automated/agentic behavior) {#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated-ai-and-agentic-behavior-\(risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated/agentic-behavior\)}

**Agentic interconnection and interdependence.** Framing point on how agentic systems’ dynamic, multi-system interactions differ structurally from more static traditional software.

#### Practice 6: Integrate visibility of the external supply chain of AI into vendor and third-party risk management / 7 (Supply chain and provenance) {#practice-6:-integrate-visibility-of-the-external-supply-chain-of-ai-into-vendor-and-third-party-risk-management-/-7-\(supply-chain-and-provenance\)}

**AI/use-case inventory.** Considering a structured example-use-case index or appendix, separate from the main practice table.

**Reference candidates:** NIST SP 800-53 AI control overlays (COSAIS, as opposed to CoSAI); additional context around the emerging AIBOM/SBOM standards cluster (SPDX AI & Datasets, OWASP AIBOM, CycloneDX ML-BOM) as candidate machine-readable formats for [Implementation 6.1.2: Require SIBOM for Mission-Critical Applications](#implementation-6.1.2:-require-sibom-for-mission-critical-applications); MITRE System of Trust as a possible supply-chain reference alongside NIST SP 800-161.

**Reference candidate:** NCCoE’s Software and AI Agent Identity and Authorization project, which is directly relevant to [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools)‘s identity requirements; worth checking for any newly published output.

#### Practice 8: Incorporate AI-aware incident analysis and response procedures (Incident analysis and response) {#practice-8:-incorporate-ai-aware-incident-analysis-and-response-procedures-\(incident-analysis-and-response\)}

**Near-miss reporting.** Expand on capturing near-misses, not just realized incidents.

**Aligning incident definitions.** Checking whether the profile’s working definition of an “incident” should explicitly cross-reference existing definitions used elsewhere (e.g., JCDC-style playbooks).

#### Practice 9: Provide role-based AI risk training that builds well-founded trust (Training) {#practice-9:-provide-role-based-ai-risk-training-that-builds-well-founded-trust-\(training\)}

**Explicit stakeholder-engagement task.** Adding task/implementation guidance ensuring the right people are involved in developing AI policies and procedures and receive adequate training, not solely technical controls.

**Maintaining skills for human oversight.** Adding guidance here (and in other practices as relevant) to better stress that human oversight and human-as-backup requires not just existing, but possibly new, training as taking over from an AI system (particularly in an emergency) can require additional skills compared to just performing the task.

### Sector-Specific References to be Included {#sector-specific-references-to-be-included}

We have compiled an initial baseline of established, sector-specific cybersecurity, process safety, and operational standards brought to our attention by the community. Moving forward, our internal roadmap aims to do more than simply index these documents; we intend to explicitly translate them into an AI risk management context.

We actively seek targeted input from domain experts on how to best frame this translation, which specific clauses or sub-sections offer the most transferable utility to AI deployment, where these references can be most effectively mapped into our profile, supporting text to properly contextualize them, and additional/alternative references that we should consider.

**Oil and Natural Gas:** API Standard 1164 (Pipeline Control Systems Cybersecurity), API RP 780 (Security Risk Assessment), API RP 754 (Process Safety Performance Indicators), IOGP Report 556 (Cybersecurity Capability and Maturity), TSA Security Directive Pipeline-2021-02, and ONG-ISAC threat advisories.

**Electric / Bulk Power:** NERC CIP-002 through CIP-014 (with emphasis on CIP-013-2 for supply chain controls), IEEE Standard 1547-2018 (Interconnection and Interoperability of Distributed Energy Resources), IEC 61850 (Power Utility Automation Networks), EPRI AI research program outputs, and DOE CESER AI guidance.

**Water and Wastewater Systems:** AWWA G430 (Security Practices for Operation and Management), AWWA M19 (Emergency Planning), the EPA Cybersecurity for the Water Sector toolkit, America’s Water Infrastructure Act (AWIA) of 2018 Section 2013 risk assessment requirements, and WaterISAC 15 Cybersecurity Fundamentals.

**Healthcare and Public Health:** HHS 405(d) Health Industry Cybersecurity Practices, FDA Good Machine Learning Practice for Medical Device Development, the HIPAA Security Rule (45 CFR Part 164, Subpart C as applied to AI processing of protected health info), and HHS HC3 sector advisories.

**Emergency Services / Public Safety:** NFPA 1500 (Fire Department Occupational Safety, Health, and Wellness), NFPA 1600 (Continuity, Emergency, and Crisis Management), and NIST Public Safety Communications Research (PSCR) AI for First Responders program outputs, and placeholders for upcoming IAFC AI working group outputs.

**Cross-Sector Industrial & Process Safety Foundations:** ISA-84 / IEC 61511 (Functional Safety: Safety Instrumented Systems for the Process Industry), ANSI/ISA-95 (Enterprise-Control System Integration), IEC 61508 (Functional Safety of Electronic Safety-Related Systems), and ISO 31000 (Risk Management Guidelines), and ISA-18.2 (Alarm Management Systems).

### Standards Bodies, Consortia, and Efforts We’re Tracking {#standards-bodies,-consortia,-and-efforts-we’re-tracking}

Here’s a broader (non-exhaustive) list of groups, standards, and initiatives already on our radar, including some we now cite in the profile and are continuing to track as their work develops. Please feel free to suggest additions or additional contextualizations, particularly with a note on which specific part is most relevant to this profile.

**AI supply chain / AIBOM:** SPDX AI & Datasets Team; OWASP AIBOM Project and GenAI AI-SBOM Initiative; CycloneDX ML-BOM guidance; OpenChain AI SBOM compliance guide; MITRE System of Trust; the G7 shared vision paper on SBOM for AI; FDA’s AIBOM effort.

**Agentic system security:** CoSAI Workstreams 1, 3, and 4 (supply chain; AI risk governance; secure design for agentic systems), including their persona/risk-map work and Project Codeguard; OWASP GenAI Agentic Security Initiative; AIUC-1 agent standards; GUAC (software security metadata aggregation).

**Cross-industry consortia and working groups:** OpenSSF’s AI/ML Working Group and GEMARA project; the Coalition for Secure AI (CoSAI) more broadly; FINOS Common Cloud Controls; OSCAL-COMPASS; the Alliance for Critical Infrastructure (ACI) launched Feb 26, 2026 as a cross-sector resilience and crisis-coordination nonprofit

**Sector-specific:** Cyber Risk Institute’s Financial Services AI RMF profile and associated guidebook/control matrix; FS-ISAC; FSSCC’s AI lexicon; Oil and Natural Gas Sector Coordinating Council (ONG-SCC); DOE’s Supply Chain Cybersecurity Principles and ICS cybersecurity testing guidance.

**Standards bodies:** ISO/IEC 22989 (AI concepts/terminology) and ISO/IEC TS 5723 (trustworthiness vocabulary); ISO/IEC TR 5469 (functional safety and AI systems); ISO/IEC 42001 (AI management systems) and ISO/IEC 38507 (governance implications of the use of AI by organizations); IEEE P7001 (transparency of autonomous systems) and IEEE 2841 (deep learning evaluation framework); the ISA/IEC 62443 series and IEC 62351 (grid automation/control protocol security).

**Risk frameworks and taxonomies:** FAIR Institute’s cyber risk scenario taxonomy and risk ontology; UC Berkeley CLTC’s work on AI risk thresholds and a standalone AI trustworthiness taxonomy.

**International:** OECD’s Framework for the Classification of AI Systems; relevant EU AI Act provisions (Articles 25 and 53); national AI governance directives and automated-decision-making frameworks in other jurisdictions where CI supply chains cross borders.

**Related NIST/NCCoE efforts already coordinated with this work:** SP 800-53 AI control overlays (COSAIS) and the associated predictive-AI outline; NCCoE’s Software and AI Agent Identity and Authorization project; the forthcoming Cyber AI Profile (IR 8596).

*As with all items above, we’re especially interested in: (1) whether these are worth including at all, (2) where they’d best fit if so, and (3) any stronger or more specific references you can point us to.*

# Conceptual Changelog {#conceptual-changelog}

This section summarizes key conceptual changes between draft versions, deliberately omitting minor edits. It is not an exhaustive diff, but a targeted summary to help reviewers identify substantive updates relevant to their feedback.

## November 9, 2026 {#november-9,-2026}

This version follows the Sep 28, 2026(a) draft, the last one shared with the community of interest. It brings in the changes made since then, including those in an Oct 15 draft shared with a small group of internal reviewers. No Practice, Task or Implementation has been removed, and apart from seven new Implementations, item numbers are unchanged, so comments keyed to earlier drafts still apply. Many titles have been reworded, as described below. This entry is written for readers of the Sep 13 and Sep 28 drafts, to point to what they may want to look at again.

**The profile is now SICI, published as a set of documents.** The SICI Summary is a four-page overview for leadership. The SICI Profile, of about thirty pages, gives a condensed introduction, the trustworthiness characteristics, each of the 13 Practices in full with the titles of its Tasks and Implementations, and a selection of scenarios. This document, the SICI Guidebook, contains everything in the Profile and adds the text of every Task and Implementation, the references, the Glossary and the appendices; the Profile and Guidebook differ only in level of detail. The Guidebook is published as a web edition, with a page for each Practice, Task and Implementation, and as a single Markdown file for LLM-based assistants, accompanied by a knowledge graph in YAML. It is no longer published as a PDF. The Introduction now describes these documents, and Section 1.4 and [Appendix E](#appendix-e:-suggested-ways-to-use-this-document-with-an-llm-based-assistant) explain how to use the web edition and the Markdown, with or without an assistant.

**How far to go: measures as a matter of degree.** A new section before the Practices, How Far to Go, says that most measures are a matter of degree, that how far to go is set by consequence weighed against finite resources, and that whatever dependency or gap remains is a decision, made within any regulatory or contractual obligations, accepted by someone with the authority to accept that level of risk, and recorded. Alternatives such as reverting or switching to a backup are available only to the extent they have been prepared. It introduces the design basis, the conditions a system is deliberately designed to withstand, with a new Glossary entry, and applies it where the text sized for an extreme ([Implementation 4.4.3](#implementation-4.4.3:-managing-correlated-multi-system-attention-surges), [Task 4.4](#task-4.4:-attention-governance-and-alert/alarm-flood-mitigation), [Practice 11](#practice-11:-maintain-si-aware-mission-continuity-and-disaster-recovery-planning), [Task 11.2](#task-11.2:-define-manual-and-alternative-operating-procedures-for-long-term-mission-continuity), [Implementation 11.2.2](#implementation-11.2.2:-develop-a-validated-“safe-operating-mode”-that-depends-minimally-on-si-infrastructure)). [Appendix A](#appendix-a:-trustworthiness-characteristics), A.3.1, relates Reliable, Robust, and Resilient to the design basis.

**Two new Implementations on records.** [Implementation 10.1.5](#implementation-10.1.5:-define-what-each-operational-record-is-for) asks what each operational record is for, who uses it and when, and how much to keep, including coarser or statistical recording where its limits are understood and accepted, and records that span several organizations. [Implementation 3.9.6](#implementation-3.9.6:-keep-a-record-of-design-decisions-and-accepted-risks) asks for a record of design decisions and accepted risks. Many items that ask for something to be recorded now point to one of them.

**Trustworthiness Effects to Consider is now Trustworthiness Side Effects to Consider**, in the sense of the side effects listed for a medicine: something to know before going ahead. The field description in [Section 2](#2:-the-profile) explains that a side effect can become a tension where the measure that would address it cannot be resourced. Handoffs (“This Task does not cover… For that, see…”) are now described as examples of where a limit is taken up, not the only place, and lists of triggers and conditions as illustrative, with a named role deciding whether other changes warrant action.

**“One resolution is” is now “One way to balance this is”** in the Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance fields, and some tensions now say that an option is available only where it has been prepared.

**Responsibility and roles.** Section 1 adds a paragraph on how SI systems challenge the way organizations divide responsibility. [Appendix A](#appendix-a:-trustworthiness-characteristics), A.1.11, and several Tasks now say that whoever holds a responsibility needs the visibility, time, resources, access, support, and authority to act on it, and where separation of roles cannot be achieved, for example in a small organization or a field office, the text asks that this and how it is offset be recorded.

**Every Practice now has a Decisions for the Organization field**, and many items have new Decisions questions on ownership, resourcing, and what happens when the preferred option is unavailable.

**Titles changed:** [Implementation 2.2.1](#implementation-2.2.1:-maintain-backup-systems-proportionate-to-consequence) (Maintain Backup Systems Proportionate to Consequence), [Implementation 8.3.2](#implementation-8.3.2:-form-an-si-incident-governance-team) (Form an SI Incident Governance Team), [Implementation 11.2.2](#implementation-11.2.2:-develop-a-validated-“safe-operating-mode”-that-depends-minimally-on-si-infrastructure) (Develop a Validated “Safe Operating Mode” that Depends Minimally on SI Infrastructure), and [Task 13.2](#task-13.2:-withdraw-all-authority-and-confirm-the-result) (Withdraw All Authority and Confirm the Result). “Table 2” is now referred to as the Trustworthiness Characteristics table.

**Field labels now in title case:** Decisions for the Organization, and Related AI RMF Subcategories Include, matching the other field labels.


**The profile now uses “Super Intelligence” (SI) in place of “Artificial Intelligence” (AI), following Executive Order 14434\.** A footnote on the title explains that “SI” refers to the same systems defined as Artificial Intelligence in 15 U.S.C. § 9401, and that cited works, proper names, quotations, identifiers, established terms of art and keyword lists keep “AI”. The update is still in progress, so both terms appear. The working title is now Automated, Agentic, and Super Intelligence in Critical Infrastructure and High-Consequence Applications, and the Scope explains why automated and agentic systems are named in it. Following the change, the AI Bill of Materials is now the SI Bill of Materials (SIBOM) in [Implementation 6.1.2](#implementation-6.1.2:-require-sibom-for-mission-critical-applications), while AIBOM remains where a cited source uses it.

**The Introduction and Scope have been rewritten.** They now state that the profile is voluntary and is not a compliance checklist; that SI systems benefit from the same controls as other software, even on purpose-built hardware, while many of the assumptions behind those controls need to be adjusted; and that operational trust rests on both governance evidence, which shows that processes exist, and technical evidence, which shows whether a particular SI system can meet a function’s requirements. The Scope now notes that many organizations already use SI systems, so that an inventory is a natural first step, and that risks can compound where newer SI systems are layered on older statistical and optimization systems. Section 1.2 explains why SI in critical infrastructure needs particular attention, applies the principle behind zero trust architecture to SI risk more generally, and distinguishes the SI Attack Surface from the wider SI Risk Surface.

**A new field, Decisions for the Organization, appears in 218 Practices, Tasks and Implementations.** It lists the choices an item leaves to the organization, such as which events trigger re-validation and who decides the response. Each Practice and Task also now says what it does not cover and where that is addressed (“This Task does not…”), and where an item leaves a matter for the organization to decide, it notes that the decision is made within any regulatory or contractual obligations.

**The trustworthiness and AI RMF fields now cover every Practice and Task.** [Practices 7](#practice-7:-manage-internal-si-supply-chain-and-data-provenance) to 12 and their Tasks now carry the Main Trustworthiness Contributions, Trustworthiness Effects to Consider, Trustworthiness Tensions to Balance and Related AI RMF Subcategories fields in the form previously used for [Practices 1](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success) to 6 and 13\.

**References have been substantially expanded, and now point to specific sections.** [Section 2](#2:-the-profile) now has about 640 reference entries across 248 of its 258 items, compared with 91 under 43 items in the Sep 28 draft. Each entry names the part of the source that applies and why, and opens with a label for the kind of document. Sources that present themselves as unfinished, such as drafts, requests for comments and concept papers, are labeled Working Document and cited deliberately, to record where practice is heading. Section 1.5 lists the sources for Section 1, and [Appendix F](#appendix-f:-consolidated-references): Consolidated References lists the 163 sources cited in Sections 1 and 2 once each, with where each is cited.

**The Glossary has been rebuilt, from seven terms to 66\.** Each entry gives a definition and, where relevant, other names for the term, terms it should be contrasted with, and senses in other fields or sectors that could cause a misreading, together with the items where it is used and references. Entries that reviewers may wish to review include AI agent, agentic AI system, super intelligence, action-level authorization, attack surface and risk surface, drift, safety wrapper and interlock, protective AI capability, fail-safe state, known-safe, root cause analysis, and prompt compromise.

**All six appendices now have content.**

* [Appendix A](#appendix-a:-trustworthiness-characteristics): Trustworthiness Characteristics is new. It gives the source definition of each characteristic and where this profile departs from it, how the grouping relates to the AI RMF’s, distinctions between characteristics that readers often merge, the tensions that recur across this Guidebook, and what the characteristics do not reach.  
* [Appendix B](#appendix-b:-scenario-to-practice-mapping) is now Scenario-to-Practice Mapping. Its 33 scenarios are illustrative composites inspired by historical incidents, not descriptions or assessments of any particular incident or organization, and each names the trustworthiness characteristics most clearly at stake.  
* [Appendix C](#appendix-c:-use-cases-and-operational-scenarios): Use Cases and Operational Scenarios sets out a common form for use cases and adds the first, C.1 Healthcare: Authorized Access versus Authorized Action, contributed by a member of the community of interest.  
* [Appendix D](#appendix-d:-crosswalks) begins with D.1, which lists common control areas, the assumption each typically makes, how SI systems can break it, and where this profile can help, with access reviews worked through as an example. Crosswalks to external frameworks remain under development.  
* [Appendix E](#appendix-e:-suggested-ways-to-use-this-document-with-an-llm-based-assistant): Suggested Ways to Use this Document with an LLM-Based Assistant covers what to give the assistant, nine common uses with example prompts, including evaluating a project against the trustworthiness characteristics, the ways an assistant can misrepresent this document, and how to check an answer. It stresses that the prompts are illustrative, and that answers should be checked against this profile and the sources it cites.  
* [Appendix F](#appendix-f:-consolidated-references): Consolidated References is described above. The reviewer material that was [Appendix E](#appendix-e:-suggested-ways-to-use-this-document-with-an-llm-based-assistant) in the Sep 13 and Sep 28 drafts is now the Additional Information for the Reviewer section at the end of the document.

**Five Implementations were added before this round.** [Implementation 3.6.4](#implementation-3.6.4:-monitor-aggregate-engagement-indicators) suggests monitoring aggregate indicators of engagement at review and approval points. [Implementation 4.6.4](#implementation-4.6.4:-distill-learned-models-into-interpretable-models-that-can-be-verified) describes distilling a trained opaque model into a self-interpretable model that can be verified and deployed in its place. [Implementation 5.3.4](#implementation-5.3.4:-limit-the-context-carried-forward-between-steps) extends least agency to the context an agentic SI system carries from one step, session or delegated agent to the next. [Implementation 7.2.4](#implementation-7.2.4:-select-and-prepare-the-inputs-each-si-system-receives) treats the selection and preparation of an SI system’s inputs, at training and at runtime, as a risk control. [Implementation 10.2.2](#implementation-10.2.2:-protect-logs-from-alteration-where-they-serve-as-evidence) asks the organization to consider how strongly logs need to be protected from later change where they may serve as evidence.

**Several additions address how separate controls on the same action fit together.** [Task 3.2](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs) notes that identity, per-action authorization and decision-level records act on the same paths as its guardrails, and suggests checking these controls together for each path. [Task 5.1](#task-5.1:-establish-identities-and-authentication-for-si-entities) states that an identity establishes which entity is acting, not what it is permitted to do. [Implementation 3.2.2](#implementation-3.2.2:-define-and-independently-enforce-deterministic-operational-constraints) adds that each constraint should hold without reference to values the SI system generates about its own output, and that a safety wrapper on a physical process does not gate commands from protective functions. [Implementation 10.1.2](#implementation-10.1.2:-runtime-telemetry-and-artifact-tracking) asks that records of what action was taken, and whether it was permitted, be generated where possible by the enforcement or validation layer rather than reported by the SI system about itself.

**Logging no longer assumes immutability.** [Task 10.2](#task-10.2:-establish-data-integrity-and-tamper-evidence-controls-for-telemetry-and-logging) and [Implementations 10.1.2](#implementation-10.1.2:-runtime-telemetry-and-artifact-tracking) and 10.2.2 now ask that logs be protected from alteration in proportion to how they will be used, particularly where they may serve as evidence, and [Implementation 10.2.1](#implementation-10.2.1:-ensure-that-existing-logging-facilities-can-absorb-si-logging) now asks whether existing logging facilities can absorb SI logging without crowding out other logs.

**Other content changes carried from the Oct 15 draft** include the SI Risk Surface now covering the SI Attack Surface ([Task 3.8](#task-3.8:-scope-and-map-the-expanded-si-attack-surface-and-risk-surface), [Task 8.1](#task-8.1:-identify-scenarios-requiring-deterministic-root-cause-analysis-and-incident-reconstruction), [Implementation 8.1.6](#implementation-8.1.6:-incident-triage-across-the-dual-attack/risk-surface)); protection for those who report near-misses ([Task 8.6](#task-8.6:-establish-non-punitive-reporting-for-si-related-near-misses), [Implementation 8.6.2](#implementation-8.6.2:-protect-reporter-identity-through-an-independent-reporting-route)); treating system prompts as sensitive and SIBOMs for internally developed systems ([Task 7.3](#task-7.3:-manage-version-control-and-logging-for-internal-si-safety-mechanisms), [Implementation 7.1.3](#implementation-7.1.3:-integrate-automated-internal-software-and-si-bill-of-material-management)); more consistent terms following the Glossary, such as oversight modes rather than levels of autonomy, operating envelope, and “independent deterministic” in place of “non-AI”; and a reading path for auditors, assessors and compliance functions in Section 1.4.

**Titles have been put in title case and many reworded**, including for the change to SI. Rewordings that change meaning include [Task 5.4](#task-5.4:-implement-continuous-monitoring-of-si-entities-against-access-and-action-boundaries-and-expectations) (Implement Continuous Monitoring of SI Entities Against Access and Action Boundaries and Expectations), [Implementation 3.6.3](#implementation-3.6.3:-cognitive-engagement-by-design) (Cognitive Engagement by Design), [Implementation 4.4.2](#implementation-4.4.2:-adapting-existing-alarm-management-for-complex,-adaptive-or-otherwise-unpredictable-systems) (Adapting Existing Alarm Management for Complex, Adaptive or Otherwise Unpredictable Systems), [Implementation 7.5.2](#implementation-7.5.2:-perform-automated-“champion-challenger”-assessment) (Perform Automated “Champion-Challenger” Assessment), [Implementation 8.6.4](#implementation-8.6.4:-share-de-identified-incident-records-for-collective-learning) (Share De-Identified Incident Records for Collective Learning), [Task 7.2](#task-7.2:-validate,-select,-and-prepare-data-for-si-systems) (Validate, Select, and Prepare Data for SI Systems), and the [Practice 10](#practice-10:-implement-multi-tiered-si-system-logging-and-audit-capabilities) Task and Implementations above.

**Corrections.** [Implementation 8.6.4](#implementation-8.6.4:-share-de-identified-incident-records-for-collective-learning) now points to [Implementation 8.6.2](#implementation-8.6.2:-protect-reporter-identity-through-an-independent-reporting-route), rather than to a cell that did not exist. [Implementation 3.4.3](#implementation-3.4.3:-monitor-validation-control-integrity) now says which controls it monitors. Several references to NIST publications that overstated what the source requires now say what it calls for, and a scope limitation attributed to this profile in [Practice 1](#practice-1:-establish-requirements-for-success) now correctly belongs to SP 800-218A.

*Version 20261109_1200a differs from 20261109_1200 only in minor presentation changes to the web edition and two notices in the front matter: that feedback shared with NIST will become part of the public record, and that the views expressed do not necessarily reflect those of NIST or the United States Government. The content is otherwise unchanged.*

## Sep 28, 2026(a) {#sep-28,-2026\(a\)}

This is a minor update to the Sep 13 draft. It adds one Task, six Implementations and a section on using the profile, and otherwise clarifies and corrects existing text. No Practice, Task or Implementation has been removed.

**Three new Implementations address how operating context and source data can change without any change to the AI system.** [Implementation 1.1.3: Establish Triggers for Re-Validating Requirements on Change of Operating Context](#implementation-1.1.3:-establish-triggers-for-re-validating-requirements-on-change-of-operating-context) covers assets whose applicable rules change when they relocate or their contract status changes, such as a mobile asset entering a different jurisdiction, and [Task 7.5: Conduct Impact Assessments and Risk Management for SI System and Model Updates](#task-7.5:-conduct-impact-assessments-and-risk-management-for-si-system-and-model-updates) now also applies where such a change alters rules encoded in the AI system, such as in its prompts, retrieval corpus, or guardrails. [Implementation 7.2.3: Assess the Conditions Under Which Source Data Is Created](#implementation-7.2.3:-assess-the-conditions-under-which-source-data-is-created) extends provenance upstream of ingestion to the point of capture, where records can be lost in manual transfer chains, overwritten, or degraded by migration between maintenance management systems. [Implementation 9.1.3: Include Data-Originating Roles in Competency Mapping](#implementation-9.1.3:-include-data-originating-roles-in-competency-mapping) brings field engineers, maintenance technicians and others who create source data into role-based training, even where they never use an AI system directly.

**A new Section 1.4, Using this Profile, suggests where different readers might start.** It gathers the guidance on non-linear reading and on starting from [Appendix B](#appendix-b:-scenario-to-practice-mapping) that was previously spread through the Introduction, adds starting points for technical staff, for those focused on a trustworthiness characteristic, for those mapping to other frameworks and for organizations with limited resources, and discusses using the document with an AI assistant, including the organizational context an assistant needs and the ways it can misrepresent the document.

**The profile now states how it relates to existing assurance regimes and to zero trust.** The Scope now says that existing assurance regimes, including authorization and continuous monitoring, can remain the foundation, and that this profile builds on them with attention to what should trigger reassessment and to monitoring what an AI system does, not only how it is configured. It also describes the profile as applying the zero trust principle, that trust is verified at each boundary rather than assumed, to AI risk more generally, including to a legitimate, uncompromised AI system that is not behaving as intended. This is carried into [Practice 3: Define Risks, Policies, and Oversight for Automated, Agentic, and SI Behavior](#practice-3:-define-risks,-policies,-and-oversight-for-automated,-agentic,-and-si-behavior), [Task 3.2: Implement Independent Guardrails for SI Outputs](#task-3.2:-implement-independent-guardrails-for-si-outputs) and [Practice 5: Implement Identity and Access Management (IdAM) for SI Agents, Systems, and Tools](#practice-5:-implement-identity-and-access-management-\(idam\)-for-si-agents,-systems,-and-tools), and zero trust is added to the Glossary.

**Language incorrectly implying guarantees removed.** Throughout the table, statements that an item “ensures” an outcome now say that it “helps ensure” it, and similar claims elsewhere, such as guardrails that structurally block unsafe commands even from a fully compromised AI system, have been restated as what the item can do.

**Terms used in their general sense do not carry sector-specific meanings.** The introduction to the table now states that where a sector, regulation or standard gives a term such as validation, verification, incident or safety function a precise meaning, this profile does not invoke that meaning, and following the profile does not by itself establish conformance with requirements stated in those terms. The Glossary adds industrial control system, noting that ICS means something different in emergency management. Table 1 now cites National Security Memorandum 22 as the source of the 16 sectors.

**Explanation features are no longer treated as evidence that a recommendation is correct.** A new [Task 4.6: Ensure that Confidence and Rationale Shown to Personnel Reflect How the SI System Reached Its Output](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output) gathers the requirements on confidence and rationale shown to personnel, previously in [Implementation 4.2.3: Human-Centered Interfaces for SI Uncertainty and Actionable Triggers](#implementation-4.2.3:-human-centered-interfaces-for-si-uncertainty-and-actionable-triggers), and adds guidance for symbolic, hybrid and self-interpretable AI systems, whose rationale can be a trace of the steps actually applied. [Implementation 4.6.1: Design Rationale Displays that Give Personnel Something to Check](#implementation-4.6.1:-design-rationale-displays-that-give-personnel-something-to-check) notes research finding that showing explanations alongside recommendations can increase acceptance whether or not the recommendation is correct, and suggests testing whether a rationale display improves decisions for the personnel who will use it, including whether they still reject incorrect recommendations. [Task 9.2: Deliver Specialized Training on Human-SI Interaction and Automation Bias](#task-9.2:-deliver-specialized-training-on-human-si-interaction-and-automation-bias) adds training on this effect. [Task 4.6: Ensure that Confidence and Rationale Shown to Personnel Reflect How the SI System Reached Its Output](#task-4.6:-ensure-that-confidence-and-rationale-shown-to-personnel-reflect-how-the-si-system-reached-its-output) also carries a new tension between the Accurate and Explainable & Interpretable characteristics, and [Implementation 10.1.2: Runtime Telemetry and Artifact Tracking](#implementation-10.1.2:-runtime-telemetry-and-artifact-tracking) notes that the inference receipt can record the rules applied, which provides the displayed trace. [Implementation 4.2.3: Human-Centered Interfaces for SI Uncertainty and Actionable Triggers](#implementation-4.2.3:-human-centered-interfaces-for-si-uncertainty-and-actionable-triggers), previously titled Human-Centered Interfaces for AI Uncertainty, Rationale, and Actionable Triggers, now addresses uncertainty and triage cues, and its Trust/Execute cue is renamed Proceed, which indicates that an output falls within the conditions the AI system was validated for rather than that it is correct.

**A refused action part-way through a sequence needs its own fail-safe state.** [Implementation 3.2.3: Specify Fail-Safe States and Fallback Behavior](#implementation-3.2.3:-specify-fail-safe-states-and-fallback-behavior) now covers the case where an AI action is refused under [Implementation 5.2.2: Action-Level, Context-Aware Authorization Policies](#implementation-5.2.2:-action-level,-context-aware-authorization-policies) after earlier steps have already executed, with a worked example of a pump changeover.

**Vendor hazard reachability attestations should be corroborated before they suppress alarms.** [Implementation 6.1.5: Operational SI Hazard Reachability Disclosures](#implementation-6.1.5:-operational-si-hazard-reachability-disclosures) now says vendor self-attestation should not be treated as sufficient to suppress a warning, and [Task 4.4: Attention Governance and Alert/Alarm Flood Mitigation](#task-4.4:-attention-governance-and-alert/alarm-flood-mitigation) applies this to alarm suppression. [Implementation 6.1.5: Operational SI Hazard Reachability Disclosures](#implementation-6.1.5:-operational-si-hazard-reachability-disclosures) also notes that the existing VEX justification for inline mitigations covers only protections built into the product, so controls that an operator deploys around an AI system would need to be stated as a separate justification.

**Retiring a protective AI capability is a change to controls as well as an asset disposal.** [Implementation 13.3.2: Treat the Retirement of a Protective SI Capability as a Change to Controls](#implementation-13.3.2:-treat-the-retirement-of-a-protective-si-capability-as-a-change-to-controls) and [Task 13.3: Preserve What Is Needed and Hand Over What Depended on the System](#task-13.3:-preserve-what-is-needed-and-hand-over-what-depended-on-the-system) previously framed these as alternatives.
